articles.title: My judgment is up to me

statement.t: What troubles me rests on my judgment; that judgment is up to me, and when I take it away there is calm.

parts.words: What troubles me rests on my judgment
that judgment is up to me
when I take it away there is calm

statement.kind: A chain: where the trouble is, whose judgment it is, and what taking it away gives
statement.form: Claim 1 places the trouble in my judgments, claim 2 says the judgment is mine to form or to withhold, and claim 3 says what taking it away gives. The statement joins these three in the order 12.16 itself gives them. Claims 4 and 5 apply it to two cases: my own body, and another person’s words.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the first and the fifth claims gain a second author. “Practice” gains questions to put to myself and words for facing a feared event, and “When it breaks” gains where false opinions come from and how they are driven out. He limits the first claim (even pain with no opinion added is still there, though light) and the fourth (the mind is struck by feelings that reason cannot take by storm), and he challenges the fifth: where everything is uncertain, he would have me believe what I prefer.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause for facing a feared event: if it does come, perhaps it is coming on my side. He limits the first claim, though: even pain with no opinion added is still there, though light.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Everything hangs on opinion; it is not only ambition and extravagance and greed that look to it
piece.follows: Everything hangs on opinion, and it is not only ambition, extravagance and greed that look to it.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness and pain, written to Lucilius, who is ill. “Opinion” is what we tell ourselves about our pain.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: we feel pain according to opinion
piece.follows: How much pain we feel depends on our opinion.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca tells the sick Lucilius not to make his pain heavier by complaining. “Opinion” is what the sufferer thinks of his own pain.
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: to take the uproar away from things and to see what is in each thing
piece.follows: I should take the uproar away from things and see what is in each one.
piece.context: Letter 24: Seneca tells Lucilius to listen calmly when his enemy threatens him over his case. “Things” are what he fears; with the uproar taken away, they hold nothing terrible but the fear.
gives: I see things as they are

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us assess each thing one by one with its reputation set aside, and ask what they are, not what they are called.
piece.follows: We should set each thing’s reputation aside and assess it by what it is, not by what it is called.
piece.context: Letter 95, on principles: what opinion we ought to hold about poverty, riches, glory, disgrace and exile. “Each thing” is one of these; its “reputation” is what people say of it.
gives: I see things as they are

items.label: practice
items.t: When people around me try to persuade me that I am wretched, I think about what I feel and not about what I hear. I ask myself whether I am in torment without cause, and whether I am making an evil of what is not one.
items.why: 4.9 deals with the person who abuses me and wants me to judge as he does. Seneca deals with people who mean well and pity me, and he gives the questions to put to myself; Marcus gives none here.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whenever people stand around you trying to persuade you that you are wretched, think not about what you hear but about what you feel
support.follows: When others try to persuade me that I am wretched, I should go by what I feel and not by what I hear.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. The “people” are those who condole with Lucilius over a trouble he expects; Seneca asks him to consult his own feeling instead of them.
gives: When people around me try to persuade me that I am wretched, I think about what I feel and not about what I hear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Be the one to question yourself: “Am I perhaps in torment and grieving without cause, and making an evil of what is not one?”
support.follows: I should ask myself whether I am in torment without cause and am making an evil out of what is not one.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: the last of the questions Seneca gives Lucilius to ask himself when the people around him tell him that he is wretched.
gives: I ask myself whether I am in torment without cause
whether I am making an evil of what is not one

items.label: practice
items.t: When I fear the worst, I say: what if it does come? We will see which of the two wins. Perhaps it is coming on my side.
items.why: 8.47 gives words for a report: say nothing further, or speak as one who recognises what happens in the universe. It gives none for facing an event I fear may come. Seneca does, and his words are again a judgment: he does not grant that the event would be an evil, but judges that it may be coming on his side.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: As for you, say: “And what if it does come? We will see which of the two wins. Perhaps it is coming on my side, and that death will bring honour to my life.”
support.follows: Lucilius is to say: suppose it does come; we will see which of the two wins; perhaps it is coming on my side.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears. After the mild remedy, “Perhaps it will not come”, Seneca gives the sterner one. “It” is the worst that Lucilius fears.
gives: I say: what if it does come? We will see which of the two wins
Perhaps it is coming on my side

items.label: breaks
items.t: I fail when I am quick to side with opinion and do not refute the things that lead me into fear. My vices were not born with me: they came upon me and were forced into me. With frequent reminders, from someone who keeps tugging at my ear, I can drive back the opinions that sound all around me.
items.why: 7.2 says my principles die when their impressions go out, and that keeping them alight is up to me. Seneca says where the false opinions come from, other people, and that the remedy is to be reminded often, by someone else if need be. Marcus speaks here only of what I do myself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: we are quick to side with opinion. We do not refute the things that lead us into fear
support.follows: We side with opinion too quickly and do not refute the things that lead us into fear.
support.context: Letter 13, on fears of what may happen. Seneca says we are troubled by suspicions and rumour more than by fact; “the things” are the reports that lead us into fear.
gives: I am quick to side with opinion and do not refute the things that lead me into fear

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For you are wrong if you think that vices are born with us: they have come upon us, they have been forced into us.
support.follows: Our vices are not born with us; they came upon us and were forced into us.
support.context: Letter 94 defends the giving of advice. Seneca has just said that parents, slaves and neighbours pass their folly on to us; the vices “have come upon us” from these people.
gives: My vices were not born with me: they came upon me and were forced into me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: let the opinions that sound all around us be driven back by frequent reminders
support.follows: If we are reminded often, we can drive back the opinions that sound all around us.
support.context: Letter 94, on the value of advice: we need a guardian to tug at our ear and drive off the common talk. The “opinions” are those of the crowd around us.
gives: with frequent reminders, from someone who keeps tugging at my ear, I can drive back the opinions that sound all around me

items.t: Seneca leaves some pain in place. Of bodily pain he says that it is light when opinion has added nothing to it, not that it is then gone (Ep. 78.13). The same section says that the weight of pain depends on opinion, and advises calling the pain nothing, or at least slight. These belong to one argument, and what is left at its end is a light pain that opinion did not make. This limits the claim that what troubles me rests on my judgments.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: pain is light if opinion has added nothing to it
support.follows: Pain to which opinion has added nothing is light.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness, to the sick Lucilius: do not make ills heavier by complaining. The “pain” is bodily pain; “opinion” is what one tells oneself about it.

items.t: Seneca allows that some shocks get past reason. Even the mind of a man over whom Fortune has lost her authority will be struck, and his colour will change (Ep. 57.3): there are some things that no virtue can escape, and such a feeling is not fear but a natural feeling that reason cannot take by storm (Ep. 57.4). The claim says that the ruling part is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself; here the mind is struck by something it did not do to itself, and reason cannot stop it. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: like Marcus, he holds that trembling, pain and turning pale are feelings of the body, and he finds the true evil only where these things drag the mind down (Ep. 71.29). He is not fully consistent: in Letter 57 the blow is to the mind; in Letter 71 such things are of the body.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: his mind too will be struck, his colour will change
support.follows: Even the mind of a man fortune cannot rule is struck by a shock, and he changes colour.
support.context: Letter 57, on passing through a dark road tunnel. The man meant is the one “over whom Fortune has lost her authority”, not Seneca himself; what strikes his mind is the shock of the darkness.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: there are some things, my Lucilius, that no virtue can escape
support.follows: Some things cannot be escaped by any virtue.
support.context: Letter 57: in a dark road tunnel Seneca felt a blow to the mind and a change in himself. The “things” are such first shocks, which he says strike even a man fortune cannot rule.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is not fear, but a natural feeling that reason cannot take by storm.
support.follows: Such a shock is not fear but a natural feeling, and reason cannot take it by storm.
support.context: Letter 57, on a journey through a dark tunnel. “This” is tightening the face at grim things, shuddering at sudden things and the sight going dim on the brink of a vast depth, in a man of virtue.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the wise man will tremble, and feel pain, and turn pale, for all these are feelings of the body. Where, then, is the disaster, where is that true evil? There, of course: if these things drag the mind down
support.follows: Trembling, pain and pallor belong to the body even in the wise man; the true evil is there only if these things drag the mind down.
support.context: Letter 71, on the supreme good: human virtue does not go beyond nature. “These things” are the trembling, pain and pallor; “There” is where they drag the mind down.

items.t: Seneca goes beyond Marcus’s “say nothing more”. Where everything is uncertain, he tells Lucilius to favour himself and believe what he prefers, and to lean towards hope even if fear has more votes (Ep. 13.13). Marcus says to add nothing to what is reported and to see things as they are in truth; a belief chosen because I prefer it is an addition. Seneca does not hold to this himself: a few lines later he says he is ashamed to be talking with Lucilius like this and to be reviving him with such mild remedies, and he goes on to a sterner one (Ep. 13.14).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whenever everything is uncertain, favour yourself: believe what you prefer
support.follows: When everything is uncertain, I should favour myself and believe what I prefer.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: Lucilius is to weigh his hopes against his fears about a trouble that may come. By “everything” Seneca means the signs on either side.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If fear has more votes, lean rather to the other side all the same, and stop disturbing yourself
support.follows: Even if fear has more on its side, I should lean the other way and stop disturbing myself.
support.context: Letter 13, on fears of what may happen. Seneca pictures hopes and fears as voting; even if fear has more votes, Lucilius is to lean towards hope.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am ashamed to be talking with you like this, and to be reviving you with such mild remedies.
support.follows: Seneca is ashamed to be talking with Lucilius like this and to be reviving him with mild remedies like these.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: said shortly after Seneca advises Lucilius to believe what he prefers. The “mild remedies” are that advice; a sterner one follows.

passages.title: On bearing illness and pain
passages.text: Do not make your own ills heavier for yourself and load yourself with complaints: pain is light if opinion has added nothing to it. If, on the other hand, you begin to encourage yourself and to say, “It is nothing, or at least it is slight; let us hold out; it will stop soon”, you will make it light in thinking it so. Everything hangs on opinion; it is not only ambition and extravagance and greed that look to it: we feel pain according to opinion.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: So, free from care, listen to your enemy’s threats; and although your own conscience gives you confidence, still, because many things outside the case carry weight, hope for what is fairest and also prepare yourself for what is most unfair. But above all remember this: to take the uproar away from things and to see what is in each thing: you will find that there is nothing terrible in those things except the fear itself.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: After gods and human beings, let us look into how things are to be used. We shall be tossing out precepts to no purpose unless this has come first: what opinion we ought to hold about each thing, about poverty, about riches, about glory, about disgrace, about homeland, about exile. Let us assess each thing one by one with its reputation set aside, and ask what they are, not what they are called.

passages.title: On needless fears about the future
passages.text: Do this for me: whenever people stand around you trying to persuade you that you are wretched, think not about what you hear but about what you feel, and take counsel with your own power to endure, and be the one to question yourself, you who know your own affairs best: “Why is it that these people are lamenting over me? Why is it that they are alarmed, that they even fear infection from me, as if misfortune could jump across? Is there any evil in that, or is that thing ill spoken of rather than evil?” Be the one to question yourself: “Am I perhaps in torment and grieving without cause, and making an evil of what is not one?”

passages.title: On needless fears about the future
passages.text: I am ashamed to be talking with you like this, and to be reviving you with such mild remedies. Let someone else say “Perhaps it will not come.” As for you, say: “And what if it does come? We will see which of the two wins. Perhaps it is coming on my side, and that death will bring honour to my life.” Hemlock made Socrates great. Wrest from Cato the sword that championed freedom: you will have taken away a great part of his glory.

passages.title: On needless fears about the future
passages.text: “But it is to come.” First look carefully at whether there are sure proofs of an evil to come. For most of the time we are troubled by suspicions, and we are made fools of by rumour, which so often finishes a war but finishes individuals far more. That is how it is, my Lucilius: we are quick to side with opinion. We do not refute the things that lead us into fear, nor do we examine them, but we panic, and turn and run like those whom dust raised by a herd in flight has driven from their camp, or whom some tale spread about with no source has terrified.

passages.title: On the usefulness of practical advice
passages.text: So let there be some guardian, and let him tug at our ear again and again, and drive off the common talk, and shout back against the praise of the crowds. For you are wrong if you think that vices are born with us: they have come upon us, they have been forced into us. So let the opinions that sound all around us be driven back by frequent reminders.

passages.title: On instinctive fear in a dark tunnel
passages.text: Still, that darkness gave me something to think about: I felt a kind of blow to the mind, and a change, without fear, brought about by the newness, and at the same time the foulness, of an unfamiliar thing. I am not speaking to you now about myself, who am a long way from being a tolerable man, let alone a perfect one, but about the man over whom Fortune has lost her authority: his mind too will be struck, his colour will change.

passages.title: On instinctive fear in a dark tunnel
passages.text: For there are some things, my Lucilius, that no virtue can escape; nature reminds virtue of its own mortality. And so he will tighten his face at grim things, and shudder at sudden things, and his sight will go dim if he stands on the brink of a vast depth and looks down into it. This is not fear, but a natural feeling that reason cannot take by storm.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: I come now to the point to which your expectation calls me. So that our virtue may not seem to wander outside the nature of things: the wise man will tremble, and feel pain, and turn pale, for all these are feelings of the body. Where, then, is the disaster, where is that true evil? There, of course: if these things drag the mind down, if they bring it to a confession of slavery, if they make it dissatisfied with itself.

passages.title: On needless fears about the future
passages.text: So weigh hope and fear, and whenever everything is uncertain, favour yourself: believe what you prefer. If fear has more votes, lean rather to the other side all the same, and stop disturbing yourself, and keep turning this over in your mind: that the greater part of mortals, though they have nothing evil upon them and nothing evil that is certain to come, seethe and run this way and that. For no one resists himself once he has begun to be pushed, and no one brings his fear down to the truth; no one says “The source is worthless, worthless: he either made it up or believed it.” We give ourselves to the breeze to be carried; we take fright at doubtful things as though they were certain; we do not keep things in proportion: a slight unease at once turns into fear.

claims.t: Everything is a matter of judgment: how anything stands for me depends on how I judge it. What troubles me rests on my judgments. It is not outside me but inside.
claims.shared: 12.16 and 2.13 open with the same saying, that everything is “judgment”. 9.30 and 9.11 both put what presses on me in “judgment”: 9.30 says the things that trouble me “rest wholly on your judgment”, 9.11 that what hemmed him in was “in my judgments”.
claims.changed: 9.30 says “many” of the things that trouble me rest on judgment; 9.11 says “all that hemmed me in”. The claim says “what troubles me” and leaves the number open. 9.11 speaks of what hemmed him in; the claim uses 9.30’s word “trouble” for both. 12.16 and 2.13 give only the bare saying, “all things are judgment” and “everything is judgment”; the claim says “a matter of” judgment, and the words after the colon, that how anything stands for me depends on how I judge it, are the editor’s reading of the saying, backed by no quote of their own.

support.quote: That all things are judgment
support.follows: All things are a matter of judgment.
gives: Everything is a matter of judgment

support.quote: That everything is judgment.
support.follows: Everything is a matter of judgment.

support.quote: those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment

support.follows: What hemmed Marcus in was not outside him. It was inside, in his judgments.
gives: What troubles me rests on my judgments

claims.t: My judgment is up to me. I am able to form the judgment I ought, and free to form none, and I need not be troubled: things themselves do not produce my verdicts, and what is outside my mind is nothing to my mind.
claims.shared: All three passages say that judging lies with me: 12.16 that the judgment “is up to you”, 7.2 “I am able to form the judgment I ought”, 6.47 “One is free to form no judgment”. 7.2 and 6.47 both go on to say that I need not be disturbed or troubled, and both then turn to “things”: things do not produce our verdicts, and things outside the mind are nothing to it.
claims.changed: 7.2 says “disturbed” and 6.47 “troubled”; the claim says “troubled” for both. The colon stands for the “for” of 6.47, where the sentence about things is given as the reason. In 7.2 the sentence about things outside the mind simply follows the question, with no “for”. Both passages speak of “this”, the matter in front of Marcus; the claim speaks generally.

support.quote: this judgment is up to you
support.follows: The judgment I form is up to me.
gives: My judgment is up to me

support.quote: I am able to form the judgment I ought about this.
support.follows: Marcus is able to form the judgment he ought to form about the matter in front of him.
gives: My judgment is up to me
I am able to form the judgment I ought

support.quote: If I am able, why am I disturbed?
support.follows: Since he is able to judge as he ought, Marcus has no reason to be disturbed.
gives: I need not be troubled

support.quote: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul
support.follows: A person is free to form no judgment about a matter, and free not to be troubled by it.

support.quote: The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind.

claims.role: What taking the judgment away gives
claims.t: When I wish, I can take away my judgment about what seems to distress me, and then I stand in the safest place: there is calm, like a bay without a wave. What hems me in I can throw out, and at once have plenty of open room.
claims.shared: 8.38 and 12.16 both say “take away” the judgment and both say what follows. The shared words are the translation’s: the Greek verbs differ (ἀφέλῃς in 8.38, ἆρον in 12.16) but are close in sense. 9.11 (“threw out”) and 9.30 (“strip away”) both speak of removing what presses on me. All four passages describe the outcome as a place: “the safest place” (8.38), “a bay without a wave” (12.16), “open room” (9.30), being out of “all that hemmed me in” (9.11).
claims.changed: 12.16 says “when you wish” and 8.38 says “if”; the claim keeps “when I wish” and drops the “if”. Only 8.38 and 12.16 name the judgment as the thing removed: in 9.11 what is thrown out is all that hemmed him in, and in 9.30 the things stripped away are needless ones among those that trouble me. 9.30 is cut in mid-sentence: the Greek goes on to say by what means the room is made, by taking the whole universe in thought, with endless time and the quick change of each thing. The claim leaves that means out, so its “open room” is not to be read as coming from the removal of a judgment alone. The headland of 12.16 is left out.

support.quote: So take the judgment away when you wish
support.follows: I can take the judgment away whenever I wish.
gives: When I wish
take away my judgment

support.quote: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place.

claims.t: My reason does not trouble or distress itself; it is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself. What happens to my body or to anything else of mine I leave to the part it happens to: the body can say so if it suffers, and whatever else of mine is in a bad way can judge that for itself.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of the judging part acting on “itself”: the ruling part “does not make trouble for itself” (7.13), and reason is not to be the one “to distress itself” (8.38). Both then turn to another part with “let”: let the body say so if it suffers (7.13), let whatever is in a bad way form its own judgment (8.38).
claims.changed: 7.13 says “the ruling part” and 8.38 says “reason”; the claim says “my reason” for both. 7.13 states it as a fact about the ruling part and 8.38 as an instruction; the claim states it as my rule. 8.38 does not name the body; 7.13 does. “Judge that for itself” follows the printed reading of 8.38, “let that form its own judgment about itself”; the translators’ other reading, “let it suppose so about itself”, says much the same: the part that is in a bad way, not reason, is to judge its own state.

support.quote: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself
support.follows: The part of me that rules does not make trouble for itself.
gives: My reason does not trouble or distress itself

support.quote: let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself
support.follows: Reason, at least, should not be the one that distresses itself.
gives: My reason does not trouble or distress itself

support.quote: it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself
support.follows: The ruling part is undisturbed and unhindered unless it disturbs and hinders itself.
gives: it is undisturbed unless it disturbs itself

support.quote: Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything.
support.follows: It is for the body to take care that it suffers nothing, and to say so if it does suffer.

claims.t: I tell myself no more than my first impressions report: if they report that someone speaks ill of me, they have not reported that I am harmed. When someone abuses me, I do not judge things as that person wants me to; I see things as they are.
claims.shared: Both passages take the case of a person who turns on me, one who “is speaking ill of you” (8.47) and one who “abuses you” (4.9). 8.47 answers that case with what has and has not been reported, and uses “see” for its second example, the sick child: “I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see”. 4.9 answers its case with “see them as they are in truth”. The shared word “see” is the translation’s: the Greek has βλέπω in 8.47 and ἴδε in 4.9, different verbs close in sense. Both refuse a judgment that goes beyond the thing.
claims.changed: In 8.47 the judgment refused is the one I would add from within; in 4.9 it is the one the abuser holds or wants me to hold. The sick child of 8.47 is a second example and is kept only in the quote. 4.9’s “in truth” is left out of the claim. For “the impressions that lead the way” the claim says “my first impressions”, the words 8.47 itself uses later.

support.quote: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report.
support.follows: I should tell myself only what the first impressions report.
gives: I tell myself no more than my first impressions report

support.quote: It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported.
support.follows: The report is that someone speaks ill of me. That I have been harmed is not part of the report.
gives: if they report that someone speaks ill of me, they have not reported that I am harmed

support.quote: I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see.
support.follows: Marcus sees that the child is sick. He does not see that the child is in danger.

support.quote: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are
support.follows: I should not take things to be what the person who abuses me decides they are or wants me to decide they are.
gives: When someone abuses me, I do not judge things as that person wants me to

support.quote: see them as they are in truth
support.follows: I should see things as they truly are.
gives: I see things as they are

single.quote: The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself
single.label: Needing nothing
single.t: So far as depends on itself, my ruling part needs nothing, unless it makes a need for itself.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of need; the others speak of trouble and distress.
single.follows: Left to itself, the ruling part needs nothing; any need it has, it makes for itself.

single.quote: Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.label: Saying something further
single.t: To what my first impressions report, I do add something: I speak to myself as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.why: Only this passage corrects the rule of saying nothing further. It does not spell out what is to be said.
single.follows: Marcus corrects himself: he may say something further, but as one who recognises each thing that happens in the universe.

single.quote: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame?
single.label: Principles going out
single.t: My principles can be killed only if the impressions that answer to them are put out, and it is up to me to keep fanning those impressions back into flame.
single.why: Only this passage says how principles are lost and how they are kept alive. It stands here as what failing looks like, and the way back.
single.follows: Principles die only when the impressions that answer to them go out, and keeping those alight is up to me.

single.quote: For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
single.label: So far as true
single.t: The saying that everything is judgment can be answered, and the answers are plain. Its usefulness is plain too, if I take what is nourishing in it, so far as it is true.
single.why: Only this passage admits that the saying has plain answers and limits it to what is true in it.
single.follows: The replies to Monimus’s saying are plain, and so is its use, if one takes from it what nourishes and only so far as it is true.

single.quote: “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted.
single.label: “I am not reason”
single.t: The self that stands in safety is my reason. If I object that I am not reason, I grant it.
single.why: Only this passage raises the objection that I am more than my reason, and it grants it. What still holds comes in the passage’s next sentence, quoted in the claim on reason and the body: reason is not to be the one that distresses itself.
single.follows: The “yourself” that stands safe is reason. To the objection that he is not reason, Marcus answers: granted.

members.text:
If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that
which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe
may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not
reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding
admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let
that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
members.english: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place. “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted. Then let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself, and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself.
members.greek: Ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὴν σὴν ὑπόληψιν περὶ τοῦ λυπεῖν σε δοκοῦντος, αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ ἀσφαλεστάτῳ ἕστηκας.—τίς αὐτός;—ὁ λόγος.—ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἰμὶ λόγος.—ἔστω. οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω, εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει, ὑπολαβέτω αὐτὸ περὶ αὑτοῦ.

members.text:
What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions
and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper
power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper
and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they
mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy
power,) are still kept fresh and alive? It is in my power concerning
this thing that is happened, what soever it be, to conceit that which is
right and true. If it be, why then am I troubled? Those things that are
without my understanding, are nothing to it at all: and that is it only,
which doth properly concern me. Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be
right.
members.english: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame? I am able to form the judgment I ought about this. If I am able, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind. Learn this and you are upright.
members.greek: Τὰ δόγματα πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ αἱ κατάλληλοι αὐτοῖς φαντασίαι σβεσθῶσιν, ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι. δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν· εἰ δύναμαι, τί ταράσσομαι; τὰ ἔξω τῆς ἐμῆς διανοίας οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν. τοῦτο μάθε καὶ ὀρθὸς εἶ.

members.text:
It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit
and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to
exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and
objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to
beget and force upon us any opinion at all.
members.english: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul; for things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts.
members.greek: Ἔξεστι περὶ τούτου μηδὲν ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ μὴ ὀχλεῖσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ· αὐτὰ γὰρ τὰ πράγματα οὐκ ἔχει φύσιν ποιητικὴν τῶν ἡμετέρων κρίσεων.

members.text:
This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that
ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon
itself. This I say; it will not put itself in any fear, it will not lead
itself into any concupiscence. If it be in the power of any other to
compel it to fear, or to grieve, it is free for him to use his power.
But sure if itself do not of itself, through some false opinion or
supposition incline itself to any such disposition; there is no fear.
For as for the body, why should I make the grief of my body, to be the
grief of my mind? If that itself can either fear or complain, let it.
But as for the soul, which indeed, can only be truly sensible of either
fear or grief; to which only it belongs according to its different
imaginations and opinions, to admit of either of these, or of their
contraries; thou mayst look to that thyself, that it suffer nothing.
Induce her not to any such opinion or persuasion. The understanding
is of itself sufficient unto itself, and needs not (if itself doth not
bring itself to need) any other thing besides itself, and by consequent
as it needs nothing, so neither can it be troubled or hindered by
anything, if itself doth not trouble and hinder itself.
members.english: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself; I mean, for example, it does not frighten itself into desire. But if anyone else can frighten or distress it, let them do so; for it will not, by its own judging, turn itself in such directions. Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything. But the little soul, the thing that fears, that is distressed, that in general forms judgments about these things, will suffer nothing at all; for you will not lead it to such a verdict. The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself; and in the same way it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself.
members.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ἐνοχλεῖ, οἷον λέγω, οὐ φοβεῖ ἑαυτὸ εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν. εἰ δέ τις ἄλλος αὐτὸ φοβῆσαι ἢ λυπῆσαι δύναται, ποιείτω· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς. τὸ σωμάτιον μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει· τὸ δὲ ψυχάριον τὸ φοβούμενον, τὸ λυπούμενον, τὸ περὶ τούτων ὅλως ὑπολαμβάνον, οὐδὲν μὴ πάθῃ· οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην. ἀπροσδεές ἐστιν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδειαν ποιῇ· κατὰ ταὐτὰ δὲ καὶ ἀτάραχον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτὸ ταράσσῃ καὶ ἐμποδίζῃ.

members.text:
Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy
power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and
then thou shalt have room enough.
members.english: You can strip away many needless things among those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment, and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself.
members.greek: Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν τῶν ἐνοχλούντων σοι δύνασαι ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα, καὶ πολλὴν εὐρυχωρίαν περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ

members.text:
Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things,
as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is
reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he
speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt
thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou
must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but
that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use
to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as
they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within
thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut
as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in
the world.
members.english: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report. It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see. So always stay like this with the first impressions and say nothing further yourself from within, and nothing happens to you. Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
members.greek: Μηδὲν πλέον σαυτῷ λέγε ὧν αἱ προηγούμεναι φαντασίαι ἀναγγέλλουσιν. ἤγγελται ὅτι ὁ δεῖνά σε κακῶς λέγει. ἤγγελται τοῦτο· τὸ δέ, ὅτι βέβλαψαι, οὐκ ἤγγελται. βλέπω ὅτι νοσεῖ τὸ παιδίον. βλέπω· ὅτι δὲ κινδυνεύει, οὐ βλέπω. οὕτως οὖν μένε ἀεὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν καὶ μηδὲν αὐτὸς ἔνδοθεν ἐπίλεγε καὶ οὐδέν σοι γίνεται· μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπίλεγε ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων.

members.text:
Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the
mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken
in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things
safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the
poet hath it.
members.english: That all things are judgment, and this judgment is up to you. So take the judgment away when you wish, and, just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave.
members.greek: Ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις καὶ αὕτη ἐπὶ σοί. ἆρον οὖν ὅτε θέλεις τὴν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκραν γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων.

members.text:
Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth,
or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see
what it is in very truth.
members.english: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are, but see them as they are in truth.
members.greek: Μὴ τοιαῦτα ὑπολάμβανε, οἷα ὁ ὑβρίζων κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται, ἀλλὰ ἴδε αὐτά, ὁποῖα κατʼ ἀλήθειάν ἐστιν.

members.text:
Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things
are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as
plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that
which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is
sweet and pleasing.
members.english: That everything is judgment. For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
members.greek: Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις. δῆλα μὲν γὰρ τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα· δῆλον δὲ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον τοῦ λεγομένου, ἐάν τις αὐτοῦ τὸ νόστιμον μέχρι τοῦ ἀληθοῦς δέχηται.

members.text:
This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all
my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever
it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but
within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before
thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
members.english: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in; for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments.
members.greek: Σήμερον ἐξῆλθον πάσης περιστάσεως, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐξέβαλον πᾶσαν περίστασιν· ἔξω γὰρ οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλὰ ἔνδον ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήψεσιν.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 8.38 is 8.40, 6.47 is 6.52, 7.13 is 7.16, 9.30 is the opening of 9.32, 8.47 is 8.49, 12.16 is 12.22, 4.9 is 4.11, 2.13 is 2.15 and 9.11 is 9.13; 7.2 is only the first part of the modern 7.2.

Reads “reason” (8.38) and “the ruling part” (7.13) as the same thing and calls both “my reason” in claim 4. Reads the unnamed “anything else of yours” of 8.38 beside the “little body” of 7.13; the Greek of 8.38 does not name the body.

The statement says “what troubles me” without “all” or “many”. 9.30 says many of the things that trouble me rest on judgment, 9.11 says all that hemmed him in was in his judgments, and 2.13 holds “everything is judgment” only so far as it is true.

Uses “trouble” in the statement and in claims 1 and 2 for three of the translation’s words: “trouble” (9.30, 6.47), “disturbed” (7.2) and “hemmed in” (9.11). “Distress” is kept as it is in claims 3 and 4. The quotes keep the difference.

Joins 8.47 and 4.9 in claim 5 although they share few words: both take a person who speaks against me, and both answer with “see” in the translation. The words “I see things as they are” rest on 4.9; 8.47 backs them only by its example of the sick child.

Quotes 9.30 although the passage is cut in mid-sentence. The Greek goes on to say that the open room is made by taking the whole universe in thought; claim 3 quotes only the room, and its notes warn that the room is not to be read as coming from removing a judgment alone. Also leaves out “it does not frighten itself into desire” (7.13), where the translators’ note says the Greek text has been doubted, and the “little soul” of the same passage.
articles.limit: 12.16 is quoted in three of the five claims and two of the three parts of the statement, so the article leans on one short passage. The passages do not agree on what to do with a judgment: 6.47 says I may form none, 7.2 that I can form the one I ought, 8.47 first says to add nothing and then to add something. Claim 2 keeps 6.47 and 7.2 side by side, and claim 5 and the said-once item on 8.47’s correction keep the two halves of 8.47; the article settles neither. Article 2 already says that I take care in my judgments and that reason is not to be overpowered by the senses. What this article adds is that the trouble itself rests on the judgment, and that the judgment can be taken away.

statement.t: My judgment is mine to give, and I give it only as far as the facts have shown, without deciding the rest.

statement.form: Pilot wording restored, 106 characters. “Acting on that much” is cut because no passage speaks of acting. “Facts” is our plain word for what impressions report in 8.47 and for things as they are in truth in 4.9. Leaving the rest undecided rests on 8.47’s unreported harm and on the freedom in 6.47, which stays a freedom in c2.

single.t: So far as depends on itself, my ruling part needs nothing, unless it makes a need for itself.
single.why: Single source, 7.13. Pilot wording stands. Both hedges are kept, so the self-sufficiency is conditional.
single.follows: Left to itself, the ruling part needs nothing; any need it has, it makes for itself.

single.quote: Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.label: Saying something further
single.t: To what my first impressions report, I do add something: I speak to myself as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
single.why: Single source, 8.47. Pilot wording stands. The passage does not spell out what the addition says, so the line does not either.
single.follows: Marcus corrects himself: he may say something further, but as one who recognises each thing that happens in the universe.

single.quote: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame?
single.label: Principles going out
single.t: My principles can be killed only if the impressions that answer to them are put out, and it is up to me to keep fanning those impressions back into flame.
single.why: Single source, 7.2. Pilot wording stands. The flame image shows that the work is continual.
single.follows: Principles die only when the impressions that answer to them go out, and keeping those alight is up to me.

single.quote: For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
single.label: So far as true
single.t: The saying that everything is judgment can be answered, and what is said in answer is plain. Its usefulness is plain too, if I take what is nourishing in it, so far as it is true.
single.why: Single source, 2.13, on its supplied quote. Pilot frame restored. “The answers” becomes “what is said in answer” because the passage does not give the reply or say there are several. The endorsement stays partial.
single.follows: The replies to Monimus’s saying are plain, and so is its use, if one takes from it what nourishes and only so far as it is true.

single.quote: “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted.
single.label: “I am not reason”
single.t: The self that stands in safety is my reason. If I object that I am not reason, I grant it.
single.why: Single source, 8.38. Pilot wording stands. It keeps the concession that the self is not simply reason.
single.follows: The “yourself” that stands safe is reason. To the objection that he is not reason, Marcus answers: granted.

members.text:
If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that
which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe
may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not
reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding
admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let
that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
members.english: If you take away your judgment about what seems to distress you, you yourself stand in the safest place. “Who is ‘yourself’?” Reason. “But I am not reason.” Granted. Then let reason, for its part, not be the one to distress itself, and if anything else of yours is in a bad way, let that form its own judgment about itself.
members.greek: Ἐὰν ἀφέλῃς τὴν σὴν ὑπόληψιν περὶ τοῦ λυπεῖν σε δοκοῦντος, αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ ἀσφαλεστάτῳ ἕστηκας.—τίς αὐτός;—ὁ λόγος.—ἀλλ’ οὐκ εἰμὶ λόγος.—ἔστω. οὐκοῦν ὁ μὲν λόγος αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν μὴ λυπείτω, εἰ δέ τι ἄλλο σοι κακῶς ἔχει, ὑπολαβέτω αὐτὸ περὶ αὑτοῦ.

members.text:
What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions
and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper
power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper
and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they
mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy
power,) are still kept fresh and alive? It is in my power concerning
this thing that is happened, what soever it be, to conceit that which is
right and true. If it be, why then am I troubled? Those things that are
without my understanding, are nothing to it at all: and that is it only,
which doth properly concern me. Be always in this mind, and thou wilt be
right.
members.english: How can the principles be killed, unless the impressions that answer to them are put out, the impressions it is up to you to keep fanning back into flame? I am able to form the judgment I ought about this. If I am able, why am I disturbed? The things outside my mind are nothing at all to my mind. Learn this and you are upright.
members.greek: Τὰ δόγματα πῶς ἄλλως δύναται νεκρωθῆναι, ἐὰν μὴ αἱ κατάλληλοι αὐτοῖς φαντασίαι σβεσθῶσιν, ἃς διηνεκῶς ἀναζωπυρεῖν ἐπὶ σοί ἐστι. δύναμαι περὶ τούτου ὃ δεῖ ὑπολαμβάνειν· εἰ δύναμαι, τί ταράσσομαι; τὰ ἔξω τῆς ἐμῆς διανοίας οὐδὲν ὅλως πρὸς τὴν ἐμὴν διάνοιαν. τοῦτο μάθε καὶ ὀρθὸς εἶ.

members.text:
It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit
and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to
exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and
objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to
beget and force upon us any opinion at all.
members.english: One is free to form no judgment about this and not to be troubled in one’s soul; for things themselves do not have a nature that produces our verdicts.
members.greek: Ἔξεστι περὶ τούτου μηδὲν ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ μὴ ὀχλεῖσθαι τῇ ψυχῇ· αὐτὰ γὰρ τὰ πράγματα οὐκ ἔχει φύσιν ποιητικὴν τῶν ἡμετέρων κρίσεων.

members.text:
This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that
ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon
itself. This I say; it will not put itself in any fear, it will not lead
itself into any concupiscence. If it be in the power of any other to
compel it to fear, or to grieve, it is free for him to use his power.
But sure if itself do not of itself, through some false opinion or
supposition incline itself to any such disposition; there is no fear.
For as for the body, why should I make the grief of my body, to be the
grief of my mind? If that itself can either fear or complain, let it.
But as for the soul, which indeed, can only be truly sensible of either
fear or grief; to which only it belongs according to its different
imaginations and opinions, to admit of either of these, or of their
contraries; thou mayst look to that thyself, that it suffer nothing.
Induce her not to any such opinion or persuasion. The understanding
is of itself sufficient unto itself, and needs not (if itself doth not
bring itself to need) any other thing besides itself, and by consequent
as it needs nothing, so neither can it be troubled or hindered by
anything, if itself doth not trouble and hinder itself.
members.english: The ruling part does not make trouble for itself; I mean, for example, it does not frighten itself into desire. But if anyone else can frighten or distress it, let them do so; for it will not, by its own judging, turn itself in such directions. Let the little body itself take care that it suffers nothing, if it can, and let it say so if it suffers anything. But the little soul, the thing that fears, that is distressed, that in general forms judgments about these things, will suffer nothing at all; for you will not lead it to such a verdict. The ruling part, so far as depends on itself, is in need of nothing, unless it makes a need for itself; and in the same way it is undisturbed and unhindered, unless it disturbs and hinders itself.
members.greek: Τὸ ἡγεμονικὸν αὐτὸ ἑαυτῷ οὐκ ἐνοχλεῖ, οἷον λέγω, οὐ φοβεῖ ἑαυτὸ εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν. εἰ δέ τις ἄλλος αὐτὸ φοβῆσαι ἢ λυπῆσαι δύναται, ποιείτω· αὐτὸ γὰρ ἑαυτὸ ὑποληπτικῶς οὐ τρέψει εἰς τοιαύτας τροπάς. τὸ σωμάτιον μὴ πάθῃ τι, αὐτὸ μεριμνάτω, εἰ δύναται, καὶ λεγέτω, εἴ τι πάσχει· τὸ δὲ ψυχάριον τὸ φοβούμενον, τὸ λυπούμενον, τὸ περὶ τούτων ὅλως ὑπολαμβάνον, οὐδὲν μὴ πάθῃ· οὐ γὰρ ἄξεις αὐτὸ εἰς κρίσιν τοιαύτην. ἀπροσδεές ἐστιν ὅσον ἐφ’ ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτῷ ἔνδειαν ποιῇ· κατὰ ταὐτὰ δὲ καὶ ἀτάραχον καὶ ἀνεμπόδιστον, ἐὰν μὴ ἑαυτὸ ταράσσῃ καὶ ἐμποδίζῃ.

members.text:
Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy
power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and
then thou shalt have room enough.
members.english: You can strip away many needless things among those that trouble you, things that rest wholly on your judgment, and you will at once make plenty of open room for yourself.
members.greek: Πολλὰ περισσὰ περιελεῖν τῶν ἐνοχλούντων σοι δύνασαι ὅλα ἐπὶ τῇ ὑπολήψει σου κείμενα, καὶ πολλὴν εὐρυχωρίαν περιποιήσεις ἤδη σεαυτῷ

members.text:
Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things,
as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them. It is
reported unto thee, that such a one speaketh ill of thee. Well; that he
speaketh ill of thee, so much is reported. But that thou art hurt
thereby, is not reported: that is the addition of opinion, which thou
must exclude. I see that my child is sick. That he is sick, I see, but
that he is in danger of his life also, I see it not. Thus thou must use
to keep thyself to the first motions and apprehensions of things, as
they present themselves outwardly; and add not unto them from within
thyself through mere conceit and opinion. Or rather add unto them: hut
as one that understandeth the true nature of all things that happen in
the world.
members.english: Say nothing more to yourself than what the impressions that lead the way report. It has been reported that so-and-so is speaking ill of you. That has been reported; but that you have been harmed has not been reported. I see that the child is sick. I see it; but that the child is in danger I do not see. So always stay like this with the first impressions and say nothing further yourself from within, and nothing happens to you. Or rather, do say something further, as one who recognises each of the things that happen in the universe.
members.greek: Μηδὲν πλέον σαυτῷ λέγε ὧν αἱ προηγούμεναι φαντασίαι ἀναγγέλλουσιν. ἤγγελται ὅτι ὁ δεῖνά σε κακῶς λέγει. ἤγγελται τοῦτο· τὸ δέ, ὅτι βέβλαψαι, οὐκ ἤγγελται. βλέπω ὅτι νοσεῖ τὸ παιδίον. βλέπω· ὅτι δὲ κινδυνεύει, οὐ βλέπω. οὕτως οὖν μένε ἀεὶ ἐπὶ τῶν πρώτων φαντασιῶν καὶ μηδὲν αὐτὸς ἔνδοθεν ἐπίλεγε καὶ οὐδέν σοι γίνεται· μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπίλεγε ὡς γνωρίζων ἕκαστα τῶν ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ συμβαινόντων.

members.text:
Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the
mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken
in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things
safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the
poet hath it.
members.english: That all things are judgment, and this judgment is up to you. So take the judgment away when you wish, and, just as for someone who has rounded the headland, there is calm: all things steady, and a bay without a wave.
members.greek: Ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις καὶ αὕτη ἐπὶ σοί. ἆρον οὖν ὅτε θέλεις τὴν ὑπόληψιν καὶ ὥσπερ κάμψαντι τὴν ἄκραν γαλήνη, σταθερὰ πάντα καὶ κόλπος ἀκύμων.

members.text:
Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth,
or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see
what it is in very truth.
members.english: Do not judge things to be such as the person who abuses you decides they are, or wants you to decide they are, but see them as they are in truth.
members.greek: Μὴ τοιαῦτα ὑπολάμβανε, οἷα ὁ ὑβρίζων κρίνει ἢ οἷά σε κρίνειν βούλεται, ἀλλὰ ἴδε αὐτά, ὁποῖα κατʼ ἀλήθειάν ἐστιν.

members.text:
Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things
are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as
plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that
which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is
sweet and pleasing.
members.english: That everything is judgment. For what is said in answer to Monimus the Cynic is plain; but plain too is the usefulness of the saying, if one takes what is nourishing in it so far as it is true.
members.greek: Ὅτι πᾶν ὑπόληψις. δῆλα μὲν γὰρ τὰ πρὸς τὸν Κυνικὸν Μόνιμον λεγόμενα· δῆλον δὲ καὶ τὸ χρήσιμον τοῦ λεγομένου, ἐάν τις αὐτοῦ τὸ νόστιμον μέχρι τοῦ ἀληθοῦς δέχηται.

members.text:
This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all
my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever
it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but
within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before
thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
members.english: Today I got out of all that hemmed me in, or rather I threw out all that hemmed me in; for it was not outside but inside, in my judgments.
members.greek: Σήμερον ἐξῆλθον πάσης περιστάσεως, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐξέβαλον πᾶσαν περίστασιν· ἔξω γὰρ οὐκ ἦν, ἀλλὰ ἔνδον ἐν ταῖς ὑπολήψεσιν.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 8.38 is 8.40, 6.47 is 6.52, 7.13 is 7.16, 9.30 is the opening of 9.32, 8.47 is 8.49, 12.16 is 12.22, 4.9 is 4.11, 2.13 is 2.15 and 9.11 is 9.13; 7.2 is only the first part of the modern 7.2.

Pilot wording restored, 106 characters. “Acting on that much” is cut because no passage speaks of acting. “Facts” is our plain word for what impressions report in 8.47 and for things as they are in truth in 4.9. Leaving the rest undecided rests on 8.47’s unreported harm and on the freedom in 6.47, which stays a freedom in c2.
marcus_revision.limit: The sources do not agree on one remedy. Some withdraw the judgment (6.47, 12.16, 8.38), while others form the right one or see truly (7.2, 4.9). Only 8.47 holds both, so the opening, which joins judging by the facts with leaving the rest undecided, is our editorial reading, not Marcus’s statement. “Facts” and “criticism” are our plain words for what impressions report, for things as they are in truth, and for ill speech or abuse. “Everything is judgment” is accepted only so far as it is true. Nothing here denies the event, the body’s suffering or the child’s sickness, and nothing says that outside things are unreal or that the child is safe. The calm is a simile for a moment when the judgment is removed, not a promise that it lasts. 9.11 reports one day, and c1 states its throwing out as a practice on our reading.

articles.title: What happens can be borne and does not harm me

statement.t: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear; what happens harms me only if I judge it bad, and it does not stop me from being good and just.

parts.words: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear
what happens harms me only if I judge it bad
it does not stop me from being good and just

statement.kind: Two grounds, what follows from them, and rules for the moment
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the grounds: what happens is within what I am fitted to bear, and the harm lies in my judgment. Claims 3 and 4 say what follows for the body and for conduct. Claims 5 and 6 are exercises for the moment a thing strikes. The statement joins the two grounds and claim 4 with no step of the editor’s.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it
groups.asks: What still holds if the statement is not true.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second voice: nothing is unbearable, I feel pain according to opinion, pain is a feeling of the body, whatever I am given is material for virtue, and pain is light when opinion adds nothing to it. The article gains a way of turning the mind from pain, a question that catches the pain I add myself, and a reason to go on living when I could leave. He challenges the first claim: a pain I cannot bear may come, though it is short. He limits the third: the mind is steady only once virtue is complete.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement is challenged in its first part. That part does not stand as it is worded: Seneca, like Marcus in 10.3, allows a pain I cannot bear, and says only that it will not last, though elsewhere he says nothing is unbearable. The rest of the statement stands.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: none of these things is an evil, none is unbearable or hard
piece.follows: None of the things Seneca has listed is an evil, and none is unbearable.
piece.context: Letter 91: after the fire that destroyed Lyon, Seneca tells Lucilius what everyone must suffer. “These things” are pain, thirst, hunger, old age, sickness, loss and death.
gives: Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: we feel pain according to opinion
piece.follows: How much pain we feel depends on our opinion.
piece.context: Letter 78 is to Lucilius, who is ill, on bearing pain. “Opinion” is what we tell ourselves about our trouble; Seneca has just said that everything depends on it.
gives: my own judgment

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: nothing is wretched for a man except that there is anything in nature which he thinks wretched
piece.follows: A person is wretched only if there is something that he thinks wretched.
piece.context: Letter 96: Seneca answers a Lucilius who is indignant and complains, and lists his own illness and losses. The one real evil in such things, he says, is being indignant and complaining.
gives: my own judgment
that it is bad

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the wise man will tremble, and feel pain, and turn pale, for all these are feelings of the body
piece.follows: Even the wise man trembles, feels pain and turns pale, because these are feelings of the body.
piece.context: Letter 71 argues that the honourable is the only good. Seneca grants that virtue does not wander outside the nature of things, and places the true evil in the mind, if these things drag it down.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: That is why a great and sensible man draws his mind apart from the body and spends much time with the better and divine part; with this complaining and fragile one, as much as is necessary.
piece.follows: A prudent person keeps the mind apart from the body and stays with the complaining body only as much as is necessary.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: the untrained cannot stand bodily pain because they live too close to the body. The “complaining and fragile one” is the body.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: If you had offered him marble, if you had offered him a still cheaper material, he would have made the best that could be made out of it. In the same way the wise man will display virtue in riches if he is allowed, and if not, in poverty
piece.follows: As a sculptor makes the best that his material allows, the wise man displays virtue in riches or in poverty.
piece.context: Letter 85 defends the view that poverty and pain do not harm the wise man: he uses bad things. “Him” is the sculptor Phidias, who worked in ivory and in bronze.
gives: What comes to hand is material
for virtue

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: pain is light if opinion has added nothing to it
piece.follows: Pain is light when opinion has added nothing to it.
piece.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: do not make your ills heavier by complaining. “Opinion” is what a person adds to the pain by what he says of it to himself.
gives: I take a hardship bare, by itself, and add nothing to it
not my opinion

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: So two things must be cut away, both the fear of what is to come and the memory of old trouble: the old trouble no longer concerns me, what is to come does not yet.
piece.follows: Fear of what is to come and memory of old trouble must both go: the old trouble no longer concerns me and what is to come does not yet.
piece.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca wants an end to complaints about past pains. Here “old trouble” is pain already gone through; “what is to come” is pain not yet here.
gives: not the rest of my life

items.label: practice
items.t: When I am in pain I turn my mind away to other thoughts: to the honourable and brave things I have done, and to the bravest men, the conquerors of pain. If pain has been conquered by laughter, it can be conquered by reason.
items.why: Marcus gives rules to recall and one example, Epicurus, who went on with philosophy in illness. Seneca makes a method of it: turn the mind away from the pain, towards my own good deeds and towards those who have beaten it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This too will help: to turn the mind aside to other thoughts and to step away from the pain.
support.follows: It helps to turn the mind away to other thoughts and to step away from the pain.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: having argued that pain is bearable or short, Seneca lists further helps. “This” is turning the mind to other thoughts.
gives: I turn my mind away to other thoughts

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Think of what you have done honourably, what you have done bravely; go over the good parts of your life in your own mind
support.follows: In pain I should think of what I have done honourably and bravely and go over the good parts of my life.
support.context: Letter 78, Seneca’s advice to the sick Lucilius on where to turn the mind when in pain: first to what he himself has done well.
gives: the honourable and brave things I have done

support.author: seneca
support.quote: then let all the bravest men, the conquerors of pain, come before you
support.follows: I should let all the bravest men, the conquerors of pain, come before me.
support.context: Letter 78, to the sick Lucilius: Seneca goes on to name such men, one who read a book during surgery and one who did not stop laughing at his torturers.
gives: the bravest men, the conquerors of pain

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Will pain not be conquered by reason, when it has been conquered by laughter?
support.follows: If laughter has conquered pain, reason can.
support.context: Letter 78, on bearing illness: Seneca has just told of a man who kept laughing under torture, and argues from him to what reason can do against pain.
gives: If pain has been conquered by laughter, it can be conquered by reason

items.label: breaks
items.role: Three ways I add to pain
items.t: When something torments me more than it should, before it should, or when it should not at all, I am increasing my pain, anticipating it or inventing it. I ask myself: am I in torment without cause, and am I making an evil of what is not one?
items.why: Marcus names one way I add to a hardship, by taking in the past and the future along with it (8.34), and says not to add to it by opinion (7.35). Seneca names three ways, and gives a question that catches them.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So some things torment us more than they ought, some torment us before they ought, some torment us when they ought not to torment us at all; we either increase our pain, or anticipate it, or invent it.
support.follows: Some things torment us too much, some too early, some with no cause: we increase our pain, anticipate it or invent it.
support.context: Letter 13 is on groundless fears; Seneca has just said that more things frighten us than crush us, and opinion troubles us more often than fact. “We” is people in general.
gives: When something torments me more than it should, before it should, or when it should not at all
I am increasing my pain, anticipating it or inventing it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Am I perhaps in torment and grieving without cause, and making an evil of what is not one?
support.follows: I should ask whether I am in torment without cause and whether I am making an evil of what is not one.
support.context: Letter 13, on groundless fears: when others try to persuade Lucilius that he is wretched, he is to consult his own feeling and put this question to himself.
gives: am I in torment without cause
am I making an evil of what is not one

items.label: doubt
items.t: When I am drawn to leave life, I do not ask how bravely I could die; I ask who would not be able to miss me bravely. Sometimes even to live is to act bravely.
items.why: 8.45 lets me leave life in a kindly spirit when it is not worth living. Seneca, who had the same impulse in a long illness, adds what held him back: his father, who could not have missed him bravely.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: For I thought not of how bravely I could die, but of how far he was from being able to miss me bravely.
support.follows: Seneca weighed not how bravely he could die but how far his father was from being able to miss him bravely.
support.context: Letter 78: Seneca recalls a long illness of his youth in which he often wanted to end his life. “He” is his old father, the thought of whom held him back.
gives: I ask who would not be able to miss me bravely

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So I ordered myself to live; for sometimes even to live is to act bravely.
support.follows: Seneca ordered himself to live; sometimes living is itself the brave act.
support.context: Letter 78: Seneca on the illness of his youth. He wanted to end his life and did not, for his father’s sake; his studies and his friends then consoled him.
gives: Sometimes even to live is to act bravely

items.t: Seneca gives the steady mind to the person whose virtue is complete. He agrees that pain belongs to the body and that the rational part cannot be conquered (Ep. 71.27, 71.29), but he says that until the good is made complete the mind wavers, and that someone still on the way will slip back at times. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus says that the mind can keep its calm; Seneca says who can count on it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Before that good is brought to fullness, there is an unsure wavering of the mind; but when it has been made complete, the mind has a stability that does not move.
support.follows: Until the highest good is brought to fullness the mind wavers; once it is complete the mind has a stability that does not move.
support.context: Letter 71: the wise man feels pain, with an irrational part that can be hurt and a rational part that cannot be conquered. By “that good” Seneca means the highest good, placed in the rational part.

support.author: seneca

items.t: Seneca disagrees with “Nothing happens to me that I cannot bear”, which is also the statement’s first part. He says that nature has made pain either bearable or short, and he tells Pain to its face that it is light if he can bear it and short if he cannot: so a pain I cannot bear may come, and what he promises is only that it will not last. Marcus’s own 10.3 allows the same case (“it will perish once it has used you up”). Seneca is inconsistent with himself here: in Letter 91 he says that none of these things, pain among them, is unbearable (Ep. 91.19), and in Letter 96 that he will not put up with himself on the day he is not able to put up with something (Ep. 96.1).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No one can be in pain both severely and for long; nature, who loves us most dearly, has so arranged us as to make pain either bearable or short
support.follows: No one is in pain both severely and for long: nature has made pain either bearable or short.
support.context: Letter 78, to Lucilius, who is ill: of the three hard things in disease Seneca takes up bodily pain, and says that extreme pain must come to an end.
