outside.section: Living now as one about to die
Living now as one about to die
Living now as one about to die

claims.t: What happens to me is a human occurrence, both usual and natural. I am fitted by nature to bear it, and I do not resent it. I am fitted to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable.
claims.shared: Wording unchanged. The fitness to bear rests on 5.16 and 8.45 together, and 10.3a now supports only the refusal of resentment because it is conditional. The human occurrence is from 8.45 alone and the role of judgment from 10.3 alone.

support.quote: Nothing happens to anyone that they are not fitted by nature to bear.
support.follows: Whatever happens to a person, that person is fitted by nature to bear it.
gives: I am fitted by nature to bear it

support.quote: For the common nature was bringing you nothing that could not be borne.
support.follows: Whatever the common nature brought me, it was something that could be borne.
gives: I am fitted by nature to bear it

support.quote: Remember, though, that you are fitted by nature to bear everything that it rests with your own judgment to make bearable and endurable
support.follows: I am fitted by nature to bear everything that my own judgment can make bearable.
gives: I am fitted to bear whatever my own judgment can make bearable

support.quote: Nothing can happen to any human being that is not a human occurrence
support.follows: Only things of the human kind can happen to a human being.
gives: a human occurrence

support.quote: So if what happens to each is what is both usual and natural, why would you resent it?
support.follows: If what happens to each thing is usual and natural for it, there is no reason to resent it.
gives: both usual and natural
I do not resent it

support.quote: So if it happens to you in a way you are fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it, but bear it as you are fitted by nature to do.
support.follows: If what happens is something I am fitted by nature to bear, I should bear it and not resent it.
gives: I do not resent it

claims.t: What troubles me is not the thing outside me but my own judgment that it is bad. Unless I make that judgment I have not yet been harmed. It is in my power not to make it, or to wipe it out at once.
claims.shared: Restores “not yet” from 7.11 and “at once” from 8.45. The claim judges the event and does not deny that it happened. Wiping out the verdict is from 8.45 alone.

support.quote: If you are distressed because of something outside you, it is not that thing that troubles you but your own verdict about it, and it is in your power to wipe that out at once.
support.follows: When something outside distresses me, what troubles me is my verdict about it, and I can wipe that verdict out at once.
gives: What troubles me is not the thing outside me
but my own judgment that it is bad
to wipe it out at once

support.quote: What is bad for you does not have its existence in another’s ruling part, nor yet in any turn and alteration of what surrounds you.
support.follows: What is bad for me is not in another person’s mind and not in any change in my surroundings.
gives: What troubles me is not the thing outside me

support.quote: Things themselves do not touch the soul in any way at all
support.follows: Things themselves do not touch the soul at all.
gives: What troubles me is not the thing outside me

support.quote: In the place where you have what judges about bad things. So let that not judge, and all is well.
support.follows: What is bad for me lies in the part of me that judges things bad; if that part does not judge, all is well.
gives: but my own judgment that it is bad
It is in my power not to make it

support.quote: But I, unless I judge that what has happened is bad, have not yet been harmed.
support.follows: Unless I judge that what has happened is bad, I have not yet been harmed.
gives: Unless I make that judgment I have not yet been harmed

support.quote: Take away the judgment, and “I have been harmed” is taken away. Take away “I have been harmed”, and the harm is taken away.
support.follows: Without the judgment there is no thought “I have been harmed”, and without that thought there is no harm.
gives: Unless I make that judgment I have not yet been harmed

support.quote: And it is possible for me not to judge so.
support.follows: It is possible for me not to make that judgment.
gives: It is in my power not to make it

claims.role: The body’s pain, the mind’s calm
claims.t: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart, the pain is for the body and its senses to see to. Neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant touches what is my mind’s own. My mind can draw a line around itself and keep its own clear sky and calm. It does not add the judgment that this is bad.
claims.shared: Replaces the blanket “nothing from outside touches my mind” with 8.39’s narrower “what is the mind’s own”. Keeps “can”, because the sources assert a possibility. The fire and iron image is from 8.39 alone, the drawn line from 5.20 alone and the clear sky from 8.26.

support.quote: Even if what is nearest to it, the little body, is cut, is burned, festers, rots, still let the part that judges about these things keep quiet.
support.follows: Even if the body is cut, burned or rotting, the part that judges about these things should keep quiet.
gives: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart

support.quote: even if the wild beasts are tearing apart the little limbs of this lump of dough that has thickened around you
support.follows: I can live unforced and glad even while wild beasts tear apart the limbs of my body.
gives: Even if my body is cut, burned or torn apart

support.quote: Pain is either a bad thing for the body, and then let the body declare it so, or for the soul.
support.follows: If pain is a bad thing for the body, it is for the body to say so.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

support.quote: Does pain, does pleasure touch you? That is for sensation to see to.
support.follows: Whether pain or pleasure touches me is a matter for sensation.
gives: the pain is for the body and its senses to see to

support.quote: let it draw a line around itself and confine those feelings within the parts of the body
support.follows: The ruling part should draw a line around itself and keep the body’s feelings within the parts of the body.
gives: draw a line around itself

support.quote: What is the mind’s own, however, no one else is in the habit of hindering: for neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant, nor slander, nor anything whatever touches it
support.follows: Nothing whatever, not fire, iron, a tyrant or slander, touches what is the mind’s own.
gives: Neither fire, nor iron, nor a tyrant touches what is my mind’s own

support.quote: For every verdict and impulse and desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to here.
support.follows: Every verdict, impulse, desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to that place.
support.note: Every verdict, impulse, desire and aversion is inside, and nothing climbs up to that place.

support.quote: For what, in all of this, prevents the mind from keeping itself in calm
support.follows: Nothing in all of this prevents the mind from keeping itself calm.
gives: keep its own clear sky and calm

support.quote: But it is possible for the soul to keep its own clear sky and calm, and not to judge that it is a bad thing.
support.follows: The soul can keep its own calm and can decline to judge that the thing is bad.
gives: keep its own clear sky and calm
does not add the judgment that this is bad

support.quote: but let the ruling part not add, from itself, the judgment that it is something good or bad
support.follows: The ruling part should not add, from itself, the judgment that the feeling is something good or bad.
gives: does not add the judgment that this is bad

claims.t: To be good and just is in my power everywhere. What is present and comes to hand is my material for virtue. Using it rightly makes me better, and to bear it nobly is good fortune.
claims.shared: Adds “everywhere”, material and right use to the opening. “Makes me better” is from 10.33 alone, where it is hedged with “if it must be said”. The good fortune is from 4.41 alone and lies in the bearing, not in the event.

support.quote: All of this is in your power: for who prevents you from being good and straightforward?
support.follows: Being good and straightforward is in my power, and no one prevents me from it.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: Surely this that has happened does not prevent you from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible, not rash, not deceived, modest, free
support.follows: What has happened does not prevent me from being just, great-hearted, self-controlled, sensible and free.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: Everywhere and without a break it is in your power to be well content, in reverence for the gods, with the present turn of events, to behave justly towards the people present
support.follows: Everywhere and at every moment I can be content with what is happening and behave justly towards the people present.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: For one must judge to be an enjoyment everything that it is possible to do in accordance with one’s own nature. And it is possible everywhere.
support.follows: Acting in accordance with my own nature is possible everywhere, and I should count it an enjoyment.
gives: To be good and just is in my power everywhere

support.quote: For to me what is present is always material for rational and civic virtue
support.follows: Whatever is present is material for rational and civic virtue.
gives: What is present and comes to hand is my material for virtue

support.quote: that, for you, is doing the things that belong to the way a human being is made, with the material that is supplied and comes to hand
support.follows: My part is to do what belongs to a human being with the material that is supplied and comes to hand.
gives: What is present and comes to hand is my material for virtue

support.quote: the human being becomes both better and more praiseworthy by using rightly the things that befall them
support.follows: A human being becomes better and more praiseworthy by using rightly what befalls them.
gives: Using it rightly makes me better

support.quote: not “this is a misfortune”, but “to bear it nobly is good fortune.”
support.follows: The thing to say is not that this is a misfortune but that bearing it nobly is good fortune.
gives: to bear it nobly is good fortune

claims.t: At every impression of harm, and at every pain, I keep a rule ready. If the city I belong to by nature is not harmed, I have not been harmed. Pain is not shameful, and what does not make me worse does not harm me.
claims.shared: The practice of keeping rules ready is shared by three passages, and the city rule by two. The line on shame is from 7.35 alone and the “worse” test from 4.7 alone. 5.19 allows that the city can be harmed, so the rule is a test, not a guarantee.

support.quote: At every impression of having been harmed, apply this rule: if the city is not harmed by this, I have not been harmed either.
support.follows: Whenever I have the impression of being harmed, I should apply the rule that if the city is not harmed, I am not harmed.
gives: At every impression of harm
I keep a rule ready
If the city I belong to by nature is not harmed, I have not been harmed

support.quote: At every pain, have this ready to hand: that it is not shameful and does not make the mind at the helm any worse
support.follows: At every pain I should have ready the thought that pain is not shameful and does not make the governing mind worse.
gives: at every pain
I keep a rule ready
Pain is not shameful

support.quote: From now on, remember, at everything that leads you towards distress, to use this principle
support.follows: At everything that leads me towards distress, I should remember to use this principle: it is not a misfortune, but bearing it nobly is good fortune.
gives: I keep a rule ready

support.quote: nothing harms one who is by nature a citizen that does not harm the city
support.follows: Nothing harms a citizen that does not harm the city.
gives: If the city I belong to by nature is not harmed, I have not been harmed

support.quote: What does not make a human being worse than they were does not make their life worse either, and does not harm them from outside or from within.
support.follows: What does not make a person worse does not make their life worse and does not harm them.
gives: what does not make me worse does not harm me

claims.t: I do not take in all my hardships at one sweep of thought. Only the present weighs on me, and it shrinks when I mark it off by itself. I add no opinion to a pain and I remember its limits. Taken this way, neither the present task nor most pain is unbearable, and most pain is not everlasting.
claims.shared: Removes “whole life”, which 8.34a does not say and which now sits in the margin. The joint phrase gives the present task to 8.34 and pain to 7.35. Both halves of the Epicurean saying are narrowed to most pain, as Marcus frames it. The shrinking present is from 8.34 alone.

support.quote: it is neither the future nor the past that weighs on you, but always the present; and this shrinks if you mark it off by itself alone and show your mind up if it cannot hold out against the present stripped bare
support.follows: Only the present weighs on me, and it shrinks when I mark it off by itself, stripped bare.
gives: Only the present weighs on me
it shrinks when I mark it off by itself

support.quote: that it is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if you remember the limits and do not add to it by opinion
support.follows: Most pain is neither unbearable nor everlasting, if I remember its limits and do not add to it by opinion.
gives: I add no opinion to a pain and I remember its limits
neither the present task nor most pain is unbearable
most pain is not everlasting

support.quote: Do not take in at one sweep of thought what hardships and how many are likely to have come on you.
support.follows: I should not take in at one sweep all the hardships that are likely to have come on me.
gives: I do not take in all my hardships at one sweep of thought

support.quote: “What is there in this task that is unbearable and not to be endured?” For you will be ashamed to admit it.
support.follows: Asked what is unbearable in the task in front of me, I would be ashamed to name anything.
gives: neither the present task nor most pain is unbearable

single.quote: That is, let it decide that what can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good.
single.label: Good and bad alike
single.t: What can happen equally to a bad man and a good one I judge neither bad nor good.
single.why: Single source, 4.32. Recast as what I judge and kept as the specific argument it is.
single.follows: What can happen equally to a bad man and a good one is neither bad nor good.

single.quote: Do not be swept off wholesale by the impression, but help as far as you are able and as far as is deserved, even if they are coming off worse in the middle things; do not, however, form the impression that it is a harm, for that is a bad habit.
single.label: Help without alarm
single.t: When people come off worse in things that are neither good nor bad, I am not swept off wholesale by the impression. Even then I help as far as I am able and as far as is deserved. I do not form the impression that their loss is a harm, for that is a bad habit.
single.why: Single source, 5.29, which breaks off incomplete. The occasion comes first so that “the impression” has a referent, and “Even then” keeps the source’s “even if”. “Things that are neither good nor bad” is our gloss on “the middle things”. Helping survives the denial of harm.
single.follows: I should help as far as I can, even when what others lose is neither good nor bad, but I should not form the impression that their loss is a harm.

single.quote: So do the same as he did, in illness, if you are ill, and in any other circumstance. For not to stand away from philosophy in anything whatever that befalls
single.label: In illness
single.t: In illness, if I am ill, and in any other circumstance, I do as Epicurus did in his illness. I do not stand away from philosophy, whatever befalls.
single.why: Single source, 9.41, truncated. Epicurus is a model for this conduct only, not an endorsement of his school.
single.follows: In illness, and in any other circumstance, I should do as Epicurus did and not stand away from philosophy, whatever befalls.

single.quote: many things that are the same as pain go unnoticed as such, though we resent them, such as being drowsy, being overheated and having no appetite. So when you are displeased at any of these, say to yourself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.label: Pain unnoticed
single.t: Many things are the same as pain and go unnoticed as such, though I resent them: being drowsy, being overheated, having no appetite. When one of these displeases me, I say to myself: “You are giving in to pain.”
single.why: Single source, 7.35. Keeps the source’s three examples and its self-address.
single.follows: Drowsiness, heat and loss of appetite are forms of pain; being displeased at them is giving in to pain.

single.quote: Did something come to stand in the way of your impulse? If your impulse was without reservation, then it is already a bad thing for you as a rational being. But if you accept the common lot, you have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.label: An unconditional impulse
single.t: If my impulse was without reservation and something came to stand in its way, that is already a bad thing for me as a rational being. If I accept the common lot, I have not yet been harmed or hindered.
single.why: Single source, 8.39, truncated. Removes the earlier explanatory gloss on “without reservation” and keeps the concession that an unreserved impulse really is thwarted.
single.follows: A blocked impulse is already bad for me if it was without reservation; if I accept the common lot I have not yet been harmed or hindered.

single.quote: But when they pass up into the mind by the other shared feeling, as in a unified body, then one should not try to go against the sensation, which is natural
single.label: The feeling is natural
single.t: When the body’s feelings pass up into my mind, as in a unified body, I do not try to go against the sensation, which is natural.
single.why: Single source, 5.20. It limits claim 3: the sensation is felt and not resisted, and only the added judgment is withheld.
single.follows: When bodily feelings reach the mind, one should not fight the sensation, which is natural.

single.quote: The same things happen to someone else, and either because they do not know that it has happened, or because they are showing off greatness of mind, they stand firm and remain unhurt. It is a terrible thing, then, that ignorance and the wish to please should be stronger than wisdom.
single.label: Outdone by ignorance
single.t: The same things that happen to me happen to someone else, who stands firm and unhurt through not knowing what has happened or through showing off greatness of mind. It is a terrible thing if ignorance and the wish to please are stronger than wisdom.
single.why: Single source, 5.16. “That happen to me” supplies the comparison the source takes from its preceding sentence. Kept in the third person as a warning, not turned into a vow.
single.follows: Others bear the same things out of ignorance or to show off; it is terrible if those are stronger than wisdom.

single.quote: And if in a way you are not fitted by nature to bear, do not resent it: for it will perish once it has used you up.
single.label: If I cannot bear it
single.t: If something happens that I am not fitted by nature to bear, I do not resent it. It will perish once it has used me up.
single.why: Single source, 10.3. It openly allows the unbearable case, which limits the opening.
single.follows: What I am not fitted to bear ends once it has used me up, so it too is not to be resented.

single.quote: “But something stronger stands in the way.” Then do not be distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with you. “But life is not worth living if this is not done.” Then leave life kindly disposed, just as the one who is doing it dies too, and at the same time gracious towards the things that stand in the way.
single.label: If I am blocked
single.t: If something stronger stands in the way of what seems sound to me, I am not distressed, for the cause of its not being done does not lie with me. If life is not worth living with this undone, I leave life kindly disposed, as the one who does it dies too, and gracious towards what stands in the way.
single.why: Single source, 8.45. The condition is the objector’s own. The line governs the manner of leaving and sets no duty to leave.
single.follows: If something stronger blocks the act, the cause is not mine and I need not be distressed; if life is not worth living without it, I may leave life kindly.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. 8.45 is 8.46–47, 10.33 is 10.32–33, 7.39 is 7.68, 7.29 is 7.53–54, 4.32 is 4.39, 4.41 is 4.49b, 5.19 is 5.22–25, 7.35 is 7.64, 8.34 is 8.36, 5.16 is 5.17–19, 5.20 is 5.26, 7.11 is 7.14, 8.39 is 8.41a, 9.41 is 9.41a, 5.29 is 5.35–36a, 8.41 is 8.42–43, 8.26 is 8.28 and 4.7 is 4.7–9; 10.3 is 10.3 in both.

137 characters, three short sentences, no semicolon. The first sentence grants that the body can be hurt, so the second is heard as a judgement about the event and not a denial of it. Bearing is narrowed to the condition in 10.3, with 7.35 as second witness that opinion decides whether pain is unbearable. 7.35 speaks of most pains only. The broader wording of 5.16 and 8.45 stays in claim 1. No promise of indefinite endurance is made.
marcus_revision.limit: These lines judge what happens. They do not deny that it happens or that it is felt. Sensation is natural and reaches the mind, pain may be bad for the body, and a hindrance is bad for an animal nature. An impulse held without reservation really is thwarted. The opening claims only that I can bear what my judgment makes bearable. 5.16 and 8.45 say more broadly that nothing comes that cannot be borne, but 10.3 allows a case that uses a person up, and 8.45 and 10.33 contemplate leaving life. The Epicurean comfort covers most pains, not all. The city rule is a test and not a promise that the city cannot be harmed. Helping others remains. The passages argue in different ways and are not one system. 8.39, 9.41 and 5.29 are truncated, and the last line of 4.7 is too obscure to build on.

articles.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself

statement.t: I keep to the few names I have given myself, do each thing as someone about to leave life, and need no one as witness.

parts.words: I keep to the few names I have given myself
do each thing as someone about to leave life
need no one as witness

statement.kind: A rule, the way it is carried out, and what it does not need
statement.form: Claim 1 is the rule: a few names, kept. Claim 4 says how each act is done under it and claim 3 what it does not need; they give the statement its second and third parts. Claim 2 is the ground, claim 5 a check on the past, and claim 6 what happens when the rule is lost. The statement joins its parts with “and” only, so it holds no inference of the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, five of the six claims gain a second author; only the review of my conduct does not. Practice gains a daily review with a test of steadiness, the side In action gains a warning against making a show of plainness, and the side When it breaks gains what Seneca says of those who are not yet consistent with themselves. He limits two claims: until I respect myself I keep a witness in mind, and a day is lived as one that could be my last, not snatched at as the last. The side If I doubt it stays empty.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a clause for the one who has not yet arrived: though more of the way to wisdom remains than I have got through, a great part of progress is wanting to make progress.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: there is more work in keeping to what you have resolved than in resolving on what is honourable
piece.follows: Keeping to what has already been resolved takes more work than resolving on what is honourable.
piece.context: Letter 16: no one lives happily without wisdom, and this must be fixed deeper by daily practice. “What you have resolved” is Lucilius’s resolve, kept until a good intention becomes a good mind.
gives: I keep myself in them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: So demand this of yourself: keep yourself, right to the end, such as you set out to show yourself.
piece.follows: I should demand of myself that I keep myself, right to the end, such as I set out to show myself.
piece.context: The close of Letter 120, on how we learn what virtue is: its mark is being always the same. To keep yourself “such as you set out to show yourself” is to play one part, not to change masks.
gives: I struggle to remain this kind of person

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.
piece.follows: The way to win the favour of the gods is to be good; whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.
piece.context: Letter 95 turns from rules of ritual to the right idea of the gods, who need no servants and do good by nature. Here “them” means the gods; to imitate them is to be good.
gives: for rational beings to become like them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory.
piece.follows: Whoever wants his virtue made public is after glory, not virtue.
piece.context: The end of Letter 113, where Seneca says justice should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation. Here “made public” means made known to other people.
gives: without craving that others call me by them

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness
piece.follows: How many people know of my fairness is nothing to the point.
piece.context: Seneca’s closing charge to Lucilius in Letter 113, after saying one must be just without reward. By “your fairness” he means your being just, whether or not anyone knows of it.
gives: any human being as witness

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: let us shape our mind as though the end had been reached
piece.follows: I should shape my mind as though the end of my life had been reached.
piece.context: Letter 101, on the futility of planning far ahead: death stands at our side and no one knows how near he is to the boundary fixed for him. Here “the end” is the end of life.
gives: as someone about to leave life
set myself in order

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: there is no day I have not looked on as if it were my last
piece.follows: Seneca has treated every day as if it were his last.
piece.context: Letter 93, on a man whose life was short but complete: a life is measured by what is done in it. Seneca speaks of himself; he never counted on the days he hoped for.
gives: as someone about to leave life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Things that are incomplete are bound to totter, and now go forward, now slip down or collapse. And they will slip down, unless they keep on going and striving
piece.follows: Whatever is incomplete totters and slips down unless it keeps on going and striving.
piece.context: Letter 71, on those who follow wisdom but have not reached it. “Things that are incomplete” means their progress, which goes backward as soon as effort slackens.
gives: I fall short

items.label: breaks
items.t: No one but the wise man plays one man; the rest of us are many-shaped. The wise man will not always go at one pace, but he will go by one road. More remains than I have got through, and a great part of progress is wanting to make progress.
items.why: Marcus says what to do when the names are lost: go back to them quickly, or go to a corner where I will prevail (10.8). Seneca adds what Marcus does not say here: that not playing one man is the common case, his own included; that one road can be kept at an uneven pace; and that wanting to make progress is a great part of progress. The three sentences come from three letters, and setting them side by side is the editor’s.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But no one except the wise man plays one; the rest of us are many-shaped.
support.follows: Only the wise man plays one man; everyone else, Seneca included, is many-shaped.
support.context: The close of Letter 120: the unwise mind does not match itself. Here “plays one” means plays one man, keeping to one mask; “the rest of us” counts Seneca among those who change.
gives: No one but the wise man plays one man; the rest of us are many-shaped

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am not saying that the wise man will always go at one pace, but that he will go by one road.
support.follows: Even the wise man’s pace may vary, but his road does not.
support.context: Letter 20 asks that deed and word agree and that a man be always the same. Asked who will achieve this, Seneca answers that few will, and then says this of the wise man.
gives: The wise man will not always go at one pace, but he will go by one road

support.author: seneca
support.quote: More remains than we have got through, but a great part of progress is wanting to make progress.
support.follows: More remains than has been got through, but wanting to make progress is a great part of progress.
support.context: Letter 71, just after Seneca says that incomplete things slip down unless they keep on going and striving. What “remains” is the rest of the way to wisdom, which he says he wants with his whole mind.
gives: More remains than I have got through
a great part of progress is wanting to make progress

items.label: practice
items.role: A daily review, and a test
items.t: I watch myself and review my day. To test whether anything has been achieved, I watch whether I want the same things today as yesterday.
items.why: Marcus looks back once over his whole conduct up to now (5.25). Seneca makes it a review of each day, and adds a test of whether I am holding steady, which Marcus does not give here.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I will watch myself at once and, what is most useful, I will review my day.
support.follows: Seneca will watch himself at once and review his day, which he calls most useful.
support.context: In Letter 83 Lucilius has asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees, and says that what makes us very bad is that no one looks back at his own life.
gives: I watch myself and review my day

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whenever you want to test whether anything has been achieved, watch whether you want the same things today as yesterday
support.follows: To test whether anything has been achieved, I should watch whether I want the same things today as yesterday.
support.context: In Letter 35 Seneca urges Lucilius to make progress and above all to be consistent with himself. This is the test he gives: a change in what one wants shows a mind adrift.
gives: To test whether anything has been achieved
I watch whether I want the same things today as yesterday

items.label: action
items.t: I make no show of plainness either: rough dress, a neglected beard, hatred declared on silver and a bed laid on the ground are another way of seeking attention. Inside, everything is different, and my outward face fits in with the people around me.
items.why: Marcus drops the show of a court and draws himself in towards a private person’s life (1.14). Seneca warns of the opposite show, which Marcus does not mention here: plainness worn in order to be noticed.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Rough dress, an uncut head of hair, a rather neglected beard, hatred declared on silver, a bed laid on the ground, and whatever else seeks attention by a perverse route: avoid them.
support.follows: Rough dress, uncut hair, a neglected beard, hatred declared on silver and a bed laid on the ground seek attention by a perverse route and should be avoided.
support.context: Letter 5 warns Lucilius, who studies philosophy, against those who want to be conspicuous rather than to improve. The list is of ways of flaunting an austere life.
gives: I make no show of plainness either
rough dress, a neglected beard, hatred declared on silver and a bed laid on the ground are another way of seeking attention

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Inside, let everything be different; let our outward face fit in with the people.
support.follows: Inside, everything should be different, while our outward face fits in with the people.
support.context: From Letter 5, on not parading philosophy in dress or habits. Here “our” means those who pursue philosophy, and “the people” are those among whom they live.
gives: Inside, everything is different, and my outward face fits in with the people around me

items.t: Seneca does not dismiss the witness so soon. Until I have come to respect myself, he has me guard myself by the authority of certain men; only after that may I dismiss my minder. This limits the claim and does not contradict it: Marcus’s man who needs no human witness has already set himself in order (3.5), and Marcus keeps a model of his own, Antoninus (6.28). Seneca’s witness is a person I picture for my own correction, not an audience whose praise I want.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men
support.follows: Until I have come to respect even myself I should guard myself by the authority of certain men; after that I may dismiss the minder.
support.context: Letter 25 passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if a great man were watching. The “minder” is that imagined guardian, a Cato, a Scipio or a Laelius, kept in mind.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a great part of wrongdoing is removed if a witness stands beside those who are about to do wrong
support.follows: A great part of wrongdoing is removed if a witness stands beside those who are about to do wrong.
support.context: Letter 11 ends with Epicurus’s advice to keep a man of high character before one’s eyes. The “witness” is that man, pictured as present; he is not an actual onlooker.

items.t: Seneca draws a line that Marcus does not draw. He works to make a day the equal of a whole life and looks at it as one that could even be his last, but he says he does not snatch at it as though it were his last. The difference is small, and he does not always keep to it himself: in Letter 93 he says there is no day he has not looked on as if it were his last (Ep. 93.6).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I do not snatch at it as though it were my last, but I look at it as though it could even be my last.
support.follows: Seneca does not snatch at a day as though it were his last; he looks at it as one that could be.
support.context: In Letter 61 Seneca, now old, writes that his one work is to put an end to old ills. Here “it” is a day, which he is working to make the equal of a whole life.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am working at this, that a day should be to me the equal of a whole life
support.follows: Seneca works at making a day the equal of a whole life.
support.context: The opening of Letter 61, on meeting death gladly. Seneca describes his own practice in old age; the letter itself, he says next, is written as if death might call him away.

passages.title: On philosophy as the guide of life
passages.text: I know that this is clear to you, Lucilius: that no one can live happily, or even tolerably, without the study of wisdom, and that the happy life is brought about by wisdom made complete, but a tolerable life even by wisdom begun. But this, which is clear, must be made firm and fixed deeper by daily practice: there is more work in keeping to what you have resolved than in resolving on what is honourable. One must persevere and add strength by constant study, until what is a good intention becomes a good mind.

passages.title: On how we come to know the good
passages.text: This above all is how an unwise mind is shown up: it comes forward now as one, now as another, and it does not match itself, and I judge nothing more shameful than that. Count it a great thing to play one man. But no one except the wise man plays one; the rest of us are many-shaped. At one moment we will seem to you thrifty and serious, at another spendthrift and frivolous; we change our mask again and again and put on the opposite of the one we have taken off. So demand this of yourself: keep yourself, right to the end, such as you set out to show yourself. Bring it about that you can be praised, or, failing that, that you can be recognised. Of someone you saw yesterday it can rightly be said, “Who is this?”: the change is so great. Farewell.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; next, to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty; to know that it is they who preside over the world, who govern all things by their power, who watch over the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals. They neither give evil nor have it; yet they chastise some people and restrain them and impose punishments, and sometimes they punish by what looks like a good. Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Fix in yourself as well what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

passages.title: On sudden death and living each day
passages.text: But what is more foolish than to be surprised that something has happened on any one day which can happen on every day? A boundary does stand for us, where the necessity of the fates, which no plea can move, has fixed it; but none of us knows how near he is to the boundary. So let us shape our mind as though the end had been reached. Let us put nothing off. Let us balance our account with life every day.

passages.title: On the quality, not the length, of life
passages.text: I would not on that account refuse to have more years added to me; yet I will say that I lacked nothing for the happy life if its span is cut short; for I have not made myself ready for the day that greedy hope had promised me as my last, but there is no day I have not looked on as if it were my last. Why do you ask me when I was born, or whether I am still registered among the younger men? I have what is mine.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: Things that are incomplete are bound to totter, and now go forward, now slip down or collapse. And they will slip down, unless they keep on going and striving; if they slacken any of their zeal and faithful exertion, they have to go backward. No one finds his progress where he had left it.

passages.title: On matching deeds to words
passages.text: Those who declaim and angle for the approval of a ring of listeners have one purpose, those who hold the ears of young men and men of leisure with varied or rapid discussion have another: philosophy teaches doing, not saying, and it demands this, that each person live by his own law, that his life not be at odds with his speech, nor his life itself at odds with itself; let all actions be of one colour. This is both the greatest duty of wisdom and its greatest sign: that deeds agree with words, that the man himself be everywhere consistent with himself and one and the same. “Who will achieve this?” Few, but some all the same. For it is difficult; and I am not saying that the wise man will always go at one pace, but that he will go by one road.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: So let us press on and persevere. More remains than we have got through, but a great part of progress is wanting to make progress. This I know of myself: I want to, and I want to with my whole mind. I see that you too have been roused and are hurrying with great force towards the finest things. Let us hurry: only so will life be a gift. Otherwise it is a delay, and a shameful one at that, for those who live among foul things. Let us see to it that all time is ours; but it will not be, unless we have first begun to be our own.

passages.title: On a daily routine and drunkenness
passages.text: So I will do what you tell me, and I will gladly write to you what I do and in what order. I will watch myself at once and, what is most useful, I will review my day. What makes us very bad is that no one looks back at his own life. We think about what we are going to do, and that rarely; we do not think about what we have done; and yet a plan for the future comes from the past.

passages.title: On steadiness and becoming a true friend
passages.text: Hurry to me, but to yourself first. Make progress, and before all else take care of this: that you be consistent with yourself. Whenever you want to test whether anything has been achieved, watch whether you want the same things today as yesterday: a change in what one wants shows that the mind is adrift, turning up now in one place and now in another, as the wind has carried it. What is fixed and set on a foundation does not wander: that falls to the perfect wise man, and to some extent also to the one who is making progress and has advanced. What then is the difference? The one who is making progress is indeed shaken, yet he does not shift his ground, but sways in his own place; the wise man is not even shaken. Farewell.

passages.title: On living philosophy without showing off
passages.text: Rough dress, an uncut head of hair, a rather neglected beard, hatred declared on silver, a bed laid on the ground, and whatever else seeks attention by a perverse route: avoid them. The very name of philosophy, even if it is handled with restraint, draws enough ill will: what if we begin to withdraw ourselves from the customs of people? Inside, let everything be different; let our outward face fit in with the people.

passages.title: On reforming friends and imagining a watcher
passages.text: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men: let it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or another at whose coming even depraved men would suppress their vices, while you are making yourself the man in whose company you would not dare to do wrong. When you have made yourself that, and have begun to have some standing in your own eyes, I will begin to allow you what the same Epicurus advises: “Withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

passages.title: On blushing and choosing a role model
passages.text: This, my Lucilius, is Epicurus’s precept. He gave us a guardian and a minder, and not without reason: a great part of wrongdoing is removed if a witness stands beside those who are about to do wrong. Let the mind have someone to revere, by whose authority it may make even its privacy purer. How fortunate is the man who corrects not only when he is present but even when he is thought of! How fortunate is the man who can revere someone in such a way that he composes and orders himself even at the memory of him! One who can revere someone in this way will soon be someone to be revered.

passages.title: On being ready and willing to die
passages.text: Let us stop wanting what we have wanted. I at any rate am working at this: that as an old man I should not want the same things I wanted as a boy. To this one thing my days go, to this my nights; this is my work, this my thought: to put an end to old ills. I am working at this, that a day should be to me the equal of a whole life; and, by Hercules, I do not snatch at it as though it were my last, but I look at it as though it could even be my last.

claims.t: I hold myself to a few things: the names I have given myself, among them good, dignified, just, affectionate and without pretence. I keep myself in them, I take care never to bear other names, and I struggle to remain this kind of person.
claims.shared: All three passages give a short list of qualities and say to keep to it. 2.2 and 6.27 both name dignity, affection and justice, and both rule out pretence (“unfeigned”, “unpretentious”); 6.27 and 10.8 both say “good” and “keep yourself”; 2.2 and 10.8 both say “few” and “take care”.
claims.changed: The claim names only the qualities that two of the lists share, and says “among them” because each list has more. Left out are freedom (2.2); simple, unspoiled, reverent, kindly and strong for fitting work (6.27); modest, truthful and the three names ending in “minded” (10.8), which have an item of their own. 2.2 speaks of “things” and 6.27 of a “kind of person”; the claim calls them names, 10.8’s word. “Unpretentious” in 6.27 stands for a Greek word meaning “without polish”, so its match with 2.2’s “unfeigned” is closer in the English than in the Greek.

claims.t: Keeping to these few things lets me live a different life, one that flows smoothly. The gods ask nothing more of me. What they want is not to be flattered, but for rational beings to become like them and for a human being to do the work of a human being.
claims.shared: Both passages say where keeping to the few things leads: in 2.2 the few things, once mastered, “let a person live a life that flows smoothly”; in 10.8 whoever keeps himself in the names “will enter a different life”. Both then say what the gods ask of a person: 2.2 that they demand nothing more, 10.8 what it is they want.
claims.changed: The claim takes the weaker verb, 2.2’s “let a person live”; 10.8 says outright “you will enter”. 2.2 adds that the life is god-fearing, and 10.8 that the person becomes a different person; the claim leaves both out. 10.8 lists the fig tree, the dog and the bee before the human being; the claim keeps only the human being.

claims.t: I keep these names without craving that others call me by them. I need neither show nor any human being as witness.
claims.shared: 1.14 and 3.5 both say “need neither … nor”: at a court one need have no bodyguards, marked clothes or similar show, and the man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness. 3.5 and 10.8 both do without what other people say of me: no human being to witness for me, no craving that others call me by the names.
