waiting for the signal to withdraw

support.quote: carry out each action as the last of your life
support.follows: Each action is to be carried out as if it were the last of my life.
gives: as someone about to leave life
each action as the last of my life

claims.t: I ask myself how I have behaved up to now towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me, and whether it holds true that I have done nothing wrong to any of them.
claims.shared: Both passages go through the same people (parents, teachers, friends, those close to me) and both speak of wrong done to them: 5.25 asks whether I have “done nothing wrong to anyone”, and 1.14 gives thanks that I was “not carried away into any offence against any of them”.
claims.changed: 5.25 asks the question; 1.14 answers it for the past and thanks the gods. The claim keeps the question. It drops what only one list has: from 5.25 the gods, brothers, wife, children, those who brought me up and household slaves; from 1.14 the grandfathers, sister and relatives.

support.quote: How have you behaved up to now towards the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves?
support.follows: Marcus asks himself how he has behaved up to now towards the gods, his family, teachers, friends, those close to him and his household.
gives: I ask myself how I have behaved up to now
my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me

support.quote: Does this hold of you up to now, towards all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”?
support.follows: Marcus asks whether, towards all the people he has listed, he has done nothing wrong and said nothing wrong.
gives: I have done nothing wrong to any of them

support.quote: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them
support.follows: Marcus thanks the gods that nearly all his family, teachers, friends and those close to him were good.
gives: my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me

support.quote: I was not carried away into any offence against any of them
support.follows: Marcus was not carried away into any offence against his family, teachers, friends or those close to him.
gives: I have done nothing wrong to any of them

claims.t: These names can be lost. It happens that a person is turned into a Caesar, made over by the office he holds. I fall short by my own fault. When I lose the names, I go back to them quickly.
claims.shared: 10.8 and 1.14 both admit failure: 10.8 speaks of “falling away” from the names and “not prevailing”, and 1.14 of Marcus’s “still falling short” of the life according to nature. 6.27 and 10.8 both warn of becoming something other than what was to be kept: being turned into a Caesar “happens”, and the names can be lost.
claims.changed: In 1.14 what Marcus falls short of is living according to nature; in 10.8 it is the names. The claim treats them as one falling short. The word “fall” is shared only in the English: in the Greek, 10.8’s verb (ἐκπίπτεις) means “fall out” and 1.14’s (ἀπολείπεσθαι) means “be left behind”. 6.27 says that being turned into a Caesar happens; it does not say that names are lost. “Made over by the office he holds” is the editor’s gloss: Caesar is Marcus’s own title as emperor.

support.quote: if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly
support.follows: The names can be lost; if they are, I should go back to them quickly.
gives: These names can be lost
When I lose the names, I go back to them quickly

support.quote: Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens.
support.follows: Being turned into a Caesar is something that happens, and care must be taken against it.
gives: It happens that a person is turned into a Caesar

support.quote: if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing
support.follows: A person can sense that he is falling away from the names and not prevailing.
gives: I fall short

support.quote: my still falling short of this is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods
support.follows: That Marcus still falls short of living according to nature is his own fault: he has not kept to the gods’ reminders.
gives: I fall short
by my own fault

single.quote: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.label: The one fruit
single.t: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions, that is, actions done for the community.
single.why: Only this passage says that life has a single fruit. “Actions done for the community” is the translators’ gloss of “social actions”.
single.follows: Life is short, and the one thing to be had from it is a pious disposition and actions done for the community.

single.quote: one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good
single.label: Leading without the show
single.t: I can draw myself in until I am very nearly a private person, and be no lowlier and no slacker for it in what I have to do as a leader for the common good.
single.why: Only this passage says it, as a thought Marcus was brought to by the ruler and father he was placed under. Its words on needing no show go into the claim on show and witness.
single.follows: Marcus’s ruler and father showed him that one can live almost as a private person and be no lowlier or slacker in a leader’s work for the common good.

single.quote: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.label: The trade I learned
single.t: I love the little trade I have learned, and I rest in it. For what is left of my life I entrust everything that is mine to the gods with my whole soul, and I make myself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of a trade to love, and of being neither tyrant nor slave. It does not say what the trade is, so it is kept apart from the names.
single.follows: I should love the trade I learned and rest in it, entrust what is mine to the gods, and be neither tyrant nor slave to anyone.

single.quote: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody.
single.label: How not to act
single.t: I do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. I do not let elegance dress up my thought, and I am not a person of many words or a busybody.
single.why: Only this passage gives this list. 2.2 has its own list of what each action should be rid of, but the two lists share no words.
single.follows: Acting unwillingly, unsocially, unexamined or divided is ruled out, and so are dressed-up thought, many words and meddling.

single.quote: Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.label: Three further names
single.t: Three further names I have given myself are clear-minded, like-minded and high-minded, and I remember what each was to mean. Clear-minded: a discerning attention to each thing, letting nothing go unheeded. Like-minded: willingly accepting what the common nature assigns. High-minded: lifting the part of me that has mind above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh (pleasure and pain), above petty reputation and above death.
single.why: Only this passage has these three names and defines them, so they are not among the names of the first claim; the definitions are kept as something to recall. “Pleasure and pain” is the translators’ gloss of the movement of the flesh.
single.follows: The three names mean attention to each thing, willing acceptance of what nature assigns, and a mind lifted above the flesh, reputation and death.

single.quote: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters
single.label: Antoninus as my model
single.t: I do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, the emperor who adopted me. I recall his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity and his ambition to grasp matters.
single.why: Only this passage sets up a person as the model. Its long list describes Antoninus and is not a list of names to keep, so it stays apart from them. That Antoninus is Antoninus Pius, who adopted Marcus, is the translators’ note.
single.follows: Marcus is to do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, whose traits he lists, beginning with these seven.

single.quote: Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
single.label: What I have come through
single.t: I call to mind what I have passed through and have been strong enough to endure; that the story of my life is now full and my service complete; how many fine things I have seen; how many pleasures and pains I have looked down on, how many honours I have looked past; and to how many inconsiderate people I have been considerate.
single.why: Only this passage looks back on what was endured and calls the life full. The question about wrongdoing in the same passage goes into the review of my conduct.
single.follows: Marcus is to recall what he has endured, seen and looked past, and that his life’s story is full and his service complete.

single.quote: although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up
single.label: Partly the gods’ kindness
single.t: I remember that my clean record towards those close to me is partly the gods’ kindness: I had a disposition from which I might well have offended them, and no circumstances came about that would have shown me up.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It sits under Practice beside the review of my conduct: what I recall when the review comes out clean, that the record is partly good fortune.
single.follows: Marcus had it in him to offend those close to him, and thanks the gods that no circumstances arose to bring it out.

single.quote: It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.
single.label: The soul giving out
single.t: It is shameful if, in a life in which my body does not give out, my soul gives out first.
single.why: Only this passage says it. It names the failure as a giving out of the soul; the other passages speak of losing names or falling short.
single.follows: It is shameful for the soul to give out before the body does.

single.quote: For to go on being what you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.label: Like the beast-fighters
single.t: To go on being as I have been up to now, torn and soiled in a life like this, is senseless clinging to life. It is to be like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown to the same claws and bites.
single.why: Only this passage gives a picture of what not changing is like.
single.follows: Going on unchanged in a life that tears and soils me is senseless clinging to life, like a mauled beast-fighter begging for one more day.

single.quote: go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail
single.label: If I am not prevailing
single.t: If I am not prevailing in keeping these names where I am, I go away with a good heart to some corner where I will prevail.
single.why: Only this passage says where to go when the names cannot be kept. It goes on to a second way out, leaving life altogether, which the article does not turn into a rule (see the editor’s decisions).
single.follows: Someone who is not prevailing should withdraw, in good heart, to a corner where he will prevail.

members.text:
Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to
perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned
gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other
cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them. Which
thou shalt do; if thou shalt go about every action as thy last action,
free from all vanity, all passionate and wilful aberration from reason,
and from all hypocrisy, and self-love, and dislike of those things,
which by the fates or appointment of God have happened unto thee. Thou
seest that those things, which for a man to hold on in a prosperous
course, and to live a divine life, are requisite and necessary, are not
many, for the gods will require no more of any man, that shall but keep
and observe these things.
members.english: At every hour take firm care, as a Roman and a man, to do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice, and to win yourself respite from all other impressions. You will win it if you carry out each action as the last of your life, rid of all aimlessness, of turning away in passion from what reason decides, of pretence, of self-love and of discontent with what has been allotted to you. You see how few the things are which, once mastered, let a person live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing: for the gods will demand nothing more of whoever keeps to these.
members.greek: Πάσης ὥρας φρόντιζε στιβαρῶς ὡς Ῥωμαῖος καὶ ἄρρην τὸ ἐν χερσὶ μετὰ τῆς ἀκριβοῦς καὶ ἀπλάστου σεμνότητος καὶ φιλοστοργίας καὶ ἐλευθερίας καὶ δικαιότητος πράσσειν καὶ σχολὴν σαυτῷ ἀπὸ πασῶν τῶν ἄλλων φαντασιῶν πορίζειν. ποριεῖς δέ, ἂν ὡς ἐσχάτην τοῦ βίου ἑκάστην πρᾶξιν ἐνεργῇς, ἀπηλλαγμένος πάσης εἰκαιότητος καὶ ἐμπαθοῦς ἀποστροφῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἱροῦντος λόγου καὶ ὑποκρίσεως καὶ φιλαυτίας καὶ δυσαρεστήσεως πρὸς τὰ συμμεμοιραμένα. ὁρᾷς πῶς ὀλίγα ἐστίν, ὧν κρατήσας τις δύναται εὔρουν καὶ θεουδῆ βιῶσαι βίον· καὶ γὰρ οἱ θεοὶ πλέον οὐδὲν ἀπαιτήσουσι παρὰ τοῦ ταῦτα φυλάσσοντος.

members.text:
If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a
shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest
of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new
tincture from the court. For it may happen if thou dost not take heed.
Keep thyself therefore, truly simple, good, sincere, grave, free
from all ostentation, a lover of that which is just, religious, kind,
tender-hearted, strong and vigorous to undergo anything that becomes
thee. Endeavour to continue such, as philosophy (hadst thou wholly and
constantly applied thyself unto it) would have made, and secured thee.
Worship the Gods, procure the welfare of men, this life is short.
Charitable actions, and a holy disposition, is the only fruit of this
earthly life.
members.english:
It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.

Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens. So keep yourself simple, good, unspoiled, dignified, unpretentious, a friend of what is just, reverent towards the gods, kindly, warmly affectionate, strong for the work that is fitting. Struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make you. Stand in awe of the gods, keep people safe. Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
members.greek:
Αἰσχρόν ἐστιν, ἐν ᾧ βίῳ τὸ σῶμά σοι μὴ ἀπαυδᾷ, ἐν τούτῳ τὴν ψυχὴν προαπαυδᾶν.

Ὅρα μὴ ἀποκαισαρωθῇς, μὴ βαφῇς· γίνεται γάρ. τήρησον οὖν σεαυτὸν ἁπλοῦν, ἀγαθόν, ἀκέραιον, σεμνόν, ἄκομψον, τοῦ δικαίου φίλον, θεοσεβῆ, εὐμενῆ, φιλόστοργον, ἐρρωμένον πρὸς τὰ πρέποντα ἔργα. ἀγώνισαι, ἵνα τοιοῦτος συμμείνῃς, οἷόν σε ἠθέλησε ποιῆσαι φιλοσοφία. αἰδοῦ θεούς, σῷζε ἀνθρώπους. βραχὺς ὁ βίος· εἶς καρπὸς τῆς ἐπιγείου ζωῆς, διάθεσις ὁσία καὶ πράξεις κοινωνικαί.

members.text:
Now that thou hast taken these names upon thee of good, modest,
true; of ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων; take heed lest at any times by
doing anything that is contrary, thou be but improperly so called, and
lose thy right to these appellations. Or if thou do, return unto them
again with all possible speed. And remember, that the word ἔμφρων notes
unto thee an intent and intelligent consideration of every object that
presents itself unto thee, without distraction. And the word σύμφρων, a
ready and contented acceptation of whatsoever by the appointment of the
common nature, happens unto thee. And the word ὑπέρφρων, a
super-extension, or a transcendent, and outreaching disposition of thy
mind, whereby it passeth by all bodily pains and pleasures, honour and
credit, death and whatsoever is of the same nature, as matters of
absolute indifferency, and in no wise to be stood upon by a wise man.
These then if inviolably thou shalt observe, and shalt not be ambitious
to be so called by others, both thou thyself shalt become a new man,
and thou shalt begin a new life. For to continue such as hitherto thou
hast been, to undergo those distractions and distempers as thou must
needs for such a life as hitherto thou hast lived, is the part of one
that is very foolish, and is overfond of his life. Whom a man might
compare to one of those half-eaten wretches, matched in the
amphitheatre with wild beasts; who as full as they are all the body
over with wounds and blood, desire for a great favour, that they may be
reserved till the next day, then also, and in the same estate to be
exposed to the same nails and teeth as before. Away therefore, ship
thyself; and from the troubles and distractions of thy former life
convey thyself as it were unto these few names; and if thou canst abide
in them, or be constant in the practice and possession of them,
continue there as glad and joyful as one that were translated unto some
such place of bliss and happiness as that which by Hesiod and Plato is
called the Islands of the Blessed, by others called the Elysian Fields.
And whensoever thou findest thyself; that thou art in danger of a
relapse, and that thou art not able to master and overcome those
difficulties and temptations that present themselves in thy present
station: get thee into any private corner, where thou mayst be better
able. Or if that will not serve forsake even thy life rather. But so
that it be not in passion but in a plain voluntary modest way: this
being the only commendable action of thy whole life that thus thou art
departed, or this having been the main work and business of thy whole
life, that thou mightest thus depart. Now for the better remembrance of
those names that we have spoken of, thou shalt find it a very good
help, to remember the Gods as often as may be: and that, the thing
which they require at our hands of as many of us, as are by nature
reasonable creation is not that with fair words, and outward show of
piety and devotion we should flatter them, but that we should become
like unto them: and that as all other natural creatures, the fig tree
for example; the dog the bee: both do, all of them, and apply
themselves unto that which by their natural constitution, is proper
unto them; so man likewise should do that, which by his nature, as he
is a man, belongs unto him.
members.english: Having given yourself these names: good, modest, truthful, clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded, take care that you never come to bear other names; and if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly. Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind. So if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life. For to go on being what you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites. So put yourself aboard these few names, and if you can stay on them, stay, like someone who has moved to some Islands of the Blessed. But if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing, go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail, or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly, having at least done this one thing, and only this, in your life: to leave it in this way. For remembering the names, though, it will help you greatly to remember the gods, and that what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being.
members.greek: Ὀνόματα θέμενος σαυτῷ ταῦτα· ἀγαθός, αἰδήμων, ἀληθής, ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων, πρόσεχε μήποτε μετονομάζῃ, κἂν ἀπολλύῃς ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα, καὶ ταχέως ἐπάνιθι ἐπ’ αὐτά. μέμνησο δὲ ὅτι τὸ μὲν ἔμφρων ἐβούλετό σοι σημαίνειν τὴν ἐφ’ ἕκαστα διαληπτικὴν ἐπίστασιν καὶ τὸ ἀπαρενθύμητον· τὸ δὲ σύμφρων τὴν ἑκούσιον ἀπόδεξιν τῶν ὑπὸ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως ἀπονεμομένων· τὸ δὲ ὑπέρφρων τὴν ὑπέρτασιν τοῦ φρονοῦντος μορίου ὑπὲρ λείαν ἣ τραχεῖαν κίνησιν τῆς σαρκὸς καὶ τὸ δοξάριον καὶ τὸν θάνατον καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα. ἐὰν οὖν διατηρῇς σεαυτὸν ὲν τούτοις τοῖς ὀνόμασι μὴ γλιχόμενος τοῦ ὑπ’ ἄλλων κατὰ ταῦτα ὀνομάζεσθαι, ἔσῃ ἕτερος καὶ εἰς βίον εἰσελεύσῃ ἕτερον. τὸ γὰρ ἔτι τοιοῦτον εἶναι οἷος μέχρι νῦν γέγονας, καὶ ἐν βίῳ τοιούτῳ σπαράσσεσθαι καὶ μολύνεσθαι, λίαν ἐστὶν ἀναισθήτου καὶ φιλοψύχου καὶ ὁμοίου τοῖς ἡμιβρώτοις θηριομάχοις, οἵτινες μεστοὶ τραυμάτων καὶ λύθρου παρακαλοῦσιν ὅμως εἰς τὴν αὔριον φυλαχθῆναι, παραβληθησόμενοι τοιοῦτοι τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὄνυξι καὶ δήγμασιν. ἐμβίβασον οὖν σαυτὸν εἰς τὰ ὀλίγα ταῦτα ὀνόματα, κἂν μὲν ἐπ’ αὐτῶν μένειν δύνῃ, μένε ὥσπερ εἰς μακάρων τινὰς νήσους μετῳκισμένος· ἐὰν δὲ αἴσθῃ ὅτι ἐκπίπτεις καὶ οὐ περικρατεῖς, ἄπιθι θαρρῶν εἰς γωνίαν τινά, ὅπου κρατήσεις, ἢ καὶ παντάπασιν ἔξιθι τοῦ βίου, μὴ ὀργιζόμενος, ἀλλὰ ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως καὶ αἰδημόνως, ἕν γε τοῦτο μόνον πράξας ἐν τῷ βίῳ τὸ οὕτως ἐξελθεῖν. πρὸς μέντοι τὸ μεμνῆσθαι τῶν ὀνομάτων μεγάλως συλλήψεταί σοι τὸ μεμνῆσθαι θεῶν καὶ ὅτιπερ οὐ κολακεύεσθαι οὗτοι θέλουσιν, ἀλλὰ ἐξομοιοῦσθαι ἑαυτοῖς τὰ λογικὰ πάντα καὶ εἶναι τὴν μὲν συκῆν τὰ συκῆς ποιοῦσαν, τὸν δὲ κύνα τὰ κυνός, τὴν δὲ μέλισσαν τὰ μελίσσης, τὸν δὲ ἄνθρωπον τὰ ἀνθρώπου.

members.text:
Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor
without due examination, nor with reluctancy. Affect not to set out thy
thoughts with curious neat language. Be neither a great talker, nor a
great undertaker. Moreover, let thy God that is in thee to rule over
thee, find by thee, that he hath to do with a man; an aged man; a
sociable man; a Roman; a prince; one that hath ordered his life, as
one that expecteth, as it were, nothing but the sound of the trumpet,
sounding a retreat to depart out of this life with all expedition. One
who for his word or actions neither needs an oath, nor any man to be a
witness.
members.english: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody. Further, let the god in you be the guardian of a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released, needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness.
members.greek: Μήτε ἀκούσιος ἐνέργει μήτε ἀκοινώνητος μήτε ἀνεξέταστος μήτε ἀνθελκόμενος· μήτε κομψεία τὴν διάνοιάν σου καλλωπιζέτω· μήτε πολυρρήμων μήτε πολυπράγμων ἔσο. ἔτι δὲ ὁ ἐν σοὶ θεὸς ἔστω προστάτης ζῴου ἄρρενος καὶ πρεσβύτου καὶ πολιτικοῦ καὶ Ῥωμαίου καὶ ἄρχοντος, ἀνατεταχότος ἑαυτόν, οἷος ἂν εἴη τις περιμένων τὸ ἀνακλητικὸν ἐκ τοῦ βίου εὔλυτος, μήτε ὅρκου δεόμενος μήτε ἀνθρώπου τινὸς μάρτυρος.

members.text:
How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards
thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy
children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy
domestics? thy servants? Is it so with thee, that hitherto thou hast
neither by word or deed wronged any of them? Remember withal through how
many things thou hast already passed, and how many thou hast been able
to endure; so that now the legend of thy life is full, and thy charge is
accomplished. Again, how many truly good things have certainly by thee
been discerned? how many pleasures, how many pains hast thou passed over
with contempt? how many things eternally glorious hast thou despised?
towards how many perverse unreasonable men hast thou carried thyself
kindly, and discreetly?
members.english: How have you behaved up to now towards the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves? Does this hold of you up to now, towards all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”? Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
members.greek: Πῶς προσενήνεξαι μέχρι νῦν θεοῖς, γονεῦσιν, ἀδελφοῖς, γυναικί, τέκνοις, διδασκάλοις, τροφεῦσι, φίλοις, οἰκείοις, οἰκέταις· εἰ πρὸς πάντας σοι μέχρι νῦν ἐστι τό· μήτε τινὰ ῥέξαι ἐξαίσιον μήτε τι εἰπεῖν. ἀναμιμνῄσκου δὲ καὶ δι’ οἵων διελήλυθας καὶ οἷα ἤρκεσας ὑπομεῖναι καὶ ὅτι πλήρης ἤδη σοι ἡ ἱστορία τοῦ βίου καὶ τελεία ἡ λειτουργία καὶ πόσα ὦπται καλὰ καὶ πόσων μὲν ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων ὑπερεῖδες, πόσα δὲ ἔνδοξα παρεῖδες, εἰς ὅσους δὲ ἀγνώμονας εὐγνώμων ἐγένου.

members.text:
Do all things as becometh the disciple of Antoninus Pius.
Remember his resolute constancy in things that were done by him
according to reason, his equability in all things, his sanctity; the
cheerfulness of his countenance, his sweetness, and how free he was from
all vainglory; how careful to come to the true and exact knowledge of
matters in hand, and how he would by no means give over till he did
fully, and plainly understand the whole state of the business; and how
patiently, and without any contestation he would bear with them, that
did unjustly condemn him: how he would never be over-hasty in anything,
nor give ear to slanders and false accusations, but examine and observe
with best diligence the several actions and dispositions of men. Again,
how he was no backbiter, nor easily frightened, nor suspicious, and in
his language free from all affectation and curiosity: and how easily he
would content himself with few things, as lodging, bedding, clothing,
and ordinary nourishment, and attendance. How able to endure labour, how
patient; able through his spare diet to continue from morning to evening
without any necessity of withdrawing before his accustomed hours to
the necessities of nature: his uniformity and constancy in matter of
friendship. How he would bear with them that with all boldness and
liberty opposed his opinions; and even rejoice if any man could better
advise him: and lastly, how religious he was without superstition. All
these things of him remember, that whensoever thy last hour shall
come upon thee, it may find thee, as it did him, ready for it in the
possession of a good conscience.
members.english: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters; and how he would not let anything at all go by without first looking into it very well and understanding it clearly; and how he bore with those who blamed him unjustly, without blaming them in return; and how he hurried towards nothing; and how he did not accept slanders; and how exact an examiner he was of characters and actions, and not one to reproach, not one to jump at a noise, not suspicious, not a sophist; and how he was content with little, for example in housing, bedding, clothing, food and service; and how hard-working he was and how patient; and that he was the kind of man who could stay at the same thing until evening, not even needing, because of his plain diet, to pass his waste except at the usual hour; and his being firm and always the same in his friendships; and his putting up with those who openly opposed his opinions, and being glad if anyone showed him something better; and how he was reverent towards the gods without superstition; so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his.
members.greek: πάντα ὡς Ἀντωνίνου μαθητής· τὸ ὑπὲρ τῶν κατὰ λόγον πρασσομένων εὔτονον ἐκείνου καὶ τὸ ὁμαλὲς πανταχοῦ καὶ τὸ ὅσιον καὶ τὸ εὔδιον τοῦ προσώπου καὶ τὸ μειλίχιον καὶ τὸ ἀκενόδοξον καὶ τὸ περὶ τὴν κατάληψιν τῶν πραγμάτων φιλότιμον· καὶ ὡς ἐκεῖνος οὐκ ἄν τι ὅλως παρῆκε μὴ πρότερον εὖ μάλα κατιδὼν καὶ σαφῶς νοήσας· καὶ ὡς ἔφερεν ἐκεῖνος τοὺς ἀδίκως αὐτὸν μεμφομένους μὴ ἀντιμεμφόμενος· καὶ ὡς ἐπ’ οὐδὲν ἔσπευδεν· καὶ ὠς διαβολὰς οὐκ ἐδέχετο· καὶ ὡς ἀκριβὴς ἦν ἐξεταστὴς ἠθῶν καὶ πράξεων καὶ οὐκ ὀνειδιστής, οὐ ψοφοδεής, οὐχ ὑπόπτης, οὐ σοφιστής· καὶ ὡς ὀλίγοις ἀρκούμενος, οἷον οἰκήσει, στρωμνῇ, ἐσθῆτι, τροφῇ, ὑπηρεσίᾳ· καὶ ὡς φιλόπονος καὶ μακρόθυμος· καὶ οἷος μένειν ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ μέχρι ἑσπέρας, διὰ τὴν λιτὴν δίαιταν μηδὲ τοῦ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα παρὰ τὴν συνήθη ὥραν χρῄζων· καὶ τὸ βέβαιον καὶ ὅμοιον ἐν ταῖς φιλίαις αὐτοῦ· καὶ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι τῶν ἀντιβαινόντων παρρησιαστικῶς ταῖς γνώμαις αὐτοῦ καὶ χαίρειν εἴ τίς τι δεικνύοι κρεῖττον· καὶ ὡς θεοσεβὴς χωρὶς δεισιδαιμονίας· ἵν’ οὕτως εὐσυνειδήτῳ σοι ἐπιστῇ ἠ τελευταία ὥρα ὡς ἐκείνῳ.

members.text:
What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to
affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life
as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs
unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either
tyrannically or servilely towards any.
members.english: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
members.greek: Τὸ τεχνίον ὃ ἔμαθες φίλει, τούτῳ προσαναπαύου· τὸ δὲ ὑπόλοιπον τοῦ βίου διέξελθε ὡς θεοῖς μὲν ἐπιτετροφὼς τὰ σεαυτοῦ πάντα ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς, ἀνθρώπων δὲ μηδενὸς μήτε τύραννον μήτε δοῦλον σεαυτὸν καθιστάς.

members.text:
From the gods I received that I had good grandfathers, and parents,
a good sister, good masters, good domestics, loving kinsmen, almost all
that I have; and that I never through haste and rashness transgressed
against any of them, notwithstanding that my disposition was such,
as that such a thing (if occasion had been) might very well have been
committed by me, but that It was the mercy of the gods, to prevent such
a concurring of matters and occasions, as might make me to incur this
blame. That I was not long brought up by the concubine of my father;
that I preserved the flower of my youth. That I took not upon me to be
a man before my time, but rather put it off longer than I needed. That
I lived under the government of my lord and father, who would take
away from me all pride and vainglory, and reduce me to that conceit and
opinion that it was not impossible for a prince to live in the court
without a troop of guards and followers, extraordinary apparel, such
and such torches and statues, and other like particulars of state and
magnificence; but that a man may reduce and contract himself almost to
the state of a private man, and yet for all that not to become the more
base and remiss in those public matters and affairs, wherein power and
authority is requisite. That I have had such a brother, who by his own
example might stir me up to think of myself; and by his respect and
love, delight and please me. That I have got ingenuous children, and
that they were not born distorted, nor with any other natural deformity.
That I was no great proficient in the study of rhetoric and poetry, and
of other faculties, which perchance I might have dwelt upon, if I had
found myself to go on in them with success. That I did by times prefer
those, by whom I was brought up, to such places and dignities, which
they seemed unto me most to desire; and that I did not put them off with
hope and expectation, that (since that they were yet but young) I would
do the same hereafter. That I ever knew Apollonius and Rusticus, and
Maximus. That I have had occasion often and effectually to consider and
meditate with myself, concerning that life which is according to nature,
what the nature and manner of it is: so that as for the gods and such
suggestions, helps and inspirations, as might be expected from them,
nothing did hinder, but that I might have begun long before to live
according to nature; or that even now that I was not yet partaker and
in present possession of that life, that I myself (in that I did not
observe those inward motions, and suggestions, yea and almost plain and
apparent instructions and admonitions of the gods,) was the only cause
of it. That my body in such a life, hath been able to hold out so long.
That I never had to do with Benedicta and Theodotus, yea and afterwards
when I fell into some fits of love, I was soon cured. That having been
often displeased with Rusticus, I never did him anything for which
afterwards I had occasion to repent. That it being so that my mother was
to die young, yet she lived with me all her latter years. That as often
as I had a purpose to help and succour any that either were poor, or
fallen into some present necessity, I never was answered by my officers
that there was not ready money enough to do it; and that I myself never
had occasion to require the like succour from any other. That I have
such a wife, so obedient, so loving, so ingenuous. That I had choice of
fit and able men, to whom I might commit the bringing up of my children.
That by dreams I have received help, as for other things, so in
particular, how I might stay my casting of blood, and cure my dizziness,
as that also that happened to thee in Cajeta, as unto Chryses when he
prayed by the seashore. And when I did first apply myself to philosophy,
that I did not fall into the hands of some sophists, or spent my time
either in reading the manifold volumes of ordinary philosophers, nor in
practising myself in the solution of arguments and fallacies, nor dwelt
upon the studies of the meteors, and other natural curiosities. All
these things without the assistance of the gods, and fortune, could not
have been.
members.english: From the gods: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them; and that I was not carried away into any offence against any of them, although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up. And that I was not brought up for longer with my grandfather’s concubine; and that I preserved the bloom of my youth; and that I was not made a man before the season, but even took some time more. That I was placed under a ruler and father who was to take all the conceit out of me and bring me to the thought that it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and other such display; but that one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good. That I happened to have such a brother, able by his character to rouse me to take care of myself, and at the same time gladdening me with his respect and affection. That my children were not born lacking in natural gifts, nor deformed in their little bodies. That I did not make more progress in rhetoric, in poetry and in the other pursuits, in which I might perhaps have been held fast, if I had felt myself getting on easily. That I was quick to set those who brought me up in the rank they seemed to me to desire, and did not put it off with the hope that, since they were still young, I would do it later. That I came to know Apollonius, Rusticus, Maximus. That I had an impression, clearly and often, of the life according to nature, of what kind of life it is, so that, as far as it rests with the gods and with the gifts, help and inspirations that come from there, nothing prevents me from living according to nature already, and my still falling short of this is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods, which are all but teachings. That my body has held out so long in a life like this. That I touched neither Benedicta nor Theodotus, but that later too, when I fell into the passions of love, I recovered. That, though I was often angry with Rusticus, I did nothing more that I would have regretted. That my mother, who was to die young, still lived with me in her last years. That whenever I wanted to help someone who was poor or in need of something else, I was never told that I had no money to do it with; and that no similar need befell me myself, so as to receive from another. That my wife is as she is, so compliant, so warmly affectionate, so unaffected. That I had no lack of suitable people to bring up my children. That remedies were given me through dreams, among others against spitting blood and against dizziness; and of this, at Caieta, as you will use. That, when I set my heart on philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor sit down to writing, or to resolving syllogisms, or to busying myself with the things in the sky. For all these things “need the gods’ help and fortune.”
members.greek: Παρὰ τῶν θεῶν τὸ ἀγαθοὺς πάππους, ἀγαθοὺς γονέας, ἀγαθὴν ἀδελφήν, ἀγαθοὺς διδασκάλους, ἀγαθοὺς οἰκείους, συγγενεῖς, φίλους σχεδὸν ἅπαντας ἔχειν· καὶ ὅτι περὶ οὐδένα αὐτῶν προέπεσον πλημμελῆσαί τι, καίτοι διάθεσιν ἔχων τοιαύτην, ἀφ’ ἧς, εἰ ἔτυχε, κἂν ἔπραξά τι τοιοῦτο· τῶν θεῶν δὲ εὐποιία τὸ μηδεμίαν συνδρομὴν πραγμάτων γενέσθαι, ἥτις ἔμελλέ με ἐλέγξειν. καὶ τὸ μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον τραφῆναι παρὰ τῇ παλλακῇ τοῦ πάππου καὶ τὸ τὴν ὥραν διασῶσαι καὶ τὸ μὴ πρὸ ὥρας ἀνδρωθῆναι, ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ ἐπιλαβεῖν τοῦ χρόνου. τὸ ἄρχοντι καὶ πατρὶ ὑποταχθῆναι, ὃς ἔμελλε πάντα τὸν τῦφον ἀφαιρήσειν μου καὶ εἰς ἔννοιαν ἄξειν τοῦ ὅτι δυνατόν ἐστιν ἐν αὐλῇ βιοῦντα μήτε δορυφορήσεων χρῄζειν μήτε ἐσθήτων σημειωδῶν μήτε λαμπάδων καὶ ἀνδριάντων τοιῶνδέ τινων καὶ τοῦ ὁμοίου κόμπου, ἀλλʼ ἔξεστιν ἐγγυτάτω ἰδιώτου συστέλλειν ἑαυτὸν καὶ μὴ διὰ τοῦτο ταπεινότερον ἢ ῥᾳθυμότερον ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ ὑπὲρ τῶν κοινῶν ἡγεμονικῶς πραχθῆναι δέοντα. τὸ ἀδελφοῦ τοιούτου τυχεῖν, δυναμένου μὲν διὰ ἤθους ἐπεγεῖραί με πρὸς ἐπιμέλειαν ἐμαυτοῦ, ἅμα δὲ καὶ τιμῇ καὶ στοργῇ εὐφραίνοντός με· τὸ παιδία μοι ἀφυῆ μὴ γενέσθαι μηδὲ κατὰ τὸ σωμάτιον διάστροφα. τὸ μὴ ἐπὶ πλέον με προκόψαι ἐν ῥητορικῇ καὶ ποιητικῇ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐπιτηδεύμασιν, ἐν οἷς ἴσως ἂν κατεσχέθην, εἰ ᾐσθόμην ἐμαυτὸν εὐόδως προιόντα. τὸ φθάσαι τοὺς τροφέας ἐν ἀξιώματι καταστῆσαι, οὗ δὴ ἐδόκουν μοι ἐπιθυμεῖν, καὶ μὴ ἀναβαλέσθαι ἐλπίδι τοῦ με, ἐπεὶ νέοι ἔτι ἦσαν, ὕστερον αὐτὸ πράξειν. τὸ γνῶναι Ἀπολλώνιον, Ῥούστικον, Μάξιμον. τὸ φαντασθῆναι περὶ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν βίου ἐναργῶς καὶ πολλάκις οἷός τίς ἐστιν, ὥστε, ὅσον ἐπὶ τοῖς θεοῖς καὶ ταῖς ἐκεῖθεν διαδόσεσι καὶ συλλήψεσι καὶ ἐπιπνοίαις, μηδὲν κωλύειν ἤδη κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν με, ἀπολείπεσθαι δὲ ἔτι τούτου παρὰ τὴν ἐμὴν αἰτίαν καὶ παρὰ τὸ μὴ διατηρεῖν τὰς ἐκ τῶν θεῶν ὑπομνήσεις καὶ μονονουχὶ διδασκαλίας· τὸ ἀντισχεῖν μοι τὸ σῶμα ἐπὶ τοσοῦτον ἐν τοιούτῳ βίῳ· τὸ μήτε Βενεδίκτης ἅψασθαι μήτε Θεοδότου, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὕστερον ἐν ἐρωτικοῖς πάθεσι γενόμενον ὑγιᾶναι· τὸ χαλεπήναντα πολλάκις Ῥουστίκῳ μηδὲν πλέον πρᾶξαι, ἐφ’ ᾧ ἂν μετέγνων· τὸ μέλλουσαν νέαν τελευτᾶν τὴν τεκοῦσαν ὅμως οἰκῆσαι μετ’ ἐμοῦ τὰ τελευταῖα ἔτη. τὸ ὁσάκις ἐβουλήθην ἐπικουρῆσαί τινι πενομένῳ ἢ εἰς ἄλλο τι χρῄζοντι, μηδέποτε ἀκοῦσαί με, ὅτι οὐκ ἔστι μοι χρήματα, ὅθεν γένηται, καὶ τὸ αὐτῷ ἐμοὶ χρείαν ὁμοίαν, ὡς παρ’ ἑτέρου μεταλαβεῖν, μὴ συμπεσεῖν· τὸ τὴν γυναῖκα τοιαύτην εἶναι, οὑτωσὶ μὲν πειθήνιον, οὕτω δὲ φιλόστοργον, οὕτω δὲ ἀφελῆ· τὸ ἐπιτηδείων τροφέων εἰς τὰ παιδία εὐπορῆσαι. τὸ δι’ ὀνειράτων βοηθήματα δοθῆναι ἄλλα τε καὶ ὡς μὴ πτύειν αἷμα καὶ μὴ ἰλιγγιᾶν, καὶ τούτου ἐν Καιήτῃ ὥσπερ χρήσῃ· τὸ ὅπως ἐπεθύμησα φιλοσοφίας, μὴ ἐμπεσεῖν εἴς τινα σοφιστὴν μηδὲ ἀποκαθίσαι ἐπὶ τὸ συγγράφειν ἢ συλλογισμοὺς ἀναλύειν ἢ περὶ τὰ μετεωρολογικὰ καταγίνεσθαι. πάντα γὰρ ταῦτα ʽθεῶν βοηθῶν καὶ τύχης δεῖται.ʼ

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.2 is 2.5, 6.27 is 6.29 with the first part of 6.30, 6.28 is the rest of 6.30, 3.5 is the first part of 3.5, 5.25 is 5.31, 4.26 is 4.31 and 1.14 is 1.17; 10.8 is the same.

Reads the qualities of 2.2, the list of 6.27 and the names of 10.8 as one short list. The first claim names only the qualities that two of the three lists have, and says “among them”; three of 10.8’s own names (clear-minded, like-minded, high-minded) stand in an item of their own with their meanings. “Names” is 10.8’s word; applying it to the qualities of 2.2 and 6.27 is the editor’s extension.

Does not put 10.8’s second way out into the first-person text. After “go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail” Marcus adds “or even leave life altogether, not in anger, but simply, freely and modestly”. The article does not write “I leave life” as a rule of life; the words stay in the passage for the reader to see.

Reads the last sentence of 10.8 as saying what the gods want (the fig tree doing a fig tree’s work, the human being a human being’s). The translators note another reading, in which the clause goes with “remember” and states what makes each thing what it is.

Uses 1.14, a list of thanks to the gods, only where it states something Marcus holds or admits: no offence against those close to him, a court without show, falling short by his own fault. The rest of its thanks are not turned into rules.

Takes the wording of the statement’s third part from 3.5 (“nor any human being as witness”). 10.8 supports its sense but not its words: it says “without craving to have others call you by them” and has neither “need” nor “witness”.
articles.limit: The article leans on 10.8, which feeds four of the six claims. Three of the article’s links between passages are loose: “without pretence” rests partly on the English of 6.27, the claim on show and witness shares only the frame “need neither”, and the claim on falling short shares the word “fall” only in the English. Much of it is said in other articles: Article 5 has the human being’s own work, Article 3 accepting what is allotted, Articles 10 and 17 doing each thing as if it were the last (Article 10 on the same Ep. 101.7, Article 17 also without pretence), and Article 11 the good life in very few things, no show and no witness (on the same Ep. 113.32) and coming back after a failure. What this section adds is a short list of names I have given myself, kept without wanting others to call me by them, and each act done as a Roman and a man who waits for the signal to withdraw and wants a good conscience at the last hour.

statement.t: I have given myself a few names, such as good. I keep to them, do each act as the last of my life, and need no human being as witness.

statement.kind: A rule, the way it is carried out, and what it does not need
statement.form: 134 characters. “Such as good” tells a first hearer that the names are qualities of character. Only “good” is named because it stands in both 10.8 and 6.27. The naming itself is 10.8’s alone. 2.2 supplies fewness and keeping to the few things. The last act is a way of acting, not an expectation of death.

claims.t: I have named myself good, modest and truthful, and I take care never to bear other names. These are few things to keep. At every hour I do what is in hand with exact and unfeigned dignity, affection, freedom and justice. I keep myself simple, good and unpretentious, and I struggle to remain the kind of person philosophy wanted to make me.
claims.shared: The opaque boarding image is replaced by plain naming, and the image moves to the margin with its condition “if you can stay”. Fewness and keeping are the joint ground of 2.2 and 10.8. The three names are 10.8’s alone, the hourly work is 2.2’s alone, and the simple character and the struggle are 6.27’s alone. Each list stays with its own passage, and none is offered as a definition of the names.

claims.t: The life I live depends on what I keep to. Once mastered, these things let me live a life that flows smoothly and is god-fearing. If I keep to these things, the gods will demand nothing more of me. If I keep myself in the names I have given myself, I will be a different person and enter a different life. The gods do not want to be flattered. They want all rational beings to become like them, the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being.
claims.shared: The first sentence is the common proposition. In 2.2 mastering the few things lets a person live a smooth life, and in 10.8 keeping in the names brings a different life. The smooth life stays with 2.2 and the different life with 10.8. What the gods demand (2.2) and what they want (10.8) remain separate sentences with one witness each.

support.quote: if you keep yourself in these names, without craving to have others call you by them, you will be a different person and will enter a different life
support.follows: Whoever keeps himself in these names becomes a different person and enters a different life.
gives: The life I live depends on what I keep to
If I keep myself in the names I have given myself, I will be a different person and enter a different life

support.quote: what they want is not to be flattered, but for all rational beings to become like them, and for the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being
support.follows: The gods do not want flattery; they want rational beings to become like them and each thing, the human being included, to do its own work.
gives: The gods do not want to be flattered
They want all rational beings to become like them, the fig tree to do the work of a fig tree, the dog the work of a dog, the bee the work of a bee, and the human being the work of a human being

claims.t: I do not look to others to confirm what I am. I do not crave to have others call me by the names I have given myself. I need neither an oath nor any human being as witness. It is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches, statues and other such display.
claims.shared: The first sentence is the common proposition of 3.5 (no human witness) and 10.8 (no craving for others to use the names). The court sentence is a single-witness detail from 1.14 and stays a statement of what is possible, not a vow.

support.quote: it is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches and statues of this sort and other such display
support.follows: The ruler and father Marcus was placed under brought him to think that one can live at a court without guards, marked clothes or similar show.
gives: It is possible to live at a court and need neither bodyguards, nor clothes that mark one out, nor torches, statues and other such display

support.quote: needing neither an oath nor any human being as witness
support.follows: The man who has set himself in order needs no oath and no human witness.
gives: I do not look to others to confirm what I am
I need neither an oath nor any human being as witness

support.quote: without craving to have others call you by them
support.follows: The names are to be kept without craving that other people call me by them.
gives: I do not look to others to confirm what I am
I do not crave to have others call me by the names I have given myself

claims.t: As a Roman and a man, I carry out each action as the last of my life. I set myself in order, as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released. I want my last hour to come upon me with a conscience as good as that of Antoninus.
claims.shared: Waiting for the signal stays a simile for being in order, not a wish to die. The conscience is measured against Antoninus, as 6.28 says. The old line repeated the last-act thought and one instance is cut.

support.quote: so that your last hour may come upon you with a conscience as good as his
support.follows: Following Antoninus is meant to bring me to my last hour with a conscience as good as his.
gives: my last hour to come upon me with a conscience as good as that of Antoninus

support.quote: as a Roman and a man
support.follows: The care over what is in hand is to be taken as a Roman and a man.
gives: As a Roman and a man

support.quote: a living being that is male, old, engaged in public affairs, a Roman and a ruler, who has set himself in order
support.follows: The god within is to guard a being who is male, old, in public life, a Roman and a ruler, and who has set himself in order.
gives: As a Roman and a man
I set myself in order

support.quote: as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released
support.follows: The man described is to be like someone who waits for the signal to withdraw from life and is easily released.
gives: as someone would be who is waiting for the signal to withdraw from life, easily released

support.quote: carry out each action as the last of your life
support.follows: Each action is to be carried out as if it were the last of my life.
gives: I carry out each action as the last of my life

claims.t: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me. They were good people, nearly all of them, and I was not carried away into any offence against any of them. I ask the same about my conduct towards the gods, my brothers, my wife, my children, those who brought me up and my household slaves. Does it hold of me up to now that I have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong?
claims.shared: The first sentence names only the people both passages list, and both passages look back on conduct towards them. The statement of no offence is 1.14’s and covers only those people. The standard from 5.25 stays a question “up to now” and is not a claim of innocence. The gods, brothers, wife, children, upbringers and household slaves are 5.25’s alone.

support.quote: How have you behaved up to now towards the gods, your parents, your brothers, your wife, your children, your teachers, those who brought you up, your friends, those close to you, your household slaves?
support.follows: Marcus asks himself how he has behaved up to now towards the gods, his family, teachers, friends, those close to him and his household.
gives: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
I ask the same about my conduct towards the gods, my brothers, my wife, my children, those who brought me up and my household slaves

support.quote: Does this hold of you up to now, towards all of them: “to have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong”?
support.follows: Marcus asks whether, towards all the people he has listed, he has done nothing wrong and said nothing wrong.
gives: Does it hold of me up to now that I have done nothing wrong to anyone, nor said anything wrong?

support.quote: that I had good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good people close to me, relatives, friends, nearly all of them
support.follows: Marcus thanks the gods that nearly all his family, teachers, friends and those close to him were good.
gives: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
They were good people, nearly all of them

support.quote: I was not carried away into any offence against any of them
support.follows: Marcus was not carried away into any offence against his family, teachers, friends or those close to him.
gives: I look back on how I have behaved towards my parents, my teachers, my friends and those close to me
I was not carried away into any offence against any of them

claims.t: I can fall away from the person I mean to be. I take care that I am not turned into a Caesar, that I am not dyed, for it happens. My still falling short of the life according to nature is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods. If I lose my names, I go back to them quickly.
claims.shared: The first sentence is the common proposition. 6.27 says being dyed happens, 10.8 speaks of sensing a falling away, and 1.14 admits still falling short. “The person I mean to be” is our summary of the three different standards. The Caesar and the dye are 6.27’s alone, the own fault is 1.14’s alone, and the quick return is 10.8’s alone. The Caesar line remains a warning to take care.

support.quote: if you do lose these names, go back to them quickly
support.follows: The names can be lost; if they are, I should go back to them quickly.
gives: If I lose my names, I go back to them quickly

support.quote: Take care that you are not turned into a Caesar, that you are not dyed: for it happens.
support.follows: Being turned into a Caesar is something that happens, and care must be taken against it.
gives: I can fall away from the person I mean to be
I take care that I am not turned into a Caesar, that I am not dyed, for it happens

support.quote: if you sense that you are falling away and are not prevailing
support.follows: A person can sense that he is falling away from the names and not prevailing.
gives: I can fall away from the person I mean to be

support.quote: my still falling short of this is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods
support.follows: That Marcus still falls short of living according to nature is his own fault: he has not kept to the gods’ reminders.
gives: I can fall away from the person I mean to be
My still falling short of the life according to nature is through my own fault and through not keeping to the reminders from the gods

single.quote: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.label: The one fruit
single.t: Life is short. There is one fruit of living on earth: a pious disposition and social actions.
single.why: Single source, 6.27. It stands as the speaker framed it. The gloss on social actions was editorial and is removed.
single.follows: Life is short, and the one thing to be had from it is a pious disposition and actions done for the community.

single.quote: one may draw oneself in until one is very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good
single.label: Leading without the show
single.t: I may draw myself in until I am very nearly a private person and not, on that account, be more lowly or more slack in what has to be done as a leader for the common good.
single.why: Single source, 1.14. “May” keeps it a permission learned at court, not a duty to withdraw.
single.follows: Marcus’s ruler and father showed him that one can live almost as a private person and be no lowlier or slacker in a leader’s work for the common good.

single.quote: Love the little trade you have learned, and rest in it; and go through what is left of your life having entrusted everything that is yours to the gods with your whole soul, and making yourself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.label: The trade I learned
single.t: I love the little trade I have learned, and I rest in it. I go through what is left of my life having entrusted everything that is mine to the gods with my whole soul, making myself neither the tyrant nor the slave of any human being.
single.why: Single source, 4.26. The trade is left unnamed, as in the source.
single.follows: I should love the trade I learned and rest in it, entrust what is mine to the gods, and be neither tyrant nor slave to anyone.

single.quote: Do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. Do not let elegance dress up your thought. Do not be a person of many words or a busybody.
single.label: How not to act
single.t: I do not act unwillingly, or unsocially, or without examining, or while pulled the other way. I do not let elegance dress up my thought. I am not a person of many words or a busybody.
single.why: Single source, 3.5. The source wording is kept in three plain sentences.
single.follows: Acting unwillingly, unsocially, unexamined or divided is ruled out, and so are dressed-up thought, many words and meddling.

single.quote: Remember that “clear-minded” was to mean for you a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded; “like-minded”, the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns; and “high-minded”, the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.label: Three further names
single.t: I remember what three of my names were to mean. “Clear-minded” was a discerning attention to each thing, and not letting things go unheeded. “Like-minded” was the willing acceptance of what the common nature assigns. “High-minded” was the lifting high of the part that has mind, above the smooth or rough movement of the flesh, above petty reputation, above death and everything of that kind.
single.why: Single source, 10.8. The bracketed gloss “pleasure and pain” was editorial and is removed.
single.follows: The three names mean attention to each thing, willing acceptance of what nature assigns, and a mind lifted above the flesh, reputation and death.

single.quote: Everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity, and his ambition to grasp matters
single.label: Antoninus as my model
single.t: I do everything as a pupil of Antoninus: his vigour on behalf of what is done according to reason, his evenness everywhere, his piety, the calm of his face, his gentleness, his freedom from vanity and his ambition to grasp matters.
single.why: Single source, 6.28. “The emperor who adopted me” is removed, because the passages do not identify him so.
single.follows: Marcus is to do everything as a pupil of Antoninus, whose traits he lists, beginning with these seven.

single.quote: Call to mind, too, what things you have passed through and what things you have been strong enough to endure; and that the story of your life is now full and your service complete; and how many fine things you have seen; and how many pleasures and pains you have looked down on, how many honours you have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people you have been considerate.
single.label: What I have come through
single.t: I call to mind what I have passed through and what I have been strong enough to endure. I call to mind that the story of my life is now full and my service complete. I call to mind how many fine things I have seen, how many pleasures and pains I have looked down on, how many honours I have looked past, and to how many inconsiderate people I have been considerate.
single.why: Single source, 5.25. Semicolons are removed. It stays a recollection to prompt me, not a verdict on my life.
single.follows: Marcus is to recall what he has endured, seen and looked past, and that his life’s story is full and his service complete.

single.quote: although I had a disposition from which, if it had so happened, I might well have done something of the kind; but it is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up
single.label: Partly the gods’ kindness
single.t: I had a disposition from which I might well have offended those close to me. It is the gods’ kindness that no combination of circumstances came about that would have shown me up.
single.why: Single source, 1.14. “Clean record” and “partly” were not in the source and are removed. “Those close to me” supplies the referent for “something of the kind”.
single.follows: Marcus had it in him to offend those close to him, and thanks the gods that no circumstances arose to bring it out.

single.quote: It is shameful that, in a life in which your body does not give out, your soul should give out first.
single.label: The soul giving out
single.t: It is shameful if, in a life in which my body does not give out, my soul gives out first.
single.why: Single source, 6.27. It is a separate remark in that passage and stands alone here.
single.follows: It is shameful for the soul to give out before the body does.

single.quote: For to go on being what you have been up to now, and to be torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life, someone like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.label: Like the beast-fighters
single.t: To go on being what I have been up to now, torn and soiled in a life like this, is the mark of someone thoroughly senseless and clinging to life. Such a person is like the half-eaten beast-fighters who, full of wounds and gore, still beg to be kept until tomorrow, to be thrown, just as they are, to the same claws and bites.
single.why: Single source, 10.8. The beast-fighters remain a comparison in the third person and are not made my identity.
single.follows: Going on unchanged in a life that tears and soils me is senseless clinging to life, like a mauled beast-fighter begging for one more day.

single.quote: go away with a good heart to some corner where you will prevail
single.label: If I am not prevailing
single.t: If I sense that I am falling away and am not prevailing, I go away with a good heart to some corner where I will prevail.
single.why: Single source, 10.8. The condition is kept so the withdrawal is not made a general rule. The further option of leaving life is held in the margin.
single.follows: Someone who is not prevailing should withdraw, in good heart, to a corner where he will prevail.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.2 is 2.5, 6.27 is 6.29 with the first part of 6.30, 6.28 is the rest of 6.30, 3.5 is the first part of 3.5, 5.25 is 5.31, 4.26 is 4.31 and 1.14 is 1.17; 10.8 is the same.

134 characters. “Such as good” tells a first hearer that the names are qualities of character. Only “good” is named because it stands in both 10.8 and 6.27. The naming itself is 10.8’s alone. 2.2 supplies fewness and keeping to the few things. The last act is a way of acting, not an expectation of death.
marcus_revision.limit: The names belong to 10.8 alone. 2.2 and 6.27 share only the fewness of what is required and overlapping but different lists of qualities, so the article joins them by theme and not as one canon. The opening names only “good”, the one quality that both 10.8 and 6.27 list. In the opening, the last-act wording is 2.2’s, and 6.28 and 3.5 witness only the shared last-hour frame. The boarding image and its condition “if you can stay” are held in the margin as 10.8’s alone. The first sentences of c2, c3, c5 and c6 are our summaries of what two passages share, and the sentences after them keep each passage’s own wording with its own witness. The gods play different parts in each passage and are not made one theology. “Service complete” (5.25) stands unresolved beside “struggle to remain” (6.27) and “still falling short” (1.14). The last-hour language is a frame for acting well and not a wish to die. The condition in 10.8i comes from the surrounding passage, and leaving life is held in the margin as 10.8’s alone. The ruler-father of 1.14 is not identified with Antoninus, and the little trade of 4.26 is not named.

articles.title: Living now as one about to die

statement.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, so I live the present justly, as one already at the end, and wait for death cheerfully.

parts.words: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
I live the present justly
as one already at the end
wait for death cheerfully

inferences.why: No passage says that I live justly because I shall soon be gone; 4.21 only sets “life is short” beside turning the present to profit.

statement.kind: A ground, the conduct that answers it, and the stance towards the end
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: I shall soon be gone and I live only the present. Claims 2 and 3 are the conduct: living as one already at the end, and what is enough meanwhile. Claim 4 is the stance towards death itself; claim 5 is the exercise that keeps the ground in view, and claim 6 says what failing would be.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it
groups.asks: What still holds if the statement is not true.
