seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three of his passages support living as one already at the end and three support waiting for death; what is enough and the view from above gain one each. Practice gains a nightly exercise and the reminder that a cheerful death is long prepared; When it breaks gains a name for the failure, a life always put off. He limits leaving the past behind, and he challenges the claim that being remembered is of no account.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a daily exercise: each night I say “I have lived”, and every morning after that is a gain. One difference bears on the statement’s last part and is left out of this article: he allows a wise man to end his own life (Ep. 70.5), where I wait for death.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: let us shape our mind as though the end had been reached
piece.follows: I should shape my mind as if I had already reached the end of my life.
piece.context: Letter 101 follows the sudden death of Cornelius Senecio amid his plans: a boundary is fixed for each of us and none knows how near it is. “The end” is that boundary.
gives: as someone already at the end of life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: That man alone has got beyond necessities, and is discharged from service and free, who lives with his life completed
piece.follows: The person who lives with his life already completed is discharged from service and free.
piece.context: Seneca’s wish for Lucilius in Letter 32: a settled mind that has no need of added years. A “completed” life is one that already has what is truly good, however long it then lasts.
gives: I live what is left
as someone already at the end of life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I write you this letter in this frame of mind: as though death were going to call me away at the very moment of writing.
piece.follows: Seneca writes this letter as if death might call him away while he is writing it.
piece.context: In Letter 61 Seneca, now old, has just said that he tries to live every day as a complete life and to regard it as possibly his last. “This frame of mind” is that thought.
gives: knowing that I may leave life at this very moment

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: That we have lived enough is brought about neither by years nor by days but by the mind.
piece.follows: Whether I have lived enough is settled by my mind, not by the number of my years or days.
piece.context: The end of Letter 61, on being ready to die: life is equipped well enough, but we are greedy and always find something lacking in it.
gives: how long I do it does not matter

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: whatever she has put together she takes apart, and whatever she has taken apart she puts together again
piece.follows: Whatever nature has put together she takes apart, and whatever she has taken apart she puts together again.
piece.context: From Letter 30, on the old and dying Bassus: death’s necessity cannot be overcome and is equal for everyone. “She” is Nature, whose law for us is the same as her own.
gives: a dissolving
it is according to nature

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I have lived, dearest Lucilius, as much as was enough; having had my fill, I await death.
piece.follows: Seneca says he has lived enough, has had his fill, and now awaits death.
piece.context: The last words of Letter 61, written in old age, where Seneca has said that dying well means dying willingly and that one should reflect on one’s end without sadness.
gives: I wait for it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: What is death? Either an end or a crossing.
piece.follows: Death is one of two things: an end, or a crossing over.
piece.context: The close of Letter 65: the mind should rule the body as god rules matter, so we should be brave. Seneca goes on to say he fears neither ceasing nor crossing over.
gives: whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: you will indeed see beneath you everything that is counted as loftiest
piece.follows: Whoever reaches the height of wisdom sees beneath him everything that people count as loftiest.
piece.context: The end of Letter 84: what seems to stand high in human affairs is really tiny. The height is wisdom, a summit before which Fortune has lowered herself; it is a place arrived at, not an exercise.
gives: I look down on human affairs as if from high above
The things people prize

items.label: practice
items.t: I order each day as if it completed my life. I go to sleep gladly, saying “I have lived”; then every morning I wake to is a gain.
items.why: 7.31 tells me to live what is left as a surplus and gives no way of doing it day by day. Seneca gives one: close each day as a finished life, so that the next day comes as a gain.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: every day must be ordered as if it were bringing up the rear of the column, and were completing and filling out life
support.follows: Each day should be ordered as if it brought up the rear of the column and completed my life.
support.context: Letter 12 is on old age. Seneca goes on to Pacuvius, who held his own funeral feast every evening. “The column” is the line of one’s days.
gives: I order each day as if it completed my life

support.author: seneca
support.quote: as we go to sleep let us say, glad and cheerful: “I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given.”
support.follows: At bedtime I should say, gladly, that I have lived and have finished the course Fortune gave me.
support.context: In Letter 12 Seneca tells of Pacuvius, carried from dinner to bed each night as if to burial, and says to do from a good conscience what he did from a bad one; the words to say are a line of verse.
gives: I go to sleep gladly, saying “I have lived”

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whoever has said “I have lived” rises every day to a gain
support.follows: Whoever has said “I have lived” rises each new morning to a gain.
support.context: The close of Seneca’s point in Letter 12 about ending each day as a finished life: if god adds a tomorrow, it is received gladly. The “gain” is that added day.
gives: every morning I wake to is a gain

items.label: practice
items.t: Leaving life with an even mind when the hour comes is something I can learn only over a long time. I shall receive death cheerfully when it comes only if I have long made myself ready for it.
items.why: Marcus says to wait for death cheerfully and gives the reasons, but he does not say here that this has to be learned. Seneca says it must be learned, and over a long time.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is a great thing, Lucilius, and one that has to be learned over a long time: to go away with an even mind when that hour which cannot be avoided draws near.
support.follows: Going away with an even mind at the hour that cannot be avoided is a great thing, and it has to be learned over a long time.
support.context: In Letter 30 Seneca describes his old friend Bassus, who is dying of age and looks on his own end with courage. “This” is what Bassus is doing: facing his death calmly.
gives: Leaving life with an even mind when the hour comes is something I can learn only over a long time

support.author: seneca
support.quote: no one has received death cheerfully when it came, except a man who had long made himself ready for it
support.follows: Only someone long prepared for death receives it cheerfully when it comes.
support.context: From Letter 30, on the dying Bassus. Seneca contrasts those who demand death in a fit of frenzy with those who wait for it calmly; death “when it came” is death that comes unsought.
gives: I shall receive death cheerfully when it comes only if I have long made myself ready for it

items.label: breaks
items.t: The great fault is a life that is never finished, with part of it always put off. Some people begin to live only when it is time to stop, and some stop before they have begun. I put nothing off and settle my account with life every day.
items.why: 12.1 names the fear of never beginning to live according to nature and does not say how that comes about. Seneca says how: by putting things off, so that the life is always unfinished. He also gives the way back, which is to settle the account daily.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The greatest fault of life is that it is always unfinished, that some part of it is put off.
support.follows: The worst fault in a life is that it is never complete: some part of it is put off.
support.context: Letter 101 follows the sudden death of Cornelius Senecio in the middle of his plans. “Unfinished” here means that part of the life is left for later.
gives: The great fault is a life that is never finished, with part of it always put off

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Some, indeed, begin just when they must stop. If you judge this a wonder, I will add something for you to wonder at more: some have stopped living before they began.
support.follows: Some people start living only when it is time to stop, and some stop living before they have started.
support.context: In Letter 23 Seneca comments on Epicurus’s saying that they live ill who are always beginning to live: such a life is always incomplete, and cannot be ready for death.
gives: Some people begin to live only when it is time to stop, and some stop before they have begun

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us put nothing off. Let us balance our account with life every day.
support.follows: I should put nothing off and settle my account with life each day.
support.context: From Letter 101: a boundary is fixed for each of us and no one knows how near it is. To “balance our account with life” is to leave nothing of one’s life owing at the end of the day.
gives: I put nothing off and settle my account with life every day

items.t: Seneca does not hold that being remembered is of no account. He agrees that time will come over everyone and that the dead do not feel the talk of those who come after, but he promises Lucilius a name among them (Ep. 21.5) and tells him to look to the thousands of years to come (Ep. 79.17). He is not consistent: his good man, told that his deed will soon be forgotten, answers that this lies outside his work (Ep. 76.29).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: few talents will lift their heads out and, though bound to depart some day into the same silence, will hold out against oblivion and will long assert their freedom
support.follows: Time covers everyone, but a few talents hold out against oblivion for a long while before they too fall silent.
support.context: In Letter 21 Seneca tells Lucilius that his name will last through these letters, as Epicurus’s letters kept Idomeneus’s name alive. What they lift their heads out of is the fathomless depth of time.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I shall have favour with those who come after; I can bring out with me names that will last.
support.follows: Seneca expects to be read by those who come after and to make the names he brings out with him last.
support.context: In Letter 21 Seneca promises Lucilius what Epicurus promised his friend Idomeneus: a name preserved by being written into letters that those who come after will read.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Many thousands of years, many thousands of peoples will come after: look to those.
support.follows: I should look to the many peoples and years that come after me, not only to the people of my own time.
support.context: Letter 79, on virtue that goes unrecognised in its own time, as with Epicurus: a day will make it public. “Those” are the later peoples, who will judge without ill will or favour.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The talk of those who come after will indeed not concern us at all; yet it will honour us and keep returning to us even though we do not feel it.
support.follows: The talk of those who come after does not concern the dead, yet it will honour them all the same.
support.context: The close of Seneca’s argument in Letter 79 that no virtue lies hidden. “Us” means those who followed virtue without recognition in their own lifetime.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: say: “Your deed will be followed by early oblivion and by a less than grateful verdict from your fellow citizens.” He will answer you: “All those things lie outside my work; I am looking at the work itself.
support.follows: Told that his deed will soon be forgotten, the good man answers that this is outside his work and that he looks only at the work itself.
support.context: In Letter 76 Seneca argues that the honourable is the only good. “He” is the good man who goes to his death rightly and dutifully, with no reward and no joy in prospect.

items.t: Seneca does not leave all the past behind. Consoling a mourner, he calls the past ours and the safest thing we have, and says that whoever is glad only at what is present sets narrow bounds to the fruits of things (Ep. 99.4–5). The limit is narrow: he means good things once had, and elsewhere he says that we are tormented by what is past and that no one is wretched from present things alone (Ep. 5.9).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The time that has gone by is ours, and nothing is in a safer place than what has been.
support.follows: The past belongs to us, and nothing we have is safer than what has already been.
support.context: A letter of consolation quoted in Letter 99: grief forgets how much was received. “The time that has gone by” is the years already had with the one who has died.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whoever is glad only at what is present sets narrow bounds to the fruits of things. Both what is to come and what is past give delight
support.follows: Whoever is glad only at what is present narrows the fruits of things; the past and the future give delight as well.
support.context: In Letter 99 Seneca, consoling a mourner, says we are ungrateful for what we have received because we hope for what is to come. The delight the past gives is memory, which is certain.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No one is made wretched by present things alone.
support.follows: Nothing in the present moment alone makes a person wretched.
support.context: The close of Letter 5: animals fear only the danger they see, while people are tormented by memory of the past and by foresight of the future.

amend.t: ; each night I say “I have lived”, and every morning after that is a gain
; but what has been is still mine, and nothing I have is safer
; yet a few names hold out long against oblivion, and I should look to the thousands of years after me

passages.title: On sudden death and living each day
passages.text: But what is more foolish than to be surprised that something has happened on any one day which can happen on every day? A boundary does stand for us, where the necessity of the fates, which no plea can move, has fixed it; but none of us knows how near he is to the boundary. So let us shape our mind as though the end had been reached. Let us put nothing off. Let us balance our account with life every day.

passages.title: On completing life before death
passages.text: I wish for you to have yourself at your own disposal: that your mind, driven about by wandering thoughts, may at last come to rest and be settled; that it may be content with itself and, once it has understood the true goods, which are possessed the moment they are understood, may have no need of added years. That man alone has got beyond necessities, and is discharged from service and free, who lives with his life completed.

passages.title: On being ready and willing to die
passages.text: I write you this letter in this frame of mind: as though death were going to call me away at the very moment of writing. I am ready to go, and I shall enjoy life for this reason, that I do not hang in too much suspense over how long this will last. Before old age I took care to live well; in old age I take care to die well. And to die well is to die willingly.

passages.title: On being ready and willing to die
passages.text: We must be prepared for death before we are prepared for life. Life is equipped well enough, but we are greedy for its equipment; something seems to us to be lacking, and always will seem so. That we have lived enough is brought about neither by years nor by days but by the mind. I have lived, dearest Lucilius, as much as was enough; having had my fill, I await death. Farewell.

passages.title: On an old man’s calm before death
passages.text: Death has a necessity that is fair and cannot be overcome: who can complain of being in a condition that no one is not in? And the first part of fairness is equality. But at this point it is needless to plead the case of nature, who wanted our law to be no other than her own: whatever she has put together she takes apart, and whatever she has taken apart she puts together again.

passages.title: On causes and the worth of studying nature
passages.text: The place that god holds in this world, the mind holds in a human being; what matter is there, the body is in us. So let the worse serve the better. Let us be brave against the things of chance; let us not tremble at wrongs, at wounds, at chains, at want. What is death? Either an end or a crossing. I am not afraid of ceasing, for it is the same as not having begun; nor of crossing over, because nowhere shall I be so cramped. Farewell.

passages.title: On reading and digesting what you read
passages.text: Whatever things seem to rise high in human affairs, though they are tiny and stand out by comparison with the lowest, are still reached by hard and steep paths. The road to the peak of rank is rough; but if you care to climb this summit, the one before which Fortune has lowered herself, you will indeed see beneath you everything that is counted as loftiest, and yet you will come to the top over level ground. Farewell.

passages.title: On old age and living each day fully
passages.text: So every day must be ordered as if it were bringing up the rear of the column, and were completing and filling out life. Whenever Pacuvius, who made Syria his own by right of possession, had made the offerings for the dead to himself with wine and those funeral feasts, he was carried from dinner to his bedroom in such a way that, amid the applause of his kept men, this was sung to music: “Life has been lived, life has been lived.”

passages.title: On old age and living each day fully
passages.text: There was no day on which he did not carry himself out for burial. What he used to do from a bad conscience let us do from a good one, and as we go to sleep let us say, glad and cheerful: “I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given.” If god adds a tomorrow, let us receive it gladly. The happiest man, and the untroubled owner of himself, is the one who waits for tomorrow without anxiety; whoever has said “I have lived” rises every day to a gain.

passages.title: On an old man’s calm before death
passages.text: This is a great thing, Lucilius, and one that has to be learned over a long time: to go away with an even mind when that hour which cannot be avoided draws near. Other kinds of death are mixed with hope: an illness comes to an end, a fire is put out, a falling building has set down the people it seemed about to crush; the sea has thrown out unharmed those it had swallowed, with the same force that was sucking them down; a soldier has drawn his sword back from the very neck of the man who was about to die. The man whom old age is leading to death has nothing to hope for; against this alone no one can step in. By no kind of death do people die more gently, but by none more slowly either.

passages.title: On an old man’s calm before death
passages.text: And further, if it has been anyone’s lot that old age should let him go gently, not torn suddenly from life but drawn away little by little, oh, that man truly ought to give thanks to all the gods that, having had his fill, he has been brought through to a rest that is necessary for a human being and welcome to a tired one. You see some people wishing for death, and indeed wishing for it more than people usually beg for life. I do not know which of the two I should think give us more courage, those who demand death or those who wait for it cheerful and quiet, since the first sometimes comes from frenzy and sudden indignation, while this calm comes from a settled judgment. Someone has come to death angry: no one has received death cheerfully when it came, except a man who had long made himself ready for it.

passages.title: On sudden death and living each day
passages.text: The greatest fault of life is that it is always unfinished, that some part of it is put off. The man who has put the finishing touch to his life every day is not in need of time. But from this need fear is born, and a craving for the future, one that eats away the mind. Nothing is more wretched than doubt about where the things that are coming will end up. The mind, anxious about how much is left or what kind of thing it is, is driven about by a fear that cannot be untangled.

passages.title: On finding true joy within
passages.text: There is no reason for you to think that these are few: they are nearly everyone. Some, indeed, begin just when they must stop. If you judge this a wonder, I will add something for you to wonder at more: some have stopped living before they began. Farewell.

passages.title: On lasting fame through philosophy
passages.text: A fathomless depth of time will come over us; few talents will lift their heads out and, though bound to depart some day into the same silence, will hold out against oblivion and will long assert their freedom. What Epicurus was able to promise his friend, this I promise you, Lucilius: I shall have favour with those who come after; I can bring out with me names that will last. Our Vergil promised everlasting memory to two men, and he is making it good: “Fortunate pair! If my songs have any power, no day shall ever take you out of time that remembers, so long as the house of Aeneas dwells beside the immovable rock of the Capitol and the Roman father holds the empire.”

passages.title: On Etna, virtue and late fame
passages.text: No virtue lies hidden, and to have lain hidden is not virtue’s own loss: a day will come to make public the virtue that was buried and held down by the spite of its own age. The man who thinks of the people of his own time is born for few. Many thousands of years, many thousands of peoples will come after: look to those. Even if envy has imposed silence on all who are alive with you, there will come those who judge without ill will, without favour. If virtue has any reward from fame, this does not perish either. The talk of those who come after will indeed not concern us at all; yet it will honour us and keep returning to us even though we do not feel it.

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: But even the man from whom this joy too is snatched away, the joy that comes from handling his greatest and last work, will leap down into death without any hesitation, content to act rightly and dutifully. Go further and set against him many things to dissuade him; say: “Your deed will be followed by early oblivion and by a less than grateful verdict from your fellow citizens.” He will answer you: “All those things lie outside my work; I am looking at the work itself. I know that this is honourable; so wherever it leads and calls, I come.”

passages.title: On excessive grief for a lost child
passages.text: But most people do not reckon up how much they have received, how much they have rejoiced. That grief has, among its other evils, this one: it is not only needless but ungrateful. So then, you had such a friend: is the effort wasted? In so many years, in so close a sharing of life, in so intimate a partnership of pursuits, was nothing achieved? Do you carry the friendship out to burial along with the friend? And why do you grieve at having lost him, if having had him does you no good? Believe me, a great part of those we have loved stays with us, even though chance has taken the people themselves away. The time that has gone by is ours, and nothing is in a safer place than what has been.

passages.title: On excessive grief for a lost child
passages.text: We are ungrateful for what we have received, out of hope for what is to come, as if what is to come, if it does turn out well for us, were not going to pass quickly into what is past. Whoever is glad only at what is present sets narrow bounds to the fruits of things. Both what is to come and what is past give delight, the one by expectation, the other by memory; but the one is in suspense and may not come about, while the other cannot not have been. What madness is it, then, to lose hold of what is surest? Let us rest in the things we have already drawn in, provided that we were not drawing them in with a mind full of holes, one that let through whatever it had received.

passages.title: On living philosophy without showing off
passages.text: Wild animals run from the dangers they see, and when they have escaped they are free from care: we are tormented both by what is coming and by what is past. Many of our good things do us harm: for memory brings back the torment of fear, and foresight takes it ahead of time. No one is made wretched by present things alone. Farewell.

claims.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, as those before me already are, and forgotten by all. All that I live is the present, an instant.
claims.shared: 8.4 and 12.15 say the same words, “you will be no one and nowhere”, one “in a little while” and the other “before long”. 8.4 and 7.16 both point to named men who are already gone. 3.10 and 12.19 both say that each person “lives only” the present.
claims.changed: The passages say “you” and “each person”; the claim says “I”. Hadrian and Augustus (8.4) and Chrysippus, Socrates and Epictetus (7.16) become “those before me”. 12.19 adds that the present is all a person loses; the claim leaves that out.

claims.t: I live what is left as someone already at the end of life, and I do, say and think each thing knowing that I may leave life at this very moment. I no longer let what rules in me be pulled about on strings, whether by unsocial impulse or by what produces the passions; I have in me something stronger and more divine than whatever pulls me so.
claims.shared: 7.31 and 1.16 both open with the same turn, “as someone who has died” and “as one already dying”, and 1.16 adds “you are old”. 1.16 and 12.15 share the image of being pulled about on strings, in 1.16 by unsocial impulse and in 12.15 by what produces the passions.
claims.changed: 7.31 says “has died”, 1.16 says “already dying” and “old”; the claim says “at the end of life” to cover both. 2.8 does not use the figure: it says only that leaving life is possible at this moment. 7.31 calls what is left “a surplus”, which the claim drops. The claim keeps each passage’s own name for what pulls: unsocial impulse (1.16), what produces the passions (12.15). It does not say that I am stronger than impulse as such; “whatever pulls me so” is 12.15’s “the things that … pull you about on strings”.

support.quote: As someone who has died and has lived out their life up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.
support.follows: I must count my life as lived and over, and live what remains as an extra, according to nature.

claims.t: Until the end comes, this is enough, and how long I do it does not matter: I steer the present towards two things, justice in what I do and being at peace with what is allotted to me. I leave the past behind and hand the future over to providence.
claims.shared: 12.1 and 4.21 both name “the present” as the thing to be steered or turned to profit, and both name justice. 12.1, 4.21 and 9.29 each set the same two things side by side: justice in what I do, and a good mind towards what is allotted or happens from outside. 5.27 and 6.21 both say “enough”; 4.21’s “content with” is the same Greek word, and it stands in the very sentence that names this pair.
claims.changed: Towards what is allotted, 12.1 says “love”, 4.21 “pleased” and 9.29 “freedom from disturbance”; the claim says “being at peace”, the least of the three. What 5.27 calls enough is its own list: to revere the gods, do good to people and bear with them. What 6.21 calls enough is hours spent treating people socially and calling on the gods.

support.quote: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present towards piety and justice

claims.t: I take death as nothing but a dissolving of the elements I am put together from; it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad. I wait for it cheerfully, whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere, and do not chafe at the delay.
claims.shared: 5.27 and 2.15 both say “wait” and “cheerful”: “You wait cheerfully” and “waiting for death with a cheerful mind”. 2.15 and 5.10 both call death a dissolving, and both tie it to nature: “according to nature” and “the natural dissolution”.
claims.changed: 5.27 leaves open what death is, an extinguishing or a move elsewhere; 2.15 and 5.10 call it a dissolution. The claim keeps both: it says how I take death, as 2.15 does (“as nothing other than”), and does not rule on what death is. 5.10 does not say “cheerfully”: it says to comfort oneself and not to chafe.

claims.t: I look down on human affairs as if from high above, and among them I stand kindly, without sneering at them. The things people prize are small and empty, and they do not last; being remembered is of no account, a name is a noise, and many will very quickly forget mine.
claims.shared: 9.29 and 12.18 both say to look down from above on human life. 5.27 and 7.3 both call what people take seriously “empty” and both use the picture of “little dogs”. 12.18 alone adds that it is all alike and short-lived.
claims.changed: 12.18 says that from above I “will despise” human affairs; 7.3 says to stand among them “kindly and without snorting at them”, which the claim puts as “without sneering at them”. The claim keeps the smallness of the things and the kindness towards the people, and leaves out the word “despise”. “They do not last” is 12.18’s “short-lived”.

support.quote: To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms

support.quote: Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.

support.quote: how many will very quickly forget it

claims.t: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living. My one fear is of living against nature: of never beginning to live according to it, or of doing what the make-up of a human being does not want.
claims.shared: Both passages narrow fear to one thing, and in both it is my own way of living measured against nature: 12.1 names “never beginning to live according to nature”, 7.16 “only one thing”, doing what “the constitution of a human being does not want”.
claims.changed: 12.1 says “fear” and 7.16 says “troubles me”; the claim says “fear” for both. “Living against nature” is the editor’s summary of the two. The translation’s “constitution” means how a human being is built; the claim says “make-up” so that it is not taken for this page’s own title. 7.16 adds doing a thing in the wrong way or at the wrong time, which the claim leaves out. 7.16 says nothing of death.

support.quote: what you fear is not some day ceasing to live but rather never beginning to live according to nature
support.follows: The thing to fear is not that life will stop one day, but never beginning to live according to nature.
gives: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living
My one fear is of living against nature

support.quote: Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.
support.follows: One thing alone troubles Marcus: doing what a human being’s make-up does not want, or doing it in the wrong way or at the wrong time.
