single.quote: Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.
single.label: Neither good nor bad
single.t: Death and life happen alike to good people and to bad, and they are neither honourable nor shameful. So death is neither good nor bad.
single.why: Only this passage argues from the fact that death comes to good and bad people alike. Other passages call death natural; none of them says that it is neither good nor bad.
single.follows: What happens alike to good and bad people is neither honourable nor shameful, so death and life are neither good nor bad.

single.quote: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead
single.label: Those who stumble
single.t: It is proper to me as a human being to love even those who stumble. This love comes if, at the moment they stumble, it strikes me that they are my kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, and that in a little while both of us will be dead.
single.why: Only this passage uses the nearness of death as a reason to love the person who wrongs me.
single.follows: I can love those who go wrong if I recall at that moment that they are kin, that they err unwillingly, and that we shall both soon be dead.

single.quote: At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them?
single.label: Those who complained
single.t: At each thing that happens, I picture the people to whom the same thing happened and who were vexed and complained. They are nowhere now, and I do not want to be like them.
single.why: Only this passage makes the dead into an exercise for the moment something happens. 8.4 and 7.16 name the dead and give no exercise.
single.follows: When something happens I should picture those who complained of the same thing, who are now nowhere, and not wish to be like them.

single.quote: You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.
single.label: Coming back to life
single.t: I can come back to life, and the way is to see things again as I used to see them.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of coming back to life. The 1634 passage leaves out the first half of the chapter, which is about principles dying when the impressions behind them go out; reading “life” here as the life of those principles leans on that half.
single.follows: Coming back to life is possible, and it consists in seeing things again as I used to see them.

single.quote: What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.
single.label: Clinging to life
single.t: When I ask what it is I want (to breathe, to have sensation and impulse, to use my voice, to think), I ask whether any of these is worth longing for. If each of them is easy to despise, I go on to the one thing left, following reason and god. To value breathing, sensing and thinking, and to be vexed that death will take them from me, conflicts with following reason and god.
single.why: Only this passage lists what death takes away and asks whether any of it is worth longing for. It shows what failing looks like: valuing these things and being vexed at losing them. “Conflicts with that” follows the translation, which supplies “with that” (following reason and god); the translators’ note gives another way of reading the sentence.
single.follows: If breathing, sensing, speaking and thinking are each easy to despise, being vexed that death takes them conflicts with following reason and god.

single.quote: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence?
single.label: With gods or without
single.t: If there are gods, leaving human life is nothing to fear, for they would not throw me into anything bad. If there are none, or they do not care about human affairs, then living on in a universe empty of gods or of providence is worth nothing to me.
single.why: Only this passage sets out both cases, gods or none. Marcus goes on to say that the gods do exist and do care; the two cases are kept here as what holds if I doubt it.
single.follows: Leaving life is nothing to fear if gods exist; and if they do not, or do not care, there is nothing in such a universe to stay for.

members.text:
Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now
enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness.
And that will be, if thou shalt forget all that is past, and for the
future, refer thyself wholly to the Divine Providence, and shalt bend
and apply all thy present thoughts and intentions to holiness and
righteousness. To holiness, in accepting willingly whatsoever is sent
by the Divine Providence, as being that which the nature of the universe
hath appointed unto thee, which also hath appointed thee for that,
whatsoever it be. To righteousness, in speaking the truth freely, and
without ambiguity; and in doing all things justly and discreetly. Now in
this good course, let not other men's either wickedness, or opinion, or
voice hinder thee: no, nor the sense of this thy pampered mass of flesh:
for let that which suffers, look to itself. If therefore whensoever the
time of thy departing shall come, thou shalt readily leave all things,
and shalt respect thy mind only, and that divine part of thine, and this
shall be thine only fear, not that some time or other thou shalt cease
to live, but thou shalt never begin to live according to nature: then
shalt thou be a man indeed, worthy of that world, from which thou hadst
thy beginning; then shalt thou cease to be a stranger in thy country,
and to wonder at those things that happen daily, as things strange and
unexpected, and anxiously to depend of divers things that are not in thy
power.
members.english: All those things you pray to reach by a roundabout road you can have already, if you do not begrudge yourself. That is: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present towards piety and justice. Piety, so that you love what is allotted, for nature brought it to you and you to it. Justice, so that, freely and without winding about, you speak the truth and do what accords with law and with what each deserves. And do not be hindered by another person’s badness, or judgment, or voice, or even by the sensation of the bit of flesh that has grown up around you, for the part that suffers will see to that. So if, whenever it is that you come close to your exit, you leave everything else behind and honour only your ruling part and what is divine in you, and if what you fear is not some day ceasing to live but rather never beginning to live according to nature, then you will be a human being worthy of the universe that gave you birth. You will stop being a stranger in your own country, stop wondering at what happens every day as if it were unexpected, and stop hanging on this and that.
members.greek: Πάντα ἐκεῖνα, ἐφ’ ἃ διὰ περιόδου εὔχῃ ἐλθεῖν, ἤδη ἔχειν δύνασαι, ἐὰν μὴ σαυτῷ φθονῇς. τοῦτο δέ ἐστιν, ἐὰν πᾶν τὸ παρελθὸν καταλίπῃς καὶ τὸ μέλλον ἐπιτρέψῃς τῇ προνοίᾳ καὶ τὸ παρὸν μόνον ἀπευθύνῃς πρὸς ὁσιότητα καὶ δικαιοσύνην. ὁσιότητα μέν, ἵνα φιλῇς τὸ ἀπονεμόμενον· σοὶ γὰρ αὐτὸ ἡ φύσις ἔφερε καὶ σὲ τούτῳ· δικαιοσύνην δέ, ἵνα ἐλευθέρως καὶ χωρὶς περιπλοκῆς λέγῃς τε τἀληθῆ καὶ πράσσῃς τὰ κατὰ νόμον καὶ κατ’ ἀξίαν· μὴ ἐμποδίζῃ δέ σε μήτε κακία ἀλλοτρία μήτε ὑπόληψις μήτε φωνὴ μηδὲ μὴν αἴσθησις τοῦ περιτεθραμμένου σοι σαρκιδίου· ὄψεται γὰρ τὸ πάσχον. ἐὰν οὖν, ὅτε δήποτε πρὸς ἐξόδῳ γένῃ, πάντα τὰ ἄλλα καταλιπὼν μόνον τὸ ἡγεμονικόν σου καὶ τὸ ἐν σοὶ θεῖον τιμήσῃς καὶ μὴ τὸ παύσεσθαί ποτε τοῦ ζῆν φοβηθῇς, ἀλλὰ τό γε μηδέποτε ἄρξασθαι κατὰ φύσιν ζῆν, ἔσῃ ἄνθρωπος ἄξιος τοῦ γεννήσαντος κόσμου καὶ παύσῃ ξένος ὢν τῆς πατρίδος καὶ θαυμάζων ὡς ἀπροσδόκητα τὰ καθ’ ἡμέραν γινόμενα καὶ κρεμάμενος ἐκ τοῦδε καὶ τοῦδε.

members.text:
From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold
here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of
navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the
general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now
first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that
are together; and some other things that are at their last. Their lives
also, who were long ago, and theirs who shall be hereafter, and the
present estate and life of those many nations of barbarians that are
now in the world, thou must likewise consider in thy mind. And how many
there be, who never so much as heard of thy name, how many that will
soon forget it; how many who but even now did commend thee, within a
very little while perchance will speak ill of thee. So that neither
fame, nor honour, nor anything else that this world doth afford, is
worth the while. The sum then of all; whatsoever doth happen unto thee,
whereof God is the cause, to accept it contentedly: whatsoever thou
doest, whereof thou thyself art the cause, to do it justly: which will
be, if both in thy resolution and in thy action thou have no further
end, than to do good unto others, as being that, which by thy natural
constitution, as a man, thou art bound unto.
members.english:
To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms, and on the differences among those coming to be, coming together, and passing away. Think too of the life lived long ago by others, the life that will be lived after you, and the life being lived now among the barbarian peoples; and how many do not even know your name, how many will very quickly forget it, how many who perhaps praise you now will very quickly blame you; and that neither being remembered is of any account, nor reputation, nor anything else at all.

Freedom from disturbance about the things that happen from the cause outside; justice in the things done through the cause that comes from you. That is, impulse and action ending in just this, acting socially, as being what is according to nature for you.
members.greek:
Ἄνωθεν ἐπιθεωρεῖν ἀγέλας μυρίας καὶ τελετὰς μυρίας καὶ πλοῦν παντοῖον ἐν χειμῶσι καὶ γαλήναις καὶ διαφορὰς γινομένων, συγγινομένων, ἀπογινομένων. ἐπινόει δὲ καὶ τὸν ὑπ’ ἄλλων πάλαι βεβιωμένον βίον καὶ τὸν μετὰ σὲ βιωθησόμενον καὶ τὸν νῦν ἐν τοῖς βαρβάροις ἔθνεσι βιούμενον· καὶ ὅσοι μὲν οὐδὲ ὄνομά σου γινώσκουσιν, ὅσοι δὲ τάχιστα ἐπιλήσονται, ὅσοι δ’ ἐπαινοῦντες ἴσως νῦν σε τάχιστα ψέξουσι· καὶ ὡς οὔτε ἡ μνήμη ἀξιόλογόν γε οὔτε ἡ δόξα οὔτε ἄλλο τι τὸ σύμπαν.

Ἀταραξία μὲν περὶ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς ἐκτὸς αἰτίας συμβαίνοντα, δικαιότης δὲ ἐν τοῖς παρὰ τὴν ἐκ σοῦ αἰτίαν ἐνεργουμένοις· τουτέστιν, ὁρμὴ καὶ πρᾶξις καταλήγουσα ἐπ’ αὐτὸ τὸ κοινωνικῶς πρᾶξαι ὡς τοῦτό σοι κατὰ φύσιν ὄν.

members.text:
As one who had lived, and were now to die by right, whatsoever is
yet remaining, bestow that wholly as a gracious overplus upon a virtuous
life. Love and affect that only, whatsoever it be that happeneth, and is
by the fates appointed unto thee. For what can be more reasonable? And
as anything doth happen unto thee by way of cross, or calamity, call
to mind presently and set before thine eyes, the examples of some other
men, to whom the self-same thing did once happen likewise. Well, what
did they? They grieved; they wondered; they complained. And where are
they now? All dead and gone. Wilt thou also be like one of them?
Or rather leaving to men of the world (whose life both in regard of
themselves, and them that they converse with, is nothing but mere
mutability; or men of as fickle minds, as fickle bodies; ever changing
and soon changed themselves) let it be thine only care and study, how to
make a right use of all such accidents. For there is good use to be made
of them, and they will prove fit matter for thee to work upon, if it
shall be both thy care and thy desire, that whatsoever thou doest, thou
thyself mayst like and approve thyself for it. And both these, see,
that thou remember well, according as the diversity of the matter of
the action that thou art about shall require. Look within; within is the
fountain of all good. Such a fountain, where springing waters can never
fail, so thou dig still deeper and deeper.
members.english:
As someone who has died and has lived out their life up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.

To love only what happens to oneself and is spun into one’s own thread. For what fits better?

At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them? Do you not rather want to leave the turns that belong to others to those who turn and are turned, and yourself to be wholly taken up with how to use the things that happen? For you will use them well, and they will be material for you. Only pay attention, and want to be honourable in your own eyes in everything you do; and remember both things, for what the action is done on also makes a difference.

Dig within. Within is the spring of the good, and it can always well up, if you always dig.
members.greek:
Ὡς ἀποτεθνηκότα δεῖ καὶ μέχρι νῦν βεβιωκότα τὸ λοιπὸν ἐκ τοῦ περιόντος ζῆσαι κατὰ τὴν φύσιν.

Μόνως φιλεῖν τὸ ἑαυτῷ συμβαῖνον καὶ συγκλωθόμενον· τί γὰρ ἁρμοδιώτερον;

Ἐφ’ ἑκάστου συμβάματος ἐκείνους πρὸ ὀμμάτων ἔχειν, οἷς τὰ αὐτὰ συνέβαινεν, ἔπειτα ἤχθοντο, ἐξενίζοντο, ἐμέμφοντο· νῦν οὗν ἐκεῖνοι ποῦ; οὐδαμοῦ. τί οὖν; καὶ σὺ θέλεις ὁμοίως; οὐχὶ δὲ τὰς μὲν ἀλλοτρίας τροπὰς καταλιπεῖν τοῖς τρέπουσι καὶ τρεπομένοις, αὐτὸς δὲ περὶ τὸ πῶς χρῆσθαι αὐτοῖς ὅλος γίνεσθαι; χρήσῃ γὰρ καλῶς καὶ ὕλη σοι ἔσται, μόνον πρόσεχε καὶ θέλε σεαυτῷ καλὸς εἶναι ἐπὶ παντός, οὖ πράσσεις, καὶ μέμνησο ἀμφοτέρων, ὅτι καὶ διάφορον ἐφ’ οὗ ἡ πρᾶξις.

Ἔνδον σκάπτε, ἔνδον ἡ πηγὴ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ ἀεὶ ἀναβλύειν δυναμένη, ἐὰν ἀεὶ σκάπτῃς.

members.text:
Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a
sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name.
And what is that but an empty sound, and a rebounding echo? Those things
which in this life are dearest unto us, and of most account, they are in
themselves but vain, putrid, contemptible. The most weighty and serious,
if rightly esteemed, but as puppies, biting one another: or untoward
children, now laughing and then crying. As for faith, and modesty, and
justice, and truth, they long since, as one of the poets hath it, have
abandoned this spacious earth, and retired themselves unto heaven. What
is it then that doth keep thee here, if things sensible be so mutable
and unsettled? and the senses so obscure, and so fallible? and our souls
nothing but an exhalation of blood? and to be in credit among such,
be but vanity? What is it that thou dost stay for? an extinction, or a
translation; either of them with a propitious and contented mind. But
still that time come, what will content thee? what else, but to worship
and praise the Gods; and to do good unto men. To bear with them, and
to forbear to do them any wrong. And for all external things belonging
either to this thy wretched body, or life, to remember that they are
neither thine, nor in thy power.
members.english: Any moment now, ash or a skeleton, and either a name or not even a name; and the name is a noise and an echo. The things highly prized in life are empty and rotten and small, little dogs biting one another, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying. But good faith, a sense of shame, justice and truth: “to Olympus from the earth of the wide ways.” What is there, then, that still holds one here, seeing that the things the senses perceive change easily and do not stand still, the organs of sense are dim and easily take false imprints, the little soul itself is a vapour rising from blood, and a good name among such people is empty? What then? You wait cheerfully for what is either an extinguishing or a move elsewhere. And until the right time for that is at hand, what is enough? What else but to revere the gods and speak well of them, to do good to human beings, to bear with them and to hold back; and, as for everything inside the limits of the bit of flesh and the little breath, to remember that it is neither yours nor up to you.
members.greek: Ὅσον οὐδέπω σποδὸς ἢ σκελετὸς καὶ ἤτοι ὄνομα ἢ οὐδὲ ὄνομα, τὸ δὲ ὄνομα ψόφος καὶ ἀπήχημα. τὰ δὲ ἐν τῷ βίῳ πολυτίμητα κενὰ καὶ σαπρὰ καὶ μικρὰ καὶ κυνίδια διαδακνόμενα καὶ παιδία φιλόνεικα, γελῶντα, εἶτα εὐθὺς κλαίοντα· πίστις δὲ καὶ αἰδὼς καὶ δίκη καὶ ἀλήθεια πρὸς Ὄλυμπον ἀπὸ χθονὸς εὐρυοδείης. τί οὖν ἔτι τὸ ἐνταῦθα κατέχον, εἴ γε τὰ μὲν αἰσθητὰ εὐμετάβλητα καὶ οὐχ ἑστῶτα, τὰ δὲ αἰσθητήρια ἀμυδρὰ καὶ εὐπαρατύπωτα, αὐτὸ δὲ τὸ ψυχάριον ἀναθυμίασις ἀφ’ αἵματος, τὸ δὲ εὐδοκιμεῖν παρὰ τοιούτοις κενόν; τί οὖν; περιμένεις ἵλεως τὴν εἴτε σβέσιν εἴτε μετάστασιν· ἕως δὲ ἐκείνης ὁ καιρὸς ἐφίσταται, τί ἀρκεῖ; τί δὲ ἄλλο ἢ θεοὺς μὲν σέβειν καὶ εὐφημεῖν, ἀνθρώπους δὲ εὖ ποιεῖν καὶ ἀνέχεσθαι αὐτῶν καὶ ἀπέχεσθαι· ὅσα δὲ ἐντὸς ὅρων τοῦ κρεᾳδίου καὶ τοῦ πνευματίου, ταῦτα μεμνῆσθαι μήτε σὰ ὄντα μήτε ἐπὶ σοί.

members.text:
Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do,
and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very
present depart out of this life. And as for death, if there be any gods,
it is no grievous thing to leave the society of men. The gods will do
thee no hurt, thou mayest be sure. But if it be so that there be no
gods, or that they take no care of the world, why should I desire to
live in a world void of gods, and of all divine providence? But gods
there be certainly, and they take care for the world; and as for those
things which be truly evil, as vice and wickedness, such things they
have put in a man's own power, that he might avoid them if he would: and
had there been anything besides that had been truly bad and evil, they
would have had a care of that also, that a man might have avoided it.
But why should that be thought to hurt and prejudice a man's life in
this world, which cannot any ways make man himself the better, or the
worse in his own person? Neither must we think that the nature of the
universe did either through ignorance pass these things, or if not as
ignorant of them, yet as unable either to prevent, or better to order
and dispose them. It cannot be that she through want either of power or
skill, should have committed such a thing, so as to suffer all things
both good and bad, equally and promiscuously, to happen unto all both
good and bad. As for life therefore, and death, honour and dishonour,
labour and pleasure, riches and poverty, all these things happen
unto men indeed, both good and bad, equally; but as things which of
themselves are neither good nor bad; because of themselves, neither
shameful nor praiseworthy.
members.english: To do and say and think each thing in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment. As for going away from among human beings: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence? But they do exist, and they do care about human affairs; and they have put it wholly in a person’s own power not to fall into the things that are truly bad. And if any of the rest were bad, they would have provided for that too, so that it would be in everyone’s power not to fall into it. But what does not make a human being worse, how could that make a human being’s life worse? The nature of the whole would not have overlooked these things, either through ignorance or because, though it knew, it could not guard against them beforehand or set them right; nor would it have made so great a mistake, through lack of power or lack of skill, that good things and bad things happen alike and in a jumble to good people and to bad. Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.
members.greek: Ὡς ἤδη δυνατοῦ ὄντος ἐξιέναι τοῦ βίου, οὕτως ἕκαστα ποιεῖν καὶ λέγειν καὶ διανοεῖσθαι. τὸ δὲ ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀπελθεῖν, εἰ μὲν θεοὶ εἰσίν, οὐδὲν δεινόν· κακῷ γάρ σε οὐκ ἂν περιβάλοιεν· εἰ δὲ ἤτοι οὐκ εἰσὶν ἢ οὐ μέλει αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀνθρωπείων, τί μοι ζῆν ἐν κόσμῳ κενῷ θεῶν ἢ προνοίας κενῷ; ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰσὶ καὶ μέλει αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀνθρωπείων καὶ τοῖς μὲν κατ’ ἀλήθειαν κακοῖς ἵνα μὴ περιπίπτῃ ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ἐπ’ αὐτῷ τὸ πᾶν ἔθεντο· τῶν δὲ λοιπῶν εἴ τι κακὸν ἦν, καὶ τοῦτο ἂν προείδοντο, ἵνα ἐπὶ παντὶ ᾖ τὸ μὴ περιπίπτειν αὐτῷ. ὃ δὲ χείρω μὴ ποιεῖ ἄνθρωπον, πῶς ἂν τοῦτο βίον ἀνθρώπου χείρω ποιήσειεν; οὔτε δὲ κατ’ ἄγνοιαν οὔτε εἰδυῖα μέν, μὴ δυναμένη δὲ προφυλάξασθαι ἢ διορθώσασθαι ταῦτα ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις παρεῖδεν ἄν, οὔτ’ ἂν τηλικοῦτον ἥμαρτεν ἤτοι παρ’ ἀδυναμίαν ἢ παρ’ ἀτεχνίαν, ἵνα τὰ ἀγαθὰ καὶ τὰ κακὰ ἐπίσης τοῖς τε ἀγαθοῖς ἀνθρώποις καὶ τοῖς κακοῖς πεφυρμένως συμβαίνῃ. θάνατος δέ γε καὶ ζωή, δόξα καὶ ἀδοξία, πόνος καὶ ἡδονή, πλοῦτος καὶ πενία, πάντα ταῦτα ἐπίσης συμβαίνει ἀνθρώπων τοῖς τε ἀγαθοῖς καὶ τοῖς κακοῖς, οὔτε καλὰ ὄντα οὔτε αἰσχρά. οὔτ’ ἄρ’ ἀγαθὰ οὔτε κακά ἐστι.

members.text:
Through the substance of the universe, as through a torrent pass
all particular bodies, being all of the same nature, and all joint
workers with the universe itself as in one of our bodies so many
members among themselves. How many such as Chrysippus, how many such
as Socrates, how many such as Epictetus, hath the age of the world
long since swallowed up and devoured? Let this, be it either men or
businesses, that thou hast occasion to think of, to the end that thy
thoughts be not distracted and thy mind too earnestly set upon anything,
upon every such occasion presently come to thy mind. Of all my thoughts
and cares, one only thing shall be the object, that I myself do nothing
which to the proper constitution of man, (either in regard of the
thing itself, or in regard of the manner, or of the time of doing,)
is contrary. The time when thou shalt have forgotten all things, is
at hand. And that time also is at hand, when thou thyself shalt be
forgotten by all. Whilst thou art, apply thyself to that especially
which unto man as he is a mart, is most proper and agreeable, and that
is, for a man even to love them that transgress against him. This shall
be, if at the same time that any such thing doth happen, thou call
to mind, that they are thy kinsmen; that it is through ignorance and
against their wills that they sin; and that within a very short while
after, both thou and he shall be no more. But above all things, that he
hath not done thee any hurt; for that by him thy mind and understanding
is not made worse or more vile than it was before.
members.english:
All bodies pass through and out of the substance of the whole, as through a winter torrent, grown together with the whole and working with it, as our limbs do with one another. How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down. Let the same thought strike you about any human being whatever and any thing.

Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.

Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all.

It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead, and above all that the person has not harmed you, for that person has not made your ruling part worse than it was before.
members.greek:
Διὰ τῆς τῶν ὅλων οὐσίας ὡς διὰ χειμάρρου διεκπορεύεται πάντα τὰ σώματα, τῷ ὅλῳ συμφυῆ καὶ συνεργὰ ὡς τὰ ἡμέτερα μέλη ἀλλήλοις. πόσους ἤδη ὁ αἰὼν Χρυσίππους, πόσους Σωκράτεις, πόσους Ἐπικτήτους καταπέπωκε. τὸ δ’ αὐτὸ καὶ ἐπὶ παντὸς οὑτινοσοῦν σοι ἀνθρώπου τε καὶ πράγματος προσπιπτέτω.

Ἐμὲ ἓν μόνον περισπᾷ, μή τι αὐτὸς ποιήσω, ὃ ἡ κατασκευὴ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐ θέλει ἢ ὡς οὐ θέλει ἢ ὃ νῦν οὐ θέλει.

Ἐγγὺς μὲν ἡ σὴ περὶ πάντων λήθη, ἐγγὺς δὲ ἡ πάντων περὶ σοῦ λήθη.

Ἴδιον ἀνθρώπου φιλεῖν καὶ τοὺς πταίοντας. τοῦτο δὲ γίνεται, ἐὰν συμπροσπίπτῃ σοι, ὅτι καὶ συγγενεῖς καὶ δι’ ἄγνοιαν καὶ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι καὶ ὡς μετ’ ὀλίγον ἀμφότεροι τεθνήξεσθε, καὶ πρὸ πάντων, ὅτι οὐκ ἔβλαψέ σε· οὐ γὰρ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν σου χεῖρον ἐποίησεν ἢ πρόσθεν ἦν.

members.text:
It is high time for thee, to understand that there is somewhat in
thee, better and more divine than either thy passions, or thy sensual
appetites and affections. What is now the object of my mind, is it fear,
or suspicion, or lust, or any such thing? To do nothing rashly without
some certain end; let that be thy first care. The next, to have no other
end than the common good. For, alas! yet a little while, and thou art no
more: no more will any, either of those things that now thou seest, or
of those men that now are living, be any more. For all things are by
nature appointed soon to be changed, turned, and corrupted, that other
things might succeed in their room.
members.english:
Notice at last that you have in yourself something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and that, in a word, pull you about on strings. What is my thought at this moment? Can it be fear? Suspicion? Desire? Anything else of that kind?

First, not at random and not without a point of reference. Second, to take as the point of reference nothing other than the social end.

That before long you will be no one and nowhere, and neither will any of the things you now see, nor any of the people now living. For it is the nature of all things to change, to turn and to perish, so that other things may come to be after them.

members.text:
These three things thou must have always in a readiness: first
concerning thine own actions, whether thou doest nothing either idly,
or otherwise, than justice and equity do require: and concerning those
things that happen unto thee externally, that either they happen unto
thee by chance, or by providence; of which two to accuse either, is
equally against reason. Secondly, what like unto our bodies are
whilest yet rude and imperfect, until they be animated: and from their
animation, until their expiration: of what things they are compounded,
and into what things they shall be dissolved. Thirdly, how vain all
things will appear unto thee when, from on high as it were, looking
down thou shalt contemplate all things upon earth, and the wonderful
mutability, that they are subject unto: considering withal, the infinite
both greatness and variety of things aerial and things celestial that
are round about it. And that as often as thou shalt behold them, thou
shalt still see the same: as the same things, so the same shortness of
continuance of all those things. And, behold, these be the things that
we are so proud and puffed up for.
members.english: These three things must be kept ready to hand. About what you do: whether it is done neither at random nor otherwise than Justice herself would have acted. About what happens from outside: that it comes either by chance or by providence, and that one must neither blame chance nor bring a charge against providence. Second: what each thing is like from seed to the receiving of a soul, and from the receiving of a soul to the giving back of the soul; and out of what kind of things it is put together and into what kind of things it is dissolved. Third: that if you were suddenly lifted high into the air and looked down on human affairs and their many turns, you will despise them, seeing at the same time how much there is that dwells all around, in the air and in the ether; and that however often you are lifted up, you will see the same things: how alike in kind, how short-lived. And over these things, the puffed-up pride.
members.greek: Τρία ταῦτα δεῖ πρόχειρα ἔχειν· ἐπὶ μὲν ὧν ποιεῖς, εἰ μήτε εἰκῇ μήτε ἄλλως ἢ ὡς ἂν ἡ Δίκη αὐτὴ ἐνήργησεν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἔξωθεν συμβαινόντων, ὅτι ἤτοι κατ’ ἐπιτυχίαν ἢ κατὰ πρόνοιαν· οὔτε δὲ τῇ ἐπιτυχίᾳ μεμπτέον οὔτε τῇ προνοίᾳ ἐγκλητέον. δεύτερον τό· ὁποῖον ἕκαστον ἀπὸ σπέρματος μέχρι ψυχώσεως καὶ ἀπὸ ψυχώσεως μέχρι τοῦ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀποδοῦναι καὶ ἐξ οἵων ἡ σύγκρισις καὶ εἰς οἷα ἡ λύσις. τρίτον, εἰ ἄφνω μετέωρος ἐξαρθεὶς κατασκέψαιο τὰ ἀνθρώπεια καὶ τὴν πολυτροπίαν, ὅτι καταφρονήσεις συνιδὼν ἅμα καὶ ὅσον τὸ περιοικοῦν ἐναερίων καὶ ἐναιθερίων· καὶ ὅτι, ὁσάκις ἂν ἐξαρθῇς, ταὐτὰ ὄψῃ, τὸ ὁμοειδές, τὸ ὀλιγοχρόνιον. ἐπὶ τούτοις ὁ τῦφος.

members.text:
Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with
those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of
this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented
and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action,
and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with
thee. Thou hast had experience of that other kind of life: make now
trial of this also. Trouble not thyself any more henceforth, reduce
thyself unto perfect simplicity. Doth any man offend? It is against
himself that he doth offend: why should it trouble thee? Hath anything
happened unto thee? It is well, whatsoever it be, it is that which
of all the common chances of the world from the very beginning in the
series of all other things that have, or shall happen, was destinated
and appointed unto thee. To comprehend all in a few words, our life is
short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion
and justice. Use recreation with sobriety.
members.english:
Try how the life of the good person, too, goes for you: the person who is pleased with what is allotted from the whole and content with their own action being just and their disposition kind.

You have seen those things; look at these too. Do not disturb yourself: make yourself simple. Someone does wrong? They do wrong to themselves. Something has happened to you? That is well: everything that happens was, from the beginning, fated along with you out of the whole and spun into your thread. In sum, life is short. The present must be turned to profit, with good reasoning and justice. Be sober, without strain.
members.greek:
Πείρασον πῶς σοι χωρεῖ καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἀνθρώπου βίος τοῦ ἀρεσκομένου μὲν τοῖς ἐκ τῶν ὅλων ἀπονεμομένοις, ἀρκουμένου δὲ τῇ ἰδίᾳ πράξει δικαίᾳ καὶ διαθέσει εὐμενεῖ.

Ἑώρακας ἐκεῖνα, ἴδε καὶ ταῦτα. σεαυτὸν μὴ τάρασσε· ἅπλωσον σεαυτόν. ἁμαρτάνει τις; ἑαυτῷ ἁμαρτάνει. συμβέβηκέ σοί τι ; καλῶς· ἐκ τῶν ὅλων ἀπʼ ἀρχῆς σοι συγκαθείμαρτο καὶ συνεκλώθετο πᾶν τὸ συμβαῖνον. τὸ δ’ ὅλον, βραχὺς ὁ βίος· κερδαντέον τὸ παρὸν σὺν εὐλογιστίᾳ καὶ δίκῃ. νῆφε ἀνειμένως.

members.text:
Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in
her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding
anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a
rational creature. The end and object of a rational constitution is, to
do nothing rashly, to be kindly affected towards men, and in all things
willingly to submit unto the gods. Casting therefore all other things
aside, keep thyself to these few, and remember withal that no man
properly can be said to live more than that which is now present, which
is but a moment of time. Whatsoever is besides either is already past,
or uncertain. The time therefore that any man doth live, is but a
little, and the place where he liveth, is but a very little corner of
the earth, and the greatest fame that can remain of a man after his
death, even that is but little, and that too, such as it is whilst it
is, is by the succession of silly mortal men preserved, who likewise
shall shortly die, and even whiles they live know not what in very deed
they themselves are: and much less can know one, who long before is dead
and gone.
members.english:
Revere the power of forming judgments. Everything lies in this, that there should no longer arise in your ruling part a judgment that does not follow nature and the constitution of the rational animal. And this promises freedom from haste, affinity with human beings, and following the gods.

So throw everything away and hold on to only these few things; and remember as well that each person lives only this present, an instant. The rest has either been lived or is uncertain. Small, then, is what each person lives, and small the little corner of the earth where they live; small too is even the longest fame after death, and even that is handed down through a line of little human beings who will die very soon and who do not know even themselves, let alone someone who died long ago.
members.greek:
Τὴν ὑποληπτικὴν δύναμιν σέβε. ἐν ταύτῃ τὸ πᾶν, ἵνα ὑπόληψις τῷ ἡγεμονικῷ σου μηκέτι ἐγγένηται ἀνακόλουθος τῇ φύσει καὶ τῇ τοῦ λογικοῦ ζῴου κατασκευῇ, αὕτη δὲ ἐπαγγέλλεται ἀπροπτωσίαν καὶ τὴν πρὸς ἀνθρώπους οἰκείωσιν καὶ τὴν τοῖς θεοῖς ἀκολουθίαν.

Πάντα οὖν ῥίψας ταῦτα μόνα τὰ ὀλίγα σύνεχε καὶ ἔτι συμμνημόνευε, ὅτι μόνον ζῇ ἕκαστος τὸ παρὸν τοῦτο, τὸ ἀκαριαῖον· τὰ δὲ ἄλλα ἢ βεβίωται ἢ ἐν ἀδήλῳ, μικρὸν μὲν οὖν ὃ ζῇ ἕκαστος· μικρὸν δὲ τὸ τῆς γῆς γωνίδιον ὅπου ζῇ· μικρὸν δὲ καὶ ἡ μηκίστη ὑστεροφημία καὶ αὕτη δὲ κατὰ διαδοχὴν ἀνθρωπαρίων τάχιστα τεθνηξομένων καὶ οὐκ εἰδότων οὐδὲ ἑαυτοὺς οὐδέ γε τὸν πρόπαλαι τεθνηκότα.

members.text:
What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang
thyself. First; let it not trouble thee. For all things both good and
evil: come to pass according to the nature and general condition of the
universe, and within a very little while, all things will be at an
end; no man will be remembered: as now of Africanus (for example) and
Augustus it is already come to pass. Then secondly; fix thy mind upon
the thing itself; look into it, and remembering thyself, that thou art
bound nevertheless to be a good man, and what it is that thy nature
requireth of thee as thou art a man, be not diverted from what thou art
about, and speak that which seemeth unto thee most just: only speak it
kindly, modestly, and without hypocrisy.
members.english:
That they will do the same things none the less, even if you burst.

First, do not be disturbed: for all things are according to the nature of the whole, and in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian is not, nor Augustus. Next, fix your eyes on the matter and see it; and, remembering as well that you must be a good human being and what the nature of a human being demands, do that without turning aside, and speak as seems to you most just: only kindly, modestly and without pretence.
members.greek:
Ὅτι οὐδὲν ἧττον τὰ αὐτὰ ποιήσουσι, κἂν σὺ διαρραγῇς.

Τὸ πρῶτον μὴ ταράσσου· πάντα γὰρ κατὰ τὴν τοῦ ὅλου φύσιν καὶ ὀλίγου χρόνου οὐδεὶς οὐδαμοῦ ἔσῃ, ὥσπερ οὐδὲ Ἁδριανὸς οὐδὲ Αὔγουστος. ἔπειτα ἀτενίσας εἰς τὸ πρᾶγμα ἴδε αὐτὸ καὶ συμμνημονεύσας ὅτι ἀγαθόν σε ἄνθρωπον εἶναι δεῖ καὶ τί τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἡ φύσις ἀπαιτεῖ, πρᾶξον τοῦτο ἀμεταστρεπτὶ καὶ εἰπέ, ὡς δικαιότατον φαίνεταί σοι· μόνον εὐμενῶς καὶ αἰδημόνως καὶ ἀνυποκρίτως.

members.text:
The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever
flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body
tending to corruption. His soul is restless, fortune uncertain, and fame
doubtful; to be brief, as a stream so are all things belonging to the
body; as a dream, or as a smoke, so are all that belong unto the soul.
Our life is a warfare, and a mere pilgrimage. Fame after life is no
better than oblivion. What is it then that will adhere and follow? Only
one thing, philosophy. And philosophy doth consist in this, for a man to
preserve that spirit which is within him, from all manner of contumelies
and injuries, and above all pains or pleasures; never to do anything
either rashly, or feignedly, or hypocritically: wholly to depend from
himself and his own proper actions: all things that happen unto him to
embrace contentedly, as coming from Him from whom he himself also came;
and above all things, with all meekness and a calm cheerfulness, to
expect death, as being nothing else but the resolution of those
elements, of which every creature is composed. And if the elements
themselves suffer nothing by this their perpetual conversion of one into
another, that dissolution, and alteration, which is so common unto all,
why should it be feared by any? Is not this according to nature? But
nothing that is according to nature can be evil.

_Whilst I was at Carnuntum._
members.english: In human life, the time is a point, the substance is in flux, perception is dim, the compound of the whole body is ready to rot, the soul is a whirl, fortune is hard to make out, fame is undiscerning. To put it briefly: everything of the body is a river, everything of the soul is a dream and smoke, life is a war and a stranger’s stay abroad, and fame after death is forgetting. What, then, can escort a person through? One thing and only one: philosophy. And this lies in keeping the spirit within free from abuse and unharmed, stronger than pleasures and pains, doing nothing at random, nothing falsely or with pretence, not needing another person to do something or not do it; and further, accepting what happens and what is allotted as coming from that same place, wherever it is, from which the spirit itself came; and, on top of all this, waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living thing is put together. And if for the elements themselves there is nothing terrible in each one continually changing into another, why should anyone look with suspicion on the change and dissolution of all? For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad. At Carnuntum.
members.greek: Τοῦ ἀνθρωπίνου βίου ὁ μὲν χρόνος στιγμή, ἡ δὲ οὐσία ῥέουσα, ἡ δὲ αἴσθησις ἀμυδρά, ἡ δὲ ὅλου τοῦ σώματος σύγκρισις εὔσηπτος, ἡ δὲ ψυχὴ ῥόμβος, ἡ δὲ τύχη δυστέκμαρτον, ἡ δὲ φήμη ἄκριτον· συνελόντι δὲ εἰπεῖν, πάντα τὰ μὲν τοῦ σώματος ποταμός, τὰ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς ὄνειρος καὶ τῦφος, ὁ δὲ βίος πόλεμος καὶ ξένου ἐπιδημία, ἡ δὲ ὑστεροφημία λήθη. τί οὖν τὸ παραπέμψαι δυνάμενον; ἓν καὶ μόνον φιλοσοφία· τοῦτο δὲ ἐν τῷ τηρεῖν τὸν ἔνδον δαίμονα ἀνύβριστον καὶ ἀσινῆ, ἡδονῶν καὶ πόνων κρείσσονα, μηδὲν εἰκῇ ποιοῦντα μηδὲ διεψευσμένως καὶ μεθ̓ ὑποκρίσεως, ἀνενδεῆ τοῦ ἄλλον ποιῆσαί τι ἢ μὴ ποιῆσαι· ἔτι δὲ τὰ συμβαίνοντα καὶ ἀπονεμόμενα δεχόμενον ὡς ἐκεῖθέν ποθεν ἐρχόμενα, ὅθεν αὐτὸς ἦλθεν· ἐπὶ πᾶσι δὲ τὸν θάνατον ἵλεῳ τῇ γνώμῃ περιμένοντα ὡς οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ λύσιν τῶν στοιχείων, ἐξ ὧν ἕκαστον ζῷον συγκρίνεται. εἰ δὲ αὐτοῖς τοῖς στοιχείοις μηδὲν δεινὸν ἐν τῷ ἕκαστον διηνεκῶς εἰς ἕτερον μεταβάλλειν, διὰ τί ὑπίδηταί τις τὴν πάντων μεταβολὴν καὶ διάλυσιν; κατὰ φύσιν γάρ· οὐδὲν δὲ κακὸν κατὰ φύσιν. Τὰ ἐν Καρνούντῳ.

members.text:
That which most men would think themselves most happy for, and
would prefer before all things, if the Gods would grant it unto them
after their deaths, thou mayst whilst thou livest grant unto thyself; to
live again. See the things of the world again, as thou hast already seen
them. For what is it else to live again? Public shows and solemnities
with much pomp and vanity, stage plays, flocks and herds; conflicts
and contentions: a bone thrown to a company of hungry curs; a bait for
greedy fishes; the painfulness, and continual burden-bearing of wretched
ants, the running to and fro of terrified mice: little puppets drawn up
and down with wires and nerves: these be the objects of the world among
all these thou must stand steadfast, meekly affected, and free from all
manner of indignation; with this right ratiocination and apprehension;
that as the worth is of those things which a man doth affect, so is in
very deed every man's worth more or less.
members.english:
You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.

The empty seriousness of a procession, plays on a stage, flocks, herds, spear fights, a little bone thrown to little dogs, a scrap of bread into the fish tanks, the toils and load-carrying of ants, the scurrying of frightened little mice, puppets pulled on strings. Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.
members.greek:
Ἀναβιῶναί σοι ἔξεστιν· ἴδε πάλιν τὰ πράγματα, ὡς ἑώρας· ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ τὸ ἀναβιῶναι.

Πομπῆς κενοσπουδία, ἐπὶ σκηνῆς δράματα, ποίμνια, ἀγέλαι, διαδορατισμοί, κυνιδίοις ὀστάριον ἐρριμμένον, ψωμίον εἰς τὰς τῶν ἰχθύων δεξαμενάς, μυρμήκων ταλαιπωρίαι καὶ ἀχθοφορίαι, μυιδίων ἐπτοημένων διαδρομαί, σιγιλλάρια νευροσπαστούμενα. χρὴ οὖν ἐν τούτοις εὐμενῶς μὲν καὶ μὴ καταφρυαττόμενον ἑστάναι, παρακολουθεῖν μέντοι, ὅτι τοσούτου ἄξιος ἕκαστός ἐστιν, ὅσου ἄξιά ἐστι ταῦτα περὶ ἃ ἐσπούδακεν.

members.text:
I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things,
whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet
deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or
distract me. For as for those creatures which are not endued with reason
and all other things and-matters of the world whatsoever I freely, and
generously, as one endued with reason, of things that have none, make
use of them. And as for men, towards them as naturally partakers of the
same reason, my care is to carry myself sociably. But whatsoever it is
that thou art about, remember to call upon the Gods. And as for the time
how long thou shalt live to do these things, let it be altogether
indifferent unto thee, for even three such hours are sufficient.
members.english:
I do my own duty; the other things do not distract me. For they are either without life, or without reason, or have gone astray and do not know the road.

Treat animals without reason, and things and objects in general, with a large mind and freely, as one who has reason treats what has none. Treat human beings socially, since they have reason. And in everything call on the gods. And do not trouble yourself about how long you will be doing this: for even three hours of this kind are enough.
members.greek:
Ἐγὼ τὸ ἐμαυτοῦ καθῆκον ποιῶ, τὰ ἄλλα με οὐ περισπᾷ· ἤτοι γὰρ ἄψυχα ἢ ἄλογα ἢ πεπλανημένα καὶ τὴν ὁδὸν ἀγνοοῦντα.

Τοῖς μὲν ἀλόγοις ζῴοις καὶ καθόλου πράγμασι καὶ ὑποκειμένοις, ὡς λόγον ἔχων λόγον μὴ ἔχουσι, χρῶ μεγαλοφρόνως καὶ ἐλευθέρως· τοῖς δὲ ἀνθρώποις, ὡς λόγον ἔχουσι, χρῶ κοινωνικῶς· ἐφ’ ἅπασι δὲ θεοὺς ἐπικαλοῦ. καὶ μὴ διαφέρου πρὸς τὸ πόσῳ χρόνῳ ταῦτα πράξεις· ἀρκοῦσι γὰρ καὶ τρεῖς ὧραι τοιαῦται.

members.text:
Whatsoever I am, is either flesh, or life, or that which we
commonly call the mistress and overruling part of man; reason. Away with
thy books, suffer not thy mind any more to be distracted, and carried to
and fro; for it will not be; but as even now ready to die, think little
of thy flesh: blood, bones, and a skin; a pretty piece of knit and
twisted work, consisting of nerves, veins and arteries; think no more of
it, than so. And as for thy life, consider what it is; a wind; not one
constant wind neither, but every moment of an hour let out, and sucked
in again. The third, is thy ruling part; and here consider; Thou art an
old man; suffer not that excellent part to be brought in subjection, and
to become slavish: suffer it not to be drawn up and down with
unreasonable and unsociable lusts and motions, as it were with wires and
nerves; suffer it not any more, either to repine at anything now
present, or to fear and fly anything to come, which the destiny hath
appointed thee.
members.english: Whatever this is that I am, it is bits of flesh, a little breath, and the ruling part. Let the books go. Be pulled no longer. It is not allowed. Instead, as one already dying, despise the bits of flesh: gore, little bones, a web, a small plaiting made of sinews, little veins and arteries. Look too at what kind of thing the breath is: wind, and not even always the same, but at every moment vomited out and gulped in again. Third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it this way: you are old. No longer let this be a slave, no longer let it be pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse, no longer let it be discontented with what is fated now or look with suspicion on what is fated to come.
members.greek: Ὅ τί ποτε τοῦτό εἰμι, σαρκία ἐστὶ καὶ πνευμάτιον καὶ τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. ἄφες τὰ βιβλία· μηκέτι σπῶ. οὐ δέδοται, ἀλλ’ ὡς ἤδη ἀποθνῄσκων τῶν μὲν σαρκίων καταφρόνησον· λύθρος καὶ ὀστάρια καὶ κροκύφαντος, ἐκ νεύρων, φλεβίων, ἀρτηριῶν πλεγμάτιον. θέασαι δὲ καὶ τὸ πνεῦμα ὁποῖόν τί ἐστιν· ἄνεμος, οὐδὲ ἀεὶ τὸ αὐτό, ἀλλὰ πάσης ὥρας ἐξεμούμενον καὶ πάλιν ῥοφούμενον. τρίτον οὖν ἐστι τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. ὧδε ἐπινοήθητι· γέρων εἶ· μηκέτι τοῦτο ἐάσῃς δουλεῦσαι, μηκέτι καθ’ ὁρμὴν ἀκοινώνητον νευροσπαστηθῆναι, μηκέτι τὸ εἱμαρμένον ἢ παρὸν δυσχερᾶναι ἢ μέλλον ὑπιδέσθαι.

members.text:
Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural
dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest
contented in those two things. First, that nothing shall happen unto
thee, which is not according to the nature of the universe. Secondly,
that it is in thy power, to do nothing against thine own proper God, and
inward spirit. For it is not in any man's power to constrain thee to
transgress against him.
members.english: One must comfort oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay, but rest in these things alone. One: that nothing will happen to me that is not according to the nature of the whole. The other: that it is in my power to do nothing against my god and spirit, for there is no one who will force me to go against him.
members.greek: δεῖ παραμυθούμενον ἑαυτὸν περιμένειν τὴν φυσικὴν λύσιν καὶ μὴ ἀσχάλλειν τῇ διατριβῇ, ἀλλὰ τούτοις μόνοις προσαναπαύεσθαι· ἑνὶ μὲν τῷ, ὅτι οὐδὲν συμβήσεταί μοι ὃ οὐχὶ κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν ἐστίν· ἑτέρῳ δέ, ὅτι ἔξεστί μοι μηδὲν πράσσειν παρὰ τὸν ἐμὸν θεὸν καὶ δαίμονα· οὐδεὶς γὰρ ὁ ἀναγκάσων τοῦτον παραβῆναι.

members.text:
Cast away from thee opinion, and thou art safe. And what is it that
hinders thee from casting of it away? When thou art grieved at anything,
hast thou forgotten that all things happen according to the nature
of the universe; and that him only it concerns, who is in fault; and
moreover, that what is now done, is that which from ever hath been done
in the world, and will ever be done, and is now done everywhere: how
nearly all men are allied one to another by a kindred not of blood, nor
of seed, but of the same mind. Thou hast also forgotten that every man's
mind partakes of the Deity, and issueth from thence; and that no man can
properly call anything his own, no not his son, nor his body, nor his
life; for that they all proceed from that One who is the giver of all
things: that all things are but opinion; that no man lives properly, but
that very instant of time which is now present. And therefore that no
man whensoever he dieth can properly be said to lose any more, than an
instant of time.
members.english:
Throw out the judgment: you are saved. Who then is stopping you from throwing it out?

Whenever you take something hard, you have forgotten that all things come about according to the nature of the whole; and that the wrong done is another’s; and, on top of these, that everything that comes about has always come about in this way, and will come about, and is coming about now everywhere; and how great is the kinship of a human being with the whole human race, for it is a sharing not of a little blood or a little seed but of mind. And you have forgotten too that each person’s mind is a god and has flowed from there; that nothing is anyone’s own, but even one’s little child and little body and the little soul itself have come from there; that everything is judgment; that each person lives only the present, and this is what they lose.
members.greek:
Βάλε ἔξω τὴν ὑπόληψιν· σέσωσαι. τίς οὖν ὁ κωλύων ἐκβάλλειν;

Ὅταν δυσφορῇς ἐπί τινι, ἐπελάθου τοῦ, ὅτι πάντα κατὰ τὴν τῶν ὅλων φύσιν γίνεται, καὶ τοῦ, ὅτι τὸ ἁμαρτανόμενον ἀλλότριον, καὶ ἐπὶ τούτοις τοῦ, ὅτι πᾶν τὸ γινόμενον οὕτως ἀεὶ ἐγίνετο καὶ γενήσεται καὶ νῦν πανταχοῦ γίνεται· τοῦ, ὅση ἡ συγγένεια ἀνθρώπου πρὸς πᾶν τὸ ἀνθρώπειον γένος· οὐ γὰρ αἱματίου ἢ σπερματίου, ἀλλὰ νοῦ κοινωνία. ἐπελάθου δὲ καὶ τοῦ, ὅτι ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς θεὸς καὶ ἐκεῖθεν ἐρρύηκεν· τοῦ, ὅτι οὐδὲν ἴδιον οὐδενός, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τεκνίον καὶ τὸ σωμάτιον καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ψυχάριον ἐκεῖθεν ἐλήλυθεν· τοῦ, ὅτι πάνθ’ ὑπόληψις· τοῦ, ὅτι τὸ παρὸν μόνον ἕκαστος ζῇ καὶ τοῦτο ἀποβάλλει.

members.text:
What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the
operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst
thou grow, and then decrease again? Wouldst thou long be able to talk,
to think and reason with thyself? Which of all these seems unto thee a
worthy object of thy desire? Now if of all these thou doest find that
they be but little worth in themselves, proceed on unto the last, which
is, in all things to follow God and reason. But for a man to grieve that
by death he shall be deprived of any of these things, is both against
God and reason.
members.english: What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.
members.greek: Τί ἐπιζητεῖς; τὸ διαπνεῖσθαι; ἀλλὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι; τὸ ὁρμᾶν; τὸ αὔξεσθαι; τὸ λήγειν αὖθις; τὸ φωνῇ χρῆσθαι; τὸ διανοεῖσθαι; τί τούτων πόθου σοι ἄξιον δοκεῖ; εἰ δὲ ἕκαστα εὐκαταφρόνητα, πρόιθι ἐπὶ τελευταῖον τὸ ἕπεσθαι τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τῷ θεῷ. ἀλλὰ μάχεται τὸ τιμᾶν ταῦτα, τὸ ἄχθεσθαι εἰ διὰ τοῦ τεθνηκέναι στερήσεταί τις αὐτῶν.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.29 is 9.30–31, 7.31 is 7.56–59, 5.27 is 5.33, 2.8 is 2.11, 7.16 is 7.19–22, 12.15 is 12.19–21, 12.18 is 12.24, 4.21 is 4.25–26, 3.10 is 3.9–10, 8.4 is 8.4–5, 2.15 is 2.17, 7.3 is 7.2b–3, 6.21 is 6.22–23, 1.16 is 2.2, 5.10 is the second half of 5.10, 12.19 is 12.25–26 and 12.24 is 12.31; 12.1 is the same.

Lets one phrase, “at the end of life”, stand in claim 2 for having died (7.31) and for being old and already dying (1.16), so that both passages support the same words; it is milder than 7.31’s “has died”.

Takes the two things that are enough (claim 3) from 12.1, 4.21 and 9.29, which share them. The word “enough” is in 5.27 and 6.21, but each calls something else enough: 5.27 revering the gods, doing good to people and bearing with them, 6.21 treating people socially and calling on the gods. 4.21 has the word in the sentence that names this pair, though the translation gives it as “content with”; the article follows the Greek, where the word is the same.

Folds what the section says about fame into the view from above (claim 5): 9.29 joins the view from above with fame, and 5.27 joins fame with the emptiness of what is prized. The lines on fame in 3.10 and 2.15 are not quoted. The puppet image shared by 1.16 and 12.15 is kept inside claim 2 and not made a claim of its own.

Leaves the word “despise” (12.18, and 1.16 of the flesh) out of the article’s own sentences and keeps 7.3’s kindness, putting its “without snorting at them” as “without sneering at them”. The section itself is harsher than the article.
articles.limit: Other articles say parts of this one. Article 3 already says that I accept what happens, and Article 2 that my work is to act well towards others; the two things named in claim 3 say both again. Article 17’s section says claim 3 too (10.12, 4.30, 6.2, 10.28), and Article 17 leaves that claim to this article; its statement (any moment now I may die; I live without pretence, here as anywhere, and I am ready to go) shares this one’s nearness of death and readiness for it, and adds that I live without pretence, here as anywhere. The first half of claim 2 is Article 9’s fourth claim (I do each thing as someone about to leave life), on the same words of Seneca (Ep. 101.7), and its second half repeats Article 2’s second claim, that reason is not to be overpowered by impulse; what claim 2 adds is the “no longer”, said to someone old and already dying. Claim 4 is near Article 33’s fourth claim (nothing terrible in my coming apart) and Article 36’s third (nature, not I, fixes the time of my death, and my death is not bad so long as it is outside my choice and not against the community); Article 36 leaves 9.3’s waiting for death to this article. Two said-once items come near others: “With gods or without” (2.8) is close to Article 4’s question why I should wish to stay in a world of confusion (6.8), and “Those who complained” (7.31) to Article 3’s fourth claim. What this article adds is the time: soon I shall be no one and nowhere and forgotten by all, I live only the present, an instant, and I live it as one already at the end. Several of these 1634 passages join separate chapters of the modern text, so a thought about death and a rule of conduct sometimes stand next to each other without Marcus joining them; the “so” in the statement is the editor’s. 5.27 feeds three claims and the statement, 12.1 two claims and the statement, and in claim 6 the words the two passages share are the editor’s summary.

statement.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, so I live the present justly, as one already at the end, and wait for death cheerfully.

parts.words: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
so I live the present justly
as one already at the end

statement.kind: A ground, the conduct that answers it, and the stance towards the end
statement.form: The existing opening stands verbatim at 130 characters. Each phrase has two passages behind it. The ‘so’ follows 4.21, which moves from the shortness of life to using the present with justice.

claims.t: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere, as those before me already are. Soon I shall forget all, and all will forget me. I live only the present, an instant, and the present is what I lose.
claims.shared: Restores the two-way forgetting of 7.16, which the earlier line had halved. Adds from 12.19 alone that the present is what is lost. The named dead are generalised to ‘those before me’.

support.quote: in a little while you will be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian is not, nor Augustus
support.follows: In a little while I shall be no one and nowhere, just as Hadrian and Augustus are not.
gives: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere
as those before me already are

support.quote: before long you will be no one and nowhere, and neither will any of the things you now see, nor any of the people now living
support.follows: Before long neither I, nor anything I now see, nor anyone now living will exist.
gives: Before long I shall be no one and nowhere

support.quote: How many a Chrysippus, how many a Socrates, how many an Epictetus has eternity already swallowed down.
support.follows: Eternity has already swallowed many a Chrysippus, many a Socrates and many an Epictetus.
gives: as those before me already are

support.quote: Your forgetting of all is near, and near is the forgetting of you by all.
support.follows: Soon I shall have forgotten everything, and soon everyone will have forgotten me.
gives: Soon I shall forget all, and all will forget me

support.quote: each person lives only this present, an instant. The rest has either been lived or is uncertain.
support.follows: A person lives only the present instant; the rest is either already lived or uncertain.
gives: I live only the present, an instant

support.quote: each person lives only the present, and this is what they lose
support.follows: A person lives only the present, and the present is what a person loses.
gives: I live only the present, an instant
the present is what I lose

claims.t: I live what is left as a surplus, like someone already at the end of life, and I do, say and think each thing knowing that I may leave life at this very moment. I no longer let what rules in me be a slave, pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse. I have in me something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions.
claims.shared: Semicolon removed. ‘Surplus’ is restored from 7.31 alone, and ‘slave’ from 1.16 alone. ‘Like’ keeps the dying person a comparison. The strings image is the jointly supported phrase.

support.quote: As someone who has died and has lived out their life up to now, one must live what is left, as a surplus, according to nature.
support.follows: I must count my life as lived and over, and live what remains as an extra, according to nature.
gives: I live what is left as a surplus
like someone already at the end of life

support.quote: as one already dying, despise the bits of flesh
support.follows: I am to despise my flesh, taking the stance of someone who is already dying.
gives: like someone already at the end of life

support.quote: Third, then, is the ruling part. Think of it this way: you are old. No longer let this be a slave, no longer let it be pulled about on strings by unsocial impulse
support.follows: I am old: I should no longer let my ruling part be a slave or be pulled about by unsocial impulse.
gives: I no longer let what rules in me be a slave
pulled about on strings
by unsocial impulse

support.quote: To do and say and think each thing in the knowledge that it is possible to leave life at this very moment.
support.follows: Everything I do, say and think should be done knowing that I could leave life right now.
gives: I do, say and think each thing knowing that I may leave life at this very moment

support.quote: you have in yourself something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and that, in a word, pull you about on strings
support.follows: There is something in me stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions and pull me about.
gives: pulled about on strings
something stronger and more divine than the things that produce the passions

claims.t: I leave the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present. I steer it towards justice in what I do and towards being pleased with what is allotted to me. Until my time comes, it is enough to do good to people and bear with them, and I do not trouble myself about how long I shall be doing this.
claims.shared: ‘Until my time comes’ gives the waiting a referent a listener can hear, where 5.27 says ‘the right time for that’ and points back to a sentence outside this line. ‘How long I shall be doing this’ now names its action, following 6.21. The future is entrusted to providence on 12.1 alone. Reverence for the gods, holding back and the three hours of 6.21 are single-source details kept in the margin.

support.quote: if you leave all the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present towards piety and justice
support.follows: I am to leave the past behind, entrust the future to providence, and steer only the present towards piety and justice.
gives: I leave the past behind, hand the future over to providence, and steer only the present
justice in what I do

support.quote: Piety, so that you love what is allotted, for nature brought it to you and you to it.
support.follows: Piety here means loving what is allotted to me, since nature brought it and me together.
gives: being pleased with what is allotted to me

support.quote: the person who is pleased with what is allotted from the whole and content with their own action being just and their disposition kind
support.follows: The good person is pleased with what the whole allots and content if their own action is just and their disposition kind.
gives: justice in what I do
being pleased with what is allotted to me

support.quote: In sum, life is short. The present must be turned to profit, with good reasoning and justice.
support.follows: Life is short; the present has to be put to good use, with good reasoning and justice.
gives: justice in what I do

support.quote: Freedom from disturbance about the things that happen from the cause outside; justice in the things done through the cause that comes from you.
support.follows: Two things are named: not being disturbed by what happens from outside, and justice in what comes from me.
gives: justice in what I do

support.quote: And until the right time for that is at hand, what is enough? What else but to revere the gods and speak well of them, to do good to human beings, to bear with them and to hold back
support.follows: Until the time of death comes, it is enough to revere the gods, do good to people, bear with them and hold back.
gives: Until my time comes
it is enough
to do good to people and bear with them

support.quote: do not trouble yourself about how long you will be doing this: for even three hours of this kind are enough
support.follows: How long I go on acting this way should not worry me; even three hours of it are enough.
gives: it is enough
I do not trouble myself about how long I shall be doing this

claims.t: I wait for death cheerfully, whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere, and I do not chafe at the delay. The dissolving of the elements I am put together from is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. 5.10a is removed from the cheerful waiting, because 5.10 speaks of comfort and patience and not of cheer, so only 2.15 and 5.27 carry that phrase. 5.10 still supports the patience and, with 2.15, the natural dissolution. The elements are from 2.15 alone, and the open alternative is from 5.27 alone.

support.quote: waiting for death with a cheerful mind, as nothing other than a dissolving of the elements of which every living thing is put together
support.follows: Philosophy includes waiting for death cheerfully, as nothing other than the coming apart of the elements a living thing is made of.
gives: I wait for death cheerfully
The dissolving of the elements I am put together from

support.quote: For it is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad.
support.follows: The change and dissolution of all is according to nature, and nothing according to nature is bad.
gives: is according to nature, and nothing that is according to nature is bad

support.quote: One must comfort oneself and wait for the natural dissolution, and not chafe at the delay
support.follows: I should comfort myself, wait for the dissolution that nature brings, and not be impatient that it is slow to come.
gives: I do not chafe at the delay
The dissolving of the elements I am put together from

support.quote: You wait cheerfully for what is either an extinguishing or a move elsewhere.
support.follows: I wait cheerfully for death, whichever it is: a going out like a flame or a move to another place.
gives: I wait for death cheerfully
whether it is an extinguishing or a move elsewhere

claims.t: I look at human affairs as if from high above, and I see how alike they are and how short-lived. The things people prize are empty and small, little dogs biting one another. A name is a noise and an echo, many will very quickly forget mine, and being remembered is of no account. Among these things I stand kindly, without sneering at them.
claims.shared: ‘Look at’ replaces ‘look down on’, so the height is a vantage and the contempt falls on prized things, not on people. The dogs and the echo are restored from 5.27 alone. The kindness is from 7.3 alone and closes the line as the limit on the contempt.

support.quote: To look down from above on countless herds and countless rites, on every kind of voyage in storms and in calms
support.follows: The exercise is to look down from above on the herds, rites and voyages of human life.
gives: I look at human affairs as if from high above

support.quote: if you were suddenly lifted high into the air and looked down on human affairs and their many turns, you will despise them
support.follows: Lifted high into the air and looking down on human affairs, I would despise them.
gives: I look at human affairs as if from high above

support.quote: Among these things, then, one must stand kindly and without snorting at them, and yet keep in view that each person is worth just as much as the things they have taken seriously are worth.
support.follows: I must stand among these things kindly and without contempt, and remember that people are worth what they take seriously.
gives: I stand kindly, without sneering at them

support.quote: The things highly prized in life are empty and rotten and small, little dogs biting one another, quarrelsome children laughing and then at once crying.
support.follows: What is highly prized in life is empty, rotten and small, like puppies biting or children quarrelling.
gives: The things people prize are empty and small
little dogs biting one another

support.quote: The empty seriousness of a procession, plays on a stage, flocks, herds, spear fights, a little bone thrown to little dogs
support.follows: A procession’s empty seriousness, plays and spear fights are listed beside a little bone thrown to little dogs.
gives: The things people prize are empty and small

support.quote: you will see the same things: how alike in kind, how short-lived
support.follows: However often I look from above, I see the same things, all alike and all short-lived.
gives: how alike they are and how short-lived

support.quote: neither being remembered is of any account, nor reputation, nor anything else at all
support.follows: Being remembered is worth nothing, and neither is reputation or anything else.
gives: being remembered is of no account

support.quote: the name is a noise and an echo
support.follows: A name left behind is only a noise and an echo.
gives: A name is a noise and an echo

support.quote: how many will very quickly forget it
support.follows: Many of those who know my name will very quickly forget it.
gives: many will very quickly forget mine

claims.t: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living but that I may never begin to live according to nature. Only one thing troubles me, that I might do what the make-up of a human being does not want, or do it in a way or at a time it does not want.
claims.shared: 12.1 states the fear inside an ‘if’, and the line adopts it as a first-person stance. The wrong way and the wrong time are restored from 7.16 alone. The earlier gloss ‘living against nature’ is dropped as our wording, not his.

support.quote: what you fear is not some day ceasing to live but rather never beginning to live according to nature
support.follows: The thing to fear is not that life will stop one day, but never beginning to live according to nature.
gives: What I fear is not that I shall some day stop living but that I may never begin to live according to nature
Only one thing troubles me

support.quote: Only one thing troubles me: that I myself might do something that the constitution of a human being does not want, or in a way it does not want, or that it does not want now.
support.follows: One thing alone troubles Marcus: doing what a human being’s make-up does not want, or doing it in the wrong way or at the wrong time.
gives: Only one thing troubles me
that I might do what the make-up of a human being does not want
or do it in a way or at a time it does not want

single.quote: Now death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty, all these happen alike to the good and to the bad among human beings, and they are neither fine nor shameful. So they are neither good nor bad.
single.label: Neither good nor bad
single.t: Death and life, good repute and ill repute, pain and pleasure, wealth and poverty all happen alike to good people and to bad. They are neither fine nor shameful, so I judge them neither good nor bad.
single.why: Single source, 2.8. The full list is restored. The verdict is strict indifference, which is weaker than the contempt of other passages and is not merged with it.
single.follows: What happens alike to good and bad people is neither honourable nor shameful, so death and life are neither good nor bad.

single.quote: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. This happens if it strikes you at the same moment that they are your kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, that in a little while both of you will be dead
single.label: Those who stumble
single.t: It is proper to a human being to love even those who stumble. That love comes if it strikes me all at once that they are my kin, that they go wrong through ignorance and against their will, and that in a little while both of us will be dead.
single.why: Single source, 7.16. ‘All at once’ corrects the earlier ‘at the moment they stumble’. The supplied quote stops before the ground Marcus puts above all, which is kept in the margin.
single.follows: I can love those who go wrong if I recall at that moment that they are kin, that they err unwillingly, and that we shall both soon be dead.

single.quote: At each thing that happens, to keep before one’s eyes the people to whom the same things happened, and who then were vexed, found it strange, complained. So where are they now? Nowhere. Well then, do you too want to be like them?
single.label: Those who complained
single.t: At each thing that happens, I keep before my eyes the people to whom the same thing happened, who were vexed, found it strange and complained. Where are they now? Nowhere. Do I want to be like them?
single.why: Single source, 7.31. The closing question stays a question, as he framed it, and is not turned into a vow.
single.follows: When something happens I should picture those who complained of the same thing, who are now nowhere, and not wish to be like them.

single.quote: You can come back to life. See things again as you used to see them: for in this lies the coming back to life.
single.label: Coming back to life
single.t: I can come back to life by seeing things again as I used to see them.
single.why: Single source, 7.3. ‘Can’ is kept as a possibility, not a duty.
single.follows: Coming back to life is possible, and it consists in seeing things again as I used to see them.

single.quote: What are you looking for? To breathe? Or to have sensation? To have impulse? To grow? And then to stop? To use your voice? To think? Which of these seems to you worth longing for? But if each of them is easy to despise, go on to the last thing, following reason and god. But to value these things, to be vexed that by being dead a person will be deprived of them, conflicts with that.
single.label: Clinging to life
single.t: I ask what I am looking for. To breathe, to have sensation, to have impulse, to grow and then to stop, to use my voice, to think? Which of these seems worth longing for? If each of them is easy to despise, I go on to the last thing, following reason and god. To value breathing, sensing and the rest, and to be vexed that death will deprive me of them, conflicts with following reason and god.
single.why: Single source, 12.24. Parentheses removed. The despising stays conditional on ‘if’. Thinking is on the list of functions, while following reason is the goal.
single.follows: If breathing, sensing, speaking and thinking are each easy to despise, being vexed that death takes them conflicts with following reason and god.

single.quote: if gods exist, it is nothing to fear, for they would not throw you into anything bad. And if either they do not exist or they do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence?
single.label: With gods or without
single.t: If gods exist, going away from among human beings is nothing to fear, for they would not throw me into anything bad. If they do not exist, or do not care about human affairs, what is it to me to live in a universe empty of gods or empty of providence?
single.why: Single source, 2.8. The second branch stays a question, where the earlier line had asserted ‘worth nothing’. Marcus goes on to affirm the gods, which is noted in the margin.
single.follows: Leaving life is nothing to fear if gods exist; and if they do not, or do not care, there is nothing in such a universe to stay for.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 9.29 is 9.30–31, 7.31 is 7.56–59, 5.27 is 5.33, 2.8 is 2.11, 7.16 is 7.19–22, 12.15 is 12.19–21, 12.18 is 12.24, 4.21 is 4.25–26, 3.10 is 3.9–10, 8.4 is 8.4–5, 2.15 is 2.17, 7.3 is 7.2b–3, 6.21 is 6.22–23, 1.16 is 2.2, 5.10 is the second half of 5.10, 12.19 is 12.25–26 and 12.24 is 12.31; 12.1 is the same.
The existing opening stands verbatim at 130 characters. Each phrase has two passages behind it. The ‘so’ follows 4.21, which moves from the shortness of life to using the present with justice.
marcus_revision.limit: The article joins notes Marcus wrote separately, so the links between brevity, justice and cheerful waiting are editorial. The theology is left unsettled: providence in 12.1, chance or providence in 12.18, extinguishing or a move elsewhere in 5.27, and dissolution only in 2.15. Cheerful waiting rests on 2.15 and 5.27 alone, while 5.10 gives patience and consolation. In c6 the fear of 12.1 is conditional in the source, and ‘only one thing’ comes from 7.16 alone. Contempt is aimed at flesh, breath, fame and prized things, never at people or at the ruling part. Nothing here recommends hastening death or withdrawing from duty.

articles.title: Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready

statement.t: When I fall short of philosophy I do not give up: I do what nature asks, keep my principles at hand and look at each thing stripped bare.

parts.words: When I fall short of philosophy I do not give up
I do what nature asks
keep my principles at hand
look at each thing stripped bare

statement.kind: A rule for failure and the three things I come back to
statement.form: Claim 5 is the rule: falling short is no reason to give up. Claims 1, 3 and 4 say what I come back to: the simple work that nature asks, principles kept ready, and the habit of looking at each thing stripped bare. Claim 2 says where I do it. No passage lists these together; the order is the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four of the five claims gain a second author: that the work needs no audience, that acting well comes from principles kept ready, that each thing is looked at bare, and that I do not give up. The article gains a measure for one who is making progress, an image for what makes the teaching hold, a way to keep principles at hand, the same stripping used on what frightens, and what stands behind “I cannot”. He limits three claims: needing no one to see, since until I respect myself I picture a good man watching; coming back, since no one finds his progress where he had left it; and the situation I am in, since the things that keep me busy are to be pushed out of the way.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains one clause: the same demands are not made of one who is making progress as of the wise man. He also warns that what I leave off goes backward, sets a pictured guard over one who is still making progress, and would push aside the things that keep me busy.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness
piece.follows: It is nothing to the point how many people know that I act fairly.
piece.context: The end of Letter 113: justice should have nothing to do with ambition or reputation and is practised without reward. “Your fairness” is one’s own just conduct.
gives: It does not need to be seen

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: One may be wise without parade, without ill will.
piece.follows: A person can be wise without making a display of it and without ill will.
piece.context: In Letter 103 Seneca tells Lucilius to take refuge in philosophy but never to vaunt it or use it to condemn others. “Parade” is the display of one’s own philosophy.
gives: I make no show of it

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: No one will carry these out as he ought unless he has something to refer them to
piece.follows: No one carries out the precepts of duty as he ought without something to refer them to.
piece.context: Letter 95 argues that advice for particular cases is not enough. “These” are Brutus’s precepts on duty; the “something to refer them to” is the goal of the highest good, like a sailor’s star.
gives: doing it well comes from principles

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: these things ought not to be stored away but at hand
piece.follows: What I know about how to act should not be stored away; it should be at hand.
piece.context: In Letter 94 Seneca defends advice that repeats the obvious: we know how to treat a friend or a wife and do not act on it. “These things” are the known truths about how to act.
gives: I keep them always at hand

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Let us assess each thing one by one with its reputation set aside, and ask what they are, not what they are called.
piece.follows: I should set aside what people say, ask of each thing what it is and not what it is called, and assess it by that.
piece.context: From Letter 95, on how to make use of things: what opinion to hold of poverty, riches, glory, disgrace, exile. “Each thing” is each of these; its “reputation” is what people say of it.
gives: what it is worth

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: to take the uproar away from things and to see what is in each thing
piece.follows: I should take the uproar away from things, and see what is in each one.
piece.context: In Letter 24 Lucilius is threatened by an enemy and fears the outcome. Seneca tells him to prepare for the worst; the “things” to be freed of uproar are what he fears, such as pain and death.
gives: I look at it stripped bare

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: So let us press on and persevere. More remains than we have got through
piece.follows: Seneca urges himself and Lucilius to press on and persevere, and adds that more remains than they have got through.
piece.context: In Letter 71 Seneca has just said that what is incomplete totters and has to go backward when it slackens. What “remains” is the progress towards wisdom still to be made; “us” is Seneca and Lucilius.
gives: I do not give up

items.label: breaks
items.role: A measure for one making progress
