items.t: It is a fault to ask of one who is making progress what is asked of the wise man. I still urge on myself what I know I should do, and I have not yet convinced myself; and even the lowest rank of those who are making progress is not to be despised.
items.why: Marcus tells himself to be content with a part and does not say by what measure a part is enough. Seneca separates the man who is making progress from the wise man, says that the same demands are not to be made of both, and counts himself among those making progress. Where Seneca speaks of urging on himself “the things I praise”, meaning what he urges on Lucilius, the article says “what I know I should do”.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Here the fault is ours, who demand the same thing of the wise man and of the man who is making progress
support.follows: The same demands should not be made of a man who is making progress as of a wise man.
support.context: In Letter 71 Seneca says the wise man conquers fortune, while many who profess wisdom are terrified by slight threats. “The man who is making progress” is anyone still on the way, himself included.
gives: It is a fault to ask of one who is making progress what is asked of the wise man

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I am still urging the things I praise on myself; I have not yet convinced myself.
support.follows: Seneca is still urging on himself the things he praises, and has not yet convinced himself.
support.context: Seneca speaks of himself, straight after saying that the wise man and the man who is making progress are not to be judged alike. “The things I praise” are what he urges on Lucilius in Letter 71.
gives: I still urge on myself what I know I should do, and I have not yet convinced myself

support.author: seneca
support.quote: but not even this third colour is to be despised.
support.follows: Even the third and lowest rank of those making progress is worth belonging to.
support.context: In Letter 75 Seneca sorts those who are making progress into three ranks. “This third colour” is the lowest: free of the great vices but not of all, still giving way to some fears.
gives: even the lowest rank of those who are making progress is not to be despised

items.label: breaks
items.t: The teaching I follow does not keep its promises if it has only coloured my mind. It has to go deep and settle for a long time, as wool takes some dyes only when it is soaked and boiled again several times.
items.why: 10.9 says that principles pictured without study of nature are wiped out day by day, and it points to that study and to keeping the contemplative side at work. Seneca adds an image for what holding takes: depth, and soaking repeated over a long time. He says it of the Stoic teaching in particular, in contrast with other branches of learning, which intellects put into practice at once.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: this one, unless it has gone down deep and settled for a long time and dyed the mind rather than coloured it, makes good on nothing it had promised
support.follows: The Stoic teaching keeps none of its promises unless it has gone deep, settled for a long time and dyed the mind rather than coloured it.
support.context: “This one” is the Stoic teaching that virtue is the only good, stated in the next lines of Letter 71. Seneca sets it against other branches of learning, which intellects put into practice at once.
gives: The teaching I follow does not keep its promises if it has only coloured my mind
It has to go deep and settle for a long time

support.author: seneca
support.quote: others it does not drink in fully unless it has been soaked and boiled again several times
support.follows: Some dyes take only after the wool has been soaked and boiled again several times.
support.context: In Letter 71, on the highest good, Seneca compares doctrines to dyes. “It” is wool, which takes on some colours in one go and “others” only after repeated soaking and boiling.
gives: as wool takes some dyes only when it is soaked and boiled again several times

items.label: practice
items.role: How principles come to be at hand
items.t: What is wholesome I stir often and turn over often, so that it is not only known to me but also ready.
items.why: Marcus says to keep principles at hand and compares them to a doctor’s instruments and a fighter’s hand; he does not say in this section how they come to be there. Seneca names the means: going over them often.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whatever is wholesome ought to be often stirred, often turned over, so that it is not only known to us but also ready
support.follows: What is wholesome should be stirred and turned over often, so that it is both known and ready.
support.context: In Letter 94 Seneca defends advice that repeats what we already know, such as how to treat a friend or a wife. “Whatever is wholesome” is any such sound truth about conduct, however obvious.
gives: What is wholesome I stir often and turn over often, so that it is not only known to me but also ready

items.label: practice
items.t: I take the mask off things as well as off people. Then I see that what I feared holds nothing terrible except the fear itself.
items.why: Marcus strips what attracts and impresses: the dishes, the wine, the purple robe, whatever seems very trustworthy. Seneca uses the same stripping on the other side, on what frightens.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The mask must be taken off not only people but things, and their own face given back to them.
support.follows: The mask should be taken off things as well as off people, so that each thing shows its own face.
support.context: In Letter 24 Seneca compares us to children frightened by friends who wear masks. The “mask” on things is the alarming show around what we fear, such as the swords and fire around death.
gives: I take the mask off things as well as off people

support.author: seneca
support.quote: there is nothing terrible in those things except the fear itself
support.follows: With the uproar taken away, the things I fear have nothing terrible in them except the fear itself.
support.context: In Letter 24 Seneca tells Lucilius, who is threatened by an enemy, to look at what he fears with the uproar taken away. “Those things” are the feared things, such as pain and death.
gives: what I feared holds nothing terrible except the fear itself

items.t: Seneca narrows “It does not need to be seen” for one who is still making progress. He agrees that being known is nothing to the point (Ep. 113.32), but until I have come to respect myself he would have me set a good man over myself as a guard and live as though under his eyes. The guard is pictured, a model to correct me, not an audience, and he is dismissed once I respect myself. Article 9 marks Ep. 25.6 as a limit on its claim that I need no human witness.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men
support.follows: Until I respect myself, I should guard myself by the authority of certain men; after that I may dismiss the minder.
support.context: In Letter 25 Seneca passes on Epicurus’s advice to act as if a respected man were watching. The “minder” is that imagined guard, a Cato or a Laelius, kept until one respects oneself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: This is indeed far grander, to live as though under the eyes of some good man who is always present
support.follows: It is grander to live as though under the eyes of a good man who is always present.
support.context: In Letter 25 Seneca takes up Epicurus’s advice to act “as though Epicurus were watching”. The “good man” is an imagined witness of one’s acts and thoughts, since solitude persuades us to every evil.

items.label: breaks
items.role: Not wanting to, rather than not being able to
items.t: When I say that I am not able, the cause is that I do not want to, and not being able is my pretext. Nature has given me strength enough if I use it, and things are difficult because I do not dare.
items.why: 6.18 says only that what is hard for me is not impossible for a human being. Seneca goes further and names what stands behind “I cannot”: not wanting to and not daring.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Not wanting to is the cause; not being able to is put forward as the pretext.
support.follows: We fail because we do not want to, and we put forward not being able as the pretext.
support.context: The last words of Letter 116, on why people say the Stoic ideal is beyond them. “The cause” is the cause of our not attaining it; “not being able to” is what we put forward.
gives: the cause is that I do not want to, and not being able is my pretext

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Nature has given man strength enough, if we would use it
support.follows: Nature has given us strength enough, provided we use it.
support.context: In Letter 116 Seneca answers the complaint that Stoic counsels are too hard for mere human beings. The “strength” is the power to do what the Stoics ask, here to be rid of the passions.
gives: Nature has given me strength enough if I use it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is not because things are difficult that we do not dare; it is because we do not dare that they are difficult.
support.follows: It is not that things are too difficult for us to dare; they are difficult because we do not dare.
support.context: In Letter 104 Seneca speaks of people who think that what they cannot do is impossible and that Stoic words are too big for human nature. What is “difficult” is bearing toil and death.
gives: things are difficult because I do not dare

items.t: Seneca agrees that I must not stop, but he does not let coming back be free of cost. Whoever slackens goes backward, and no one finds his progress where he had left it (Ep. 71.35); philosophy studied with breaks runs back all the way to its beginnings (Ep. 72.3). Seneca limits the claim without contradicting it: Marcus says to come back and to be content with a part, and does not say that nothing was lost.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: No one finds his progress where he had left it.
support.follows: After a break, no one finds his progress where he had left it.
support.context: In Letter 71 Seneca describes anyone still incomplete as tottering, now going forward, now slipping down. “Progress” is progress towards wisdom; to leave it is to slacken in zeal and faithful effort.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: they will slip down, unless they keep on going and striving
support.follows: What is incomplete slips down unless it keeps on going and striving.
support.context: From Letter 71, on those who follow wisdom without having reached it. “They” are the things that are incomplete: the state of a person who is still on the way.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: it does not stay where it was interrupted, but, like things stretched tight that spring apart, it runs back all the way to its beginnings, because it has left off being continuous
support.follows: Philosophy that is interrupted does not stay where it was; having left off being continuous, it runs back all the way to its beginnings.
support.context: Letter 72 says that philosophy must not wait for free time. “It” is philosophy studied with interruptions, which Seneca compares to things stretched tight that spring apart.

items.t: Seneca narrows the claim. Marcus says that no situation suits philosophy better than the one he is in (11.6), and no passage says what that situation is. Seneca names one that does not suit it: being busy. He tells Lucilius to let go of what hinders him and push it out of the way, because no one reaches a sound mind while he is busy (Ep. 53.9, 72.3). If Marcus’s situation is read as the things that keep him busy, the two disagree outright; that reading is the editor’s, so this is marked as a limit and not as a challenge. Seneca is not consistent: in the same section of Letter 72 he says that no time is ill suited to study, and in Ep. 62.1 that a crowd of business does not stand between a person and study. Both are quoted below.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let go of everything that hinders you and make yourself free for a sound mind: no one reaches it while he is busy.
support.follows: I should let go of everything that hinders me and make myself free for a sound mind, which no one reaches while he is busy.
support.context: In Letter 53 Seneca argues that a sick man drops his business to get well, and the mind deserves the same. “It” is a sound mind; “everything that hinders you” is business and other concerns.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We must resist the things that keep us busy: they are not to be untangled but pushed out of the way.
support.follows: The things that keep me busy are to be resisted and pushed out of the way, not untangled one by one.
support.context: In Letter 72 Seneca writes on a day full of business and says new employments always spring up. “The things that keep us busy” are these occupations, which he would push away, not settle one by one.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: There is in fact no time that is ill suited to a study that brings health; and yet many do not study in the midst of the things on account of which one ought to study
support.follows: No time is ill suited to a study that brings health, yet many do not study in the midst of the very things on account of which one ought to study.
support.context: Letter 72 adds this after saying that what keeps us busy must be pushed away. “The things on account of which one ought to study” are those in which a person is pressed and most needs it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: They are lying, those who want it to look as though the press of business stands between them and liberal studies
support.follows: People who want it to look as though a crowd of business keeps them from study are lying.
support.context: The opening of Letter 62, where Seneca says he has time and is his own wherever he is, since he lends himself to affairs and does not hand himself over. “Liberal studies” include philosophy.

amend.t: ; and I do not make the same demands on one who is making progress as on the wise man
; but I do not find my progress where I had left it, and what I leave off goes backward
; but within it I push out of the way the things that keep me busy, for no one reaches a sound mind while he is busy
; but until I respect myself, I live as though under the eyes of a good man set over me as a guard

passages.title: On whether the virtues are living beings
passages.text: Fix in yourself as well what I was saying a little earlier: that it is nothing to the point how many people know of your fairness. Anyone who wants his virtue made public is working not for virtue but for glory. Are you unwilling to be just without glory? But, by Hercules, you will often have to be just with a bad name, and then, if you are wise, let a bad reputation well won delight you. Farewell.

passages.title: On the danger people pose to each other
passages.text: But philosophy herself you must not show off. To many she has been a cause of danger when handled arrogantly and defiantly. Let her strip vices from you, not reproach others with theirs. Let her not be at odds with the ways of people at large, nor make it her business to seem to condemn whatever she does not do. One may be wise without parade, without ill will. Farewell.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: Marcus Brutus, in the book he titled “Peri kathekontos” (“On Duty”), gives many precepts to parents and to children and to brothers. No one will carry these out as he ought unless he has something to refer them to. We must set before us the goal of the highest good, towards which we may strive, towards which every deed and word of ours may look, just as those who sail must direct their course towards some star.

passages.title: On the usefulness of practical advice
passages.text: You know that friendships are to be cultivated religiously, but you do not do it. You know that a man is shameless who demands chastity of his wife while he himself is a seducer of other men’s wives; you know that, just as she ought to have nothing to do with an adulterer, so you ought to have nothing to do with a mistress, and you do not do it. So you must be reminded again and again; for these things ought not to be stored away but at hand. Whatever is wholesome ought to be often stirred, often turned over, so that it is not only known to us but also ready. Add now that even plain things usually become plainer.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: After gods and human beings, let us look into how things are to be used. We shall be tossing out precepts to no purpose unless this has come first: what opinion we ought to hold about each thing, about poverty, about riches, about glory, about disgrace, about homeland, about exile. Let us assess each thing one by one with its reputation set aside, and ask what they are, not what they are called.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: So, free from care, listen to your enemy’s threats; and although your own conscience gives you confidence, still, because many things outside the case carry weight, hope for what is fairest and also prepare yourself for what is most unfair. But above all remember this: to take the uproar away from things and to see what is in each thing: you will find that there is nothing terrible in those things except the fear itself.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: So let us press on and persevere. More remains than we have got through, but a great part of progress is wanting to make progress. This I know of myself: I want to, and I want to with my whole mind. I see that you too have been roused and are hurrying with great force towards the finest things. Let us hurry: only so will life be a gift. Otherwise it is a delay, and a shameful one at that, for those who live among foul things. Let us see to it that all time is ours; but it will not be, unless we have first begun to be our own.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: The wise man, it is true, conquers fortune by virtue, but many who have professed wisdom have at times been terrified by the slightest threats. Here the fault is ours, who demand the same thing of the wise man and of the man who is making progress. I am still urging the things I praise on myself; I have not yet convinced myself. Even if I had convinced myself, I would not yet have them so ready or so practised that they would run out to meet whatever happens.

passages.title: On plain writing and stages of progress
passages.text: Let us give some thought to this rank: it will go well with us if we are admitted to this group. The second step is won through great good fortune in one’s nature and through great and unremitting effort in study; but not even this third colour is to be despised. Think how much evil you see around you; look how there is no outrage without a precedent, how much progress wickedness makes every day, how much wrong is done in public and in private: you will understand that we attain enough if we are not among the worst.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: Just as wool takes on some colours at a single dyeing, and others it does not drink in fully unless it has been soaked and boiled again several times, so there are other branches of learning that intellects put into practice at once, as soon as they have received them: this one, unless it has gone down deep and settled for a long time and dyed the mind rather than coloured it, makes good on nothing it had promised.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: What you see happen to children happens to us too, who are slightly bigger children: the people they love, the people they are used to, the people they play with, if they see them wearing masks, they take fright. The mask must be taken off not only people but things, and their own face given back to them.

passages.title: On reforming friends and imagining a watcher
passages.text: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men: let it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or another at whose coming even depraved men would suppress their vices, while you are making yourself the man in whose company you would not dare to do wrong. When you have made yourself that, and have begun to have some standing in your own eyes, I will begin to allow you what the same Epicurus advises: “Withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

passages.title: On reforming friends and imagining a watcher
passages.text: “Do everything,” he says, “as though Epicurus were watching.” It is without doubt useful to have set a guard over oneself and to have someone you look to, someone you judge to be present at your thoughts. This is indeed far grander, to live as though under the eyes of some good man who is always present; but I am content even with this, that you do whatever you do as though someone were watching. Solitude talks us into every evil.

passages.title: On removing the passions altogether
passages.text: Do you know why we cannot do those things? Because we do not believe that we can. Or rather, by Hercules, the fact of the matter is something else: we defend our vices because we love them, and we would rather excuse them than shake them off. Nature has given man strength enough, if we would use it, if we would gather our powers and rouse all of them on our own behalf, or at any rate not against ourselves. Not wanting to is the cause; not being able to is put forward as the pretext. Farewell.

passages.title: On travel, health and the examples of great men
passages.text: But how much better I think of them! They too can do these things, but they do not want to. And after all, whom have those things ever failed when he tried them? To whom have they not appeared easier in the doing? It is not because things are difficult that we do not dare; it is because we do not dare that they are difficult.

passages.title: On virtue as the only good
passages.text: Things that are incomplete are bound to totter, and now go forward, now slip down or collapse. And they will slip down, unless they keep on going and striving; if they slacken any of their zeal and faithful exertion, they have to go backward. No one finds his progress where he had left it.

passages.title: On not letting business postpone philosophy
passages.text: It is not when you have time free that you are to do philosophy, but you are to make time free so that you may do philosophy. Everything else is to be neglected so that we may sit in attendance on philosophy, for which no time is long enough, even if life is drawn out from boyhood to the farthest limits of a human lifetime. It does not matter much whether you give philosophy up or leave it off for a time; for it does not stay where it was interrupted, but, like things stretched tight that spring apart, it runs back all the way to its beginnings, because it has left off being continuous. We must resist the things that keep us busy: they are not to be untangled but pushed out of the way. There is in fact no time that is ill suited to a study that brings health; and yet many do not study in the midst of the things on account of which one ought to study.

passages.title: On hidden faults and giving all to philosophy
passages.text: If you were ill, you would have set aside the care of your property, and your business in the forum would have dropped out of your mind, and you would not think anyone worth so much that you would go down as his advocate during a remission; with your whole mind you would work at this, to be freed from the illness as soon as possible. Well then? Will you not do the same now too? Let go of everything that hinders you and make yourself free for a sound mind: no one reaches it while he is busy. Philosophy exercises her own royal power; she gives out time, she does not accept it; she is not a thing for leftover hours; she belongs to the regular hours, she is the mistress, she is present and gives orders.

passages.title: On making time for study anywhere
passages.text: They are lying, those who want it to look as though the press of business stands between them and liberal studies: they feign occupations, they make more of them, and they are the ones who keep themselves occupied. I have time, Lucilius, I have time, and wherever I am, there I am my own. For I do not hand myself over to affairs but lend myself to them, and I do not go hunting for reasons to waste time. And in whatever place I have come to a stop, there I work on my own thoughts and turn something wholesome over in my mind.

claims.t: Philosophy wants only what my nature wants: the good life lies in very few things, in doing what nature asks of me, and that is a simple and modest work. It does not need to be seen: I make no show of it, I let go of reputation, and I do not look around to see whether anyone will know.
claims.shared: 5.9, 8.1 and 9.28 speak of what nature wants or asks: 5.9 and 8.1 both have “your nature wants”, 8.1 has “what human nature asks for” and 9.28 “what nature now demands”. All four, 7.38 included, set being seen aside: “no show” (5.9), “reputation” (8.1), “whether anyone will know” (9.28), “recognised by no one” (7.38).
claims.changed: “It does not need to be seen” is the editor’s summary: 7.38 says that one can become godlike and be recognised by no one, and 9.28 says not to look whether anyone will know. 9.28 says “simple and modest” of “the work of philosophy”; the claim says it of doing what nature asks, which the same passage names a few lines earlier, and that step is the editor’s. 8.1 says “human nature” and 9.28 “nature”; the claim says “nature”. 7.38 says “living happily” and 8.1 “the good life”; the claim says “the good life” for both.

support.quote: philosophy wants only what your nature wants
support.follows: Philosophy asks for nothing beyond what my own nature asks for.
gives: Philosophy wants only what my nature wants

support.quote: living happily lies in very few things
support.follows: Very few things are needed for living happily.
gives: the good life lies in very few things

support.quote: nowhere found the good life: not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature asks for.
support.follows: The good life is not in argument, wealth, reputation or enjoyment; it is in doing what human nature asks for.
gives: in doing what nature asks of me

support.quote: Do what nature now demands.
support.follows: The thing to do is what nature demands at this moment.
gives: in doing what nature asks of me

support.quote: The work of philosophy is simple and modest
support.follows: What philosophy has to do is simple and modest.
gives: a simple and modest work

support.quote: it is very possible to become a godlike man and to be recognised by no one
support.follows: A man can become godlike without anyone recognising it.
gives: It does not need to be seen

support.quote: Set out, if it is given to you, and do not look around to see whether anyone will know.
support.follows: I should start if I am given the chance, and not look around to see whether anyone will know of it.
gives: It does not need to be seen
I do not look around to see whether anyone will know

support.quote: For in this way you will make no show of obeying reason, but will find rest in it.
support.follows: Coming to philosophy in the right way, I shall not display my obedience to reason; I shall rest in it.
gives: I make no show of it

support.quote: let go of what reputation you will have
support.follows: I should let go of the question of what reputation I shall have.
gives: I let go of reputation

claims.t: The situation I am in now may fight against a philosopher’s reputation, but no other is so suited to philosophy. It is material for my reason, and I do not run away from it: I stay until I have made it my own.
claims.shared: 8.1 and 11.6 both speak of my “situation”: in 8.1 it fights against the reputation of a philosopher, in 11.6 none is so suited to philosophy. 10.32 calls what I would run from “material” and “a subject”; the Greek word behind “subject” is the one translated “situation” in the other two, though its sense there is a subject set before me to work on.
claims.changed: The “but” that sets 8.1 against 11.6 is the editor’s way of joining them; neither passage mentions the other’s point. 10.32 speaks of “all these things”, which point back to something before the passage begins; the claim reads them as the things of my life, as 10.32’s own words “the things in life” allow, and so lets “Stay” be said of my situation. No passage says what the situation is.

support.quote: winning the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and your situation fights against it too
support.follows: Being known as a philosopher is no longer easy for Marcus, and his situation works against it as well.
gives: The situation I am in now
may fight against a philosopher’s reputation

support.quote: there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be
support.follows: No situation in life is better suited to philosophy than the one I happen to be in now.
gives: The situation I am in now
no other is so suited to philosophy

support.quote: What material, what a subject, you are running away from! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has seen the things in life accurately and as a student of nature?
support.follows: What I am running away from is material: exercises for a reason that has looked exactly at the things in life.
gives: It is material for my reason
I do not run away from it

support.quote: Stay, then, until you have made these things too your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw into it.
support.follows: I should stay until I have made these things my own, as a strong stomach does with food and a bright fire with whatever is thrown into it.
gives: I stay until I have made it my own

claims.t: Being good is my craft, and doing it well comes from principles. I keep them always at hand, as a doctor has his instruments ready, and as the fighter whose weapon is his own hand, which he never puts down and needs only to clench.
claims.shared: 3.14 and 12.6 both say “principles” and both say “always”: doctors “always have their instruments and blades at hand”, the fighter “always has his hand”. 11.4 wants one thought that “always comes to hand”. 8.1 and 11.4 both say where acting well comes from: “principles from which your impulses and actions come”, “from points of theory”.
claims.changed: 11.4 says “points of theory”; the claim says “principles”, the word of 8.1, 3.14 and 12.6. 11.4 wants one thought kept at hand (that a social act is its own benefit); the claim says it of the principles in general. 12.6’s “all-in fighter”, who fights with his hands, is given as “the fighter whose weapon is his own hand”; the gladiator, who puts his sword down and picks it up, is left out.

support.quote: What is your craft? To be good. And how does that come about well, except from points of theory
support.follows: My craft is to be good, and it is done well only from points of theory.
gives: Being good is my craft
doing it well comes from principles

support.quote: How, then, will you do these things? If you have principles from which your impulses and actions come.
support.follows: I shall do what is asked of me if I have principles from which my impulses and actions come.
gives: doing it well comes from principles

support.quote: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready
support.follows: I should have my principles ready in the way doctors always keep their instruments at hand for emergencies.
gives: I keep them always at hand
as a doctor has his instruments ready

support.quote: in the use of principles one must be like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator. For the gladiator puts down the sword he uses and picks it up; but the other always has his hand, and needs only to clench it.
support.follows: Principles should be used like a fighter’s own hand, which is always there, and not like a sword that is put down and picked up.
gives: I keep them always at hand
as the fighter whose weapon is his own hand, which he never puts down and needs only to clench

support.quote: I have done something as a social being: then I have been benefited. See that this always comes to hand, and never stop.
support.follows: The thought that acting as a social being is itself my benefit should always be at hand.
gives: I keep them always at hand

claims.t: Whatever comes up in my life, I look at it stripped bare: what it is in its substance, what it is put together from, what it will change into, how long it lasts and what it is worth. Nothing does more for greatness of mind, and what seemed very trustworthy turns out cheap.
claims.shared: 3.11, 6.11 and 12.6 all say “bare”. 3.11 and 10.9 both ask what a thing is “in its substance” and what it is “put together from”. 3.11 and 10.11 have the same sentence, “nothing so produces greatness of mind”, and both speak of what things turn into.
claims.changed: In 12.6 what is looked at bare is “what is causal”; the claim says it of each thing. 3.11 says “into which it will be broken up”; the claim says “what it will change into”, which is nearer to 10.11’s “change into one another”. In 3.11 greatness of mind comes from testing each thing, in 10.11 from contemplating how things change; the claim joins the two. The meals, the wine, the robe and sex in 6.11 are dropped.

support.quote: always to make a definition or outline of the thing that comes up in an impression, so as to see it as it is in its substance, bare, whole and entire, and taken apart, and to say to oneself its own name and the names of the things from which it was put together and into which it will be broken up
support.follows: I should define each thing that comes up, see it bare and in its parts, and name what it was made from and what it will break up into.
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
I look at it stripped bare
what it is in its substance
what it is put together from
what it will change into

support.quote: the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is in its nature to last, what it is put together from
support.follows: Marcus asks when he will enjoy recognising, case by case, what a thing is, how long it lasts and what it is made of.
gives: what it is in its substance
what it is put together from
how long it lasts

support.quote: so one must do through the whole of life, and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare, see their cheapness plainly, and strip off the story on which they pride themselves
support.follows: All through life, where things look very trustworthy, I should strip them bare, see how cheap they are and take away their story.
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
I look at it stripped bare
what seemed very trustworthy turns out cheap

support.quote: To look at what is causal, bare of its husks.
support.follows: One thing to keep in mind is to look at what is causal with its husks taken off.
gives: I look at it stripped bare
support.note: The passage is a list of headings. What is seen bare here is the causal element in things, not each thing as a whole.

support.quote: How all things change into one another: get yourself a method for contemplating it, attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this field. For nothing so produces greatness of mind.
support.follows: I should get a method for contemplating how all things change into one another and train in it; nothing does more for greatness of mind.
gives: what it will change into
Nothing does more for greatness of mind

support.quote: nothing so produces greatness of mind as being able to test methodically and truly each of the things that come up in life
support.follows: Nothing makes the mind greater than being able to test, by method and truly, each thing that comes up in life.
gives: Whatever comes up in my life
Nothing does more for greatness of mind

support.quote: what it is worth to the whole, and what to the human being
support.follows: Of each thing I should ask what it is worth to the whole and what it is worth to a human being.
gives: what it is worth

claims.t: When I fail to act from my principles, or I see what I can no longer be, I do not give up. I come back, and I am content if most of what I do befits a human being, if I live at least the rest of my life as my nature wants, or if even the smallest thing goes forward in what I do.
claims.shared: 8.1 and 9.28 both say “be content if”, and 5.9 says “be glad if”. 5.9 and 7.38 both say “give up”. In each passage the full measure is out of reach (acting rightly every time, a whole life as a philosopher, a logician’s knowledge, Plato’s republic) and a part of it is declared enough.
claims.changed: 5.9 says “be glad”; the claim says “content”, the word of 8.1 and 9.28. “Most of what I do befits a human being” rests on words the translation supplies: the Greek of 5.9 has only “if the greater part more human”, which can also mean “human enough”, and the claim drops the comparative. 9.28 is about public affairs: the smallest thing that goes forward there is a result among other people; “in what I do” is the editor’s, and so is “even”. 5.9’s “disgusted” and “lose patience” are dropped.

support.quote: Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose patience, if doing each thing from right principles does not come to you time after time
support.follows: If I do not manage to act from right principles every time, that is no reason for disgust, for giving up or for impatience.
gives: When I fail to act from my principles
I do not give up

support.quote: you can no longer have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy
support.follows: Marcus can no longer have lived his whole life as a philosopher, and he and many others can see that he is far from philosophy.
gives: I see what I can no longer be

support.quote: because you have given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, do not for that reason give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god
support.follows: Having lost hope of being a logician or a student of nature is no reason to give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god.
gives: I see what I can no longer be
I do not give up

support.quote: when you have been knocked aside, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being
support.follows: Knocked aside, I should come back, and be glad if most of what I do is more fitting for a human being.
gives: I come back
I am content if
most of what I do befits a human being

support.quote: be content if you live at least the rest of your life, however much it may be, as your nature wants
support.follows: It is enough to live what is left of my life, however much that is, as my nature wants.
gives: I am content if
I live at least the rest of my life as my nature wants

support.quote: Do not hope for Plato’s republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward
support.follows: I should not hope for a perfect state, and should be content if the smallest thing moves forward.
gives: I am content if
the smallest thing goes forward

single.quote: What principles? Those about good things and bad: that nothing is a good thing for a human being which does not make them just, self-controlled, brave, free, and nothing is a bad thing which does not make them the opposite of these.
single.label: What the principles say
single.t: My principles are about what is good and what is bad: nothing is good for a human being that does not make them just, self-controlled, brave and free, and nothing is bad that does not make them the opposite.
single.why: Only 8.1 says what the principles are. 5.12 names nearly the same list as the true goods, but it does so inside a test of what most people call good, and it is set aside.
single.follows: The principles are about good and bad: only what makes a person just, self-controlled, brave and free is good, and only what does the opposite is bad.

single.quote: love what you are coming back to. And do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash.
single.label: As to a remedy
single.t: I love what I come back to. I do not come back to philosophy as a schoolboy to the slave who minds him, but as a person with sore eyes goes to the remedies for them, the sponge and the egg, or as another goes to a poultice.
single.why: Only this passage says in what spirit I come back. 3.14 also takes an image from medicine, but there the principles are the doctor’s instruments, not the patient’s remedy. That the sponge and the egg are remedies for sore eyes is from the translators’ note.
single.follows: I should love what I return to, and return to philosophy as a sick person goes to a remedy, not as a boy to the slave who keeps him in order.

single.quote: Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery: day by day those sacred principles of yours will be wiped out, all those that you picture without study of nature and let go by.
single.label: How principles fade
single.t: Principles that I only picture without studying nature, and then let pass, are wiped out day by day, amid farce, war, panic, numbness and slavery.
single.why: Only this passage says how principles are lost. The Greek opens with five bare nouns and does not say how they connect with the rest; “amid” is the editor’s reading of that link. The Greek of the last clause is uncertain.
single.follows: After naming farce, war, panic, numbness and slavery, Marcus says that principles pictured without study of nature will be wiped out day by day.

single.quote: If something is hard for you yourself to carry out, do not judge it impossible for a human being; but if something is possible for a human being and proper to them, consider it within your own reach too.
single.label: Hard, not impossible
single.t: If something is hard for me to carry out, I do not judge it impossible for a human being. If it is possible for a human being and proper to them, I count it within my own reach too.
single.why: Only this passage answers the thought that I am not able to do it. It is also the passage farthest from the centre of the section.
single.follows: What is hard for me is not for that reason impossible for a human being, and what a human being can properly do is within my reach too.

single.quote: to the Stoics themselves, at least, they seem hard to grasp. And every assent of ours can shift: for where is the person who does not shift? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap
single.label: If I cannot be sure
single.t: The Stoics themselves find the truth of things hard to grasp, and everything I agree to can shift, as it does for everyone. Then I pass on to the things themselves and see how short-lived and how cheap they are.
single.why: Only this passage admits that what I hold to may be wrong. It stands under doubt because it says what I can still do then: look at the objects themselves. What Marcus goes on to rest in lies outside this passage.
single.follows: The Stoics themselves find things hard to grasp and no one’s assent is fixed; Marcus then turns to the objects and finds them short-lived and cheap.

members.text:
Be not discontented, be not disheartened, be not out of hope, if
often it succeed not so well with thee punctually and precisely to do
all things according to the right dogmata, but being once cast off,
return unto them again: and as for those many and more frequent
occurrences, either of worldly distractions, or human infirmities, which
as a man thou canst not but in some measure be subject unto, be not thou
discontented with them; but however, love and affect that only which
thou dust return unto: a philosopher's life, and proper occupation after
the most exact manner. And when thou dust return to thy philosophy,
return not unto it as the manner of some is, after play and liberty as
it were, to their schoolmasters and pedagogues; but as they that have
sore eyes to their sponge and egg: or as another to his cataplasm; or
as others to their fomentations: so shalt not thou make it a matter of
ostentation at all to obey reason but of ease and comfort. And
remember that philosophy requireth nothing of thee, but what thy
nature requireth, and wouldest thou thyself desire anything that is
not according to nature? for which of these sayest thou; that which is
according to nature or against it, is of itself more kind and pleasing?
Is it not for that respect especially, that pleasure itself is to so
many men's hurt and overthrow, most prevalent, because esteemed commonly
most kind, and natural? But consider well whether magnanimity rather,
and true liberty, and true simplicity, and equanimity, and holiness;
whether these be not most kind and natural? And prudency itself, what
more kind and amiable than it, when thou shalt truly consider with
thyself, what it is through all the proper objects of thy rational
intellectual faculty currently to go on without any fall or stumble?
As for the things of the world, their true nature is in a manner so
involved with obscurity, that unto many philosophers, and those no
mean ones, they seemed altogether incomprehensible, and the Stoics
themselves, though they judge them not altogether incomprehensible,
yet scarce and not without much difficulty, comprehensible, so that
all assent of ours is fallible, for who is he that is infallible in his
conclusions? From the nature of things, pass now unto their subjects
and matter: how temporary, how vile are they I such as may be in the
power and possession of some abominable loose liver, of some common
strumpet, of some notorious oppressor and extortioner. Pass from thence
to the dispositions of them that thou doest ordinarily converse with,
how hardly do we bear, even with the most loving and amiable! that I may
not say, how hard it is for us to bear even with our own selves, in such
obscurity, and impurity of things: in such and so continual a flux both
of the substances and time; both of the motions themselves, and things
moved; what it is that we can fasten upon; either to honour, and respect
especially; or seriously, and studiously to seek after; I cannot so much
as conceive For indeed they are things contrary.
members.english:
Do not be disgusted, do not give up, do not lose patience, if doing each thing from right principles does not come to you time after time; but when you have been knocked aside, come back again, and be glad if most of what you do is more in keeping with a human being, and love what you are coming back to. And do not come back to philosophy as to a schoolboy’s minder, but as people with sore eyes go to the little sponge and the egg, as another goes to a poultice, as to a medicinal wash. For in this way you will make no show of obeying reason, but will find rest in it. Remember that philosophy wants only what your nature wants; but you were wanting something else, not in accord with nature. For what is more agreeable than these things? For is it not through this that pleasure trips us up? But look whether greatness of soul, freedom, simplicity, fairness of mind, piety are more agreeable. For what is more agreeable than wisdom itself, when you think of how the power of understanding and knowledge never stumbles and flows smoothly in everything?

Things are, in a way, so veiled that to not a few philosophers, and not ordinary ones, they have seemed altogether impossible to grasp; except that to the Stoics themselves, at least, they seem hard to grasp. And every assent of ours can shift: for where is the person who does not shift? Pass on, then, to the objects themselves: how short-lived they are, how cheap, how they can be in the possession of a catamite, a prostitute or a robber. After that go on to the characters of the people you live with: one can hardly put up with even the most charming of them, not to mention that a person can hardly bear even themselves. In such gloom and filth, then, and in so great a flow of substance and of time, of movement and of the things moved, what there is that can be highly valued, or pursued in earnest at all, I cannot even imagine. For on the contrary …
members.greek:
Μὴ σικχαίνειν μηδὲ ἀπαυδᾶν μηδὲ ἀποδυσπετεῖν, εἰ μὴ καταπυκνοῦταί σοι τὸ ἀπὸ δογμάτων ὀρθῶν ἕκαστα πράσσειν, ἀλλὰ ἐκκρουσθέντα πάλιν ἐπανιέναι καὶ ἀσμενίζειν, εἰ τὰ πλείω ἀνθρωπικώτερα, καὶ φιλεῖν τοῦτο, ἐφ̓ ὃ ἐπανέρχῃ, καὶ μὴ ὡς πρὸς παιδαγωγὸν τὴν φιλοσοφίαν ἐπανιέναι, ἀλλ’ ὡς οἱ ὀφθαλμιῶντες πρὸς τὸ σπογγάριον καὶ τὸ ᾠόν, ὡς ἄλλος πρὸς κατάπλασμα, ὡς πρὸς καταιόνησιν. οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲν ἐπιδείξῃ τὸ πειθαρχεῖν τῷ λόγῳ, ἀλλὰ προσαναπαύσῃ αὐτῷ. μέμνησο δὲ ὅτι φιλοσοφία μόνα θέλει ἃ ἡ φύσις σου θέλει· σὺ δὲ ἄλλο ἤθελες οὐ κατὰ φύσιν. τί γὰρ τούτων προσηνέστερον; ἡ γὰρ ἡδονὴ οὐχὶ διὰ τοῦτο σφάλλει; ἀλλὰ θέασαι, εἰ προσηνέστερον μεγαλοψυχία, ἐλευθερία, ἁπλότης, εὐγνωμοσύνη, ὁσιότης, αὐτῆς γὰρ φρονήσεως τί προσηνέστερον, ὅταν τὸ ἄπταιστον καὶ εὔρουν ἐν πᾶσι τῆς παρακολουθητικῆς καὶ ἐπιστημονικῆς δυνάμεως ἐνθυμηθῇς;

Τὰ μὲν πράγματα ἐν τοιαύτῃ τρόπον τινὰ ἐγκαλύψει ἐστίν, ὥστε φιλοσόφοις οὐκ ὀλίγοις οὐδὲ τοῖς τυχοῦσιν ἔδοξε παντάπασιν ἀκατάληπτα εἶναι, πλὴν αὐτοῖς γε τοῖς Στωικοῖς δυσκατάληπτα δοκεῖ· καὶ πᾶσα ἡ ἡμετέρα συγκατάθεσις μεταπτώτη· ποῦ γὰρ ὁ ἀμετάπτωτος; μέτιθι τοίνυν ἐπ’ αὐτὰ τὰ ὑποκείμενα ὡς ὀλιγοχρόνια καὶ εὐτελῆ καὶ δυνάμενα ἐν κτήσει κιναίδου ἢ πόρνης ἢ λῃστοῦ εἶναι. μετὰ τοῦτο ἔπιθι ἐπὶ τὰ τῶν συμβιούντων ἤθη, ὧν μόλις ἐστὶ καὶ τοῦ χαριεστάτου ἀνασχέσθαι, ἵνα μὴ λέγω, ὅτι καὶ ἑαυτόν τις μόγις ὑπομένει. ἐν τοιούτῳ οὖν ζόφῳ καὶ ῥύπῳ καὶ τοσαύτῃ ῥύσει τῆς τε οὐσίας καὶ τοῦ χρόνου καὶ τῆς κινήσεως καὶ τῶν κινουμένων τί ποτέ ἐστι τὸ ἐκτιμηθῆναι ἢ τὸ ὅλως σπουδασθῆναι δυνάμενον, οὐδ’ ἐπινοῶ. τοὐναντίον γὰρ

members.text:
This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory;
if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the
commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least,
hath lived a philosopher's life. For both unto others, and to thyself
especially, it is well known, that thou hast done many things contrary
to that perfection of life. Thou hast therefore been confounded in thy
course, and henceforth it will be hard for thee to recover the title and
credit of a philosopher. And to it also is thy calling and profession
repugnant. If therefore thou dost truly understand, what it is that is
of moment indeed; as for thy fame and credit, take no thought or care
for that: let it suffice thee if all the rest of thy life, be it more or
less, thou shalt live as thy nature requireth, or according to the true
and natural end of thy making. Take pains therefore to know what it is
that thy nature requireth, and let nothing else distract thee. Thou
hast already had sufficient experience, that of those many things that
hitherto thou hast erred and wandered about, thou couldst not find
happiness in any of them. Not in syllogisms, and logical subtilties, not
in wealth, not in honour and reputation, not in pleasure. In none of all
these. Wherein then is it to be found? In the practice of those things,
which the nature of man, as he is a man, doth require. How then shall
he do those things? if his dogmata, or moral tenets and opinions (from
which all motions and actions do proceed), be right and true. Which be
those dogmata? Those that concern that which is good or evil, as that
there is nothing truly good and beneficial unto man, but that which
makes him just, temperate, courageous, liberal; and that there is
nothing truly evil and hurtful unto man, but that which causeth the
contrary effects.
members.english: This too helps you not to care for empty reputation: that you can no longer have lived your whole life, or at least your life since youth, as a philosopher, but to many others, and to you yourself, it has become plain that you are far from philosophy. You are muddied, then, so that winning the reputation of a philosopher is no longer easy for you; and your situation fights against it too. If, then, you have truly seen where the matter lies, let go of what reputation you will have, and be content if you live at least the rest of your life, however much it may be, as your nature wants. So understand what it wants, and let nothing else pull you away. For you have learned by trial how many things you wandered among and nowhere found the good life: not in syllogisms, not in wealth, not in reputation, not in enjoyment, nowhere. Where is it, then? In doing what human nature asks for. How, then, will you do these things? If you have principles from which your impulses and actions come. What principles? Those about good things and bad: that nothing is a good thing for a human being which does not make them just, self-controlled, brave, free, and nothing is a bad thing which does not make them the opposite of these.
members.greek: Καὶ τοῦτο πρὸς τὸ ἀκενόδοξον φέρει, ὅτι οὐκέτι δύνασαι τὸν βίον ὅλον ἢ τόν γε ἀπὸ νεότητος φιλόσοφον βεβιωκέναι, ἀλλὰ πολλοῖς τε ἄλλοις καὶ αὐτὸς σεαυτῷ δῆλος γέγονας πόρρω φιλοσοφίας ὤν. πέφυρσαι οὖν, ὥστε τὴν μὲν δόξαν τὴν τοῦ φιλοσόφου κτήσασθαι οὐκέτι σοι ῥᾴδιον· ἀνταγωνίζεται δὲ καὶ ἡ ὑπόθεσις. εἴπερ οὖν ἀληθῶς ἑώρακας ποῦ κεῖται τὸ πρᾶγμα, τὸ μὲν τί δόξεις ἄφες, ἀρκέσθητι δέ, εἰ κἂν τὸ λοιπὸν τοῦ βίου ὅσον δήποτε, ὡς ἡ σὴ φύσις θέλει, βιώσῃ. κατανόησον οὖν τί θέλει, καὶ ἄλλο μηδέν σε περισπάτω· πεπείρασαι γὰρ περὶ πόσα πλανηθεὶς οὐδαμοῦ εὗρες τὸ εὖ ζῆν, οὐκ ἐν συλλογισμοῖς, οὐκ ἐν πλούτῳ, οὐκ ἐν δόξῃ, οὐκ ἐν ἀπολαύσει, οὐδαμοῦ. ποῦ οὖν ἐστιν; ἐν τῷ ποιεῖν ἃ ἐπιζητεῖ ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου φύσις. πῶς οὖν ταῦτα ποιήσεις; ἐὰν δόγματα ἔχῃς ἀφ’ ὧν αἱ ὁρμαὶ καὶ αἱ πράξεις. τίνα δόγματα; περὶ ἀγαθῶν καὶ κακῶν, ὡς οὐδενὸς μὲν ἀγαθοῦ ὄντος ἀνθρώπῳ ὃ οὐχὶ ποιεῖ δίκαιον, σώφρονα, ἀνδρεῖον, ἐλεύθερον, οὐδενὸς δὲ κακοῦ ὃ οὐχὶ ποιεῖ τἀναντία τοῖς εἰρημένοις.

members.text:
Toys and fooleries at home, wars abroad: sometimes terror, sometimes
torpor, or stupid sloth: this is thy daily slavery. By little and
little, if thou doest not better look to it, those sacred dogmata will
be blotted out of thy mind. How many things be there, which when as
a mere naturalist, thou hast barely considered of according to their
nature, thou doest let pass without any further use? Whereas thou
shouldst in all things so join action and contemplation, that thou
mightest both at the same time attend all present occasions, to perform
everything duly and carefully and yet so intend the contemplative part
too, that no part of that delight and pleasure, which the contemplative
knowledge of everything according to its true nature doth of itself
afford, might be lost. Or, that the true and contemnplative knowledge
of everything according to its own nature, might of itself, (action
being subject to many lets and impediments) afford unto thee sufficient
pleasure and happiness. Not apparent indeed, but not concealed. And when
shalt thou attain to the happiness of true simplicity, and unaffected
gravity? When shalt thou rejoice in the certain knowledge of every
particular object according to its true nature: as what the matter and
substance of it is; what use it is for in the world: how long it can
subsist: what things it doth consist of: who they be that are capable of
it, and who they that can give it, and take it away?
members.english: Farce, war, panic, numbness, slavery: day by day those sacred principles of yours will be wiped out, all those that you picture without study of nature and let go by. But everything must be looked at and done in such a way that at one and the same time the practical side is carried out and the contemplative side is at work, and that the self-assurance which comes from knowledge of each thing is kept, unnoticed but not hidden. For when will you enjoy simplicity? When dignity? When the recognition, in each case, of what the thing is in its substance, what place it has in the universe, how long it is in its nature to last, what it is put together from, who can have it, and who can give it and take it away?
members.greek: Μῖμος, πόλεμος, πτοία, νάρκα, δουλεία· καθ’ ἡμέραν ἀπαλείψεταί σου τὰ ἱερὰ ἐκεῖνα δόγματα, ὁπόσα ἀφυσιολογήτως φαντάζῃ καὶ παραπέμπεις. δεῖ δὲ πᾶν οὕτω βλέπειν καὶ πράσσειν ὥστε καὶ τὸ πρακτικὸν ἅμα συντελεῖσθαι καὶ ἅμα τὸ θεωρητικὸν ἐνεργεῖσθαι καὶ τὸ ἐκ τῆς περὶ ἑκάστων ἐπιστήμης αὔθαδες σῴζεσθαι λανθάνον, οὐχὶ κρυπτόμενον. πότε γὰρ ἁπλότητος ἀπολαύσεις; πότε δὲ σεμνότητος; πότε δὲ τῆς ἐφ’ ἑκάστου γνωρίσεως, τί τε ἐστὶ κατ’ οὐσίαν καὶ τίνα χώραν ἔχει ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ καὶ ἐπὶ πόσον πέφυκεν ὑφίστασθαι καὶ ἐκ τίνων συγκέκριται καὶ τίσι δύναται ὑπάρχειν καὶ τίνες δύνανται αὐτὸ διδόναι τε καὶ ἀφαιρεῖσθαι;

members.text:
Let these be the objects of thy ordinary meditation: to consider,
what manner of men both for soul and body we ought to be, whensoever
death shall surprise us: the shortness of this our mortal life: the
immense vastness of the time that hath been before, and will he after
us: the frailty of every worldly material object: all these things to
consider, and behold clearly in themselves, all disguisement of external
outside being removed and taken away. Again, to consider the efficient
causes of all things: the proper ends and references of all actions:
what pain is in itself; what pleasure, what death: what fame or
honour, how every man is the true and proper ground of his own rest and
tranquillity, and that no man can truly be hindered by any other: that
all is but conceit and opinion. As for the use of thy dogmata, thou must
carry thyself in the practice of them, rather like unto a pancratiastes,
or one that at the same time both fights and wrestles with hands and
feet, than a gladiator. For this, if he lose his sword that he fights
with, he is gone: whereas the other hath still his hand free, which he
may easily turn and manage at his will.
members.english:
What a person ought to be like, in body and in soul, when death catches them. The shortness of life. The gaping expanse of time behind and ahead. The weakness of all matter.

To look at what is causal, bare of its husks. The aims of actions. What pain is. What pleasure is. What death is. What reputation is. Who is the cause of a person’s own busyness. How no one is hindered by another. That everything is judgment.

And in the use of principles one must be like the all-in fighter, not the gladiator. For the gladiator puts down the sword he uses and picks it up; but the other always has his hand, and needs only to clench it.
members.greek:
Ὁποῖον δεῖ καταληφθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ θανάτου καὶ σώματι καὶ ψυχῇ· τὴν βραχύτητα τοῦ βίου· τὴν ἀχάνειαν τοῦ ὀπίσω καὶ πρόσω αἰῶνος· τὴν ἀσθένειαν πάσης ὕλης.

Γυμνὰ τῶν φλοιῶν θεάσασθαι τὰ αἰτιώδη· τὰς ἀναφορὰς τῶν πράξεων· τί πόνος· τί ἡδονή· τί θάνατος· τί δόξα· τίς ὁ ἑαυτῷ ἀσχολίας αἴτιος· πῶς οὐδεὶς ὑπ’ ἄλλου ἐμποδίζεται· ὅτι πάντα ὑπόληψις.

Ὅμοιον δ’ εἶναι δεῖ ἐν τῇ τῶν δογμάτων χρήσει παγκρατιαστῇ, οὐχὶ μονομάχῳ· ὁ μὲν γὰρ τὸ ξίφος ᾧ χρῆται ἀποτίθεται καὶ ἀναιρεῖται· ὁ δὲ τὴν χεῖρα ἀεὶ ἔχει καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο ἢ συστρέψαι αὐτὴν δεῖ.

members.text:
To these ever-present helps and mementoes, let one more be added,
ever to make a particular description and delineation as it were of
every object that presents itself to thy mind, that thou mayest wholly
and throughly contemplate it, in its own proper nature, bare and naked;
wholly, and severally; divided into its several parts and quarters: and
then by thyself in thy mind, to call both it, and those things of which
it doth consist, and in which it shall be resolved, by their own proper
true names, and appellations. For there is nothing so effectual to beget
true magnanimity, as to be able truly and methodically to examine and
consider all things that happen in this life, and so to penetrate
into their natures, that at the same time, this also may concur in our
apprehensions: what is the true use of it? and what is the true nature
of this universe, to which it is useful? how much in regard of the
universe may it be esteemed? how much in regard of man, a citizen of the
supreme city, of which all other cities in the world are as it were but
houses and families?
members.english: To the precepts already named let one more be added: always to make a definition or outline of the thing that comes up in an impression, so as to see it as it is in its substance, bare, whole and entire, and taken apart, and to say to oneself its own name and the names of the things from which it was put together and into which it will be broken up. For nothing so produces greatness of mind as being able to test methodically and truly each of the things that come up in life, and always looking into them in such a way as to take in at the same time what kind of use this thing supplies to what kind of universe, what it is worth to the whole, and what to the human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, of which the other cities are like houses.
members.greek: Τοῖς δὲ εἰρημένοις παραστήμασιν ἓν ἔτι προσέστω, τὸ ὅρον ἢ ὑπογραφὴν ἀεὶ ποιεῖσθαι τοῦ ὑποπίπτοντος φανταστοῦ, ὥστε αὐτὸ ὁποῖόν ἐστι κατ’ οὐσίαν, γυμνόν, ὅλον δι’ ὅλων διῃρημένως βλέπειν καὶ τὸ ἴδιον ὄνομα αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἐκείνων, ἐξ ὧν συνεκρίθη καὶ εἰς ἃ ἀναλυθήσεται, λέγειν παρ’ ἑαυτῷ. οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν, ὡς τὸ ἐλέγχειν ὁδῷ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ ἕκαστον τῶν τῷ βίῳ ὑποπιπτόντων δύνασθαι καὶ τὸ ἀεὶ οὕτως εἰς αὐτὰ ὁρᾶν, ὥστε συνεπιβάλλειν ὁποίῳ τινὶ τῷ κόσμῳ ὁποίαν τινὰ τοῦτο χρείαν παρεχόμενον τίνα μὲν ἔχει ἀξίαν ὡς πρὸς τὸ ὅλον, τίνα δὲ ὡς πρὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον, πολίτην ὄντα πόλεως τῆς ἀνωτάτης, ἧς αἱ λοιπαὶ πόλεις ὥσπερ οἰκίαι εἰσίν·

members.text:
To find out, and set to thyself some certain way and method of
contemplation, whereby thou mayest clearly discern and represent unto
thyself, the mutual change of all things, the one into the other. Bear
it in thy mind evermore, and see that thou be throughly well exercised
in this particular. For there is not anything more effectual to beget
true magnanimity.
members.english: How all things change into one another: get yourself a method for contemplating it, attend to it constantly, and train yourself in this field. For nothing so produces greatness of mind.
members.greek: Πῶς εἰς ἄλληλα πάντα μεταβάλλει, θεωρητικὴν μέθοδον κτῆσαι καὶ διηνεκῶς πρόσεχε καὶ συγγυμνάσθητι περὶ τοῦτο τὸ μέρος· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτως μεγαλοφροσύνης ποιητικόν.

members.text:
How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself
meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right
apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a
fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog. And again more generally; This
phalernum, this excellent highly commended wine, is but the bare juice
of an ordinary grape. This purple robe, but sheep's hairs, dyed with
the blood of a shellfish. So for coitus, it is but the attrition of an
ordinary base entrail, and the excretion of a little vile snivel, with
a certain kind of convulsion: according to Hippocrates his opinion. How
excellent useful are these lively fancies and representations of things,
thus penetrating and passing through the objects, to make their true
nature known and apparent! This must thou use all thy life long, and
upon all occasions: and then especially, when matters are apprehended
as of great worth and respect, thy art and care must be to uncover
them, and to behold their vileness, and to take away from them all those
serious circumstances and expressions, under which they made so grave
a show. For outward pomp and appearance is a great juggler; and then
especially art thou most in danger to be beguiled by it, when (to
a man's thinking) thou most seemest to be employed about matters of
moment.
members.english: Just as, over cooked dishes and other such things to eat, one takes the impression that this is the dead body of a fish, and this the dead body of a bird or a pig; and again, that Falernian wine is a little juice from a little bunch of grapes, and the purple-bordered robe is little hairs of a little sheep soaked in a little blood from a shellfish; and, over what belongs to sex, that it is the rubbing of a bit of gut and, with a kind of spasm, the discharge of a little slime: just as these impressions reach the things themselves and go right through them, so that one sees what they really are, so one must do through the whole of life, and where things give the impression of being very trustworthy, strip them bare, see their cheapness plainly, and strip off the story on which they pride themselves. For conceit is a formidable cheat, and it is when you think you are most occupied with serious things that you are most bewitched.
members.greek: Οἷον δὴ τὸ φαντασίαν λαμβάνειν ἐπὶ τῶν ὄψων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων ἐδωδίμων, ὅτι νεκρὸς οὗτος ἰχθύος, οὗτος δὲ νεκρὸς ὄρνιθος ἢ χοίρου· καὶ πάλιν, ὅτι ὁ Φάλερνος χυλάριόν ἐστι σταφυλίου καὶ ἡ περιπόρφυρος τριχία προβατίου αἱματίῳ κόγχης δεδευμένα· καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κατὰ τὴν συνουσίαν ἐντερίου παράτριψις καὶ μετά τινος σπασμοῦ μυξαρίου ἔκκρισις· οἷαι δὴ αὗταί εἰσιν αἱ φαντασίαι καθικνούμεναι αὐτῶν τῶν πραγμάτων καὶ διεξιοῦσαι δι’ αὐτῶν, ὥστε ὁρᾶν οἷά τινά ποτέ ἐστιν· οὕτως δεῖ παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον ποιεῖν καὶ ὅπου λίαν ἀξιόπιστα τὰ πράγματα φαντάζεται, ἀπογυμνοῦν αὐτὰ καὶ τὴν εὐτέλειαν αὐτῶν καθορᾶν καὶ τὴν ἱστορίαν ἐφ’ ᾗ σεμνύνεται περιαιρεῖν. δεινὸς γὰρ ὁ τῦφος παραλογιστὴς καὶ ὅτε δοκεῖς μάλιστα περὶ τὰ σπουδαῖα καταγίνεσθαι, τότε μάλιστα καταγοητεύῃ.

members.text:
And these your professed politicians, the only true practical
philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of
affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what
wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves?
O man! what ado doest thou keep? Do what thy nature doth now require.
Resolve upon it, if thou mayest: and take no thought, whether anybody
shall know it or no. Yea, but sayest thou, I must not expect a Plato's
commonwealth. If they profit though never so little, I must be content;
and think much even of that little progress. Doth then any of them
forsake their former false opinions that I should think they profit? For
without a change of opinions, alas! what is all that ostentation, but
mere wretchedness of slavish minds, that groan privately, and yet would
make a show of obedience to reason, and truth? Go too now and tell me
of Alexander and Philippus, and Demetrius Phalereus. Whether they
understood what the common nature requireth, and could rule themselves
or no, they know best themselves. But if they kept a life, and
swaggered; I (God be thanked) am not bound to imitate them. The effect
of true philosophy is, unaffected simplicity and modesty. Persuade me
not to ostentation and vainglory.
members.english: And how cheap, too, are these little people who are busy with public affairs and, as they suppose, practical in a philosophic way: full of snot. Man, what then? Do what nature now demands. Set out, if it is given to you, and do not look around to see whether anyone will know. Do not hope for Plato’s republic, but be content if the smallest thing goes forward, and think of the outcome of even this as a small thing. For who will change a principle of theirs? And without a change of principles, what is there but the slavery of people who groan and pretend to be persuaded? Go on now and tell me of Alexander and Philip and Demetrius of Phalerum. It is for them to see whether they saw what the common nature wanted and schooled themselves; but if they played the tragic hero, no one has condemned me to imitate them. The work of philosophy is simple and modest: do not lead me off into solemn conceit.
members.greek: ὡς εὐτελῆ δὲ καὶ τὰ πολιτικὰ ταῦτα καί, ὡς οἴεται, φιλοσόφως πρακτικὰ ἀνθρώπια· μυξῶν μεστά.—ἄνθρωπε, τί ποτε; ποίησον ὃ νῦν ἡ φύσις ἀπαιτεῖ, ὅρμησον, ἐὰν διδῶται, καὶ μὴ περιβλέπου εἴ τις εἴσεται. μὴ τὴν Πλάτωνος πολιτείαν ἔλπιζε, ἀλλὰ ἀρκοῦ, εἰ τὸ βραχύτατον πρόεισι, καὶ τούτου αὐτοῦ τὴν ἔκβασιν ὡς μικρόν τί ἐστι διανοοῦ. δόγμα γὰρ αὐτῶν τίς μεταβαλεῖ; χωρὶς δὲ δογμάτων μεταβολῆς τί ἄλλο ἢ δουλεία στενόντων καὶ πείθεσθαι προσποιουμένων; ὕπαγε νῦν καὶ Ἀλέξανδρον καὶ Φίλιππον καὶ Δημήτριον τὸν Φαληρέα μοι λέγε. ὄψονται, εἰ εἶδον, τί ἡ κοινὴ φύσις ἤθελε, καὶ ἑαυτοὺς ἐπαιδαγώγησαν· εἰ δὲ ἐτραγῴδησαν, οὐδείς με κατακέκρικε μιμεῖσθαι. ἁπλοῦν ἐστι καὶ αἰδῆμον τὸ φιλοσοφίας ἔργον· μή με ἄπαγε ἐπὶ σεμνοτυφίαν.

members.text:
What a subject, and what a course of life is it, that thou doest
so much desire to be rid of. For all these things, what are they, but
fit objects for an understanding, that beholdeth everything according to
its true nature, to exercise itself upon? Be patient, therefore, until
that (as a strong stomach that turns all things into his own nature; and
as a great fire that turneth in flame and light, whatsoever thou doest
cast into it) thou have made these things also familiar, and as it were
natural unto thee.
members.english: What material, what a subject, you are running away from! For what are all these things but exercises for a reason that has seen the things in life accurately and as a student of nature? Stay, then, until you have made these things too your own, as a strong stomach makes everything its own, as a bright fire makes flame and light out of whatever you throw into it.
members.greek: Οἵαν ὕλην καὶ ὑπόθεσιν φεύγεις· τί γάρ ἐστι πάντα ταῦτα ἄλλο πλὴν γυμνάσματα λόγου ἑωρακότος ἀκριβῶς καὶ φυσιολόγως τὰ ἐν τῷ βίῳ; μένε οὖν, μέχρι ἐξοικειώσῃς σεαυτῷ καὶ ταῦτα, ὡς ὁ ἐρρωμένος στόμαχος πάντα ἐξοικειοῖ, ὡς τὸ λαμπρὸν πῦρ, ὅ τι ἂν ἐμβάλῃς, φλόγα ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ αὐγὴν ποιεῖ.

members.text:
For it is a thing very possible, that a man should be a very
divine man, and yet be altogether unknown. This thou must ever be
mindful of, as of this also, that a man's true happiness doth consist
in very few things. And that although thou dost despair, that thou shalt
ever be a good either logician, or naturalist, yet thou art never the
further off by it from being either liberal, or modest, or charitable,
or obedient unto God.
members.english: For it is very possible to become a godlike man and to be recognised by no one. Remember this always, and this as well: that living happily lies in very few things. And because you have given up hope of being a logician and a student of nature, do not for that reason give up on being free, modest, social and obedient to god.
members.greek: λίαν γὰρ ἐνδέχεται θεῖον ἄνδρα γενέσθαι καὶ ὑπὸ μηδενὸς γνωρισθῆναι. τούτου μέμνησο ἀεὶ καὶ ἔτι ἐκείνου, ὅτι ἐν ὀλιγίστοις κεῖται τὸ εὐδαιμόνως βιῶσαι καὶ μή, ὅτι ἀπήλπισας διαλεκτικὸς καὶ φυσικὸς ἔσεσθαι, διὰ τοῦτο ἀπογνῷς καὶ ἐλεύθερος καὶ αἰδήμων καὶ κοινωνικὸς καὶ εὐπειθὴς θεῷ.

members.text:
Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See
that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never
cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good. And how should
this be well brought to pass, but by certain theorems and doctrines;
some Concerning the nature of the universe, and some Concerning the
proper and particular constitution of man?
members.english:
I have done something as a social being: then I have been benefited. See that this always comes to hand, and never stop.

What is your craft? To be good. And how does that come about well, except from points of theory, some about the nature of the whole, others about the constitution proper to the human being?
members.greek:
Πεποίηκά τι κοινωνικῶς· οὐκοῦν ὠφέλημαι. τοῦτο ἵνα ἀεὶ πρόχειρον ἀπαντᾷ, καὶ μηδαμοῦ παύου.

Τίς σου ἡ τέχνη; ἀγαθὸν εἶναι. τοῦτο δὲ πῶς καλῶς γίνεται ὴ ἐκ θεωρημάτων, τῶν μὲν περὶ τῆς τοῦ ὅλου φύσεως, τῶν δὲ περὶ τῆς ἰδίας τοῦ ἀνθρώπου κατασκευῆς.

members.why: A test of what most people call good, made with a line of comedy. Its list of true goods is close to 8.1’s, but its subject is which things are good, not how I keep to philosophy or come back to it.
members.text:
What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are
esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this. For if a man shall
hear things mentioned as good, which are really good indeed, such as are
prudence, temperance, justice, fortitude, after so much heard and
conceived, he cannot endure to hear of any more, for the word good is
properly spoken of them. But as for those which by the vulgar are
esteemed good, if he shall hear them mentioned as good, he doth hearken
for more. He is well contented to hear, that what is spoken by the
comedian, is but familiarly and popularly spoken, so that even the
vulgar apprehend the difference. For why is it else, that this offends
not and needs not to be excused, when virtues are styled good: but that
which is spoken in commendation of wealth, pleasure, or honour, we
entertain it only as merrily and pleasantly spoken? Proceed therefore,
and inquire further, whether it may not be that those things also which
being mentioned upon the stage were merrily, and with great applause of
the multitude, scoffed at with this jest, that they that possessed them
had not in all the world of their own, (such was their affluence and
plenty) so much as a place where to avoid their excrements. Whether, I
say, those ought not also in very deed to be much respected, and
esteemed of, as the only things that are truly good.
members.english: What kind of things they are that seem good to most people, you can gather from this as well. For if a person had in mind certain things that truly are good, such as wisdom, self-control, justice, courage, then, with these first in mind, they could not listen to the words “because of the good things”, for it will not fit. But a person who has first in mind the things that appear good to most people will listen, and will readily accept what the comic poet said as a fitting thing to add. So even most people have an impression of the difference. For otherwise this line would not jar and be refused in the one case, while, when it is said of wealth and of the pieces of good luck that make for luxury or reputation, we accept it as aptly and wittily said. Go on, then, and ask whether one should honour and judge to be good the kind of things which, when they have first been brought to mind, can fittingly be followed by the line that their owner, because of the plenty, “has nowhere to shit”.
members.greek: Ὁποῖά τινά ἐστι τὰ τοῖς πολλοῖς δοκοῦντα ἀγαθά, κἂν ἐντεῦθεν λάβοις. εἰ γάρ τις ἐπινοήσειεν ὑπάρχοντά τινα ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθά, οἷον φρόνησιν, σωφροσύνην, δικαιοσύνην, ἀνδρείαν, οὐκ ἂν ταῦτα προεπινοήσας ἐπακοῦσαι δυνηθείη τό· ʽὑπὸ τῶν ἀγαθῶνʼ, οὐ γὰρ ἐφαρμόσει. τὰ δέ γε τοῖς πολλοῖς φαινόμενα ἀγαθὰ προεπινοήσας τις ἐπακούσεται καὶ ῥᾳδίως δέξεται ὡς οἰκείως ἐπιλεγόμενον τὸ ὑπὸ τοῦ κωμικοῦ εἰρημένον. οὕτως καὶ οἱ πολλοὶ φαντάζονται τὴν διαφοράν· οὐ γὰρ ἂν τοῦτο μὲν οὐ προσέκοπτε καὶ ἀπηξιοῦτο, τὸ δὲ ἐπὶ τοῦ πλούτου καὶ τῶν πρὸς τρυφὴν ἢ δόξαν εὐκληρημάτων παρεδεχόμεθα ὡς ἱκνουμένως καὶ ἀστείως εἰρημένον. πρόιθι οὖν καὶ ἐρώτα, εἰ τιμητέον καὶ ἀγαθὰ ὑποληπτέον τὰ τοιαῦτα, ὧν προεπινοηθέντων οἰκείως ἂν ἐπιφέροιτο τὸ τὸν κεκτημένον αὐτὰ ὑπὸ τῆς εὐπορίας ʽοὐκ ἔχειν ὅποι χέσῃʼ.

members.text:
How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy
life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very
course, that thou art now already in?
members.english: How plainly it comes home that there is no other situation in life so suited to philosophy as this one in which you now happen to be.
members.greek: Πῶς ἐναργὲς προσπίπτει τὸ μὴ εἶναι ἄλλην βίου ὑπόθεσιν εἰς τὸ φιλοσοφεῖν οὕτως ἐπιτήδειον ὡς ταύτην, ἐν ᾗ νῦν ὢν τυγχάνεις.

members.text:
As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready
at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a
readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and
whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou
must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between
these two things divine, and things human. For without relation unto
God, thou shalt never speed in any worldly actions; nor on the other
side in any divine, without some respect had to things human.
members.english: As doctors always have their instruments and blades at hand for emergency treatments, so have your principles ready for knowing things divine and human, and for doing everything, even the smallest thing, as one who remembers the bond that ties the two to each other. For you will not do any human thing well without referring it at the same time to the divine, nor the other way round.
members.greek: Ὥσπερ οἱ ἰατροὶ ἀεὶ τὰ ὄργανα καὶ σιδήρια πρόχειρα ἔχουσι πρὸς τὰ αἰφνίδια τῶν θεραπευμάτων, οὕτω τὰ δόγματα σὺ ἕτοιμα ἔχε πρὸς τὸ τὰ θεῖα καὶ ἀνθρώπινα εἰδέναι, καὶ πᾶν καὶ τὸ μικρότατον οὕτω ποιεῖν ὡς τῆς ἀμφοτέρων πρὸς ἄλληλα συνδέσεως μεμνημένον. οὔτε γὰρ ἀνθρώπινόν τι ἄνευ τῆς ἐπὶ τὰ θεῖα συναναφορᾶς εὖ πράξεις οὔτ’ ἔμπαλιν.

members.why: Says that what moves a person is hidden inside and that the body is its tool. Nothing in it is about principles, their use or falling short; it belongs with the passages on the ruling part and the body.
members.text:
Remember, that that which sets a man at work, and hath power
over the affections to draw them either one way, or the other way, is
not any external thing properly, but that which is hidden within every
man's dogmata, and opinions: That, that is rhetoric; that is life; that
(to speak true) is man himself. As for thy body, which as a vessel, or
a case, compasseth thee about, and the many and curious instruments
that it hath annexed unto it, let them not trouble thy thoughts. For
of themselves they are but as a carpenter's axe, but that they are born
with us, and naturally sticking unto us. But otherwise, without the
inward cause that hath power to move them, and to restrain them, those
parts are of themselves of no more use unto us, than the shuttle is
of itself to the weaver, or the pen to the writer, or the whip to the
coachman.
members.english: Remember that what pulls the strings is that thing hidden inside. That is oratory, that is life, that, if one must say it, is the human being. Never picture along with it the vessel-like thing that surrounds it and these little tools moulded around it. For they are like a carpenter’s axe, differing only in being grown on. For without the cause that moves them and holds them in check, these parts are in fact of no more use than the weaver’s shuttle, the writer’s pen and the charioteer’s little whip.
