and concordant with the Gods; that is, accepting with praises whatsoever
they shall think good to appoint and allot unto thee.
members.english: It is not breathing through the surface as plants do that is of value, nor breathing as cattle and wild beasts do, nor being stamped by an impression, nor being pulled on strings by impulse, nor herding together, nor taking in food; for this last is like passing out the waste from the food. What then is of value? Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well. What is left that is of value? I think it is this: to move and to hold back in keeping with the way one is oneself made, which is also where tending and the crafts lead. For every craft aims at this, that the thing made should be fit for the work it was made for. The planter and the one who tends the vine, the breaker of colts and the one who tends the dog are after this. And the upbringing of children, and teaching: what are they pressing towards? Here, then, is what is of value. And if this is in a good state, you will not be acquiring any of the other things for yourself. Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and, what is more, to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself, well fitted to your fellows and in tune with the gods, that is, praising all that they deal out and have arranged.
members.greek: Οὔτε τὸ διαπνεῖσθαι ὡς τὰ φυτὰ τίμιον οὔτε τὸ ἀναπνεῖν ὡς τὰ βοσκήματα καὶ τὰ θηρία οὔτε τὸ τυποῦσθαι κατὰ φαντασίαν οὔτε τὸ νευροσπαστεῖσθαι καθ’ ὁρμὴν οὔτε τὸ συναγελάζεσθαι οὔτε τὸ τρέφεσθαι· τοῦτο γὰρ ὅμοιον τῷ ἀποκρίνειν τὰ περιττώματα τῆς τροφῆς. τί οὖν τίμιον; τὸ κροτεῖσθαι; οὐχί. οὐκοῦν οὐδὲ τὸ ὑπὸ γλωσσῶν κροτεῖσθαι· αἱ γὰρ παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν εὐφημίαι κρότος γλωσσῶν. ἀφῆκας οὖν καὶ τὸ δοξάριον· τί καταλείπεται τίμιον; δοκῶ μὲν τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἰδίαν κατασκευὴν κινεῖσθαι καὶ ἴσχεσθαι, ἐφ’ ὅ καὶ αἱ ἐπιμέλειαι ἄγουσι καὶ αἱ τέχναι. ἥ τε γὰρ τέχνη πᾶσα τούτου στοχάζεται, ἵνα τὸ κατασκευασθὲν ἐπιτηδείως ἔχῃ πρὸς τὸ ἔργον πρὸς ὅ κατεσκεύασται· ὅ τε φυτουργὸς καὶ ὁ ἐπιμελούμενος τῆς ἀμπέλου, καὶ ὁ πωλοδάμνης καὶ ὁ τοῦ κυνὸς ἐπιμελούμενος τοῦτο ζητεῖ. αἱ δὲ παιδαγωγίαι, αἱ δὲ διδασκαλίαι ἐπὶ τί σπεύδουσιν; ὧδε οὖν τὸ τίμιον καὶ τοῦτο μὲν ἂν εὖ ἔχῃ, οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων περιποιήσεις σεαυτῷ. οὐ παύσῃ καὶ ἄλλα πολλὰ τιμῶν; οὔτ’ οὖν ἐλεύθερος ἔσῃ οὔτε αὐτάρκης οὔτε ἀπαθής· ἀνάγκη γὰρ φθονεῖν, ζηλοτυπεῖν, ὑφορᾶσθαι τοὺς ἀφελέσθαι ἐκεῖνα δυναμένους, ἐπιβουλεύειν τοῖς ἔχουσι τὸ τιμώμενον ὑπὸ σοῦ. ὅλως πεφύρθαι ἀνάγκη τὸν ἐκείνων τινὸς ἐνδεῆ, προσέτι δὲ πολλὰ καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς μέμφεσθαι. ἡ δὲ τῆς ἰδίας διανοίας αἰδὼς καὶ τιμὴ σεαυτῷ τε ἀρεστόν σε ποιήσει καὶ τοῖς κοινωνοῖς εὐάρμοστον καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς σύμφωνον, τουτέστιν ἐπαινοῦντα ὅσα ἐκεῖνοι διανέμουσι καὶ διατετάχασιν.

members.text:
O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple,
single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed.
Thou wilt one day be sensible of their happiness, whose end is love, and
their affections dead to all worldly things. Thou shalt one day be full,
and in want of no external thing: not seeking pleasure from anything,
either living or insensible, that this world can afford; neither wanting
time for the continuation of thy pleasure, nor place and opportunity,
nor the favour either of the weather or of men. When thou shalt have
content in thy present estate, and all things present shall add to thy
content: when thou shalt persuade thyself, that thou hast all things;
all for thy good, and all by the providence of the Gods: and of things
future also shalt be as confident, that all will do well, as tending to
the maintenance and preservation in some sort, of his perfect welfare
and happiness, who is perfection of life, of goodness, and beauty; who
begets all things, and containeth all things in himself, and in himself
doth recollect all things from all places that are dissolved, that of
them he may beget others again like unto them. Such one day shall be thy
disposition, that thou shalt be able, both in regard of the Gods, and
in regard of men, so to fit and order thy conversation, as neither
to complain of them at any time, for anything that they do; nor to do
anything thyself, for which thou mayest justly be condemned.
members.english: Will you ever, soul, be good and simple and one and bare, plainer to see than the body wrapped round you? Will you ever taste the loving and affectionate disposition? Will you ever be full and in need of nothing, longing for nothing and desiring nothing, whether living or lifeless, for the enjoyment of pleasures? Nor time in which to enjoy them longer? Nor a place or a country or a mild climate? Nor people who suit you well? But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present, and persuade yourself that all things are present to you, from the gods, that all things are well with you and will be well, all that pleases them and all that they are going to give for the preservation of the perfect living being, the good and just and beautiful one, which begets all things and holds them together and surrounds them and takes them into itself as they are dissolved for the birth of others like them? Will you ever be such as to live as a fellow citizen with gods and human beings in such a way that you neither find any fault with them nor are condemned by them?
members.greek: Ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα, ὦ ψυχή, ἀγαθὴ καὶ ἁπλῆ καὶ μία καὶ γυμνή, φανερωτέρα τοῦ περικειμένου σοι σώματος; γεύσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα τῆς φιλητικῆς καὶ στερκτικῆς διαθέσεως; ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα πλήρης καὶ ἀνενδεὴς καὶ οὐδὲν ἐπιποθοῦσα οὐδὲ ἐπιθυμοῦσα οὐδενὸς οὔτε ἐμψύχου οὔτε ἀψύχου πρὸς ἡδονῶν ἀπολαύσεις; οὐδὲ χρόνου, ἐν ᾧ ἐπὶ μακρότερον ἀπολαύσεις; οὐδὲ τόπου ἢ χώρας ἢ ἀέρων εὐκρασίας; οὐδὲ ἀνθρώπων εὐαρμοστίας; ἀλλὰ ἀρκεσθήσῃ τῇ παρούσῃ καταστάσει καὶ ἡσθήσῃ τοῖς παροῦσι πᾶσι καὶ συμπείσεις σεαυτὴν ὅτι πάντα σοι παρὰ τῶν θεῶν πάρεστι, πάντα σοι εὖ ἔχει καὶ εὖ ἕξει, ὅσα φίλον αὐτοῖς καὶ ὅσα μέλλουσι δώσειν ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ τοῦ τελείου ζῴου, τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ δικαίου καὶ καλοῦ καὶ γεννῶντος πάντα καὶ συνέχοντος καὶ περιέχοντος καὶ περιλαμβάνοντος διαλυόμενα εἰς γένεσιν ἑτέρων ὁμοίων; ἔσῃ ποτὲ ἆρα τοιαύτη, οἵα θεοῖς τε καὶ ἀνθρώποις οὕτως συμπολιτεύεσθαι ὡς μήτε μέμφεσθαί τι αὐτοῖς μήτε καταγινώσκεσθαι ὑπ’ αὐτῶν;

members.text:
Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much
distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease
roving and wandering to and fro. Thou must also take heed of another
kind of wandering, for they are idle in their actions, who toil and
labour in this life, and have no certain scope to which to direct all
their motions, and desires.
members.english: Do the things that fall on you from outside distract you at all? Then give yourself leisure to learn some further good thing, and stop wandering. But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too: those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.
members.greek: Περισπᾷ τί σε τὰ ἔξωθεν ἐμπίπτοντα; καὶ σχολὴν πάρεχε σεαυτῷ τοῦ προσμανθάνειν ἀγαθόν τι καὶ παῦσαι ῥεμβόμενος. ἤδη δὲ καὶ τὴν ἑτέραν περιφορὰν φυλακτέον· ληροῦσι γὰρ καὶ διὰ πράξεων οἱ κεκμηκότες τῷ βίῳ καὶ μὴ ἔχοντες σκοπόν, ἐφ’ ὃν πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν καὶ καθάπαξ φαντασίαν ἀπευθύνουσιν.

members.text:
What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts
of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy
mind at all? What now is to be done, if thou mayest search and inquiry
into that, what needs thou care for more? And if thou art well able to
perceive it alone, let no man divert thee from it. But if alone thou
doest not so well perceive it, suspend thine action, and take advice
from the best. And if there be anything else that doth hinder thee, go
on with prudence and discretion, according to the present occasion
and opportunity, still proposing that unto thyself, which thou doest
conceive most right and just. For to hit that aright, and to speed in
the prosecution of it, must needs be happiness, since it is that only
which we can truly and properly be said to miss of, or miscarry in.
members.english: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back; and if you do not see it clearly, to hold off and use the best advisers; and if some other things stand in the way of this, to go forward as present means allow, in a considered way, holding to what appears just? For to reach this is best, since failure, at any rate, is falling away from this.
members.greek: Τίς ὑπονοίας χρεία παρὸν σκοπεῖν τί δεῖ πραχθῆναι, κἂν μὲν συνορᾷς, εὐμενῶς, ἀμεταστρεπτὶ ταύτῃ χωρεῖν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ συνορᾷς, ἐπέχειν καὶ συμβούλοις τοῖς ἀρίστοις χρῆσθαι· ἐὰν δὲ ἕτερά τινα πρὸς ταῦτα ἀντιβαίνῃ, προιέναι κατὰ τὰς παρούσας ἀφορμὰς λελογισμένως, ἐχόμενον τοῦ φαινομένου δικαίου; ἄριστον γὰρ κατατυγχάνειν τούτου, ἐπεί τοι ἥ γε ἀπόπτωσις ἀπὸ τούτου ἐστίν.

members.text:
The things themselves (which either to get or to avoid thou art put
to so much trouble) come not unto thee themselves; but thou in a manner
goest unto them. Let then thine own judgment and opinion concerning
those things be at rest; and as for the things themselves, they stand
still and quiet, without any noise or stir at all; and so shall all
pursuing and flying cease.
members.english: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them. At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay still, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν Οὐκ ἔρχεται ἐπὶ σὲ τὰ πράγματα ὧν αἱ διώξεις καὶ φυγαὶ θορυβοῦσί σε, ἀλλὰ τρόπον τινὰ αὐτὸς ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνα ἔρχῃ· τὸ γοῦν κρῖμα τὸ περὶ αὐτῶν ἡσυχαζέτω κἀκεῖνα μενεῖ ἀτρεμοῦντα καὶ οὔτε διώκων οὔτε φεύγων ὀφθήσῃ.

members.text:
Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know
what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only
what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in
Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others,
but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant
agitation.
members.english: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing, so that this very thing may be just and holy, or in keeping with the good man: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that.
members.greek: Ὅσην εὐσχολίαν κερδαίνει ὁ μὴ βλέπων τί ὁ πλησίον εἶπεν ἢ ἔπραξεν ἢ διενοήθη, ἀλλὰ μόνον τί αὐτὸς ποιεῖ, ἵνα αὐτὸ τοῦτο δίκαιον ᾖ καὶ ὅσιον ἢ † κατὰ τὸν ἀγαθὸν· μὴ μέλαν ἦθος περιβλέπεσθαι, ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ τῆς γραμμῆς τρέχειν ὀρθόν, μὴ διερριμμένον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.11 is 2.12–13, 7.20 is 7.27–28, 10.24 is 10.23–24, 6.15 is 6.16, 2.4 is 2.7, 10.13 is 10.12, 11.10 is 11.11, 4.15 is 4.18 and 12.2 is 12.2–3; 4.3, 3.4 and 10.1 are the same.

Reads the soul (4.3), the ruling part (3.4, 7.20, 10.24), the guardian spirit within (2.11) and the mind (4.3, 12.2) as one thing, called “my mind” or “what is within me”. This section does not say that the guardian spirit is the mind; the identification is the editor’s.

Puts praise in claim 2, beside not watching other people, in 6.15’s words (“the many”) rather than 3.4’s narrower ones. 4.3’s own reasons against petty fame (that everything is soon forgotten, and that the whole earth is a point) are not quoted.

Keeps claim 6, acting with an aim, though its passages do not speak of retreat. 2.4 begins with distraction from outside and 4.15 with the leisure gained by not watching a neighbour; the editor reads them as where the retreat sends me back to.
articles.limit: The section holds together less well than its title suggests: 2.4, 10.13 and 4.15 are about aim rather than retreat, and 4.3 feeds three claims, so much rests on one long passage. Much of it is said elsewhere: going back into myself, and doing it continually (claim 1 and the item from 4.3), is in Article 25’s claims 1 and 3; that the place makes no difference is Article 17’s claim 4 and Article 18’s claim 1; claim 3 repeats Articles 7 and 8; claim 4 comes near Article 2’s claim on the body; claim 5 comes near Articles 10 and 16; and asking what my mind is being used for (10.24) and going straight towards a target (claim 6) are in Article 31’s claims 3 and 6, with holding to one aim and going straight on in Articles 1 and 2. Articles 22, 26 and 27 turn my attention to other people’s minds for a purpose, which claim 2’s exception for the common good may allow, though no passage here says so. What this article adds is the retreat as a place I can reach at any hour, keeping to my own mind instead of to what others say and do, and, in claim 6, seeing clearly what has to be done and not being thrown about.

statement.t: I can retreat into myself wherever I am, and I watch what is within me, not what others say or do.

statement.form: Every phrase rests on two passages. “At any hour” is in 4.3 only, so it moves to c1. “What is within me” replaces “my own mind” because 3.4 speaks of the ruling part and 2.11 of the guardian spirit, and the sources do not equate them.

claims.t: I do not need a country place, a seashore or a mountain. Where I am is just like them, and at any hour I am free to retreat into myself. No retreat is quieter than my own soul. Ease in my soul is nothing other than good order. My ruling part is content with itself when it acts justly, and by that very fact it has calm.
claims.shared: “Ease in my soul” names the place so the definition is clear when heard. “At any hour” and “free” are 4.3 only, and 7.20a supports only the turn inward. The definition of ease is 4.3 only. The tie between calm and just action is 7.20 only. “Free to” keeps this a permission, not a duty.

support.quote: People look for retreats for themselves: country places, seashores, mountains. You too are in the habit of longing very much for such things. But all of this is the mark of someone with no training at all, when you are free, at whatever hour you wish, to retreat into yourself.
support.follows: Longing for a retreat in the country, by the sea or in the mountains is untrained, since I can retreat into myself whenever I wish.

support.quote: Let it always be clear that the country place over there is just like this, and how everything here is the same as on the top of the mountain or on the seashore or wherever you like.
support.follows: The place where I am is no different from a country place, a mountain top or a seashore.

support.quote: Draw in upon yourself.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to draw in upon himself.

support.quote: nowhere that a person retreats to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul
support.follows: No place a person can retreat to is quieter or freer from business than their own soul.
gives: No retreat is quieter than my own soul
Ease in my soul is nothing other than good order

support.quote: they are at once in complete ease; and by ease I mean nothing other than good order
support.follows: Whoever has the right things within and looks into them is at once at ease; by ease Marcus means nothing but good order.
gives: Ease in my soul is nothing other than good order

support.quote: It is the nature of the rational ruling part to be content with itself when it acts justly and by that very fact has calm.
support.follows: When the rational ruling part acts justly, it is content with itself and, by that very fact, calm.
gives: My ruling part is content with itself when it acts justly, and by that very fact it has calm

claims.t: I do not wear away what is left of my life on thoughts about other people, unless those thoughts serve the common benefit. I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking. I look only at what I am doing and keep watch over what is within me. The praise of the many is a clapping of tongues, and I set no store by it.
claims.shared: The common-benefit exception is 3.4 only and is attached to the thoughts it qualifies. The clapping image is 6.15 only. In 3.4c the praise set aside comes from people who do not live in agreement with nature, so the margin keeps the good opinion that 3.4 still values.

support.quote: Do not wear away what is left of your life in impressions about other people, when you are not referring them to something of common benefit
support.follows: I should not use up what is left of my life on impressions of other people, unless they serve some common benefit.
gives: I do not wear away what is left of my life on thoughts about other people
unless those thoughts serve the common benefit

support.quote: forming impressions of what so-and-so is doing, and for what purpose, and what they are saying, and what they have in mind, and what they are contriving, and all such things as make you wander away from watching over your own ruling part
support.follows: Picturing what others do, say, mean and plot draws me away from watching over my own ruling part.
gives: I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking
keep watch over what is within me

support.quote: looks by guesswork for what is in the souls of their neighbours, but does not notice that it is enough to keep only to the guardian spirit within them and to serve it truly
support.follows: Guessing at what is in other people’s souls is wretched; it is enough to keep to the guardian spirit within me and serve it.
gives: I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking
keep watch over what is within me

support.quote: How much leisure a person gains who does not look at what their neighbour said or did or thought, but only at what they themselves are doing
support.follows: Whoever looks only at what they are doing, not at what a neighbour said, did or thought, gains much leisure.
gives: I do not guess at what a neighbour is doing, saying or thinking
I look only at what I am doing

support.quote: So he sets no store either by praise that comes from such people, who are not even pleased with themselves.
support.follows: The good man sets no store by praise from people who do not live by nature and are not even pleased with themselves.
gives: I set no store by it

support.quote: Being clapped? No. Then not being clapped by tongues either; for the praises of the many are a clapping of tongues. So you have let petty fame go as well.
support.follows: Applause has no value, and the praise of the many is only applause by tongues, so petty fame has no value either.
gives: The praise of the many is a clapping of tongues
I set no store by it

claims.t: The things I chase or flee in turmoil do not come to me. They stand outside, unmoving, and in a way I go to them. My turmoil comes only from my own judgment about them. When I let that judgment be quiet, they stay still, and I am seen neither chasing nor fleeing.
claims.shared: The scope stays with the things that cause turmoil and keeps the hedge “in a way” from 11.10. This is not a ban on all pursuit. The line judges how events disturb me and does not deny that they occur.

support.quote: The things whose pursuit and avoidance throw you into turmoil do not come to you, but in a way you yourself go to them.
support.follows: The things I chase or flee do not come to me; in a way I go to them.
gives: The things I chase or flee in turmoil do not come to me
They stand outside, unmoving
in a way I go to them

support.quote: things do not touch the soul but stand outside it, unmoving, and disturbances come only from the judgment within
support.follows: Things stay outside the soul and do not touch it; every disturbance comes from the judgment within.
gives: They stand outside, unmoving
My turmoil comes only from my own judgment about them

support.quote: At least let your judgment about them be quiet, and they will stay still, and you will be seen neither pursuing nor avoiding.
support.follows: If my judgment about these things is quiet, they stay where they are, and I neither pursue nor avoid them.
gives: My turmoil comes only from my own judgment about them
When I let that judgment be quiet, they stay still
I am seen neither chasing nor fleeing

claims.t: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine. The other two are mine so far as I must take care of them. I keep my mind apart from body and breath, and from whatever they attach to me unchosen. Once my mind has taken itself back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, smooth or rough. I ask whether my ruling part can be melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns.
claims.shared: The threefold division and the care owed to body and breath are 12.2 only. The image of melting into the flesh is a question in 10.24, so it stays a question and does not become a vow. In 12.2 the separation is the condition of a promise. Here it is stated as a practice.

support.quote: There are three things of which you are made up: a little body, a little breath, mind. Of these the other two are yours so far as you must take care of them, but only the third is properly yours.
support.follows: Of body, breath and mind, only the mind is properly mine; body and breath are mine to care for.
gives: Of body, breath and mind, only my mind is properly mine
The other two are mine so far as I must take care of them

support.quote: So if you separate from yourself, that is, from your thought, all that others do or say, or all that you yourself have done or said, and all that troubles you as something to come, and all that attaches to you, without your choosing it, from the little body that surrounds you or the little breath born with you
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to separate from his thought, among other things, all that comes to him unchosen from his body and breath.
gives: I keep my mind apart from body and breath
from whatever they attach to me unchosen

support.quote: the mind does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly, once the mind has taken itself back and come to know its own power
support.follows: Once the mind has drawn back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, whether that moves smoothly or roughly.
gives: I keep my mind apart from body and breath
Once my mind has taken itself back and knows its own power, it does not mix with the breath, smooth or rough

support.quote: Can it be melted into the bit of flesh and blended with it, so that it turns as the flesh turns?
support.follows: Marcus asks, with misgiving, whether his ruling part has been melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns.
gives: I ask whether my ruling part can be melted into the flesh, so that it turns as the flesh turns

claims.t: I keep to what is present. I practise living only what I am living, that is, the present. I do not think of absent things as already here, and I reckon up the best of what is here. I ask my soul whether it will be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present.
claims.shared: 10.1 is an unanswered question to the soul, so the old “I am content” claimed an achievement the source does not. It is restored as a question. “Already here” follows 7.20, which does not say “already mine”.

support.quote: practise living only what you are living, that is, the present
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to practise living only what he is living now, the present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I practise living only what I am living, that is, the present

support.quote: Not to think of absent things as already there, but to reckon up the best of the things that are present
support.follows: I should not treat absent things as already there, but count up the best of what is present.
gives: I keep to what is present
I do not think of absent things as already here
I reckon up the best of what is here

support.quote: But will you be content with your present state and take pleasure in all that is present
support.follows: Marcus asks his soul whether it will ever be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present.
gives: I ask my soul whether it will be content with its present state and take pleasure in all that is present

claims.t: I guard against drifting in what I do, as people drift who have no target for their impulses and impressions. I have no need of guessing when I am free to look at what has to be done. When I see it clearly, I go that way with good will and without turning back. I run straight along the line, not looking round and not thrown this way and that.
claims.shared: 2.4 is a warning about people with no target, so the line guards against their drifting and does not vow a target. The lack of a target now clearly belongs to those people, not to me. The runner image is 4.15 only. The case where I do not see clearly is 10.13 only and stays in the margin.

support.quote: But now there is the other kind of drifting to guard against as well. For people play the fool through their actions too: those who are worn out by life and have no target at which to direct every impulse and, in general, every impression.
support.follows: People with no target for their impulses play the fool in what they do, and this drifting has to be guarded against.
gives: I guard against drifting in what I do
as people drift who have no target for their impulses and impressions

support.quote: What need is there of guessing, when you are free to look at what has to be done, and, if you see it clearly, to go that way with good will and without turning back
support.follows: Instead of guessing, I can look at what has to be done and, if I see it clearly, go that way without turning back.
gives: I have no need of guessing when I am free to look at what has to be done
When I see it clearly, I go that way with good will
without turning back

support.quote: not to look round at a dark character, but to run straight along the line, not thrown this way and that
support.follows: I should not look round at a bad character but run straight along my line, not thrown from side to side.
gives: without turning back
I run straight along the line
not looking round
not thrown this way and that

single.quote: So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary which, as soon as they meet you, will be enough to wash away all distress and to send you back without resentment at the things you are returning to.
single.label: Renewing the retreat
single.t: I retreat into myself continually and renew myself. I keep short, elementary truths ready, enough to wash away all distress and to send me back without resentment at what I return to.
single.why: Single source, 4.3f: “So give yourself this retreat continually, and renew yourself. And let the things be short and elementary”. It adds that the retreat is repeated, brief and ends in a return. “A few” is dropped because the source does not say it.
single.follows: The retreat should be taken continually, with a few short truths that wash away distress and send me back without resentment.

single.quote: And you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”, you would answer at once and frankly, “This, and this”
single.label: A test for my thoughts
single.t: I accustom myself to form only thoughts that I could name at once and frankly if someone suddenly asked, “What are you thinking now?”
single.why: Single source, 3.4d: “you must accustom yourself to form only those impressions about which, if someone suddenly asked”. The question is kept in the speaker’s framing as a test of my own thoughts.
single.follows: I should form only impressions I could name at once and frankly if someone suddenly asked what I was thinking.

single.quote: What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now?
single.label: Three questions
single.t: I ask what my ruling part is to me, what kind of thing I am making it now, and what I am using it for now.
single.why: Single source, 10.24c: “What is my ruling part to me, and what kind of thing am I making it now, and what am I using it for now?” The gloss “my mind” is removed because 10.24 goes on to ask whether the ruling part can be empty of mind.
single.follows: Marcus asks himself what his ruling part is to him, what he is making of it now and what he is using it for.

single.quote: To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.label: Serving what is within
single.t: I serve the guardian spirit within me by keeping it clean of passion, of aimlessness, and of discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.
single.why: Single source, 2.11b: “To serve it is to keep it clean of passion and aimlessness and discontent with what comes from the gods and from people.” The guardian spirit is 2.11’s own term and is not merged with mind or ruling part. The pilot wording stands.
single.follows: Serving the guardian spirit within means keeping it free of passion, aimlessness and discontent with what gods and people send.

single.quote: Will you not stop valuing many other things as well? Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion. For you are bound to envy, to be jealous, to look with suspicion on those who can take those things away, to plot against those who have what you value. In short, anyone who is in need of any of those things is bound to be in confusion, and, what is more, to find much fault even with the gods. But respect for your own mind, and the value you set on it, will make you pleasing to yourself
single.label: Valuing other things
single.t: If I go on valuing many things besides my own mind, I will be neither free nor sufficient to myself nor without passion. Then I am bound to envy, to suspect those who can take those things away, and to plot against those who have them. Respect for my own mind, and the value I set on it, makes me pleasing to myself.
single.why: Single source, 6.15b: “Then you will be neither free nor sufficient to yourself nor without passion.” It is a warning stated as a consequence, not a vow. “Besides my own mind” is our gloss on the source’s “many other things”, taken from its closing contrast.
single.follows: Valuing many outside things leaves me unfree, envious and confused; respect for my own mind makes me pleasing to myself.

single.quote: be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much that, if ever they are not present, you will be troubled.
single.label: Not prizing what I have too much
single.t: Glad as I am of what is present, I guard against prizing it so much that I would be troubled if it were ever absent.
single.why: Single source, 7.20d: “be on your guard that through being so glad of them you do not accustom yourself to prize them so much”. It is the counterweight to c5 and keeps the gladness.
single.follows: Being glad of what I have, I should not get used to prizing it so much that losing it would trouble me.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 2.11 is 2.12–13, 7.20 is 7.27–28, 10.24 is 10.23–24, 6.15 is 6.16, 2.4 is 2.7, 10.13 is 10.12, 11.10 is 11.11, 4.15 is 4.18 and 12.2 is 12.2–3; 4.3, 3.4 and 10.1 are the same.

Every phrase rests on two passages. “At any hour” is in 4.3 only, so it moves to c1. “What is within me” replaces “my own mind” because 3.4 speaks of the ruling part and 2.11 of the guardian spirit, and the sources do not equate them.
marcus_revision.limit: This article describes a brief, repeatable return to oneself that sends me back to people and to work. It is not permanent solitude, a ban on all thought about others, or contempt for the body or for present goods. “Soul”, “mind”, “ruling part” and “guardian spirit” are each source’s own terms, and the passages do not equate them. Several sources are conditional or interrogative (4.3, 10.1, 12.2), so the lines state practices and questions, not attainments. In c4 the keeping apart is a condition in 12.2, and what 12.2 separates from the mind is what body and breath attach unchosen. In c2 the praise set aside in 3.4 is that of people who do not live in agreement with nature, and “the many” comes from 6.15. Rendering the sources in the first person, treating “impressions” as thoughts, and glossing the “many other things” of 6.15 as things besides my own mind are our editorial reading and not primary evidence.

statement.t: Nothing is better than the spirit within me and its virtue, and no one can prevent me from living by it.

parts.words: Nothing is better than the spirit within me and its virtue

statement.form: Claim 1 says what is best: the spirit within and its virtue, beside which everything else is small. Claim 2 says that no one can prevent me from living by it. The other claims say what follows for what I do, how I practise it, and how it fails.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, three claims gain a second author: the good that is my own, keeping to what is necessary, and what pulls me away from my own good. “Why” gains his argument that reason is a human being’s own good, and “In action” gains where the good in a choice lies. He limits the claim that no one can prevent me from living well: nothing can break the happiness of the wise, but my gladness can be cut apart while I am still imperfect, and old age can shake the mind.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a ground: each thing is judged by its own good, and a human being’s own good is reason brought to perfection. Its second half is narrowed in the second claim: he grants it fully only to the wise.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: go back to your own good
piece.follows: There is a good that is truly my own, and I should go back to it.
piece.context: Letter 124, on the good grasped by reason. Seneca tells Lucilius to stop rivalling animals in strength and looks; “your own good” is a mind freed from faults and pure: perfected reason.
gives: That is the good that is my own

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: how pleasant life is, how unencumbered, for those who follow them, how bitter and entangled is the life of those who have trusted opinion more than nature
piece.follows: Life is pleasant and unencumbered for those who follow nature’s laws, and bitter and entangled for those who trust opinion more than nature.
piece.context: Letter 48, against logic games. Philosophy should show people what nature makes necessary and what superfluous; “them” are the easy laws that nature has laid down.
gives: spares me toil and trouble

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: leave at once those things that people run about after
piece.follows: The things that people run about after are to be left at once.
piece.context: Letter 84, on how the mind can become one whole: by listening to reason, which Seneca imagines speaking. “Those things” are the riches, pleasures and ambition it tells one to leave next.
gives: it pulls me about

items.label: why
items.role: Why reason is my own good
items.t: Everything is judged by its own good, as a vine is recommended by its wine and a stag by its speed. Strength, beauty and speed I share with animals; reason brought to perfection is the good that is my own as a human being.
items.why: Marcus says that nothing is better than the spirit within and its virtue, and does not say why. Seneca argues it: each thing is judged by what is its own, and what is a human being’s own is reason, which no animal shares.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Every thing rests on its own good. What recommends the vine is its fruitfulness and the flavour of its wine; what recommends the stag is speed.
support.follows: Each thing is recommended by the good that is its own, as a vine by its wine and a stag by its speed.
support.context: Letter 76 sets out to prove that there is only one good. Each thing, whether vine, stag or dog, is rated by what it is born for.
gives: Everything is judged by its own good
as a vine is recommended by its wine and a stag by its speed

support.author: seneca
support.quote: He is strong: so are lions. He is handsome: so are peacocks. He is swift: so are horses.
support.follows: Strength, beauty and speed a human being shares with lions, peacocks and horses.
support.context: Letter 76, in the argument that there is only one good: qualities a human being shares with animals, which therefore cannot be his own good.
gives: Strength, beauty and speed I share with animals

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So perfected reason is the good peculiar to him; everything else he has in common with animals and plants.
support.follows: Perfected reason is the good peculiar to a human being; everything else he has in common with animals and plants.
support.context: Letter 76, in the argument that there is only one good: what is best in a human being is reason, by which he goes ahead of the animals.
gives: reason brought to perfection is the good that is my own as a human being

items.label: action
items.role: Where the good lies in a choice
items.t: I may seek health, rest and freedom from pain, not because they are goods but because they are according to nature. What is good is not the thing I choose but the kind of choice I make.
items.why: 10.2 says I am to take up what my animal nature asks for unless it makes me worse as a rational being, and 3.7 says to admit it when a benefit is only an animal’s. Neither says what is good in such a choice. Seneca says: not the thing chosen but the kind of choice.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why would I not seek them? Not because they are goods, but because they are according to nature
support.follows: Health, rest and freedom from pain may be sought because they are according to nature, not because they are goods.
support.context: Letter 92, on the happy life. An objector asks whether health, rest and freedom from pain, which do not hinder virtue, should be sought; “them” are those three.
gives: I may seek health, rest and freedom from pain
not because they are goods but because they are according to nature

support.author: seneca
support.quote: the good is not in the thing but in a choice of a certain kind
support.follows: The good lies not in the thing chosen but in the kind of choice made.
support.context: Letter 92, on choosing clean clothing: the choice of it is a good, the clothing is not. Here “the thing” is whatever is chosen, clothing or health.
gives: What is good is not the thing I choose but the kind of choice I make

items.t: Seneca agrees that nothing from outside can break the wise man’s happiness (Ep. 72.4), but no one else’s: the gladness of anyone still imperfect is cut apart. He also names a case Marcus does not name here, old age shaking the mind (Ep. 58.35). He gives it as the premise of his rule on when to leave life, not as an objection, and old age is not plainly a thing from outside. This narrows the claim; it does not deny it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: In those who are still imperfect, gladness is cut apart; but the wise man’s joy is woven in one piece: it is torn by no cause, by no fortune
support.follows: The gladness of one still imperfect is cut apart; no cause and no fortune can tear the wise man’s joy.
support.context: Letter 72, on business crowding out philosophy. Someone says that something will come up to get in the way; Seneca answers that only the gladness of the imperfect is cut apart.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: if it begins to shake my mind, if it begins to tear its parts loose
support.follows: Old age can begin to shake the mind and tear its parts loose.
support.context: Letter 58 ends on when one may leave life. Seneca will not leave old age while it keeps the whole of his better part; here “it”, which may shake the mind, is old age.
