passages.title: On the good belonging to reason alone
passages.text: Will you not leave the things in which you are bound to be beaten while you strive for what is not your own, and go back to your own good? What is this? A mind, of course, freed from faults and pure, striving to equal god, lifting itself above human things, placing nothing of its own outside itself. You are a rational animal. What, then, is the good in you? Perfected reason. Summon it from here to its own goal, as far as it can possibly grow.

passages.title: On logic puzzles versus real help
passages.text: Say what nature has made necessary and what superfluous, how easy the [laws] are that it has laid down, how pleasant life is, how unencumbered, for those who follow them, how bitter and entangled is the life of those who have trusted opinion more than nature [gap in the Latin] if you have first shown what part of them they are going to relieve. Which of those things takes away desires? Which moderates them? I wish it were only that they do no good! They do harm. Whenever you like I will make this perfectly clear to you: that a well-born character is crushed and weakened when it is thrown into those quibbles.

passages.title: On reading and digesting what you read
passages.text: “How,” you say, “will it be possible to bring this about?” By constant attention: if we do nothing except at reason’s urging and avoid nothing except at reason’s urging. If you are willing to listen to reason, it will say to you: leave at once those things that people run about after; leave riches, either a danger or a burden to those who own them; leave the pleasures of body and of mind, they soften and weaken; leave ambition, it is a swollen thing, empty, windy, it has no limit, it is as anxious not to see anyone ahead of it as not to see anyone level with it, it suffers from envy, and a double envy at that. And you see how wretched a man is if he is envied and also envies.

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: Every thing rests on its own good. What recommends the vine is its fruitfulness and the flavour of its wine; what recommends the stag is speed. Of pack animals, whose one use is to carry a load, you ask how strong they are in the back. In a dog the first thing is keenness of scent if it has to track wild animals, running if it has to catch them, boldness if it has to bite and attack. In each thing, what ought to be best is that for which it is born, that by which it is rated.

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: What is best in a human being? Reason: by this he goes ahead of the animals and comes next after the gods. So perfected reason is the good peculiar to him; everything else he has in common with animals and plants. He is strong: so are lions. He is handsome: so are peacocks. He is swift: so are horses. I say nothing of his being outdone in all these; I am not asking what he has in him that is greatest, but what is his own. He has a body: so do trees. He has impulse and voluntary movement: so do beasts and worms. He has a voice: but how much louder is the dogs’, how much shriller the eagles’, deeper the bulls’, sweeter and more supple the nightingales’?

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: “What then?” he says. “If good health and rest and freedom from pains are not going to hinder virtue in any way, will you not seek them?” Why would I not seek them? Not because they are goods, but because they are according to nature, and because I will take them with good judgment. What then will be good in them? This one thing: being well chosen. For when I take the kind of clothing that is fitting, when I walk as I ought, when I dine as I should, it is not the dinner or the walk or the clothing that is a good, but my purpose in them, the purpose of one who keeps, in each thing, the measure that agrees with reason.

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: I will add this as well: the choice of clean clothing is something a human being should seek; for a human being is by nature a clean animal and one that chooses with care. And so clean clothing is not a good in itself, but the choice of clean clothing is, because the good is not in the thing but in a choice of a certain kind; it is our actions that are honourable, not the things themselves that are done.

passages.title: On not letting business postpone philosophy
passages.text: “Something will come up to get in the way.” Not, at any rate, in the way of the man whose mind is glad and lively in every piece of business. In those who are still imperfect, gladness is cut apart; but the wise man’s joy is woven in one piece: it is torn by no cause, by no fortune. He is calm always and everywhere. For he does not hang on what is not his own, and he does not wait for the favour of fortune or of a man. His happiness is home-grown: it would go out of the mind if it came into it. It is born there.

passages.title: On what exists, Plato’s ideas and old age
passages.text: Do not listen to me unwillingly, as though this pronouncement already applied to you; and weigh what I am saying. I shall not leave old age, if it keeps the whole of me for myself, the whole, that is, as far as that better part goes. But if it begins to shake my mind, if it begins to tear its parts loose, if it leaves me not life but breath, I shall leap out of a building that is rotten and falling down.

claims.t: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else: nothing in human life is better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. That is the good that is my own. Everything else is small beside it, and I chase after none of it and run from none of it.
claims.shared: Both 3.7 and 3.8 put the spirit within first: in 3.7 nothing appears better than “the spirit itself that is seated in you”, in 3.8 the good person “has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue”. 3.7 and 5.28 both name a good that is one’s own (“that good which is proper to you and is yours”; “to have its good in a just disposition and just action”), and 3.8 and 3.13 both say the person flees nothing (“neither pursuing nor fleeing”; “waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing”).
claims.changed: 3.7 puts it as a test, “if nothing appears better”; the claim states the answer that 3.7 expects. 3.8 says “neither pursuing nor fleeing” and 3.13 “waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing”, with no object; the claim limits both to the things set below the spirit, so it does not forbid choosing the better and holding on to it. 5.28 speaks of every rational being; the claim says “me”.

support.quote: But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you
support.follows: If nothing appears better than the spirit seated within me, that spirit is the best thing I have.
gives: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else

support.quote: whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue
support.follows: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.
gives: I prefer the spirit within me and its virtue to everything else

support.quote: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage
support.follows: Justice, truth, self-control and courage are the standard that anything better in human life would have to beat.
gives: nothing in human life is better than justice, truth, self-control and courage

support.quote: that good which is proper to you and is yours
support.follows: There is a good that belongs to me as my own, and I am to honour it above everything else.
gives: That is the good that is my own

support.quote: to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there
support.follows: A rational being’s good lies in being just and acting justly, and its desire should go no further than that.
gives: That is the good that is my own

support.quote: if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else
support.follows: If everything else looks smaller and cheaper than the spirit within, nothing else should be given room.
gives: Everything else is small beside it

support.quote: Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
support.follows: Whoever prefers their own mind and spirit lives without chasing things and without running from them.
gives: I chase after none of it and run from none of it
run from none of it

support.quote: waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing
support.follows: Living well comes from joining several things, among them waiting for nothing and running from nothing.
gives: run from none of it

claims.t: No one can prevent me from living well, or from doing and saying what is according to nature. Nothing from outside stands in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and good sense.
claims.shared: Four passages say that there is something no one can prevent: “there is no one who can prevent this” (3.13), “there is no one who prevents you” (2.6), “No one will prevent you” (6.53), “no one at all can prevent you” (8.30). 3.13 and 11.15 both speak of living well and say it is in my power; 2.6 and 6.53 both say that what no one can prevent is what accords with nature.
claims.changed: The four passages name different things that no one can prevent: living well (3.13), doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole (2.6), living by the reason of my own nature (6.53), each action doing its part (8.30). The claim puts living well first and names doing and saying after it. 2.6 speaks of the nature of which I am a part, 6.53 of my own nature; the claim says “according to nature” and does not choose between them. 8.30 says “at least” of acting justly, with self-control and good sense, and grants that some other activity may be prevented; the claim’s second sentence keeps to those three.

support.quote: you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
support.follows: Whoever does the present work by right reason and keeps their spirit pure will live well, and no one can prevent it.
gives: No one can prevent me
living well

support.quote: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul
support.follows: The power to live in the finest way lies in the soul itself.
gives: living well

support.quote: there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part
support.follows: No one can stop me from always doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole I am part of.
gives: No one can prevent me
doing and saying
what is according to nature

support.quote: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature.
support.follows: No one can stop me from living by the reason of my own nature.
gives: No one can prevent me
what is according to nature

support.quote: And no one at all can prevent you from making sure that it does its own part.
support.follows: No one can stop each of my actions from doing its own part as far as it can.
gives: No one can prevent me

support.quote: “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
support.follows: Nothing outside me can stop me from acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
gives: Nothing from outside stands in the way
acting justly, with self-control and good sense

claims.t: In all I say and do, I keep to what is necessary, what reason requires of a being made for life among fellow citizens, and I strip away the rest, needless impressions as well as needless acts. Keeping to it is taking the short road, the one according to nature, and it spares me toil and trouble.
claims.shared: Both passages are about everything one says and does (4.20: “most of what we say and do”; 4.43: “say and do everything in the soundest way”), and both say that keeping to the right course frees one from burden: 4.20 “more leisure and be less troubled”, 4.43 “frees you from toil”.
claims.changed: 4.20 puts this as a cautious question (“Might it not be better…?”) that suggests its answer; the claim states the answer. 4.20 says doing only what is necessary leaves one “less troubled”; 4.43 says the short road “frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation”. The claim says “spares me toil and trouble” for both, and drops hanging back, contriving and affectation. That the necessary road and the short road are the same road is the editor’s reading.

support.quote: For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled.
support.follows: Most of what we say and do is unnecessary, and stripping it away gives more leisure and less trouble.
gives: In all I say and do
I strip away the rest
spares me toil and trouble

support.quote: Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires?
support.follows: Doing what is necessary, as reason requires of a being made for civic life, may be better than simply doing few things.
gives: I keep to what is necessary, what reason requires of a being made for life among fellow citizens

support.quote: And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too
support.follows: Needless impressions should be stripped away as well as needless actions.
gives: needless impressions as well as needless acts

support.quote: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way.
support.follows: The short road is the road of nature, and taking it lets me say and do everything in the soundest way.
gives: In all I say and do
taking the short road, the one according to nature

support.quote: For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
support.follows: Keeping to that road frees one from toil, from hanging back, and from contriving and affectation.
gives: spares me toil and trouble

claims.role: Benefit to the rational or the animal in me
claims.t: When something seems to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal. If as an animal, I admit plainly that it is only an animal’s benefit, and I take what my animal nature asks for only if it does not make me worse as a rational being. What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens.
claims.shared: Both passages tell apart what I am as an animal and what I am as a rational being, and both put the rational first: 3.7 “If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so”; 10.2 “unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state”. Both also join the rational to the civic: 3.7 “the rational and civic good”, 10.2 “what is rational is by that very fact also civic”.
claims.changed: 10.2 speaks of what my animal nature asks for, not of a benefit, and asks no question; that the two passages speak of one thing is the editor’s reading. 10.2 begins one step lower, with what I need simply as a growing body, and climbs to the animal and then to the rational; the claim keeps only the last step. 3.7 answers a speaker who says “the better is what benefits”; the claim makes the question my own. “Civic” in both passages is put as “made for life among fellow citizens”.

support.quote: “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so
support.follows: If something benefits me as a rational being I should keep to it; if only as an animal, I should admit that.
gives: When something seems to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me
as a rational being or as an animal
If as an animal, I admit plainly that it is only an animal’s benefit

support.quote: Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and take up all of this, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state.
support.follows: What my animal nature asks for is to be taken up, unless it would make my rational nature worse.
gives: as a rational being or as an animal
I take what my animal nature asks for only if it does not make me worse as a rational being

support.quote: should take up a position against the rational and civic good
support.follows: The good of a rational being is also a civic good, and nothing of another kind may be set against it.
gives: What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens

support.quote: And what is rational is by that very fact also civic.
support.follows: Whatever is rational is, for that very reason, also civic.
gives: What is rational in me is also made for life among fellow citizens

claims.t: I put my life together one action at a time. I carry through what lies before me step by step, as I would spell out a name letter by letter, and I join one good to the next without leaving a gap.
claims.shared: 5.28 and 6.24 both say “step by step”: to “judge and act step by step, as along a road” (5.28) and to “carry through step by step what lies before you” (6.24). 8.30 says something near it of a whole life: “put your life together one action at a time”.
claims.changed: 6.24 speaks of each duty, 8.30 of a life, 5.28 of the road a life travels; the claim speaks of my life. The link between “step by step” and 8.30’s “one action at a time” leans on the translation: in 5.28 and 6.24 the Greek is an idiom for “methodically, in due order”, rendered “step by step”. 12.22 adds the joining of one good to the next.

support.quote: You must put your life together one action at a time
support.follows: A life is to be built one action at a time.
gives: I put my life together one action at a time

support.quote: if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road
support.follows: Life goes well for whoever can judge and act step by step, as one goes along a road.
gives: step by step

support.quote: carry through step by step what lies before you
support.follows: Whatever lies before me is to be carried through step by step.
gives: I carry through what lies before me
step by step

support.quote: Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters?
support.follows: Asked how a name is written, one calmly counts off its letters one by one.
gives: as I would spell out a name letter by letter

support.quote: joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap
support.follows: Once I do what is just and say what is true, what is left is to enjoy living, linking one good to the next.
gives: I join one good to the next without leaving a gap

claims.t: If I lean towards anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me, such as praise, office, wealth or pleasure, it pulls me about, takes control of me and carries me off course. I count nothing as a benefit that will force me to break faith, to hate or to play a part. The way back is to choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.
claims.shared: Both passages warn against giving weight to what is not my own good: 3.7 against having “tipped and turned aside towards anything else”, 3.8 against valuing “as a benefit to yourself” what will one day harm me.
claims.changed: 3.8 does not say that praise or wealth forces anyone to break faith; it forbids counting as a benefit whatever will do so. The claim keeps that as a rule of its own. 3.8 lists seven things such a benefit forces: to break faith, abandon self-respect, hate, suspect, curse, play a part, and want what must be hidden behind walls and curtains; the claim keeps three. “The way back” is the editor’s name for 3.7’s command to choose the better.

support.quote: Once you have tipped and turned aside towards anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honour above all else
support.follows: Once I lean towards anything else, I can no longer honour my own good above all without being pulled about.
gives: If I lean towards anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me
it pulls me about

support.quote: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains.
support.follows: Nothing that will one day force me to break faith, hate, suspect or pretend should count as a benefit to me.
gives: If I lean towards anything other than the good that is my own and count it as a benefit to me
I count nothing as a benefit that will force me to break faith, to hate or to play a part

support.quote: such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures
support.follows: Praise from the many, offices, wealth and pleasures are things of another kind than the rational and civic good.
gives: such as praise, office, wealth or pleasure

support.quote: All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course.
support.follows: Such things may seem to fit for a while, but then they suddenly take control and carry one off course.
gives: takes control of me and carries me off course

support.quote: But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it.
support.follows: I should choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.
gives: choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it

single.quote: if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best
single.label: If I find better
single.t: If I ever see anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage and a mind content with itself, I shall turn to it with my whole soul and enjoy what I have found to be best.
single.why: Only 3.7 allows that something might be better than justice and the spirit within, and says what to do then. No other passage of the section considers it.
single.follows: If something better than justice and a mind content with itself is ever seen, one should turn to it wholeheartedly.

single.quote: keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment
single.label: Keeping it pure
single.t: I keep my own spirit pure, as if I had to give it back this very moment.
single.why: Only 3.13 speaks of keeping the spirit pure and of giving it back. 3.8 shares the readiness (“even if they have to depart this moment”) but not the purity or the giving back.
single.follows: I should keep my spirit pure as though I had to hand it back right now.

single.quote: none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once
single.label: Wiping out a verdict
single.t: Things do not put judgments about themselves into me; I write the verdicts myself. I need not write them, and if one gets written without my noticing, I can wipe it out at once.
single.why: Only 11.15 says where my verdicts about things come from and that I can wipe one out. It is kept as a way back when a wrong verdict has been written.
single.follows: Things do not judge themselves in me; I write the verdicts, and I can refuse to write them or wipe one out at once.

single.quote: if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation
single.label: When things go against nature
single.t: When what I meet is contrary to nature, I look for what there is for me that is according to my own nature and hurry towards it, even if it brings me no reputation.
single.why: Only 11.15 says what to do when things are contrary to nature. In 11.15 “they” are the indifferent things just named, and the translators note that the sentence before is obscure.
single.follows: When things are contrary to nature, I should seek what accords with my own nature and go for it, even if it brings no fame.

members.text:
If thou shalt find anything in this mortal life better than
righteousness, than truth, temperance, fortitude, and in general better
than a mind contented both with those things which according to right
and reason she doth, and in those, which without her will and knowledge
happen unto thee by the providence; if I say, thou canst find out
anything better than this, apply thyself unto it with thy whole heart,
and that which is best wheresoever thou dost find it, enjoy freely. But
if nothing thou shalt find worthy to be preferred to that spirit which
is within thee; if nothing better than to subject unto thee thine own
lusts and desires, and not to give way to any fancies or imaginations
before thou hast duly considered of them, nothing better than to
withdraw thyself (to use Socrates his words) from all sensuality, and
submit thyself unto the gods, and to have care of all men in general: if
thou shalt find that all other things in comparison of this, are but
vile, and of little moment; then give not way to any other thing, which
being once though but affected and inclined unto, it will no more be in
thy power without all distraction as thou oughtest to prefer and to
pursue after that good, which is thine own and thy proper good. For it
is not lawful, that anything that is of another and inferior kind and
nature, be it what it will, as either popular applause, or honour, or
riches, or pleasures; should be suffered to confront and contest as it
were, with that which is rational, and operatively good. For all these
things, if once though but for a while, they begin to please, they
presently prevail, and pervert a man's mind, or turn a man from the
right way. Do thou therefore I say absolutely and freely make choice of
that which is best, and stick unto it. Now, that they say is best, which
is most profitable. If they mean profitable to man as he is a rational
man, stand thou to it, and maintain it; but if they mean profitable, as
he is a creature, only reject it; and from this thy tenet and conclusion
keep off carefully all plausible shows and colours of external
appearance, that thou mayest be able to discern things rightly.
members.english: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage, and, in a word, than your thought being content with itself in the things where it has you acting according to right reason, and in fate, in the things that are allotted without your choosing; if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best. But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you, which has put its own impulses under itself, which examines the impressions, which has pulled itself away, as Socrates used to say, from the feelings of the senses, and has put itself under the gods, and cares for human beings; if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else. Once you have tipped and turned aside towards anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honour above all else that good which is proper to you and is yours. For it is not permitted that anything whatever of a different kind, such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures, should take up a position against the rational and civic good. All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course. But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so, and guard your verdict without conceit. Only see that you make the examination without slipping.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν κρεῖττον εὑρίσκεις ἐν τῷ ἀνθρωπίνῳ βίῳ δικαιοσύνης, ἀληθείας, σωφροσύνης, ἀνδρείας καὶ καθάπαξ τοῦ ἀρκεῖσθαι ἑαυτῇ τὴν διάνοιάν σου, ἐν οἷς κατὰ τὸν λόγον τὸν ὀρθὸν πράσσοντά σε παρέχεται, καὶ ἐν τῇ εἱμαρμένῃ ἐν τοῖς ἀπροαιρέτως ἀπονεμομένοις· εἰ τούτου, φημί, κρεῖττόν τι ὁρᾷς, ἐπʼ ἐκεῖνο ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τραπόμενος τοῦ ἀρίστου εὑρισκομένου ἀπόλαυε. εἰ δὲ μηδὲν κρεῖττον φαίνεται αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἐνιδρυμένου ἐν σοὶ δαίμονος, τάς τε ἰδίας ὁρμὰς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτῷ καὶ τὰς φαντασίας ἐξετάζοντος καὶ τῶν αἰσθητικῶν πείσεων, ὡς ὁ Σωκράτης ἔλεγεν, ἑαυτὸν ἀφειλκυκότος καὶ τοῖς θεοῖς ὑποτεταχότος ἑαυτὸν καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων προκηδομένου· εἰ τούτου πάντα τὰ ἄλλα μικρότερα καὶ εὐτελέστερα εὑρίσκεις, μηδενὶ χώραν δίδου ἑτέρῳ, πρὸς ὃ ῥέψας ἅπαξ καὶ ἀποκλίνας οὐκέτι ἀπερισπάστως τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἐκεῖνο, τὸ ἴδιον καὶ τὸ σόν, προτιμᾶν δυνήσῃ. ἀντικαθῆσθαι γὰρ τῷ λογικῷ καὶ πολιτικῷ ἀγαθῷ οὐ θέμις οὐδʼ ὁτιοῦν ἑτερογενές, οἷον τὸν παρὰ τῶν πολλῶν ἔπαινον ἢ ἀρχὰς ἢ πλοῦτον ἢ ἀπολαύσεις ἡδονῶν· πάντα ταῦτα, κἂν πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐναρμόζειν δόξῃ, κατεκράτησεν ἄφνω καὶ παρήνεγκεν. σὺ δέ, φημί, ἁπλῶς καὶ ἐλευθέρως ἑλοῦ τὸ κρεῖττον καὶ τούτου ἀντέχου· “κρεῖττον δὲ τὸ συμφέρον.” εἰ μὲν τὸ ὡς λογικῷ, τοῦτο τήρει· εἰ δὲ τὸ ὡς ζῴῳ, ἀπόφηναι, καὶ ἀτύφως φύλασσε τὴν κρίσιν· μόνον ὅπως ἀσφαλῶς τὴν ἐξέτασιν ποιήσῃ.

members.text:
If thou shalt intend that which is present, following the rule of
right and reason carefully, solidly, meekly, and shalt not intermix
any other businesses, but shall study this only to preserve thy spirit
unpolluted, and pure, and shall cleave unto him without either hope
or fear of anything, in all things that thou shalt either do or speak,
contenting thyself with heroical truth, thou shalt live happily; and
from this, there is no man that can hinder thee.
members.english: If you do the work that is present, following right reason, earnestly, vigorously, with good will, and with nothing as a side business, but keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment; if you join this together, waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing, but content with the present work that is according to nature and with heroic truth in what you say and utter, you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
members.greek: Ἐὰν τὸ παρὸν ἐνεργῇς ἑπόμενος τῷ ὀρθῷ λόγῳ, ἐσπουδασμένως, ἐρρωμένως, εὐμενῶς, καὶ μηδὲν παρεμπόρευμα, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ δαίμονα καθαρὸν ἑστῶτα τηρῇς, ὡσεὶ καὶ ἤδη ἀποδοῦναι δέοι· ἐὰν τοῦτο συνάπτῃς μηδὲν περιμένων μηδὲ Φεύγων, ἀλλὰ τῇ παρούσῃ κατὰ Φύσιν ἐνεργείᾳ καὶ τῇ ὧν λέγεις καὶ Φθέγγῃ ἡρωικῇ ἀληθείᾳ ἀρκούμενος, εὐζωήσεις. ἔστι δὲ οὐδεὶς ὁ τοῦτο κωλῦσαι δυνάμενος.

members.text:
To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected
with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature
indifferent. To be thus affected she must consider all worldly objects
both divided and whole: remembering withal that no object can of itself
beget any opinion in us, neither can come to us, but stands without
still and quiet; but that we ourselves beget, and as it were print in
ourselves opinions concerning them. Now it is in our power, not to print
them; and if they creep in and lurk in some corner, it is in our
power to wipe them off. Remembering moreover, that this care and
circumspection of thine, is to continue but for a while, and then thy
life will be at an end. And what should hinder, but that thou mayest do
well with all these things? For if they be according to nature, rejoice
in them, and let them be pleasing and acceptable unto thee. But if
they be against nature, seek thou that which is according to thine own
nature, and whether it be for thy credit or no, use all possible speed
for the attainment of it: for no man ought to be blamed, for seeking his
own good and happiness.
members.english: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul, if a person is indifferent towards the things that are indifferent. And a person will be indifferent if they look at each of these things taken apart and as a whole, and remember that none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once; and remember that this kind of attention will be for a short time, and after that life will be over. But what is hard about these things being otherwise? For if they are according to nature, rejoice in them and let them be easy for you. And if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation. For there is pardon for everyone who looks for their own good.
members.greek: Κάλλιστα διαζῆν, δύναμις αὕτη ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ, ἐὰν πρὸς τὰ ἀδιάφορά τις ἀδιαφορῇ. ἀδιαφορήσει δέ, ἐὰν ἕκαστον αὐτῶν θεωρῇ διῃρημένως καὶ ὁλικῶς καὶ μεμνημένος ὅτι οὐδὲν αὐτῶν ὑπόληψιν περὶ αὐτοῦ ἡμῖν ἐμποιεῖ οὐδὲ ἔρχεται ἐφ’ ἡμᾶς, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἀτρεμεῖ, ἡμεῖς δέ ἐσμεν οἱ τὰς περὶ αὐτῶν κρίσεις γεννῶντες καὶ οἷον γράφοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς, ἐξὸν μὲν μὴ γράφειν, ἐξὸν δέ, κἄν που λάθῃ, εὐθὺς ἐξαλεῖψαι· ὅτι ὀλίγου χρόνου ἔσται ἡ τοιαύτη προσοχὴ καὶ λοιπὸν πεπαύσεται ὁ βίος. τί μέντοι δύσκολον ἄλλως ἔχειν ταῦτα; εἰ μὲν γὰρ κατὰ φύσιν ἐστί, χαῖρε αὐτοῖς καὶ ῥᾴδια ἔστω σοι· εἰ δὲ παρὰ φύσιν, ζήτει τί ἐστί σοι κατὰ τὴν σὴν φύσιν καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦτο σπεῦδε, κἂν ἄδοξον ᾖ· παντὶ γὰρ συγγνώμη τὸ ἴδιον ἀγαθὸν ζητοῦντι.

members.text:
Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain
thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man,
to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that
requireth the secret of walls or veils. But he that preferreth before
all things his rational part and spirit, and the sacred mysteries of
virtue which issueth from it, he shall never lament and exclaim, never
sigh; he shall never want either solitude or company: and which is
chiefest of all, he shall live without either desire or fear. And as for
life, whether for a long or short time he shall enjoy his soul thus
compassed about with a body, he is altogether indifferent. For if even
now he were to depart, he is as ready for it, as for any other action,
which may be performed with modesty and decency. For all his life long,
this is his only care, that his mind may always be occupied in such
intentions and objects, as are proper to a rational sociable creature.
members.english: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains. For whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue, does not make a tragedy of things, does not groan, will need neither solitude nor a crowd. Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing. Whether they will have the use of the soul, enclosed in the body, for a longer stretch of time or a shorter one matters to them not at all. For even if they have to depart this moment, they will go as free of ties as if they were about to do anything else that can be done with self-respect and in good order, on their guard through their whole life against this one thing only: that their thought should take any turn foreign to a living being that has mind and is civic.
members.greek: Μὴ τιμήσῃς ποτὲ ὡς συμφέρον σεαυτοῦ, ὃ ἀναγκάσει σέ ποτε τὴν πίστιν παραβῆναι, τὴν αἰδῶ ἐγκαταλιπεῖν, μισῆσαί τινα, ὑποπτεῦσαι, καταράσασθαι, ὑποκρίνασθαι, ἐπιθυμῆσαί τινος τοίχων καὶ παραπετασμάτων δεομένου. ὁ γὰρ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ νοῦν καὶ δαίμονα καὶ τὰ ὄργια τῆς τούτου ἀρετῆς προελόμενος τραγῳδίαν οὐ ποιεῖ, οὐ στενάζει, οὐκ ἐρημίας, οὐ πολυπληθείας δεήσεται· τὸ μέγιστον, ζήσει μήτε διώκων μήτε φεύγων, πότερον δὲ ἐπὶ πλέον διάστημα χρόνου τῷ σώματι περιεχομένῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ἢ ἐπ’ ἔλασσον χρήσεται, οὐδ᾽ ὁτιοῦν αὐτῷ μέλει· κἂν γὰρ ἤδη ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι δέῃ, οὕτως εὐλύτως ἄπεισιν, ὡς ἄλλο τι τῶν αἰδημόνως καὶ κοσμίως ἐνεργεῖσθαι δυναμένων ἐνεργήσων, τοῦτο μόνον παρ’ ὅλον τὸν βίον εὐλαβούμενος, τὸ τὴν διάνοιαν ἔν τινι ἀνοικείῳ νοεροῦ καὶ πολιτικοῦ ζῴου τροπῇ γενέσθαι.

members.text:
Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know
thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what
is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is
just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life
in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately
succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?
members.english: What keeps a life safe: to see each thing through and through, what it is in itself, what in it is the material and what the cause; with the whole soul to do what is just and to say what is true. What is left but to enjoy living, joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap?
members.greek: Σωτηρία βίου ἕκαστον δι’ ὅλου αὐτὸ τί ἐστιν ὁρᾶν, τί μὲν αὐτοῦ τὸ ὑλικόν, τί δὲ τὸ αἰτιῶδες· ἐξ ὅλης τῆς ψυχῆς τὰ δίκαια ποιεῖν καὶ τἀληθῆ λέγειν. τί λοιπὸν ἢ ἀπολαύειν τοῦ ζῆν συνάπτοντα ἄλλο ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ ἀγαθόν, ὥστε μηδὲ τὸ βραχύτατον διάστημα ἀπολείπειν;

members.text:
As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to
observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require. That
done, if thou find not that thy nature, as thou art a living sensible
creature, will be the worse for it, thou mayest proceed. Next then thou
must examine, what thy nature as thou art a living sensible creature,
doth require. And that, whatsoever it be, thou mayest admit of and do
it, if thy nature as thou art a reasonable living creature, will not be
the worse for it. Now whatsoever is reasonable, is also sociable, Keep
thyself to these rules, and trouble not thyself about idle things.
members.english: Watch what your nature asks for, taking yourself as something governed by nature only. Then do it and accept it, unless your nature as an animal is going to be put in a worse state. Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and take up all of this, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state. And what is rational is by that very fact also civic. Using these rules, then, do not busy yourself with anything further.
members.greek: Παρατήρει τί σου ἡ φύσις ἐπιζητεῖ ὡς ὑπὸ φύσεως μόνον διοικουμένου· εἶτα ποίει αὐτὸ καὶ προσίεσο, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαί σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις. ἑξῆς δὲ παρατηρητέον τί ἐπιζητεῖ σου ἡ ὡς ζῴου φύσις, καὶ πᾶν τοῦτο παραληπτέον, εἰ μὴ χεῖρον μέλλει διατίθεσθαι ἡ ὡς ζῴου λογικοῦ φύσις· ἔστι δὲ τὸ λογικὸν εὐθὺς καὶ πολιτικόν. τούτοις δὴ κανόσι χρώμενος μηδὲν περιεργάζου.

members.text:
These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature
of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what
relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And
that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always
both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature,
whereof thou art a part.
members.english: These things must always be remembered: what the nature of the whole is, and what mine is, and how this one stands to that one, and what kind of part it is of what kind of whole; and that there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part.
members.greek: Τούτων ἀεὶ δεῖ μεμνῆσθαι, τίς ἡ τῶν ὅλων φύσις καὶ τίς ἡ ἐμὴ καὶ πῶς αὕτη πρὸς ἐκείνην ἔχουσα καὶ ὁποῖόν τι μέρος ὁποίου τοῦ ὅλου οὖσα καὶ ὅτι οὐδεὶς ὁ κωλύων τὰ ἀκόλουθα τῇ φύσει, ἧς μέρος εἶ, πράσσειν τε ἀεὶ καὶ λέγειν.

members.text:
Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single
action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is
fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee. And who can
hinder thee, but that thou mayest perform what is fitting? But there may
be some outward let and impediment. Not any, that can hinder thee, but
that whatsoever thou dost, thou may do it, justly, temperately, and
with the praise of God. Yea, but there may be somewhat, whereby some
operation or other of thine may be hindered. And then, with that very
thing that doth hinder, thou mayest he well pleased, and so by this
gentle and equanimious conversion of thy mind unto that which may be,
instead of that which at first thou didst intend, in the room of that
former action there succeedeth another, which agrees as well with this
contraction of thy life, that we now speak of.
members.english: You must put your life together one action at a time, and if each action does its own part as far as it can, be content. And no one at all can prevent you from making sure that it does its own part. “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense. Some other kind of activity will perhaps be prevented; but through being well pleased with the very thing that prevents it, and through moving over with good grace to what is given, another action at once takes its place, one that will fit into the putting together of which we are speaking.
members.greek: Συντιθέναι δεῖ τὸν βίον κατὰ μίαν πρᾶξιν καὶ εἰ ἑκάστη τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχει ὡς οἷόν τε, ἀρκεῖσθαι· ἵνα δὲ τὸ ἑαυτῆς παρέχῃ, οὐδὲ εἷς σε κωλῦσαι δύναται.—ἀλλʼ ἐνστήσεταί τι ἔξωθεν.—οὐδὲν εἴς γε τὸ δικαίως καὶ σωφρόνως καὶ εὐλογίστως, ἄλλο δέ τι ἴσως ἐνεργητικὸν κωλυθήσεται, ἀλλὰ τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸ τὸ κώλυμα εὐαρεστήσει καὶ τῇ ἐπὶ τὸ διδόμενον εὐγνώμονι μεταβάσει εὐθὺς ἄλλη πρᾶξις ἀντικαθίσταται ἐναρμόσουσα εἰς τὴν σύνθεσιν, περὶ ἧς ὁ λόγος.

members.text:
They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt
live cheerfully. Certainly there is nothing better, than for a man
to confine himself to necessary actions; to such and so many only, as
reason in a creature that knows itself born for society, will command
and enjoin. This will not only procure that cheerfulness, which from the
goodness, but that also, which from the paucity of actions doth usually
proceed. For since it is so, that most of those things, which we either
speak or do, are unnecessary; if a man shall cut them off, it must needs
follow that he shall thereby gain much leisure, and save much trouble,
and therefore at every action a man must privately by way of admonition
suggest unto himself, What? may not this that now I go about, be of the
number of unnecessary actions? Neither must he use himself to cut off
actions only, but thoughts and imaginations also, that are unnecessary
for so will unnecessary consequent actions the better be prevented and
cut off.
members.english: “Do few things,” he says, “if you mean to be cheerful.” Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires? For this brings not only the cheerfulness that comes from doing things well, but also the cheerfulness that comes from doing few things. For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled. So on each occasion one must also remind oneself: “Is this perhaps one of the things that are not necessary?” And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too, for then superfluous actions will not follow after them either.
members.greek: ʽὈλίγα πρῆσσε, φησίν, εἰ μέλλεις εὐθυμήσειν.ʼ μήποτε ἄμεινον τἀναγκαῖα πράσσειν καὶ ὅσα ὁ τοῦ φύσει πολιτικοῦ ζῴου λόγος αἱρεῖ καὶ ὡς αἱρεῖ; τοῦτο γὰρ οὐ μόνον τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ καλῶς πράσσειν εὐθυμίαν φέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀλίγα πράσσειν. τὰ πλεῖστα γὰρ ὧν λέγομεν καὶ πράσσομεν οὐκ ἀναγκαῖα ὄντα ἐάν τις περιέλῃ, εὐσχολώτερος καὶ ἀταρακτότερος ἔσται. ὅθεν δεῖ καὶ παῤ ἕκαστα ἑαυτὸν ὑπομιμνῄσκειν· μήτι τοῦτο τῶν οὐκ ἀναγκαίων; δεῖ δὲ μὴ μόνον πράξεις τὰς μὴ ἀναγκαίας περιαιρεῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ φαντασίας· οὕτως γὰρ οὐδὲ πράξεις παρέλκουσαι ἐπακολουθήσουσιν.

members.why: Its subject is that I am a part of the whole and kin to those of my own kind, and so welcome what the whole allots and do nothing unsocial; Articles 1 and 3 say this, and it does not speak of what is best or of what no one can prevent.
members.text:
Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the
cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature. Let this then be
thy first ground, that thou art part of that universe, which is governed
by nature. Then secondly, that to those parts that are of the same kind
and nature as thou art, thou hast relation of kindred. For of these,
if I shall always be mindful, first as I am a part, I shall never be
displeased with anything, that falls to my particular share of the
common chances of the world. For nothing that is behoveful unto the
whole, can be truly hurtful to that which is part of it. For this
being the common privilege of all natures, that they contain nothing in
themselves that is hurtful unto them; it cannot be that the nature of
the universe (whose privilege beyond other particular natures, is,
that she cannot against her will by any higher external cause be
constrained,) should beget anything and cherish it in her bosom that
should tend to her own hurt and prejudice. As then I bear in mind that
I am a part of such an universe, I shall not be displeased with anything
that happens. And as I have relation of kindred to those parts that
are of the same kind and nature that I am, so I shall be careful to
do nothing that is prejudicial to the community, but in all my
deliberations shall they that are of my kind ever be; and the common
good, that, which all my intentions and resolutions shall drive unto,
as that which is contrary unto it, I shall by all means endeavour to
prevent and avoid. These things once so fixed and concluded, as thou
wouldst think him a happy citizen, whose constant study and practice
were for the good and benefit of his fellow citizens, and the carriage
of the city such towards him, that he were well pleased with it; so must
it needs be with thee, that thou shalt live a happy life.
members.english: Whether it is atoms or nature, let this first be laid down: that I am a part of the whole, which is governed by nature. Next, that I have a certain kinship with the parts that are of the same kind as I am. For if I remember these things, then insofar as I am a part, I will not be displeased with anything that is allotted from the whole. For nothing that is good for the whole is harmful to the part. For the whole has nothing that is not good for itself. All natures have this in common, but the nature of the universe has this in addition, that it is not even forced by any cause from outside to produce anything harmful to itself. So by remembering that I am a part of a whole of this kind, I will be well pleased with everything that comes about. And insofar as I have a certain kinship with the parts of the same kind, I will do nothing unsocial. Rather I will make those of my own kind my aim, and I will lead my every impulse towards what is good for all in common and lead it away from the opposite. When these things are carried through in this way, life must flow well, just as you would think that a citizen’s life flows well when that citizen goes forward through actions that profit the citizens, and welcomes whatever the city allots.
members.greek: Εἴτε ἄτομοι εἴτε φύσις, πρῶτον κείσθω ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ τοῦ ὅλου ὑπὸ φύσεως διοικουμένου· ἔπειτα, ὅτι ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη. τούτων γὰρ μεμνημένος, καθότι μὲν μέρος εἰμί, οὐδενὶ δυσαρεστήσω τῶν ἐκ τοῦ ὅλου ἀπονεμομένων· οὐδὲν γὰρ βλαβερὸν τῷ μέρει ὃ τῷ ὅλῳ συμφέρει. οὐ γὰρ ἔχει τι τὸ ὅλον ὃ μὴ συμφέρει ἑαυτῷ, πασῶν μὲν φύσεων κοινὸν ἐχουσῶν τοῦτο, τῆς δὲ τοῦ κόσμου προσειληφυίας τὸ μηδὲ ὑπό τινος ἔξωθεν αἰτίας ἀναγκάζεσθαι βλαβερόν τι ἑαυτῇ γεννᾶν. κατὰ μὲν δὴ τὸ μεμνῆσθαι ὅτι μέρος εἰμὶ ὅλου τοῦ τοιούτου, εὐαρεστήσω παντὶ τῷ ἀποβαίνοντι, καθόσον δὲ ἔχω πως οἰκείως πρὸς τὰ ὁμογενῆ μέρη, οὐδὲν πράξω ἀκοινώνητον, μᾶλλον δὲ στοχάσομαι τῶν ὁμογενῶν καὶ πρὸς τὸ κοινῇ συμφέρον πᾶσαν ὁρμὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἄξω καὶ ἀπὸ τοὐναντίου ἀπάξω. τούτων δὲ οὕτως περαινομένων ἀνάγκη τὸν βίον εὐροεῖν, ὡς ἂν καὶ πολίτου βίον εὔρουν ἐπινοήσειας προιόντος διὰ πράξεων τοῖς πολίταις λυσιτελῶν καὶ ὅπερ ἂν ἡ πόλις ἀπονέμῃ, τοῦτο ἀσπαζομένου.

members.text:
Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the
right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou
wilt observe a true method. These two things be common to the souls, as
of God, so of men, and of every reasonable creature, first that in their
own proper work they cannot be hindered by anything: and secondly, that
their happiness doth consist in a disposition to, and in the practice of
righteousness; and that in these their desire is terminated.
members.english: You can always have your life flow well, if indeed you can also travel a good road, if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road. These two things are common to the soul of god, and of a human being, and of every rational living being: not to be hindered by anything else; and to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there.
members.greek: Δύνασαι ἀεὶ εὐροεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ εὐοδεῖν, εἴ γε καὶ ὁδῷ ὑπολαμβάνειν καὶ πράσσειν. δύο ταῦτα κοινὰ τῇ τε τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τῇ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ παντὸς λογικοῦ ζῴου ψυχῇ· τὸ μὴ ἐμποδίζεσθαι ὑπ’ ἄλλου καὶ τὸ ἐν τῇ δικαικῇ διαθέσει καὶ πράξει ἔχειν τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ἐνταῦθα τὴν ὄρεξιν ἀπολήγειν.

members.text:
Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most
compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both
words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect.
For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife,
dissembling, and ostentation.
members.english: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way. For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
members.greek: Ἐπὶ τὴν σύντομον ἀεὶ τρέχε· σύντομος δὲ ἡ κατὰ φύσιν, ὥστε κατὰ τὸ ὑγιέστατον πᾶν λέγειν καὶ πράσσειν. ἀπαλλάσσει γὰρ ἡ τοιαύτη πρόθεσις κόπων καὶ στραγγείας καὶ πάσης οἰκονομίας καὶ κομψείας.

members.text:
No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing
can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.
members.english: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature. Nothing will happen to you contrary to the reason of the common nature.
members.greek: Κατὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς σῆς φύσεως βιοῦν σε οὐδεὶς κωλύσει· παρὰ τὸν λόγον τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως οὐδέν σοι συμβήσεται.

members.text:
if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus
is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and
utter out in order every letter of it? And if any shall begin to gainsay
thee, and quarrel with thee about it; wilt thou quarrel with him again,
or rather go on meekly as thou hast begun, until thou hast numbered out
every letter? Here then likewise remember, that every duty that belongs
unto a man doth consist of some certain letters or numbers as it were,
to which without any noise or tumult keeping thyself thou must orderly
proceed to thy proposed end, forbearing to quarrel with him that would
quarrel and fall out with thee.
members.english: If someone sets you the question how the name Antoninus is written, surely you will not strain as you bring out each of its letters? What then if they get angry: surely you will not get angry back? Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters? So here too, remember that every duty is made complete out of certain counted parts. These you must keep to, and, without being thrown into confusion and without being annoyed in turn at those who are annoyed, carry through step by step what lies before you.
members.greek: Ἐάν τίς σοι προβάλῃ πῶς γράφεται τὸ Ἀντωνίνου ὄνομα, μήτι κατεντεινόμενος προοίσῃ ἕκαστον τῶν στοιχείων; τί οὖν ἐὰν ὀργίζωνται, μήτι ἀντοργιῇ; μήτι οὐκ ἐξαριθμήσῃ πρᾴως προιὼν ἕκαστον τῶν γραμμάτων; οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐνθάδε μέμνησο ὅτι πᾶν καθῆκον ἐξ ἀριθμῶν τινῶν συμπληροῦται. τούτους δεῖ τηροῦντα καὶ μὴ θορυβούμενον μηδὲ τοῖς δυσχεραίνουσιν ἀντιδυσχεραίνοντα περαίνειν ὁδῷ τὸ προκείμενον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 3.7 is 3.6, 3.8 is 3.7, 3.13 is 3.12, 11.15 is 11.16, 12.22 is 12.29, 2.6 is 2.9, 8.30 is 8.32, 4.20 is 4.24, 4.43 is 4.51, 5.28 is 5.34, 6.53 is 6.58, 6.24 is 6.26; 10.2 and 10.6 are the same.

Reads 3.7’s “if nothing appears better than the spirit” as the answer Marcus expects, and states it in claim 1 as my view; what 3.7 leaves open, that something better might be found, is the said-once item under “If I doubt it”. Under “Why” the section gives the statement’s two halves at length (claims 1 and 2), not an argument for them.
Claim 2 gathers four passages that each say no one can prevent something, though each names a different thing. Only the words “No one can prevent me” are said by all four.

Claim 4 pairs 3.7’s question (does it benefit me as a rational being or as an animal?) with 10.2’s ladder of natures, and places it under “In action”, not under “If I doubt it”, though in 3.7 it answers an objection.
articles.limit: Article 8’s claim 4 already says that nothing that happens prevents me from being good and just, and Article 2 that reason leads my work; what this article adds is the ranking, that nothing is better than the spirit within and its virtue. Article 17’s claim 4 allows that the people around me may not let me live according to nature, so “no one can prevent me” in claim 2 is read here as holding of the inner act, not of my outward life. The said-once item on verdicts (11.15) repeats Article 7’s claims 2 and 3 and Article 8’s claim 2. Much of the article rests on 3.7, and the article asserts that nothing is better without arguing for it. Seneca’s item under “Why” and the statement clause come close to Article 5, which already quotes Ep. 76.8 and has an item on 76.10 and 41.8; what they add here is 76.9’s comparison with animals.

statement.t: I find nothing better than the spirit within me and its virtue, and no one can prevent me from living by it.

statement.form: “I find” keeps 3.7’s open test, which a flat “nothing is better” would close. The freedom claimed covers living by the spirit, not outward success.
