claims.t: I find nothing in human life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage. My own good lies in a just disposition and just action, and my desire stops there. I hold everything else smaller and cheaper, and I live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
claims.shared: Names the four virtues and adds 5.28’s limit on desire. “Smaller and cheaper” is 3.7 alone. The joint anchors are the good that is my own (3.7 with 5.28) and living without fleeing (3.8 with 3.13). “Pursuing” is 3.8’s word, where 3.13 says “waiting for nothing”. The finding stays a judgement reached under 3.7’s conditional.

support.quote: But if nothing appears better than the spirit itself that is seated in you
support.follows: If nothing appears better than the spirit seated within me, that spirit is the best thing I have.
gives: I find nothing in human life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage

support.quote: whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit, and the rites of its virtue
support.follows: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.
support.note: Whoever has preferred their own mind and spirit and its virtue does not make a tragedy of things and does not groan.

support.quote: If you find in human life anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage
support.follows: Justice, truth, self-control and courage are the standard that anything better in human life would have to beat.
gives: I find nothing in human life better than justice, truth, self-control and courage

support.quote: that good which is proper to you and is yours
support.follows: There is a good that belongs to me as my own, and I am to honour it above everything else.
gives: My own good lies in a just disposition and just action, and my desire stops there

support.quote: to have its good in a just disposition and just action, and to have its desire stop there
support.follows: A rational being’s good lies in being just and acting justly, and its desire should go no further than that.
gives: My own good lies in a just disposition and just action, and my desire stops there

support.quote: if you find everything else smaller and cheaper than this, give room to nothing else
support.follows: If everything else looks smaller and cheaper than the spirit within, nothing else should be given room.
gives: I hold everything else smaller and cheaper

support.quote: Greatest of all, they will live neither pursuing nor fleeing.
support.follows: Whoever prefers their own mind and spirit lives without chasing things and without running from them.
gives: I live neither pursuing nor fleeing

support.quote: waiting for nothing and fleeing nothing
support.follows: Living well comes from joining several things, among them waiting for nothing and running from nothing.
gives: I live neither pursuing nor fleeing

claims.t: No one can prevent me from living well, for that power is in my own soul. No one prevents me from doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which I am a part. No one can stop me from making sure that each action does its own part. Nothing from outside stands in the way, at least not in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
claims.shared: “At least not” keeps 8.30’s limit: only virtuous action is unhinderable. The soul’s power is from 11.15 alone. The concession that other activity may be blocked is kept in the margin.

support.quote: you will live well. And there is no one who can prevent this.
support.follows: Whoever does the present work by right reason and keeps their spirit pure will live well, and no one can prevent it.
gives: No one can prevent me from living well

support.quote: To live life through in the finest way: this power is in the soul
support.follows: The power to live in the finest way lies in the soul itself.
gives: that power is in my own soul

support.quote: there is no one who prevents you from always doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which you are a part
support.follows: No one can stop me from always doing and saying what fits the nature of the whole I am part of.
gives: No one prevents me from doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which I am a part

support.quote: No one will prevent you from living according to the reason of your own nature.
support.follows: No one can stop me from living by the reason of my own nature.
gives: No one can prevent me from living well
No one prevents me from doing and saying what is in keeping with the nature of which I am a part

support.quote: And no one at all can prevent you from making sure that it does its own part.
support.follows: No one can stop each of my actions from doing its own part as far as it can.
gives: No one can stop me from making sure that each action does its own part

support.quote: “But something from outside will stand in the way.” Nothing will, at least not in the way of acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
support.follows: Nothing outside me can stop me from acting justly, with self-control and with good sense.
gives: Nothing from outside stands in the way, at least not in the way of my acting justly, with self-control and with good sense

claims.t: In what I say and do, I do what is necessary and what reason requires of a being made by nature for life among fellow citizens, in the way reason requires it. Most of what I say and do is not necessary. I strip away what is not necessary, impressions as well as actions, and I am less troubled. I run to the short road, the one according to nature, and say and do everything in the soundest way. That purpose frees me from toil, from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
claims.shared: The second sentence now names whose words and acts are meant and what is stripped away. The necessary (4.20) and the short road (4.43) stand side by side and are not equated. The joint anchor is saying and doing. “Short” means sound, not less effort.

support.quote: For most of what we say and do is not necessary, and if a person strips it away they will have more leisure and be less troubled.
support.follows: Most of what we say and do is unnecessary, and stripping it away gives more leisure and less trouble.
gives: In what I say and do
Most of what I say and do is not necessary
I strip away what is not necessary, impressions as well as actions, and I am less troubled

support.quote: Might it not be better to do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of a living being that is civic by nature requires, and in the way it requires?
support.follows: Doing what is necessary, as reason requires of a being made for civic life, may be better than simply doing few things.
gives: I do what is necessary and what reason requires of a being made by nature for life among fellow citizens, in the way reason requires it

support.quote: And one must strip away not only the actions that are not necessary but impressions too
support.follows: Needless impressions should be stripped away as well as needless actions.
gives: I strip away what is not necessary, impressions as well as actions, and I am less troubled

support.quote: Always run to the short road. And the short road is the one according to nature, so that you say and do everything in the soundest way.
support.follows: The short road is the road of nature, and taking it lets me say and do everything in the soundest way.
gives: In what I say and do
I run to the short road, the one according to nature, and say and do everything in the soundest way

support.quote: For a purpose of this kind frees you from toil and from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation.
support.follows: Keeping to that road frees one from toil, from hanging back, and from contriving and affectation.
gives: That purpose frees me from toil, from hanging back, and from all contriving and affectation

claims.role: Benefit to the rational or the animal in me
claims.t: When something is said to benefit me, I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal. If as a rational being, I keep to it. If as an animal, I say so. I take up all that my nature as an animal asks for, unless my nature as a rational animal would be put in a worse state. What is rational is by that very fact also civic, and I let nothing take up a position against the rational and civic good.
claims.shared: Animal nature’s demands are affirmed and only capped, as 10.2 has it. The candour clause is 3.7 alone, and the cap and “by that very fact” are 10.2 alone. The joint point, anchored on “the rational and civic good”, is that the rational and the civic go together.

support.quote: “But the better is what benefits.” If it benefits you as a rational being, keep to that. But if as an animal, say so
support.follows: If something benefits me as a rational being I should keep to it; if only as an animal, I should admit that.
gives: When something is said to benefit me
I ask whether it benefits me as a rational being or as an animal
If as a rational being, I keep to it
If as an animal, I say so

support.quote: Next you must watch what your nature as an animal asks for, and take up all of this, unless your nature as a rational animal is going to be put in a worse state.
support.follows: What my animal nature asks for is to be taken up, unless it would make my rational nature worse.
gives: I take up all that my nature as an animal asks for, unless my nature as a rational animal would be put in a worse state

support.quote: should take up a position against the rational and civic good
support.follows: The good of a rational being is also a civic good, and nothing of another kind may be set against it.
gives: I let nothing take up a position against
the rational and civic good

support.quote: And what is rational is by that very fact also civic.
support.follows: Whatever is rational is, for that very reason, also civic.
gives: What is rational is by that very fact also civic
the rational and civic good

claims.t: I put my life together one action at a time. I judge and act step by step, as along a road. I carry through what lies before me as I would gently count off the letters of a name. I join one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap.
claims.shared: Step by step is shared by 5.28 and 6.24. The road is 5.28 alone, the letters 6.24 alone, the gapless joining 12.22 alone and the assembled life 8.30 alone. Each image is kept because it explains the method, and the letters stay a comparison.

support.quote: You must put your life together one action at a time
support.follows: A life is to be built one action at a time.
gives: I put my life together one action at a time

support.quote: if indeed you can also judge and act step by step, as along a road
support.follows: Life goes well for whoever can judge and act step by step, as one goes along a road.
gives: I judge and act step by step
as along a road

support.quote: carry through step by step what lies before you
support.follows: Whatever lies before me is to be carried through step by step.
gives: I judge and act step by step
I carry through what lies before me

support.quote: Will you not gently go on counting off each of the letters?
support.follows: Asked how a name is written, one calmly counts off its letters one by one.
gives: as I would gently count off the letters of a name

support.quote: joining one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap
support.follows: Once I do what is just and say what is true, what is left is to enjoy living, linking one good to the next.
gives: I join one good to another so as to leave not even the shortest gap

claims.t: I simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it. Once I tip and turn aside towards anything else, I am pulled about. Praise from the many, offices, wealth and the enjoyment of pleasures seem to fit for a little while, then suddenly take control and carry me off course. I never value as a benefit to myself anything that will one day force me to break faith, to abandon my self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, or to desire something that needs walls and curtains.
claims.shared: The choice comes first so that “anything else” has a clear referent. The warning about rival goods stays a warning. The joint anchor is narrowed to the compelling: 3.7 says such things take control and 3.8 says they force. Valuing as a benefit and the full list, with its walls and curtains, are 3.8 alone.

support.quote: Once you have tipped and turned aside towards anything else, you will no longer be able, without being pulled about, to honour above all else
support.follows: Once I lean towards anything else, I can no longer honour my own good above all without being pulled about.
gives: Once I tip and turn aside towards anything else, I am pulled about

support.quote: Never value as a benefit to yourself anything that will one day force you to break faith, to abandon your self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, to desire something that needs walls and curtains.
support.follows: Nothing that will one day force me to break faith, hate, suspect or pretend should count as a benefit to me.
gives: I never value as a benefit to myself
anything that will one day force me
to break faith, to abandon my self-respect, to hate someone, to suspect, to curse, to play a part, or to desire something that needs walls and curtains

support.quote: such as praise from the many, or offices, or wealth, or the enjoyment of pleasures
support.follows: Praise from the many, offices, wealth and pleasures are things of another kind than the rational and civic good.
gives: Praise from the many, offices, wealth and the enjoyment of pleasures

support.quote: All these, even if for a little while they seem to fit, suddenly take control and carry you off course.
support.follows: Such things may seem to fit for a while, but then they suddenly take control and carry one off course.
gives: seem to fit for a little while, then suddenly take control and carry me off course
anything that will one day force me

support.quote: But you, I say, simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it.
support.follows: I should choose the better, simply and freely, and hold on to it.
gives: I simply and freely choose the better and hold on to it

single.quote: if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best
single.label: If I find better
single.t: If I see anything better than justice, truth, self-control, courage and a mind content with its own right action and with what fate allots, I turn to it with my whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best.
single.why: Single source 3.7, quote 3.7b: “if, I say, you see anything better than this, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy what is found to be best”. “This” is spelled out from the same passage so the line reads alone. It stays an open conditional test and is not a vow to search.
single.follows: If something better than justice and a mind content with itself is ever seen, one should turn to it wholeheartedly.

single.quote: keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment
single.label: Keeping it pure
single.t: I keep my own spirit standing pure, as if I had to give it back this very moment.
single.why: Single source 3.13, quote 3.13a: “keep your own spirit standing pure, as if you had to give it back this very moment”. “Standing” is restored from the source. Readiness to give the spirit back is not made the article’s common theme.
single.follows: I should keep my spirit pure as though I had to hand it back right now.

single.quote: none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once
single.label: Wiping out a verdict
single.t: Things do not put a judgment about themselves into me. They stay still, and I produce the verdicts about them and write them in myself. It is in my power not to write them, and if one escapes my notice, to wipe it out at once.
single.why: Single source 11.15, quote 11.15b: “none of them puts a judgment about itself into us, nor comes to us, but the things stay still, and it is we who produce the verdicts about them and, as it were, write them in ourselves, when it is in our power not to write them, and in our power, even if one of them somehow escapes our notice, to wipe it out at once”. The semicolon is removed and “stay still” restored. The line concerns my verdict about a thing and does not deny the thing.
single.follows: Things do not judge themselves in me; I write the verdicts, and I can refuse to write them or wipe one out at once.

single.quote: if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation
single.label: When things go against nature
single.t: When things are contrary to nature, I look for what there is for me that is according to my own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation.
single.why: Single source 11.15, quote 11.15c: “if they are contrary to nature, look for what there is for you that is according to your own nature and hurry towards that, even if it brings no reputation”. In the source “they” are the indifferent things. The companion case, rejoicing in what accords with nature, is in the margin.
single.follows: When things are contrary to nature, I should seek what accords with my own nature and go for it, even if it brings no fame.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 3.7 is 3.6, 3.8 is 3.7, 3.13 is 3.12, 11.15 is 11.16, 12.22 is 12.29, 2.6 is 2.9, 8.30 is 8.32, 4.20 is 4.24, 4.43 is 4.51, 5.28 is 5.34, 6.53 is 6.58, 6.24 is 6.26; 10.2 and 10.6 are the same.
“I find” keeps 3.7’s open test, which a flat “nothing is better” would close. The freedom claimed covers living by the spirit, not outward success.
marcus_revision.limit: The claim that nothing is better than the spirit and its virtue is a finding under 3.7’s open test, not a closed dogma. What no one can prevent is just, truthful, rational and civic action and judgement, not outward success or events matching my wishes. 8.30 concedes that other activity may be blocked. 3.13’s promise of living well holds only when all its parts are joined, and 11.15 places the power in the soul on condition of indifference to indifferent things. Shortness of life and readiness to depart appear only in 3.8, 3.13 and 11.15, so they are not made common doctrine. The single-source lines speak for their own passages only. In the fused claims, single-witness details such as the road, the letters, the walls and curtains, “smaller and cheaper” and “by that very fact” are anchored to their one passage and are not joint doctrine.

articles.title: Living with the gods

statement.t: I live with the gods and meet their power always, revere both them and reason, and keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old.

parts.words: I live with the gods and meet their power always
revere both them and reason
keep before me the dawn sky and a good person of old

statement.kind: A way of living with the gods, what I revere, and two exercises of reminding
statement.form: Claim 1 says that I live with the gods and experience their power all the time, and what living with them consists in. Claim 2 names what is revered: the gods, reason and the unseen soul. Claim 3 gives two exercises of reminding, and the statement names what each keeps before me: the dawn sky I look at (11.25) and the good person I am reminded of (11.24). No passage joins the three, so the statement lists them with “and” and draws no conclusion from one to another. “Always”, which stands for 12.21’s “on every occasion” and 5.21’s “constantly”, is placed at the end of the first part so that it covers that part only: 11.25 is an exercise at dawn, and 4.13 gives no frequency.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it
groups.asks: What still holds if the statement is not true.
groups.empty: No passage in this section asks what still holds if there are no gods; 12.21 answers those who ask where Marcus has seen them by giving his grounds for holding that they exist, and those grounds stand under “Why”.

near.title: Keeping the few names I have given myself
Coming back to my principles and keeping them ready
Blaming no one for what is not up to me
Living now as one about to die

outside.section: Keeping the few names I have given myself
What happens to me
The retreat within

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, claim 1 gains a second author for saying that the spirit, which is reason, is a fragment of the divine, and claim 3 a second author for keeping one good person in mind. The article gains what Marcus leaves out here: God as an observer within me, what worship consists in, the chosen person as a watcher, an example of what I turn back from when I return to reason, and what holds if no minder was given to me. Seneca limits claim 3: I need the person as a guard over me only until I respect myself.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains two watchers: God, who is present in my mind, and the good person of old, whom I treat as if he were looking on. He sets a term to the second: once I have come to respect myself, I need no longer keep that person over me as a guard.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Now reason is nothing other than a part of the divine breath sunk into a human body
piece.follows: Human reason is a part of the divine breath, sunk into a human body.
piece.context: Letter 66 argues that all goods are equal, since the divine is of one nature. Here “reason” is human reason; in 5.21 Marcus says the spirit Zeus gave each person is that person’s mind and reason.
gives: a fragment of himself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: We must hold some good man dear and keep him always before our eyes
piece.follows: The counsel is to pick one good man, hold him dear and keep him always in view.
piece.context: The closing motto of Letter 11, which Seneca gives as the counsel of Epicurus. Here “some good man” is a man one chooses; the motto does not say that he must be of old.
gives: I constantly remind myself of one
who practised virtue

items.label: why
items.t: God is near me, with me and within me. A sacred spirit sits within me, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are mine, and as I treat it, so it treats me. Nothing is shut to God: he is present in my mind and comes into the midst of my thoughts.
items.why: Marcus says that I show the gods my soul and that the spirit is my protector and leader. He does not say that the spirit observes the bad and the good that are mine, that it treats me as I treat it, or that nothing in me is shut to God.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: god is near you, he is with you, he is within.
support.follows: God is near a person, with that person and within that person.
support.context: The opening of Letter 41: Lucilius need not pray at a temple for a sound mind, since he can get it from himself. Here “you” is Lucilius, and through him anyone.
gives: God is near me, with me and within me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn.
support.follows: A sacred spirit within us observes and guards the bad and the good that are ours, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41, just after “he is with you, he is within”. The “sacred spirit” is the one that sits within each person; no one, Seneca adds, is good without God’s help.
gives: A sacred spirit sits within me, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are mine
as I treat it, so it treats me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Nothing is shut to god; he is present in our minds and comes into the midst of our thoughts
support.follows: Nothing is shut to God; he is present in our minds and enters into our thoughts.
support.context: The opening of Letter 83: Lucilius asked for an account of Seneca’s whole day. One should live and think as if seen, since God sees into our minds and thoughts.
gives: Nothing is shut to God: he is present in my mind and comes into the midst of my thoughts

items.label: action
items.t: The first way I worship the gods is to believe in them, and the next is to give them their majesty and their goodness. Whoever knows God worships him.
items.why: Marcus stands in awe of the gods, and those who question him say that he reveres them; in this section he does not say what worship consists in. Seneca does, and he begins where the questioners of 12.21 begin: with holding that the gods exist.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; next, to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty
support.follows: Worship of the gods begins with believing in them and goes on to giving them their majesty and their goodness.
support.context: Letter 95 holds that rules for ritual are useless without a right idea of God. This sentence begins Seneca’s own account of what worshipping the gods is.
gives: The first way I worship the gods is to believe in them, and the next is to give them their majesty and their goodness

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whoever knows god worships him
support.follows: Anyone who knows God worships him.
support.context: Letter 95, on worship: Seneca would forbid lamps, morning calls at temples and gifts to Jupiter’s and Juno’s statues, and sets knowing God against these rites.
gives: Whoever knows God worships him

items.label: practice
items.t: To keep a good man before my eyes, I choose Cato, or, if he seems to me too stiff, Laelius, a man of a more relaxed mind. I live as if he were looking on and do everything as if he saw it. With a witness standing beside me when I am about to do wrong, a great part of my wrongdoing is removed.
items.why: 11.24 gives the Epicurean rule in one line: remind yourself of a person of old. Seneca gives a similar counsel, which he quotes from Epicurus and comments on. In it the person is more than a reminder: he is a witness, and I act as if he saw me. Seneca also names whom to choose.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So choose Cato. If he seems to you too stiff, choose Laelius, a man of a more relaxed mind.
support.follows: The person to choose is Cato, or, for someone who finds Cato too stiff, the more relaxed Laelius.
support.context: Letter 11: Seneca applies Epicurus’s counsel to keep a good man always before one’s eyes. Cato and Laelius are Romans of earlier centuries, offered as that man.
gives: I choose Cato, or, if he seems to me too stiff, Laelius, a man of a more relaxed mind

support.author: seneca
support.quote: we live just as if he were looking on and do everything as if he saw it
support.follows: One should live and do everything as if the chosen man were looking on.
support.context: The second half of a motto that Seneca quotes from Epicurus at the end of Letter 11. Here “he” is the good man whom one is to keep before one’s eyes.
gives: I live as if he were looking on and do everything as if he saw it

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a great part of wrongdoing is removed if a witness stands beside those who are about to do wrong
support.follows: Having a witness close by at the moment of going wrong removes a great part of wrongdoing.
support.context: Letter 11, Seneca’s comment on Epicurus’s counsel to keep a good man before one’s eyes. Here the “witness” is the man one imagines looking on, as in the motto.
gives: With a witness standing beside me when I am about to do wrong, a great part of my wrongdoing is removed

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I have been striving for what is not my own, such as the strength of my body, which nature has granted in greater measure to farm animals and wild beasts, I go back to my own good. I am a rational animal, and the good in me is perfected reason. The greatest use my teacher can be to me is to show me that good, to separate me from the mute animals and place me with God.
items.why: 4.13 says that I pass from seeming a beast to seeming a god if I turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason; it does not say what I had turned to instead. Seneca gives an example: the strength of the body, which farm animals and wild beasts have in greater measure. He speaks of what I am, where 4.13 speaks of how I seem to others.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Why, I say, do you feed and exercise the strength of your body? Nature has granted that strength in greater measure to farm animals and wild beasts.
support.follows: Seneca asks why anyone feeds and exercises the strength of the body, when nature has granted more of it to farm animals and wild beasts.
support.context: Near the end of Letter 124, on the good as grasped by reason. Seneca asks Lucilius why he cultivates strength, beauty, hair and speed, in each of which some animal surpasses him.
gives: such as the strength of my body, which nature has granted in greater measure to farm animals and wild beasts

support.author: seneca
support.quote: while you strive for what is not your own, and go back to your own good
support.follows: Whoever is striving for what is not his own is asked to go back to his own good.
support.context: Letter 124: Seneca has asked why Lucilius trains strength, beauty and speed, in which animals surpass him. Those are the things “not your own”; the good is a mind freed from faults and pure.
gives: When I have been striving for what is not my own
I go back to my own good

support.author: seneca
support.quote: You are a rational animal. What, then, is the good in you? Perfected reason.
support.follows: A human being is a rational animal, and the good in one is perfected reason.
support.context: The close of Letter 124. “You” is Lucilius as a human being; Seneca’s answer to his own question is that a human’s good is reason brought to perfection.
gives: I am a rational animal, and the good in me is perfected reason

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I can in no way be of more use than if I show you your own good, if I separate you from the mute animals, if I place you with god
support.follows: Seneca can be of no more use to Lucilius than by showing him his own good, separating him from the mute animals and placing him with God.
support.context: The end of Letter 124, which argues that the good is grasped by reason and not by the senses. Seneca says what use the argument is to Lucilius, the “you”.
gives: The greatest use my teacher can be to me is to show me that good, to separate me from the mute animals and place me with God

items.label: doubt
items.t: I can set aside for now what some hold, that each of us is given a god as a minder. Whether I have been assigned to such a god or am neglected and given over to fortune, nothing worse can be called down on me than to have myself angry with me.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section asks what holds if no spirit was given to me. Seneca sets that belief aside and says what holds either way: the worst thing is to have myself angry with me. He sets aside only the god given to each person as a minder, not the gods; and in Letter 41 he himself says that a sacred spirit within us is our guardian.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Set aside for now what some hold, that each one of us is given a god as a minder
support.follows: What some hold, that each person is given a god as a minder, can be set aside for now.
support.context: The opening of Letter 110, just after the greeting. Seneca sets aside, for the moment, the popular belief in a lesser god attached to each person, which Roman ancestors held.
gives: I can set aside for now what some hold, that each of us is given a god as a minder

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whether we have been assigned or neglected and given over to fortune, you can call down on no one anything worse than if you call down on him that he should have his own self angry with him
support.follows: Whether or not a person has been assigned to such a god, nothing worse can be called down on him than to have himself angry with him.
support.context: Letter 110: Seneca leaves open whether gods attend to individuals. Here “assigned” means assigned to a god as minder; either way the worst for anyone is to have himself angry with him.

items.t: Claim 3 says that I constantly remind myself of a person of old, by a rule from the writings of the Epicureans. Seneca gives a similar Epicurean practice an end: the man is a minder who guards me until I have come to respect myself, and then I may dismiss him (Ep. 25.6). Seneca limits the claim without contradicting it: he does not say that the reminding ever does harm. Letter 11 sets no such term: at its end he says to show the chosen man to oneself always.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men
support.follows: The imagined guard is to be kept until one respects oneself; after that he may be dismissed.
support.context: Letter 25, on Epicurus’s saying that one should do everything as if Epicurus were watching. The “minder” is the good man one imagines as a guard over oneself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Show him to yourself always, either as guardian or as example
support.follows: The chosen man is to be shown to oneself always, as guardian or as example; no end to this is named.
support.context: The last lines of Letter 11, after the advice to choose Cato or Laelius. Here “him” is that chosen man, against whom one measures one’s character as against a ruler.

passages.title: On all goods being equal
passages.text: Mortal things dwindle and fall, are worn away and grow, are drained and filled; and so, in a lot so uncertain, there is inequality among them. Divine things have one nature. Now reason is nothing other than a part of the divine breath sunk into a human body. If reason is divine, and no good is without reason, then every good is divine. Further, there is no difference between divine things; so there is none between goods either. Therefore joy and the brave, unyielding endurance of torture are equal; for in both there is the same greatness of mind, in the one slackened and loose, in the other fighting and taut.

passages.title: On blushing and choosing a role model
passages.text: Now the letter calls for its close. Take one, and a useful and wholesome one at that, which I want you to fix in your mind: “We must hold some good man dear and keep him always before our eyes, so that we live just as if he were looking on and do everything as if he saw it.”

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: You are doing a very good thing, and one that is healthy for you, if, as you write, you keep on making your way towards a sound mind. It is foolish to pray for this when you can obtain it from yourself. There is no need to lift hands to heaven, or to beg the temple-keeper to admit us to the ear of the statue, as if we could be heard better: god is near you, he is with you, he is within.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: This is what I say, Lucilius: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn. And indeed no one is a good man without god: or can anyone rise above fortune unless helped by him? It is he who gives advice that is grand and lofty. In each and every good man a god (which god is uncertain) lives.

passages.title: On a daily routine and drunkenness
passages.text: You tell me to report to you each of my days, and the whole of each: you judge well of me if you think there is nothing in them that I would hide. Certainly we must live as if we were living in plain sight, and think as if someone could look into the inmost heart: and someone can. For what is the use of something being kept secret from a human being? Nothing is shut to god; he is present in our minds and comes into the midst of our thoughts. I say “comes into” as if he ever went away.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; next, to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty; to know that it is they who preside over the world, who govern all things by their power, who watch over the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals. They neither give evil nor have it; yet they chastise some people and restrain them and impose punishments, and sometimes they punish by what looks like a good. Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: It is usual to give precepts on how the gods are to be worshipped. Let us forbid anyone to light lamps on the sabbath, since the gods have no need of light and not even human beings take pleasure in soot. Let us forbid anyone to perform morning greetings and to sit at the doors of temples: it is human vanity that is won by such attentions; whoever knows god worships him. Let us forbid anyone to bring towels and bath scrapers to Jupiter and to hold a mirror for Juno: god does not look for servants. Why would he? He himself serves the human race; he is at hand everywhere and for everyone.

passages.title: On blushing and choosing a role model
passages.text: So choose Cato. If he seems to you too stiff, choose Laelius, a man of a more relaxed mind. Choose the man whose life and speech and very face, which carries his mind in plain view, have pleased you. Show him to yourself always, either as guardian or as example. Someone is needed, I say, against whom our character may measure itself: you will not straighten what is crooked except against a ruler. Farewell.

passages.title: On blushing and choosing a role model
passages.text: This, my Lucilius, is Epicurus’s precept. He gave us a guardian and a minder, and not without reason: a great part of wrongdoing is removed if a witness stands beside those who are about to do wrong. Let the mind have someone to revere, by whose authority it may make even its privacy purer. How fortunate is the man who corrects not only when he is present but even when he is thought of! How fortunate is the man who can revere someone in such a way that he composes and orders himself even at the memory of him! One who can revere someone in this way will soon be someone to be revered.

passages.title: On the good belonging to reason alone
passages.text: Why, I say, do you feed and exercise the strength of your body? Nature has granted that strength in greater measure to farm animals and wild beasts. Why do you cultivate your beauty? When you have done everything, you will be beaten in looks by the mute animals. Why do you dress your hair with enormous care? When you have let it flow in the manner of the Parthians, or tied it up in the way of the Germans, or, as is the habit of the Scythians, spread it loose, a thicker mane will toss on any horse you like, and a more beautiful one will bristle on the necks of lions. When you have trained yourself for speed, you will not be the equal of a little hare.

passages.title: On the good belonging to reason alone
passages.text: Will you not leave the things in which you are bound to be beaten while you strive for what is not your own, and go back to your own good? What is this? A mind, of course, freed from faults and pure, striving to equal god, lifting itself above human things, placing nothing of its own outside itself. You are a rational animal. What, then, is the good in you? Perfected reason. Summon it from here to its own goal, as far as it can possibly grow.

passages.title: On the good belonging to reason alone
passages.text: Do you ask what this discussion now leads to, and what use it will be to your mind? I say: it exercises the mind and sharpens it, and it keeps the mind, which will be doing something in any case, in an honourable occupation. And it is also of use in that it delays those who are hurrying towards what is wrong. But I say this: I can in no way be of more use than if I show you your own good, if I separate you from the mute animals, if I place you with god.

passages.title: On empty fears and true riches
passages.text: From my place at Nomentum I greet you and tell you to have a good mind, that is, all the gods well disposed; and whoever has made himself well disposed to himself has them appeased and favouring him. Set aside for now what some hold, that each one of us is given a god as a minder, not one of the regular rank, to be sure, but this one of a lower grade, among those whom Ovid calls “gods from the common people”. Yet I want you to set this aside in such a way that you remember that our ancestors, who believed it, were Stoics; for to individuals, one by one, they gave both Genius and Juno.

passages.title: On empty fears and true riches
passages.text: We shall see later whether the gods have so much leisure that they manage the affairs of private persons. For the present know this: whether we have been assigned or neglected and given over to fortune, you can call down on no one anything worse than if you call down on him that he should have his own self angry with him. But there is no reason for you to wish on anyone you think deserving of punishment that he should have the gods hostile: he has them so, I say, even if he seems to be carried forward by their favour.

passages.title: On reforming friends and imagining a watcher
passages.text: When you have made so much progress that you have respect even for yourself, you may dismiss your minder. Meanwhile guard yourself by the authority of certain men: let it be the famous Cato, or Scipio, or Laelius, or another at whose coming even depraved men would suppress their vices, while you are making yourself the man in whose company you would not dare to do wrong. When you have made yourself that, and have begun to have some standing in your own eyes, I will begin to allow you what the same Epicurus advises: “Withdraw into yourself most of all when you are forced to be in a crowd.”

claims.role: With the gods at every moment
claims.t: I live with the gods and experience their power all the time. I constantly show them my own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that is wanted by the spirit Zeus gave me as protector and leader, a fragment of himself.
claims.shared: Both passages speak of dealings with the gods that never stop. In 12.21 Marcus experiences their power “on every occasion”; in 5.21 the one who lives with the gods shows them their own soul “constantly”. “All the time” stands for both. Only 5.21 calls this living with the gods.
claims.changed: 12.21 gives this experience as the way Marcus knows that the gods exist; the claim takes from it only that the experience comes on every occasion, and sets it beside living with the gods without making it a part of that life. 5.21 says “each person” and “their own soul”; the claim says “me” and “my own soul”.

support.follows: To live with the gods is to show them, constantly, a soul content with its lot that does all that the spirit given by Zeus wants.

claims.changed: In 12.21 the word “revere” is spoken by those who question Marcus; his answer accepts it and ends with his awe of the gods. 4.13 does not say whether the reason to be revered is a person’s own or the reason of the whole, and the claim leaves that open as well.

claims.t: I give myself reminders, by rules taken from schools of philosophy. At dawn I turn my eyes to the sky and am reminded of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way; and I constantly remind myself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
claims.shared: Both passages give a rule for reminding oneself, and both use the same verb: 11.25 “so that we are reminded”, 11.24 “to remind oneself”. Both name the school the rule comes from: “The Pythagoreans” in 11.25, “the writings of the Epicureans” in 11.24. Each names something to be reminded of that does its part well: those in the sky that always complete their own work, and a person of old who practised virtue.
claims.changed: The claim takes both rules as my own and says “schools of philosophy” for the Pythagoreans and the Epicureans. 11.25 says “we” and 11.24 “oneself”; the claim says “I”. Only 11.24 uses the word “rule”; 11.25 gives the Pythagoreans’ instruction without a verb. 11.25 says “those”; the claim says “those in the sky”, since the passage has just named the sky.

single.quote: this spirit is each person’s mind and reason
single.label: What the spirit is
single.t: The spirit that Zeus gave me as my leader is my own mind and reason.
single.why: Only this passage says what the spirit is. 4.13 names reason and does not connect it with a spirit or with Zeus.
single.follows: The spirit Zeus gives each person as protector and leader is that person’s own mind and reason.

single.quote: they are visible even to the eye
single.label: Seen with the eye
single.t: The gods can be seen, even with the eye.
single.why: Only this passage says that the gods are visible, and it does not say which gods. 11.25 looks at the sky but does not call what is seen there gods.
single.follows: Marcus’s first answer to those who ask where he has seen the gods is that they can be seen with the eye.

single.quote: from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them
single.label: Known by their power
single.t: It is from my experience of their power that I grasp that the gods exist, and I stand in awe of them.
single.why: Only this passage says how I know that the gods exist. No other passage of the section argues for it.
single.follows: Marcus’s ground for holding that the gods exist, and for his awe of them, is what he has just named: his experience of their power.

single.quote: and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.label: What the sky shows
single.t: The sky at dawn also reminds me of order, of purity and of nakedness: a star has no veil in front of it.
single.why: Only this passage names order, purity and nakedness. 5.21 speaks of showing the gods my soul, but it does not say that the soul is shown uncovered.
single.follows: Those in the sky are also a reminder of order, purity and nakedness, since a star has nothing hung in front of it.

single.quote: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles
single.label: From beast to god
single.t: To the very people to whom I now seem a beast and an ape, I shall seem a god within ten days, if I turn back to the principles.
single.why: Only this passage says what it looks like to have left the principles, and that there is a way back. It speaks of how I seem to people, not of living with the gods. Its last words, “reverence for reason”, are quoted in claim 2.
single.follows: Whoever turns back to the principles will soon seem a god to the same people who now take him for a beast and an ape.

members.text:
To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how
knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in
their worship? I answer first of all, that even to the very eye, they
are in some manner visible and apparent. Secondly, neither have I ever
seen mine own soul, and yet I respect and honour it. So then for the
Gods, by the daily experience that I have of their power and providence
towards myself and others, I know certainly that they are, and therefore
worship them.
members.english: To those who ask: “Well, where have you seen the gods, or from what have you grasped that they exist, that you revere them as you do?” First, they are visible even to the eye. Second, though, I have not seen my own soul either, and yet I honour it. So with the gods too: from what I experience of their power on every occasion, from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.
members.greek: Πρὸς τοὺς ἐπιζητοῦντας· ποῦ γὰρ ἰδὼν τοὺς θεοὺς ἢ πόθεν κατειληφὼς ὅτι εἰσὶν οὕτως σέβεις; πρῶτον μὲν καὶ ὄψει ὁρατοί εἰσιν· ἔπειτα μέντοι οὐδὲ τὴν ψυχὴν τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ ἑώρακα καὶ ὅμως τιμῶ· οὕτως οὖν καὶ τοὺς θεούς, ἐξ ὧν τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτῶν ἑκάστοτε πειρῶμαι, ἐκ τούτων ὅτι τε εἰσὶ καταλαμβάνω καὶ αἰδοῦμαι.

members.text:
To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times
affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well
pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and
performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of
himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
members.english: “To live with the gods.” And the one who lives with the gods is the one who constantly shows them their own soul, content with what is allotted and doing all that the spirit wants, the spirit that Zeus has given to each person as protector and leader, a fragment of himself. And this spirit is each person’s mind and reason.
members.greek: ʽΣυζῆν θεοῖς.ʼ συζῇ δὲ θεοῖς ὁ συνεχῶς δεικνὺς αὐτοῖς τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ψυχὴν ἀρεσκομένην μὲν τοῖς ἀπονεμομένοις, ποιοῦσαν δὲ ὅσα βούλεται ὁ δαίμων, ὃν ἑκάστῳ προστάτην καὶ ἡγεμόνα ὁ Ζεὺς ἔδωκεν, ἀπόσπασμα ἑαυτοῦ. οὗτος δέ ἐστιν ὁ ἑκάστου νοῦς καὶ λόγος.

members.text:
Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of
them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring
of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an
ape.
members.english: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles and to reverence for reason.
members.greek: Ἐντὸς δέκα ἡμερῶν θεὸς αὐτοῖς τούτοις δόξεις οἷς νῦν θηρίον καὶ πίθηκος, ἐὰν ἀνακάμψῃς ἐπὶ τὰ δόγματα καὶ τὸν σεβασμὸν τοῦ λόγου.

members.text:
The Pythagoreans were wont betimes in the morning the first thing
they did, to look up unto the heavens, to put themselves in mind of them
who constantly and invariably did perform their task: as also to put
themselves in mind of orderliness, or good order, and of purity, and of
naked simplicity. For no star or planet hath any cover before it.
members.english: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way, and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
members.greek: Οἱ Πυθαγόρειοι· ἕωθεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν ἀφορᾶν, ἵν’ ὑπομιμνῃσκώμεθα τῶν ἀεὶ κατὰ τὰ αὐτὰ καὶ ὡσαύτως τὸ ἑαυτῶν ἔργον διανυόντων καὶ τῆς τάξεως καὶ τῆς καθαρότητος καὶ τῆς γυμνότητος· οὐδὲν γὰρ προκάλυμμα ἄστρου.

members.text:
In the ancient mystical letters of the Ephesians, there was an
item, that a man should always have in his mind some one or other of the
ancient worthies.
members.english: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
members.greek: Ἐν τοῖς τῶν Ἐπικουρείων γράμμασι παράγγελμα ἔκειτο συνεχῶς ὑπομιμνῄσκεσθαι τῶν παλαιῶν τινος τῶν ἀρετῇ χρησαμένων.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.21 is 12.28, 5.21 is 5.27, 4.13 is 4.16, 11.25 is 11.27 and 11.24 is 11.26.

Sets living with the gods (5.21) and experiencing their power (12.21) side by side, in claim 1 and in the first part of the statement, joined only by what both say: that it goes on all the time. The claim, its heading and the statement do not say that the experience is part of living with them.

Takes “I revere the gods” from words that 12.21 gives to Marcus’s questioners (“that you revere them as you do”), because they share a Greek root with “reverence for reason” in 4.13. Marcus’s own verbs in 12.21 are “honour”, of his soul, and “stand in awe”, of the gods.

Does not say that the reason I revere is the reason that leads me. 4.13 says “reverence for reason”, and its Greek leaves open whether a person’s own reason or the reason of the whole is meant; 5.21 says that the spirit leads and is mind and reason, but not that it is revered. The two stand side by side: the reverence in claim 2 and in the statement, the leading spirit in claim 1 and in the said-once item from 5.21.

Reads “those that always complete their own work” (11.25) as the stars, as the passage’s last sentence suggests, but writes “those in the sky” in the claim and does not name them. Does not join them to the gods who are “visible even to the eye” in 12.21: neither passage says that the stars are gods.

Says in claim 3 that both rules come from schools of philosophy. For 11.24 this follows the edition’s text, “Epicureans”; the translators’ note says, from memory and unchecked, that the manuscripts read “Ephesians” and that “Epicureans” is an editor’s correction.
articles.limit: Article 4 already says that what rules in me is of one kind with the reason that governs the world, and that I honour what is supreme in myself (5.18); Article 3 already says that I accept what happens, which here is “content with what is allotted”. What this article adds is that life with the gods goes on all the time, that it consists in what I show them, and two exercises of reminding. Of Seneca’s additions, the one on what I go back from comes near Article 5’s Seneca item from Ep. 76.10, that reason is what is peculiar to me; what it adds here is the turning back from what is not my own. The article is weakest where it joins its parts: the section holds three passages on the gods and reason and two on reminders, and no passage connects the two groups; the statement only sets them side by side.

claims.t: I keep in mind two reminders from other schools. The Pythagoreans say to turn the eyes to the sky at dawn, and so be reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way. The Epicureans laid down a rule to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
claims.shared: Both are reported practices of other schools, so the line keeps them as reports and claims only that I keep them in mind. The semicolon is removed. The sky practice is 11.25 alone, and the exemplar rule is 11.24 alone and has no gods in it.

support.quote: The Pythagoreans: to turn our eyes to the sky at dawn, so that we are reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way
support.follows: The Pythagoreans’ instruction is to look at the sky at dawn, as a reminder of those in the sky that always complete their own work in the same way.
gives: I keep in mind two reminders from other schools
The Pythagoreans say to turn the eyes to the sky at dawn, and so be reminded of those that always complete their own work along the same lines and in the same way

support.quote: In the writings of the Epicureans a rule was laid down: to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue
support.follows: The Epicureans had a written rule: keep reminding yourself of one of the people of old who practised virtue.
gives: I keep in mind two reminders from other schools
The Epicureans laid down a rule to remind oneself constantly of one of the people of old who practised virtue

single.quote: this spirit is each person’s mind and reason
single.label: What the spirit is
single.t: The spirit in me is my own mind and reason.
single.why: Single source, 5.21. Narrowed to what the quote says, which is that the spirit is a person’s mind and reason. Zeus’s gift and the role of leader belong to c1.
single.follows: The spirit Zeus gives each person as protector and leader is that person’s own mind and reason.

single.quote: they are visible even to the eye
single.label: Seen with the eye
single.t: The gods are visible even to the eye.
single.why: Single source, 12.21. This is the first of two separate answers. The passage does not say which visible things the gods are.
single.follows: Marcus’s first answer to those who ask where he has seen the gods is that they can be seen with the eye.

single.quote: from that I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them
single.label: Known by their power
single.t: From what I experience of the gods’ power, I both grasp that they exist and stand in awe of them.
single.why: Single source, 12.21. ‘What I experience of the gods’ power’ spells out the quote’s ‘from that’ as the passage itself does, so the line can stand alone. The ground is experienced power producing awe, not sight of the gods and not a proof.
single.follows: Marcus’s ground for holding that the gods exist, and for his awe of them, is what he has just named: his experience of their power.

single.quote: and of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.label: What the sky shows
single.t: The stars remind me of their order, their purity and their nakedness. For a star has no veil.
single.why: Single source, 11.25, from a reported Pythagorean practice. The stars are named from the quote’s own image so that ‘their’ has a referent. The image stands in the third person as given, and the line does not call the stars gods.
single.follows: Those in the sky are also a reminder of order, purity and nakedness, since a star has nothing hung in front of it.

single.quote: Within ten days you will seem a god to the very people to whom you now seem a beast and an ape, if you turn back to the principles
single.label: From beast to god
single.t: If I turn back to the principles, within ten days I will seem a god to the very people to whom I now seem a beast and an ape.
single.why: Single source, 4.13. It is conditional and concerns how I seem to the same onlookers, not what I become. It is not a vow, and their opinion is not the aim.
single.follows: Whoever turns back to the principles will soon seem a god to the same people who now take him for a beast and an ape.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.21 is 12.28, 5.21 is 5.27, 4.13 is 4.16, 11.25 is 11.27 and 11.24 is 11.26.

Each phrase rests on two passages. Reverence for the gods is 12.21 and reverence for reason is 4.13. The reminders are the Pythagorean one of work always done the same way and the Epicurean one of virtue. ‘Live with the gods’ is left to c1 because only 5.21 says it.
marcus_revision.limit: The article joins reverence for the gods and reason (12.21, 5.21, 4.13) with reminder practices that Marcus only reports from other schools (11.25, 11.24). The first-person form suggests more adoption of those practices than the sources state. 4.13’s ‘seem a god’ is about reputation and is kept apart from 5.21’s living with the gods. 12.21 offers experience of the gods’ power and awe, not a demonstration.

articles.title: Blaming no one for what is not up to me

statement.t: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me, and I blame no one for it, neither the gods nor people.

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: Claims 1 and 3 are the ground: I count only what is up to me as good or bad, and the gods go wrong in nothing. Claims 2 and 4 are the conduct that follows: no one is to be blamed, and my own wrong is what I can stop. 6.36 itself draws the line from the ground to the conduct, so the “and” of the statement needs no inference of the editor’s. Claim 5 is the failure and the way back.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, the slavery of claim 1 and the case against the gods in claim 5 gain a second author; “In action” gains philosophy turned on my own vices, “Practice” gains a way to be fortunate without prayers, and “If I doubt it” gains a second answer to the gods’ neglect. He limits two claims: the gods are sometimes without concern for individuals (claim 3), and for the harm we bring on ourselves we can complain of no one but ourselves (claim 2).
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands, and he adds what holds if the gods do neglect me: the worst would be to be at odds with myself.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: To be a slave to no thing, to no necessity, to no accidents
piece.follows: To be free is to be a slave to no thing, no necessity and no accident.
piece.context: Letter 51, on the pleasure resort of Baiae: Seneca resolves not to yield to Fortune or to pleasure. The words answer the question of what freedom is, the goal for which the toil is done.
gives: letting it would be slavery

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: For if he considers anything else a good, first, he passes an unfavourable judgment on providence
piece.follows: Whoever counts anything but the honourable as good ends by judging providence unfavourably.
piece.context: Letter 74 says that whoever wants to be happy must hold that only the honourable is good. “He” is that person; the next words give his grievance: many troubles happen to just men.
gives: I make a case against the gods

items.label: action
items.t: I use philosophy to strip vices from myself, not to reproach others with theirs, and I do not use it to condemn every way of living that I do not follow myself.
items.why: 7.41 and 8.15 say that my own wrong is the one I can deal with. Seneca says what that means for philosophy: it is for my own vices, not a means of reproaching other people with theirs.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let her strip vices from you, not reproach others with theirs.
support.follows: Philosophy should be used to remove my own vices, not to reproach other people with theirs.
support.context: The end of Letter 103, on the dangers that come from other people. “Her” is philosophy, in which Seneca has just told Lucilius to take refuge, without vaunting it.
gives: I use philosophy to strip vices from myself, not to reproach others with theirs

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let her not be at odds with the ways of people at large, nor make it her business to seem to condemn whatever she does not do.
support.follows: Philosophy should not be at odds with ordinary ways or seem to condemn whatever it does not itself do.
support.context: Letter 103, on the dangers that come from other people, ends by warning that philosophy must not be vaunted. “She” is philosophy, which must not set itself against everyone else’s ways.
gives: I do not use it to condemn every way of living that I do not follow myself

items.label: practice
items.t: I do not pick out by prayer what I would want to come to me. I make myself fortunate by my own doing, knowing that what has virtue mixed into it is good and what has wickedness joined to it is shameful.
items.why: 9.40 keeps praying and turns the prayer towards what is up to me. Seneca asks what need there is of prayers at all: the good fortune I would pray for I make myself. Here the two differ: 9.40 answers that very objection (“who told you that the gods do not also lend a hand with the things that are up to us?”), and Seneca himself elsewhere tells Lucilius to pray for a sound mind (Ep. 10.4).

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So there is no reason for you to pick out, from that old prayer of your parents, what you would want to come to you, what you would wish for
support.follows: Lucilius has no reason to pick out, from what his parents once prayed for him, what he would want to come to him.
support.context: Letter 31 tells Lucilius to be deaf to the wishes of those who love him. The “old prayer” is what his parents prayed for him, which Seneca says he no longer needs.
gives: I do not pick out by prayer what I would want to come to me

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What need is there of prayers? Make yourself fortunate by your own doing; and you will, if you understand that those things are good which have virtue mixed into them, and those shameful which have wickedness joined to them.
support.follows: No prayers are needed: I can make myself fortunate by my own doing once I see that what has virtue mixed into it is good.
support.context: Letter 31, on not heeding the prayers of those who love us. A man who has passed through the greatest things should stop wearying the gods; “you will” means he will make himself fortunate.
gives: I make myself fortunate by my own doing
what has virtue mixed into it is good and what has wickedness joined to it is shameful

items.label: doubt
items.t: Whether I have been assigned to a guardian or neglected and given over to fortune, nothing worse can be wished on me than to be at odds with myself.
items.why: Marcus’s answer in 7.25 to being neglected by the gods is that this too has its reason. Seneca adds a second answer that does not depend on the gods: whether I am guarded or neglected, the worst that can happen to me is to be at odds with myself.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: whether we have been assigned or neglected and given over to fortune, you can call down on no one anything worse than if you call down on him that he should have his own self angry with him
support.follows: Whether or not the gods look after us, nothing worse can be called down on anyone than to be angry with himself.
support.context: Letter 110 opens on whether each of us has a guardian god. Seneca puts off asking whether the gods care for individuals; “him” is anyone one might wish harm on.
gives: Whether I have been assigned to a guardian or neglected and given over to fortune
nothing worse can be wished on me than to be at odds with myself

items.t: Marcus says that if the gods have neglected me, this too has its reason (7.25), and that they would not let anything be neglected unjustly (12.4). Seneca states as a fact that the gods, who watch over the human race, are sometimes without concern for individuals, and he gives no reason for it (Ep. 95.50). In Ep. 110.2 he leaves open whether the gods care for individuals at all, which sits uneasily with his stating it as a fact. This limits the claim; Ep. 95.50 itself affirms the gods’ goodness.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: who watch over the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals
support.follows: The gods guard the human race, though they sometimes do not attend to individuals.
support.context: Letter 95 says how to worship the gods: believe in them and acknowledge their goodness. “Who” refers to the gods, who preside over the world.

items.t: Seneca does not blame God, but he does not say that no one is to blame: for the harm humankind has brought on itself by bringing out what the nature of things was hiding, we can complain of nothing but ourselves (Ep. 110.10). Marcus excuses people because they go wrong only unwillingly; Seneca keeps one complaint, against ourselves. This limits the claim; the complaint he keeps is not against the gods.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We can complain of nothing but ourselves: the things we were to perish by we have brought out, though the nature of things was unwilling and was hiding them.
support.follows: For the harm we suffer from what we brought out, though the nature of things was unwilling, we can complain only of ourselves.
support.context: Letter 110, on true and false riches: God put good things within reach and buried what harms. “We” are humankind, who dug up gold and the like out of greed.

amend.t: ; whether or not the gods watch over me, the worst for me is to be at odds with myself
; but they watch over the human race and are sometimes without concern for individuals

passages.title: On luxurious resorts and soft living
passages.text: Freedom is what has been set as the goal; it is for this prize that the toil is done. You ask what freedom is? To be a slave to no thing, to no necessity, to no accidents; to bring Fortune down to level ground. On the day I understand that she has more power, she will have no power: am I to put up with her, when death is in my hand?

passages.title: On virtue as the only safe good
passages.text: Whoever resolves to be happy should think that the only good is what is honourable. For if he considers anything else a good, first, he passes an unfavourable judgment on providence, because many troubles happen to just men, and because whatever it has given us is short and slight, if you compare it with the lifetime of the whole world.

passages.title: On the danger people pose to each other
passages.text: But philosophy herself you must not show off. To many she has been a cause of danger when handled arrogantly and defiantly. Let her strip vices from you, not reproach others with theirs. Let her not be at odds with the ways of people at large, nor make it her business to seem to condemn whatever she does not do. One may be wise without parade, without ill will. Farewell.

passages.title: On trusting yourself and scorning popular goods
passages.text: Hard work feeds noble minds. So there is no reason for you to pick out, from that old prayer of your parents, what you would want to come to you, what you would wish for; and altogether, for a man who has already passed through the greatest things, it is shameful still to be wearying the gods. What need is there of prayers? Make yourself fortunate by your own doing; and you will, if you understand that those things are good which have virtue mixed into them, and those shameful which have wickedness joined to them. Just as nothing is bright without a mixture of light, and nothing is black unless it has darkness in it or has drawn something dark into itself; just as nothing is hot without the help of fire, and nothing cold without air; so it is partnership with virtue and with wickedness that makes things honourable and shameful.

passages.title: On empty fears and true riches
passages.text: We shall see later whether the gods have so much leisure that they manage the affairs of private persons. For the present know this: whether we have been assigned or neglected and given over to fortune, you can call down on no one anything worse than if you call down on him that he should have his own self angry with him. But there is no reason for you to wish on anyone you think deserving of punishment that he should have the gods hostile: he has them so, I say, even if he seems to be carried forward by their favour.

passages.title: On why advice needs underlying principles
passages.text: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods; next, to give them the majesty that is theirs, to give them the goodness without which there is no majesty; to know that it is they who preside over the world, who govern all things by their power, who watch over the human race, sometimes without concern for individuals. They neither give evil nor have it; yet they chastise some people and restrain them and impose punishments, and sometimes they punish by what looks like a good. Do you want to win the favour of the gods? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough.

passages.title: On empty fears and true riches
passages.text: Whatever was going to be for our good, our god and parent placed close at hand; he did not wait for us to search and gave it of his own accord: the things that would harm us he pressed down very deep. We can complain of nothing but ourselves: the things we were to perish by we have brought out, though the nature of things was unwilling and was hiding them. We have bound the mind over to pleasure, and to indulge pleasure is the beginning of all evils; we have handed it over to ambition and reputation, and to the rest, things equally empty and hollow.

claims.role: What counts as good or bad
claims.t: I count only what is up to me as good or bad for me. I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me: letting it would be slavery, and doing so leads me into many wrongs.
claims.shared: Both passages set what is up to me against what is not, and both name the same mistake in the same words: letting what is not up to me “make a difference” (6.36: “the difference these things make to us”; 9.40: “make a difference to you”).
claims.changed: 6.36 says “we” and 9.40 says “you”; the claim says “I”. 6.36 calls the other things “not yours to choose”, 9.40 “not up to you”; the claim uses 9.40’s phrase for both. 9.40 asks a question (“is it not better…?”); the claim states its answer. 6.36 gives a condition (“if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad”); the claim states it as a rule I keep: I count only these things as good or bad.

support.quote: if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad
support.follows: Marcus proposes that we count only the things that are up to us as good or bad.
gives: I count only what is up to me as good or bad for me

support.quote: And indeed we do many wrongs because of the difference these things make to us.
support.follows: When things outside our choice make a difference to us, that leads us into many wrongs.
gives: make a difference to me
doing so leads me into many wrongs

support.quote: is it not better to use what is up to you in freedom than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you, in slavery and degradation?
support.follows: It is better to use freely what is up to me than to let what is not up to me make a difference to me, which is slavery.
gives: I do not let what is not up to me make a difference to me
make a difference to me
letting it would be slavery

claims.t: No one is to be blamed: not the gods, not people, and not things. I do not accuse a god, I do not take an enemy’s stand against a person, and I am not angry with things, which do not care at all.
claims.shared: 8.15 and 12.9 both contain the same words, “no one is to be blamed”. 12.9 and 6.36 both name the gods and people together. 8.15’s “no one” can equally mean “nothing” in the Greek, and 7.25 says of things that one must not be angry with them.
claims.changed: 6.36 says there is no cause left for accusing a god or taking an enemy’s stand, once only what is up to us counts as good or bad; the claim states the conduct without the condition, which claim 1 gives. 7.25 speaks of anger at things, not of blame; the claim puts both under “not to be blamed”.

support.quote: No one is to be blamed.
support.follows: No one, and nothing, is to be blamed for what goes wrong.

support.follows: The gods are not to be blamed.

support.quote: So no one is to be blamed.
support.follows: Since neither the gods nor people are to be blamed, no one is.

support.follows: Once only what is up to us counts as good or bad, there is no cause to accuse a god or to stand against a person as an enemy.

claims.role: When the gods seem to neglect us
claims.t: The gods go wrong in nothing. If they have neglected me and my children, or seem to have overlooked very good people, who, once dead, may not come to be again, this too has its reason: they would not let anything be neglected unjustly and against reason, and if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise.
claims.shared: 7.25 and 12.4 both face the thought that the gods neglect someone, and both answer that this is not without reason: in 7.25, if I and my two children have been “neglected by the gods, this too has its reason”; in 12.4 the gods, who seem to have “overlooked” very good people, would not let anything be “neglected unjustly and against reason”. 12.9 gives the ground both rest on: the gods go wrong in nothing.
claims.changed: 7.25 supposes the neglect and says that it too has its reason. 12.4 asks how the gods could have overlooked the very good and answers that nothing is neglected unjustly; “seem” is said of 12.4’s case only. 12.4’s case is particular: very good people who, once dead, may not come to be again.

support.quote: for they go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly
support.follows: The gods go wrong in nothing, neither on purpose nor against their will.
gives: The gods go wrong in nothing

support.quote: But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.
support.follows: Even if the gods have neglected me and my children, there is a reason for that too.
gives: If they have neglected me and my children
this too has its reason

support.quote: overlooked this one thing only: that some people, and very good ones
support.follows: It looks as if the gods, who arranged everything well, overlooked one thing: what becomes of very good people after death.
gives: seem to have overlooked very good people

support.quote: they would not have let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason
support.follows: If the gods are best and most just, nothing in the order of things has been neglected unjustly or against reason.
gives: this too has its reason
they would not let anything be neglected unjustly and against reason

support.quote: be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise

claims.t: My own wrongdoing is up to me, and I can stop it. Another person’s wrong is up to them, and I cannot escape it. My part is to set that person right if I can, or else at least put the situation right; and if I can do neither, blaming serves no end.
claims.shared: 8.15 and 7.41 both split a wrong into mine and another’s, and both say that mine is the one I can deal with: 8.15 “If it is up to you, why do you do it? If it is up to another …”; 7.41 “one’s own vice, which is in fact possible” to flee, and “that of others, which is impossible”.
claims.changed: 8.15 asks questions; the claim states their answers. 8.15 does not say what “it” is; the claim takes it to be a wrong, as 7.41’s “vice” is. 7.41’s “flee” becomes “stop” for my own vice and “escape” for another’s: I cannot rid myself of other people’s vice as I can of my own. 8.15’s “the thing itself” is rendered “the situation”.

support.quote: If it is up to you, why do you do it?
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to me, I have no reason to go on doing it.
gives: My own wrongdoing is up to me, and I can stop it

support.quote: It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.
support.follows: I can get clear of my own vice and cannot get clear of other people’s, so it is ridiculous to try the second and not the first.
gives: My own wrongdoing is up to me, and I can stop it
Another person’s wrong
I cannot escape it

support.quote: If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame?
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to someone else, there is no one and nothing for me to blame.
