is up to them

support.quote: For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you?
support.follows: I should correct the other person if I can, or else the thing itself; if I can do neither, blaming serves no end.

claims.t: When I let what is not up to me count as good or bad, I make a case against the gods: I blame them for what I meet with or miss, or I argue with them about what is just; and I hate the people who caused it. The way back is to stop grumbling and become simpler and better towards the gods.
claims.shared: 6.36 and 12.4 both describe a charge brought against the gods: 6.36 “you blame the gods”, 12.4 “you are arguing a case of justice with god”. 9.35 calls a halt to the grumbling and gives the way back: “towards the gods too … become simpler and better”.
claims.changed: In 12.4 the prying is part of an argument: that we argue a case of justice with god shows we hold the gods to be just. The claim keeps the arguing only as a failure: the word “prying” marks it as going beyond what is proper. 9.35 does not say what the grumbling is about. Joining 12.4’s arguing with god to 6.36’s condition (letting what is not up to me count as good or bad) is the editor’s reading: 12.4 pries into the fate of the very good after death and does not name that condition as its cause. 12.4 says “god” in the singular; the claim says “them”, the gods named in the same sentence.

support.quote: Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause
support.follows: Whoever counts things outside their choice as good or bad will blame the gods and hate people when they meet or miss those things.
gives: When I let what is not up to me count as good or bad
I make a case against the gods
I blame them for what I meet with or miss
I hate the people who caused it

support.quote: For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god.
support.follows: Prying into why the good do not come to be again after death is arguing a case of justice with god.
gives: I make a case against the gods
I argue with them about what is just

support.quote: Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to have done with a wretched life of grumbling and putting on an act.
gives: stop grumbling

support.quote: But towards the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.
support.follows: It is time to become simpler and better towards the gods as well.
gives: and become simpler and better towards the gods

single.quote: Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.
single.label: Turning prayers round
single.t: I turn my prayers round. Instead of praying not to lose my child, I pray not to be afraid of losing it.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of prayer. It is kept as the article’s practice: a way of asking for what is up to me.
single.follows: I should pray not to be afraid of losing my child, instead of praying not to lose it, and see what happens.

single.quote: Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing.
single.label: Looking at what troubles me
single.t: When something troubles me, I ask what is new in it, and I look at its cause and at what it is made of. There is nothing more to it than these.
single.why: Only this passage gives questions to put to whatever troubles me. Article 4 asks about causes in general; here the questions come at the moment of trouble.
single.follows: When something troubles me, I should look at its cause and at what it is made of, since there is nothing more to it.

single.quote: No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.
single.label: Not joining in
single.t: When others lament, I do not join in the wailing, and I do not let my pulse race.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of others’ lamenting and of my own agitation. Its two instructions are kept as a practice.
single.follows: I should not join others in lamenting, and I should not let myself grow agitated.

single.quote: The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people of such a kind and in such numbers. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?
single.label: Giving up on bad people
single.t: When I give up on bad people, I remember that the gods, who are immortal, put up with them and care for them. I am about to come to an end, and I am one of the bad ones myself.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of the gods’ patience with bad people. It names a failure, giving up on them, and sets the gods’ care against it.
single.follows: If the immortal gods bear with bad people and care for them, I, who will soon die and am bad myself, have no ground to give up on them.

single.quote: The atoms or the gods? Both are madness.
single.label: Either way
single.t: Whether what happens comes from the atoms or from the gods, blaming either is madness.
single.why: Only this passage argues by cases: blaming is madness whichever account of the world is true, chance or the gods. It is kept as what still holds if I doubt that the gods govern.
single.follows: Whether things come about by the atoms or by the gods, blaming either is madness.

members.text:
What things soever are not within the proper power and
jurisdiction of thine own will either to compass or avoid, if thou shalt
propose unto thyself any of those things as either good, or evil; it
must needs be that according as thou shalt either fall into that which
thou dost think evil, or miss of that which thou dost think good, so
wilt thou be ready both to complain of the Gods, and to hate those men,
who either shall be so indeed, or shall by thee be suspected as the
cause either of thy missing of the one, or falling into the other. And
indeed we must needs commit many evils, if we incline to any of these
things, more or less, with an opinion of any difference. But if we mind
and fancy those things only, as good and bad, which wholly depend of our
own wills, there is no more occasion why we should either murmur against
the Gods, or be at enmity with any man.
members.english: Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause, or are suspected of being about to be the cause, of your missing the one or meeting with the other. And indeed we do many wrongs because of the difference these things make to us. But if we judge only the things that are up to us to be good and bad, no cause is left either for accusing a god or for taking an enemy’s stand against a person.
members.greek: Ὅ τι ἂν τῶν ἀπροαιρέτων ὑποστήσῃ σαυτῷ ἀγαθὸν ἢ κακόν, ἀνάγκη κατὰ τὴν περίπτωσιν τοῦ τοιούτου κακοῦ ἢ τὴν ἀπότευξιν τοῦ τοιούτου ἀγαθοῦ μέμψασθαί σε θεοῖς καὶ ἀνθρώπους δὲ μισῆσαι τοὺς αἰτίους ὄντας ἢ ὑποπτευομένους ἔσεσθαι τῆς ἀποτεύξεως ἢ τῆς περιπτώσεως· καὶ ἀδικοῦμεν δὴ πολλὰ διὰ τὴν πρὸς ταῦτα διαφοράν. ἐὰν δὲ μόνα τὰ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν ἀγαθὰ καὶ κακὰ κρίνωμεν, οὐδεμία αἰτία καταλείπεται οὔτε θεῷ ἐγκαλέσαι οὔτε πρὸς ἄνθρωπον στῆναι στάσιν πολεμίου.

members.text:
how come it to pass that the Gods having ordered all other things
so well and so lovingly, should be overseen in this one only thing, that
whereas then hath been some very good men that have made many covenants
as it were with God and by many holy actions and outward services
contracted a kind of familiarity with Him; that these men when once they
are dead, should never be restored to life, but be extinct for ever. But
this thou mayest be sure of, that this (if it be so indeed) would
never have been so ordered by the Gods, had it been fit otherwise. For
certainly it was possible, had it been more just so and had it been
according to nature, the nature of the universe would easily have borne
it. But now because it is not so, (if so be that it be not so indeed) be
therefore confident that it was not fit it should be so for thou seest
thyself, that now seeking after this matter, how freely thou doest argue
and contest with God. But were not the Gods both just and good in the
highest degree, thou durst not thus reason with them. Now if just and
good, it could not be that in the creation of the world, they should
either unjustly or unreasonably oversee anything.
members.english: How can it be that the gods, who arranged all things well and with love for humankind, overlooked this one thing only: that some people, and very good ones, who have made a great many contracts, so to speak, with the divine, and who through holy deeds and sacred rites have come to be on the closest terms with the divine, once they have died, never come to be again, but are completely extinguished? But if this really is so, be sure that if it ought to have been otherwise, they would have made it otherwise. For if it were just, it would also be possible, and if it were in accord with nature, nature would have brought it about. So from its not being so, if indeed it is not so, be assured that it ought not to have come about so. For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god. And we would not be reasoning with the gods like this unless they are best and most just. And if that is so, they would not have let anything in the order of things be neglected unjustly and against reason.
members.greek: Πῶς ποτε πάντα καλῶς καὶ φιλανθρώπως διατάξαντες οἱ θεοὶ τοῦτο μόνον παρεῖδον, τὸ ἐνίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ πάνυ χρηστοὺς καὶ πλεῖστα πρὸς τὸ θεῖον ὥσπερ συμβόλαια θεμένους καὶ ἐπὶ πλεῖστον δι’ ἔργων ὁσίων καὶ ἱερουργιῶν συνήθεις τῷ θείῳ γενομένους, ἐπειδὰν ἅπαξ ἀποθάνωσι, μηκέτι αὖθις γίνεσθαι, ἀλλ’ εἰς τὸ παντελὲς ἀπεσβηκέναι; τοῦτο δὲ εἴπερ ἄρα καὶ οὕτως ἔχει, εὖ ἴσθι ὅτι, εἰ ὡς ἑτέρως ἔχειν ἔδει, ἐποίησαν ἄν· εἰ γὰρ δίκαιον ἦν, ἦν ἃν καὶ δυνατόν, καὶ εἰ κατὰ φύσιν, ἤνεγκεν ἂν αὐτὸ ἡ φύσις. ἐκ δὴ τοῦ μὴ οὕτως ἔχειν, εἴπερ οὐχ οὕτως ἔχει, πιστούσθω σοι τὸ μὴ δεῆσαι οὕτως γίνεσθαι· ὁρᾷς γὰρ καὶ αὐτὸς ὅτι τοῦτο παραζητῶν δικαιολογῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν· οὐκ ἂν δ’ οὕτως διελεγόμεθα τοῖς θεοῖς, εἰ μὴ ἄριστοι καὶ δικαιότατοί εἰσιν. εἰ δὲ τοῦτο, οὐκ ἄν τι περιεῖδον ἀδίκως καὶ ἀλόγως ἠμελημένον τῶν ἐν τῇ διακοσμήσει.

members.text:
If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do
it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to
do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but
if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end
is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.
members.english: If it is up to you, why do you do it? If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame? The atoms or the gods? Both are madness. No one is to be blamed. For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you? For nothing is to be done without an aim.
members.greek: Εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ ·σοί, τί αὐτὸ ποιεῖς; εἰ δὲ ἐπ’ ἄλλῳ, τίνι μέμφῃ; ταῖς ἀτόμοις ἢ τοῖς θεοῖς; ἀμφότερα μανιώδη. Οὐδενὶ μεμπτέον. εἰ μὲν γὰρ δύνασαι, διόρθωσον· εἰ δὲ τοῦτο μὴ δύνασαι, τό γε πρᾶγμα αὐτό· εἰ δὲ μηδὲ τοῦτο, πρὸς τί ἔτι σοι φέρει τὸ μέμψασθαι; εἰκῇ γὰρ οὐδὲν ποιητέον.

members.text:
Out of several poets and comics. 'It will but little avail thee,
to turn thine anger and indignation upon the things themselves that have
fallen across unto thee. For as for them, they are not sensible of it,
&c. Thou shalt but make thyself a laughing-stock; both unto the Gods and
men, &c. Our life is reaped like a ripe ear of corn; one is yet
standing and another is down, &c. But if so be that I and my children be
neglected by the gods, there is some reason even for that, &c. As long
as right and equity is of my side, &c. Not to lament with them, not to
tremble, &c.'
members.english:
“For one must not be angry with things, for they do not care at all.”

“May you give joys to the immortal gods and to us.”

“To reap life like a ripe ear of grain, and for one to be and another not.”

“But if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods, this too has its reason.”

“For what is right is with me, and what is just.”

No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.
members.greek:
Τοῖς πράγμασιν γὰρ οὐχὶ θυμοῦσθαι χρεών· μέλει γὰρ αὐτοῖς οὐδέν.

Ἀθανάτοις τε θεοῖς καὶ ἡμῖν χάρματα δοίης.

Βίον θερίζειν ὥστε κάρπιμον στάχυν καὶ τὸν μὲν εἶναι, τὸν δὲ μή.

Εἰ δ’ ἠμελήθην ἐκ θεῶν καὶ παῖδ’ ἐμώ, ἔχει λόγον καὶ τοῦτο.

Τὸ γὰρ εὖ μετ’ ἐμοῦ καὶ τὸ δίκαιον.

Μὴ συνεπιθρηνεῖν, μὴ σφύζειν.

members.text:
Can the Gods, who are immortal, for the continuance of so many ages
bear without indignation with such and so many sinners, as have ever
been, yea not only so, but also take such care for them, that they want
nothing; and dust thou so grievously take on, as one that could bear
with them no longer; thou that art but for a moment of time? yea thou
that art one of those sinners thyself? A very ridiculous thing it is,
that any man should dispense with vice and wickedness in himself, which
is in his power to restrain; and should go about to suppress it in
others, which is altogether impossible.
members.english:
The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people of such a kind and in such numbers. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?

It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.
members.greek:
Οἱ θεοί, ἀθάνατοι ὄντες, οὐ δυσχεραίνουσιν ὅτι ἐν τοσούτῳ αἰῶνι δεήσει αὐτοὺς πάντως ἀεὶ τοιούτων ὄντων καὶ τοσούτων φαύλων ἀνέχεσθαι· προσέτι δὲ καὶ κήδονται αὐτῶν παντοίως. σὺ δέ, ὅσον οὐδέπω λήγειν μέλλων, ἀπαυδᾷς, καὶ ταῦτα εἶς ὢν τῶν φαύλων;

Γελοῖόν ἐστι τὴν μὲν ἰδίαν κακίαν μὴ φεύγειν, ὃ καὶ δυνατόν ἐστι, τὴν δὲ τῶν ἄλλων φεύγειν, ὅπερ ἀδύνατον.

members.text:
Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and
allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind. If they can do
nothing, why doest thou pray? If they can, why wouldst not thou rather
pray, that they will grant unto thee, that thou mayst neither fear, nor
lust after any of those worldly things which cause these distractions
and distempers of it? Why not rather, that thou mayst not at either
their absence or presence, be grieved and discontented: than either that
thou mayst obtain them, or that thou mayst avoid them? For certainly
it must needs be, that if the Gods can help us in anything, they may in
this kind also. But thou wilt say perchance, 'In those things the Gods
have given me my liberty: and it is in mine own power to do what I
will.' But if thou mayst use this liberty, rather to set thy mind at
true liberty, than wilfully with baseness and servility of mind to
affect those things, which either to compass or to avoid is not in thy
power, wert not thou better? And as for the Gods, who hath told thee,
that they may not help us up even in those things that they have put in
our own power? whether it be so or no, thou shalt soon perceive, if
thou wilt but try thyself and pray. One prayeth that he may compass his
desire, to lie with such or such a one, pray thou that thou mayst not
lust to lie with her. Another how he may be rid of such a one; pray thou
that thou mayst so patiently bear with him, as that thou have no such
need to be rid of him. Another, that he may not lose his child. Pray
thou that thou mayst not fear to lose him. To this end and purpose, let
all thy prayer be, and see what will be the event.
members.english: Either the gods can do nothing or they can. Now if they cannot, why do you pray? But if they can, why do you not rather pray that they grant you not to fear any of these things, not to desire any of them, not to be pained at any of them, rather than that any of them be absent or be present? For certainly, if they can work with people, they can work with them towards these things too. But perhaps you will say: “The gods have left these things up to me.” Then is it not better to use what is up to you in freedom than to let what is not up to you make a difference to you, in slavery and degradation? And who told you that the gods do not also lend a hand with the things that are up to us? Begin, at any rate, to pray about these, and you will see. This man prays: “How may I sleep with that woman?” You: “How may I not desire to sleep with that woman?” Another: “How may I be rid of that one?” You: “How may I not want to be rid of that one?” Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.
members.greek: Ἤτοι οὐδὲν δύνανται οἱ θεοὶ ἢ δύνανται. εἰ μὲν οὖν μὴ δύνανται, τί εὔχῃ; εἰ δὲ δύνανται, διὰ τί οὐχὶ μᾶλλον εὔχῃ. διδόναι αὐτοὺς τὸ μήτε φοβεῖσθαί τι τούτων μήτε ἐπιθυμεῖν τινος τούτων μήτε λυπεῖσθαι ἐπί τινι τούτων, μᾶλλον ἤπερ τὸ μὴ παρεῖναί τι τούτων ἢ τὸ παρεῖναι; πάντως γάρ, εἰ δύνανται συνεργεῖν ἀνθρώποις, καὶ εἰς ταῦτα δύνανται συνεργεῖν. ἀλλὰ ἴσως ἐρεῖς ὅτι· ἐπ’ ἐμοὶ αὐτὰ οἱ θεοὶ ἐποίησαν. εἶτα οὐ κρεῖσσον χρῆσθαι τοῖς ἐπὶ σοὶ μετ’ ἐλευθερίας ἣ διαφέρεσθαι πρὸς τὰ μὴ ἐπὶ σοὶ μετὰ δουλείας καὶ ταπεινότητος; τίς δέ σοι εἶπεν ὅτι οὐχὶ καὶ εἰς τὰ ἐφ̓ ἡμῖν οἱ θεοὶ συλλαμβάνουσιν; ἄρξαι γοῦν περὶ τούτων εὔχεσθαι καὶ ὄψει. οὗτος εὔχεται· πῶς κοιμηθῶ μετ’ ἐκείνης· σύ· πῶς μὴ ἐπιθυμήσω τοῦ κοιμηθῆναι μετ’ ἐκείνης. ἄλλος· πῶς στερηθῶ ἐκείνου· σύ· πῶς μὴ χρῄζω τοῦ στερηθῆναι. ἄλλος· πῶς μὴ ἀποβάλω τὸ τεκνίον· σύ· πῶς μὴ φοβηθῶ ἀποβαλεῖν. ὅλως ὧδε ἐπίστρεψον τὰς εὐχὰς καὶ θεώρει τί γίνεται.

members.text:
Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and
dissembling never be at an end? What then is it, that troubleth thee?
Doth any new thing happen unto thee? What doest thou so wonder at? At
the cause, or the matter? Behold either by itself, is either of that
weight and moment indeed? And besides these, there is not anything. But
thy duty towards the Gods also, it is time thou shouldst acquit thyself
of it with more goodness and simplicity.
members.english: Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping. Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing. But towards the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.
members.greek: Ἅλις τοῦ ἀθλίου βίου καὶ γογγυσμοῦ καὶ πιθηκισμοῦ.—τί ταράσσῃ; τί τούτων καινόν; τί σε ἐξίστησι; τὸ αἴτιον; ἴδε αὐτό. ἀλλ’ ἡ ὕλη; ἴδε αὐτήν. ἔξω δὲ τούτων οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς θεοὺς ἤδη ποτὲ ἁπλούστερος καὶ χρηστότερος γενοῦ.

members.text:
Whatsoever doth happen in the ordinary course and consequence of
natural events, neither the Gods, (for it is not possible, that they
either wittingly or unwittingly should do anything amiss) nor men, (for
it is through ignorance, and therefore against their wills that they do
anything amiss) must be accused. None then must be accused.
members.english:
What follows in order on nature.

The gods are not to be blamed, for they go wrong in nothing, willingly or unwillingly. Nor are people, for they go wrong in nothing except unwillingly. So no one is to be blamed.
members.greek: τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ φύσει. Μήτε θεοῖς μεμπτέον· οὐδὲν γὰρ ἑκόντες ἢ ἄκοντες ἁμαρτάνουσι· μήτε ἀνθρώποις· οὐδὲν γὰρ οὐχὶ ἄκοντες. ὥστε οὐδενὶ μεμπτέον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 6.36 is 6.41, 12.4 is 12.5, 8.15 is 8.17, 7.25 is 7.38 to 7.43, 7.41 is 7.70 to 7.71, 9.35 is 9.37a and 12.9 is 12.11b to 12.12; 9.40 is the same.

Changes the title from “What is not in my power” to “Blaming no one for what is not up to me”. Five of the eight passages are about blame or anger at gods, people or things; what is up to me is the ground they give for it.

Reads the “prying” of 12.4 as a failure, as the Greek word marks it (going beyond what is proper). In 12.4 the same sentence is also a step of an argument that the gods are just; the article does not quote that step and mentions it only in its notes.

Takes “make a difference” as the translators render the idiom shared by 6.36 (διαφορά) and 9.40 (διαφέρεσθαι πρός). Their notes give another reading, “quarrels over” or “be at odds with”; on either reading the two passages use the same idiom, so claim 1 holds.

Reads 8.15’s “No one is to be blamed” as also “nothing”, as the Greek allows (Οὐδενί), so that 8.15 and 7.25 meet on “not things” in claim 2. 8.15’s two cases, the atoms or the gods, are kept apart under “If I doubt it”.

Reads 7.41’s “do you give up” as giving up on bad people, from the gods’ patience with them in the sentence before. The Greek verb (ἀπαυδᾷς) has no object and could mean giving up from weariness in general.

Every line of 7.25 but the last is a quoted verse, which the translators, from memory, take to be from lost plays; the two used here, “one must not be angry with things” and “if I and my two children have been neglected by the gods”, are verses Marcus copied out and keeps as his own maxims. Leaves out three of the other lines: the wish for joys to the gods, the line on reaping life like grain, and “what is right is with me”; none says anything about blame. Also leaves out 12.9’s fragment “What follows in order on nature.” and most of the question that opens 12.4; claim 3 quotes only its words on the very good being overlooked.
articles.limit: Articles 3, 4, 7 and 8 already say that I do not complain of what happens, that the reason governing the world has no cause to do evil, that my judgment is up to me, and that only my judgment makes a thing harm me; Article 19 says that I teach or bear with whoever wrongs me and that the gods too are kind to such people (close to claim 4 and to the said-once item on giving up on bad people), Article 28 that I leave another person’s wrong with them, and Article 4 already quotes Seneca’s Ep. 95.50. What this article adds concerns blame: since I count only what is up to me as good or bad, I have no one to blame, the gods, people or things, and my own wrongdoing is the one thing I can stop. Its weak point is claim 3: the gods’ justice is asserted, not argued, apart from 12.4’s step that we would not argue a case of justice with gods who were not just.

statement.t: I judge only what is up to me to be good or bad, and I blame no one, neither the gods nor people.

statement.kind: A ground and the conduct that follows from it
statement.form: Replaces the double negative with a positive statement of what externals cannot settle, my judgement of good and bad. The words good or bad are from 6.36. 9.40 supports the same point only as not letting what is not up to me make a difference. The refusal of blame is flat in 8.15 and 12.9 and conditional on right judgement in 6.36. The first sentence of c1 now overlaps the opening, though c1 still adds freedom, slavery and the many wrongs.

claims.t: If a wrong is up to me, I ask why I do it. It is ridiculous to flee the vice of others, which is impossible, and not to flee my own vice, which is possible. If a wrong is up to another, I set that person right if I can. If I cannot, I set right at least the thing itself. If I can do neither, blaming serves no end.
claims.shared: Text unchanged. The joint anchor now covers only what both passages say, that my own wrong is within my power. The ridicule and the fleeing are from 7.41 alone, and the order of setting right is from 8.15 alone.

support.quote: If it is up to you, why do you do it?
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to me, I have no reason to go on doing it.
gives: If a wrong is up to me, I ask why I do it
my own vice, which is possible

support.quote: It is ridiculous not to flee one’s own vice, which is in fact possible, but to flee that of others, which is impossible.
support.follows: I can get clear of my own vice and cannot get clear of other people’s, so it is ridiculous to try the second and not the first.
gives: It is ridiculous to flee the vice of others, which is impossible
not to flee
my own vice, which is possible

support.quote: If it is up to another, whom or what do you blame?
support.follows: If what is going wrong is up to someone else, there is no one and nothing for me to blame.
gives: If a wrong is up to another

support.quote: For if you can, set the other right. If you cannot do that, set right at least the thing itself. And if not even that, what end does blaming still serve for you?
support.follows: I should correct the other person if I can, or else the thing itself; if I can do neither, blaming serves no end.
gives: I set that person right if I can
I set right at least the thing itself
blaming serves no end

claims.t: When I set up as good or bad something that is not mine to choose, I make a case against the gods. Then I blame the gods when I meet such a bad thing or miss such a good one, and I hate the people who are the cause. When I pry into what the gods have allowed, I am arguing a case of justice with god. Enough of the grumbling. Towards the gods too, now at last, I become simpler and better.
claims.shared: Describes the lapse, with “Then” tying the blame to the misjudgement so it is not heard as a vow. “What the gods have allowed” gives the prying an object. In 12.4 that object is specifically the fate of good people after death. Hatred of people is from 6.36 alone. 9.35 stands beside the lapse without being called its cure, and “simpler” is left undefined.

support.quote: Whatever you set up for yourself as good or bad among the things that are not yours to choose, it must follow that when you meet with such a bad thing or miss such a good one, you blame the gods, and hate people too: those who are the cause
support.follows: Whoever counts things outside their choice as good or bad will blame the gods and hate people when they meet or miss those things.
gives: I set up as good or bad something that is not mine to choose
I make a case against the gods
I blame the gods when I meet such a bad thing or miss such a good one
I hate the people who are the cause

support.quote: For you see for yourself that in prying into this you are arguing a case of justice with god.
support.follows: Prying into why the good do not come to be again after death is arguing a case of justice with god.
gives: I make a case against the gods
When I pry into what the gods have allowed
I am arguing a case of justice with god

support.quote: Enough of the wretched life, the grumbling, the aping.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself to have done with a wretched life of grumbling and putting on an act.
gives: Enough of the grumbling

support.quote: But towards the gods too, now at last, become simpler and better.
support.follows: It is time to become simpler and better towards the gods as well.
gives: Towards the gods too, now at last, I become simpler and better

single.quote: Another: “How may I not lose my little child?” You: “How may I not be afraid of losing it?” In short, turn your prayers round like this and watch what happens.
single.label: Turning prayers round
single.t: I turn my prayers round and watch what happens. Another prays, “How may I not lose my little child?” I pray, “How may I not be afraid of losing it?”
single.why: Single source, 9.40. Restores the paired prayers and “watch what happens”. Prayer is redirected, not abolished, and no result is promised.
single.follows: I should pray not to be afraid of losing my child, instead of praying not to lose it, and see what happens.

single.quote: Why are you troubled? What in this is new? What puts you beside yourself? The cause? Look at it. Or the material? Look at it. Beyond these there is nothing.
single.label: Looking at what troubles me
single.t: When I am troubled, I ask what is new in the thing that troubles me. I look at the cause, and I look at the material. Beyond these there is nothing.
single.why: Single source, 9.35. Keeps the source’s terms cause and material and its closing sentence.
single.follows: When something troubles me, I should look at its cause and at what it is made of, since there is nothing more to it.

single.quote: No joining in the wailing, no racing pulse.
single.label: Not joining in
single.t: I do not join in the wailing, and I do not let my pulse race.
single.why: Single source, 7.25. This is the only line of that passage in Marcus’s own voice. The added “When others lament” is dropped as unneeded.
single.follows: I should not join others in lamenting, and I should not let myself grow agitated.

single.quote: The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed that through so long a time they will certainly always have to put up with bad people of such a kind and in such numbers. More than that, they care for them in every kind of way. But you, who are about to come to an end any moment now, do you give up, and that when you are one of the bad ones?
single.label: Giving up on bad people
single.t: When I am ready to give up on bad people, I remember the gods. The gods, who are immortal, are not vexed at having to put up with so many bad people for so long, and the gods care for those people in every kind of way. I am about to come to an end, and I am one of the bad ones myself.
single.why: Single source, 7.41. Kept as a rebuke to giving up, not turned into a vow. Blame is not mentioned in the source.
single.follows: If the immortal gods bear with bad people and care for them, I, who will soon die and am bad myself, have no ground to give up on them.

single.quote: The atoms or the gods? Both are madness.
single.label: Either way
single.t: Blaming the atoms is madness, and blaming the gods is madness.
single.why: Single source, 8.15. Names blaming as the madness and leaves the choice between atoms and gods undecided, as in the source.
single.follows: Whether things come about by the atoms or by the gods, blaming either is madness.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 6.36 is 6.41, 12.4 is 12.5, 8.15 is 8.17, 7.25 is 7.38 to 7.43, 7.41 is 7.70 to 7.71, 9.35 is 9.37a and 12.9 is 12.11b to 12.12; 9.40 is the same.

Replaces the double negative with a positive statement of what externals cannot settle, my judgement of good and bad. The words good or bad are from 6.36. 9.40 supports the same point only as not letting what is not up to me make a difference. The refusal of blame is flat in 8.15 and 12.9 and conditional on right judgement in 6.36. The first sentence of c1 now overlaps the opening, though c1 still adds freedom, slavery and the many wrongs.
marcus_revision.limit: The passages agree in refusing blame, but on different grounds: misplaced valuation in 6.36, aimlessness in 8.15, divine inerrancy and unwilling human error in 12.9, the justice presupposed by questioning in 12.4. The article does not merge these into one argument. The opening’s words good or bad come from 6.36, and 9.40 supports them only as the difference that what is not up to me should not make. The article does not settle whether the gods govern or can act, nor whether the dead are extinguished. The lines from 7.25 are quoted verses, and “simpler” in 9.35 is left undefined. In c5 the prying of 12.4 is stated generally, though the passage concerns good people after death. 7.41 does not mention blame. Not blaming does not deny that people do wrong, and it does not replace setting things right. Only the opening was reviewed here, and its repair leaves the first sentence of c1 overlapping it.

articles.title: Happiness and unhappiness are my own doing

statement.t: My happiness is decided in my own soul and I need nothing besides; if I do not want what happens, I desert nature and the law that send it.

parts.words: My happiness is decided in my own soul
I need nothing besides
if I do not want what happens
I desert nature and the law that send it

statement.kind: A ground, what follows from it, and the failure named
statement.form: Claim 1 says where happiness and unhappiness are decided; “is decided in my own soul” is the editor’s summary of 7.14’s “ruling part” and 2.5’s “their own soul”. Claim 2 draws what follows for me: what I have in myself is enough (9.24, 4.24, 7.14). Claim 3 names the failure: whoever does not want what happens deserts what sends it, the common nature in 4.24 and the law in 10.25. No passage joins the first two claims to the third; setting them in one statement is the editor’s.

groups.name: Why
groups.asks: The ground for the statement.

groups.name: In action
groups.asks: What follows for what I do.

groups.name: Practice
groups.asks: An exercise I can repeat.

groups.name: When it breaks
groups.asks: What failing looks like, and the way back.

groups.name: If I doubt it
groups.asks: What still holds if the statement is not true.
groups.empty: No passage in this section considers what would still hold if my happiness were not decided in my own soul, so Marcus gives nothing under this label.

The retreat within
The work that belongs to me
near.chapter: The whole and my place in it

near.title: Whether anything is better than virtue

outside.section: What happens to me

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, two of his passages back the first claim and one backs the second. The article gains a sentence that the editor reads as joining its two halves (being under orders does not make me unhappy; acting against my will does), the spirit within, a daily review, a way back, and an answer to an objection. He limits the second claim: the wise man is content with himself for a happy life, not for staying alive.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a sentence that the editor reads as joining its two halves: being under orders does not make me unhappy; acting against my will does. “I need nothing besides” holds for a happy life, not for staying alive.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the mind is stronger than any fortune, and itself leads its own things in either direction, and is for itself the cause of a happy life and of a wretched one
piece.follows: The mind is stronger than any fortune, and it is itself the cause of a happy life or a wretched one.
piece.context: Letter 98, on not leaning on Fortune’s gifts: Fortune hands us only the material for goods and evils. In the quote, “its own things” are the mind’s own, led by it to good or to evil.
gives: Whether I am happy or unhappy
is decided in my own soul

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: the happy life rests on this one thing, that reason in us should be perfect
piece.follows: The happy life rests on one thing only: that reason in us should be perfect.
piece.context: Opening of Letter 92, on the happy life: the soul has a primary part whose rational side commands the rest. “This” is perfect reason in that commanding part.
gives: Happiness is a good ruling part

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: he holds the heights, and leans on no one at all except himself; for a man who is held up by some support can fall
piece.follows: The happy man leans on no one and nothing but himself, because whoever is held up by some support can fall.
piece.context: Letter 92, on the happy life: Seneca calls happy the man whom nothing makes smaller. “He” is that man; a “support” is anything outside himself that he leans on.
gives: I need nothing besides

items.label: why
items.t: Being under orders does not make me unhappy; doing a thing unwillingly does. If I take my orders willingly, I escape the bitterest part of slavery, which is doing what I do not want to do.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section joins the article’s two halves: happiness in my own soul, and the runaway who does not want what happens. Seneca ties unhappiness to unwillingness, with the same picture of orders and slavery; he does not speak here of where happiness is decided. The editor reads his sentence as joining the two halves: what makes me unhappy is not the order but my unwillingness. His slave does not run; he stays and takes the order willingly.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: It is not the man who does something under orders who is wretched, but the man who does it unwillingly.
support.follows: Acting under orders does not make a person wretched; acting unwillingly does.
support.context: Letter 61, on meeting death gladly. Seneca explains why a necessity stops being one if I want it; the orders are those of circumstances, not of a human master.
gives: Being under orders does not make me unhappy; doing a thing unwillingly does

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The man who takes orders willingly escapes the bitterest part of slavery: doing what he does not want to do
support.follows: Whoever takes his orders willingly escapes the bitterest part of slavery, which is doing what one does not want to do.
support.context: Letter 61: Seneca, now old, says that dying well means dying gladly and that one should do nothing unwillingly. The “orders” are what necessity demands, death above all.
gives: If I take my orders willingly, I escape the bitterest part of slavery, which is doing what I do not want to do

items.label: why
items.t: A sacred spirit sits within me. It is the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are mine, and as I treat it, so it treats me.
items.why: 7.14 calls happiness “a good spirit” and says nothing more about it; the claim keeps its other name, a good ruling part. Seneca says what the spirit within does: it observes and guards the bad and the good that are mine, and it treats me as I treat it. He does not call it my happiness.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn.
support.follows: A sacred spirit sits within us, observes and guards the bad and the good that are ours, and treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41: Lucilius need not pray for a sound mind, because God is near him, with him and within him. The “sacred spirit” is that god within each person.
gives: A sacred spirit sits within me
It is the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are mine
as I treat it, so it treats me

items.label: practice
items.t: I watch myself and review my day. I consult myself: am I ever sad, does any hope make my mind anxious with expectation of the future, does my mind keep its even course day and night, pleased with itself?
items.why: 2.5 says that I am bound to be unhappy if I do not keep track of my own soul, and gives no way of doing it. Seneca gives two: a review of my day, and questions to put to myself. In Letter 83 he says that not looking back at one’s life makes people very bad, where Marcus says unhappy.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I will watch myself at once and, what is most useful, I will review my day. What makes us very bad is that no one looks back at his own life
support.follows: Seneca will watch himself and review his day, because not looking back at one’s own life is what makes people very bad.
support.context: Letter 83: Lucilius has asked for an account of each of Seneca’s days. Seneca agrees, having said that God is witness of our souls. “Us” is people in general.
gives: I watch myself and review my day

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Now consult yourself: if you are never sad, if no hope makes your mind anxious with expectation of the future, if by day and by night the course of your mind, lifted up and pleased with itself, is even and level, you have reached the height of human good.
support.follows: If I am never sad, if no hope makes my mind anxious about the future, and my mind keeps an even course, pleased with itself, I have reached the height of human good.
support.context: Letter 59, on joy: Seneca shows Lucilius how to tell that he is not yet wise, since the wise man is full of joy, cheerful and peaceful. “Yourself” is Lucilius, testing his own mind.
gives: I consult myself: am I ever sad, does any hope make my mind anxious with expectation of the future, does my mind keep its even course day and night, pleased with itself

items.label: breaks
items.t: When I stray from nature I am forced to desire and to fear, and to be a slave to the things of chance. I can return to the road and be restored to my original condition.
items.why: Marcus names the exile and the runaway and, in this section, gives no return; 9.24 only says “enough”. Seneca says the return is open. His order also differs: for Marcus the fear is itself the flight from the master; for Seneca the straying comes first and brings the fear, and with it another master, chance.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: one who strays from her must desire and fear and be a slave to the things of chance
support.follows: Whoever strays from nature must desire and fear and be a slave to the things of chance.
support.context: Letter 98, on Fortune: after naming men who scorned riches and bore pain, Seneca asks why we lose heart. By “her” Seneca means nature, which we are to follow; “things of chance” are Fortune’s gifts.
gives: When I stray from nature I am forced to desire and to fear, and to be a slave to the things of chance

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We may return to the road, we may be restored to our original condition
support.follows: We can go back to the road and be restored to our original condition.
support.context: Letter 98: Seneca has just said that straying from nature brings desire, fear and slavery to chance. The “road” is following nature; “we” are he and Lucilius.
gives: I can return to the road and be restored to my original condition

items.label: doubt
items.t: If what I myself think made me happy, a man who is rich to his shame would be happy as soon as he called himself so. What matters is not what I say but what I think, and not on one day but constantly; and only the wise are pleased with what is their own.
items.why: No passage of Marcus in this section meets an objection. Seneca meets the nearest one: cannot anyone then decide that he is happy? He raises it against a poet’s line, that a man is unhappy if he thinks himself so, and the objection keeps the poet’s terms: happiness by what one thinks oneself. Placing it beside this article’s statement, which says my happiness is decided in my own soul, is the editor’s step; Seneca does not speak of the soul here. This is an objection answered, not the case in which the statement is false; Seneca does not consider that case here. His answer is that what counts is what I think constantly, and that only the wise are pleased with what is theirs.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If that man who is rich to his shame calls himself happy, and that one who is master of many but slave of more, will he become happy by what he himself thinks?
support.follows: Seneca puts the objection: if a man rich to his shame, or one who is master of many but slave of more, calls himself happy, does his own opinion make him so?
support.context: End of Letter 9, on the wise man content with himself. Seneca has quoted a poet’s line, that a man is unhappy if he thinks himself so, and lets Lucilius object to it.
gives: If what I myself think made me happy
a man who is rich to his shame would be happy as soon as he called himself so

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What matters is not what he says but what he thinks, and not what he thinks on one day but what he thinks constantly.
support.follows: What counts is what a person thinks, not what he says, and what he thinks constantly, not on one day.
support.context: End of Letter 9, on the wise man content with himself. Seneca answers the objection that a man rich to his shame could make himself happy merely by calling himself happy.
gives: What matters is not what I say but what I think, and not on one day but constantly

support.author: seneca
support.quote: what is his own pleases no one but the wise man; all folly suffers from disgust with itself.
support.follows: Only the wise man is pleased with what is his; all folly suffers from disgust with itself.
support.context: End of Letter 9: Seneca tells Lucilius not to fear that happiness by one’s own judgment will come to someone unworthy. “His own” is what the wise man has and is.
gives: only the wise are pleased with what is their own

items.t: Seneca agrees that the wise man is content with himself, and says how far that reaches: for living happily, not for living, since for living he has use for many things (Ep. 9.13). He adds Chrysippus’s distinction: the wise man has use for hands and eyes and many things for daily use, and yet is in want of nothing (Ep. 9.14). And the wise man still wants friends, though he would live happily without them (Ep. 9.15). Marcus’s beggar is whoever is “in need of another” for what is useful for life; Seneca’s wise man has use for many things and is in want of none. This limits the claim without contradicting it, provided two readings hold, both the editor’s: that 4.24’s “useful for life” means useful for living well, not for staying alive, and that “I do not need you” (7.14), said just after Marcus defines happiness, is about happiness. Seneca says all this of the wise man, and tells Lucilius that he is not yet one (Ep. 59.14); the clause on the claim says “I”, as Marcus’s claims do. Seneca also warns against reading the saying so that the wise man is pushed back on every side and forced inside his own skin.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The wise man is content with himself for living happily, not for living, since for living he has use for many things, and for living happily he has use only for a mind that is sound and held high and looks down on fortune.
support.follows: The wise man is content with himself for a happy life, not for staying alive; for happiness he has use only for a mind that is sound and held high.
support.context: Letter 9, on friendship: Seneca explains the saying “The wise man is content with himself”, which most people, he says, read so as to push the wise man back on every side.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: The wise man has use for hands and eyes and many things necessary for daily use; he is in want of nothing.
support.follows: The wise man has use for hands, eyes and much else for daily use, and yet he is in want of nothing.
support.context: Letter 9: Seneca reports Chrysippus’s distinction between having use for a thing and being in want of it. Want is a matter of necessity, and nothing is necessary to the wise man.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: So, although he is content with himself, he has use for friends. He desires to have as many of them as possible, not in order to live happily, for he will live happily even without friends.
support.follows: Though content with himself, the wise man wants as many friends as possible, but not in order to be happy; he is happy without them.
support.context: Letter 9, answering whether the wise man, content with himself, needs friendship. “He” is the wise man; the sentence draws on the distinction between having use for a thing and being in want of it.

amend.t: ; being under orders does not make me unhappy, but acting against my will does
; nothing, that is, for a happy life: to stay alive I have use for many things, and I still want friends

passages.title: On not depending on fortune’s gifts
passages.text: All the things that Fortune looks on become fruitful and pleasant on this condition: that the one who has them also has himself and is not in the power of his own things. For those people are wrong, Lucilius, who judge that Fortune gives us anything good or anything evil: she gives the material for goods and evils, and the beginnings of things that, in our keeping, will turn out for evil or for good. For the mind is stronger than any fortune, and itself leads its own things in either direction, and is for itself the cause of a happy life and of a wretched one.

passages.title: On reason and virtue sufficing for happiness
passages.text: If we agree on this, it follows that we also agree on that: the happy life rests on this one thing, that reason in us should be perfect. For it alone does not let the mind sink; it stands against fortune; in whatever state things are, it keeps [a word here is corrupt in the Latin]. And the only good is what is never broken off. That man, I say, is happy whom nothing makes smaller; he holds the heights, and leans on no one at all except himself; for a man who is held up by some support can fall. If it is otherwise, things that are not ours will begin to have great power in us. But who wants to owe his standing to fortune, or what sensible man admires himself for things that are not his own?

passages.title: On being ready and willing to die
passages.text: Take care that you never do anything unwillingly. Whatever is going to be necessary for one who resists is no necessity for one who wants it. This is what I mean. The man who takes orders willingly escapes the bitterest part of slavery: doing what he does not want to do. It is not the man who does something under orders who is wretched, but the man who does it unwillingly. So let us set our mind in order so that we want whatever the situation demands, and above all so that we think of our own end without sadness.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: This is what I say, Lucilius: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn. And indeed no one is a good man without god: or can anyone rise above fortune unless helped by him? It is he who gives advice that is grand and lofty. In each and every good man a god (which god is uncertain) lives.

passages.title: On a daily routine and drunkenness
passages.text: So I will do what you tell me, and I will gladly write to you what I do and in what order. I will watch myself at once and, what is most useful, I will review my day. What makes us very bad is that no one looks back at his own life. We think about what we are going to do, and that rarely; we do not think about what we have done; and yet a plan for the future comes from the past.

passages.title: On pleasure, true joy and self-flattery
passages.text: I shall now show you how you may understand that you are not a wise man. The wise man is full of joy, cheerful and peaceful, unshaken; he lives with the gods as an equal. Now consult yourself: if you are never sad, if no hope makes your mind anxious with expectation of the future, if by day and by night the course of your mind, lifted up and pleased with itself, is even and level, you have reached the height of human good. But if you go after all pleasures, from every side, know that you fall as far short of wisdom as you do of joy. This is what you long to reach, but you go wrong in hoping that you will get there among riches, among honours, that is, in looking for joy among anxieties: those things, which you go after as though they would give gladness and pleasure, are causes of pain.

passages.title: On not depending on fortune’s gifts
passages.text: Why have we given up? Why do we despair? Whatever it has been possible to do, it is possible to do. Only let us cleanse our mind and follow nature: one who strays from her must desire and fear and be a slave to the things of chance. We may return to the road, we may be restored to our original condition. Let us be restored, so that we can bear pains to the end, in whatever way they invade the body, and say to Fortune: “It is a man you have to deal with. Look for someone you can conquer.”

passages.title: On self-sufficiency and why the wise want friends
passages.text: “What then?” you say. “If that man who is rich to his shame calls himself happy, and that one who is master of many but slave of more, will he become happy by what he himself thinks?” What matters is not what he says but what he thinks, and not what he thinks on one day but what he thinks constantly. But there is no reason for you to fear that so great a thing may come to someone unworthy: what is his own pleases no one but the wise man; all folly suffers from disgust with itself. Farewell.

passages.title: On self-sufficiency and why the wise want friends
passages.text: “The wise man is content with himself.” Most people, my Lucilius, interpret this wrongly: they push the wise man back on every side and force him inside his own skin. But a distinction must be drawn: what does that saying promise, and how far? The wise man is content with himself for living happily, not for living, since for living he has use for many things, and for living happily he has use only for a mind that is sound and held high and looks down on fortune.

passages.title: On self-sufficiency and why the wise want friends
passages.text: I want to point out to you Chrysippus’s distinction as well. He says that the wise man is in want of nothing, and yet has use for many things: “on the other hand there is nothing the fool has use for, since he does not know how to use anything, but he is in want of everything.” The wise man has use for hands and eyes and many things necessary for daily use; he is in want of nothing. For to be in want is a matter of necessity; nothing is necessary to the wise man.

passages.title: On self-sufficiency and why the wise want friends
passages.text: So, although he is content with himself, he has use for friends. He desires to have as many of them as possible, not in order to live happily, for he will live happily even without friends. The highest good does not look for equipment from outside; it is cultivated at home, it comes wholly from itself. It begins to be subject to fortune if it looks for any part of itself outside the house.

claims.t: Whether I am happy or unhappy is decided in my own soul. Happiness is a good ruling part. If I do not keep track of what moves in my own soul, I am bound to be unhappy; not attending to what goes on in someone else’s soul hardly ever makes anyone unhappy.

members.text:
He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are
sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding.
He poor, that stands in need of another, and hath not in himself all
things needful for this life. He an aposteme of the world, who by being
discontented with those things that happen unto him in the world,
doth as it were apostatise, and separate himself from common nature's
rational administration. For the same nature it is that brings this
unto thee, whatsoever it be, that first brought thee into the world. He
raises sedition in the city, who by irrational actions withdraws his own
soul from that one and common soul of all rational creatures.
members.english: An exile is whoever exiles themselves from the reason that belongs to citizens. Blind is whoever shuts the eye of the mind. A beggar is whoever is in need of another and does not have from themselves everything that is useful for life. An abscess standing apart from the universe is whoever stands apart and separates themselves from the reason of the common nature by being displeased with what happens: for that nature brings this forth, the same one that brought you forth too. A piece split off from the city is whoever splits their own soul off from the soul of rational beings, which is one.
members.greek: φυγὰς ὁ φεύγων τὸν πολιτικὸν λόγον· τυφλὸς ὁ καταμύων τῷ νοερῷ ὄμματι· πτωχὸς ὁ ἐνδεὴς ἑτέρου καὶ μὴ πάντα ἔχων παρ’ ἑαυτοῦ τὰ εἰς τὸν βίον χρήσιμα· ἀπόστημα κόσμου ὁ ἀφιστάμενος καὶ χωρίζων ἑαυτὸν τοῦ τῆς κοινῆς φύσεως λόγου διὰ τοῦ δυσαρεστεῖν τοῖς συμβαίνουσιν· ἐκείνη γὰρ φέρει τοῦτο, ἣ καὶ σὲ ἤνεγκεν· ἀπόσχισμα πόλεως ὁ τὴν ἰδίαν ψυχὴν τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ἀποσχίζων, μιᾶς οὔσης.

members.text:
For not observing the state of another
man's soul, scarce was ever any man known to be unhappy. Tell whosoever
they be that intend not, and guide not by reason and discretion the
motions of their own souls, they must of necessity be unhappy.

members.text:
What is εὐδαιμονία, or happiness: but ἀγαθὸς δαίμων, or, a good
dæmon, or spirit? What then dost thou do here, O opinion? By the Gods
I adjure thee, that thou get thee gone, as thou earnest: for I need thee
not. Thou earnest indeed unto me according to thy ancient wonted manner.
It is that, that all men have ever been subject unto. That thou camest
therefore I am not angry with thee, only begone, now that I have found
thee what thou art.

members.greek: Εὐδαιμονία ἐστὶ δαίμων ἀγαθὸς ἢ ἡγεμονικὸν ἀγαθόν. τί οὖν ὧδε ποιεῖς, ὦ φαντασία; ἀπέρχου, τοὺς θεούς σοι, ὡς ἦλθες· οὐ γὰρ χρῄζω σου. ἐλήλυθας δὲ κατὰ τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἔθος. οὐκ ὀργίζομαί σοι· μόνον ἄπιθι.

members.text:
Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already
been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness
it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient
happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural
constitution.
members.english: You have endured countless things because you were not content with your ruling part doing the kind of things it is made to do. But enough.
members.greek: Ἀνέτλης μύρια διὰ τὸ μὴ ἀρκεῖσθαι τῷ σῷ ἡγεμονικῷ ποιοῦντι ταῦτα, οἷα κατεσκεύασται. ἀλλὰ ἅλις.

members.text:
He that runs away from his master is a fugitive. But the law is
every man's master. He therefore that forsakes the law, is a fugitive.
So is he, whosoever he be, that is either sorry, angry, or afraid, or
for anything that either hath been, is, or shall be by his appointment,
who is the Lord and Governor of the universe. For he truly and properly
is Νόμος, or the law, as the only νέμων, or distributor and dispenser
of all things that happen unto any one in his lifetime--Whatsoever then
is either sorry, angry, or afraid, is a fugitive.
members.english: Whoever flees from their master is a runaway slave. And the law is master, so whoever breaks the law is a runaway slave too. But whoever is distressed or angry or afraid also does not want one of the things appointed by the one who governs all things to have happened, or to be happening, or to be going to happen; and the one who governs all things is law, as the one who deals out all that falls to each. So whoever is afraid or distressed or angry is a runaway slave.
members.greek: Ὁ τὸν κύριον φεύγων δραπέτης· κύριος δὲ ὁ νόμος καὶ ὁ παρανομῶν οὖν δραπέτης. ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ λυπούμενος ἢ ὀργιζόμενος ἢ φοβούμενος οὐ βούλεταί τι γεγονέναι ἢ γίνεσθαι ἢ γενήσεσθαι τῶν ὑπὸ τοῦ τὰ πάντα διοικοῦντος τεταγμένων, ὅς ἐστι νόμος, νέμων ὅσα ἑκάστῳ ἐπιβάλλει. ὁ ἄρα φοβούμενος ἢ λυπούμενος ἢ ὀργιζόμενος δραπέτης.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 4.24 is 4.29 without its first sentence, 2.5 is 2.8, 7.14 is 7.17 and 9.24 is 9.26; 10.25 is the same.

Keeps “a good ruling part” and leaves “a good spirit” (7.14) to the quote. The Greek word for happiness contains the word for spirit, which English cannot show, and the “or” between the two names can also mean “that is”.

Turns two descriptions of a failure into a rule: 9.24’s “you were not content” becomes “I am content”, and 4.24’s beggar, who is “in need of another”, becomes “I need nothing besides”. Neither passage states the rule in the positive.

Reads the common nature that “brings this forth” (4.24) and the one who governs all things, who is law (10.25), as the sender of what happens; “the very thing that sends it” (claim 3), “nature and the law that send it” (the statement) and “I desert” are the editor’s words for what the two say. Keeps 4.24’s exile out of that claim, because the exile leaves the reason that belongs to citizens and is not said to be against what happens.

Leaves out two sentences of quoted passages. The last sentence of 4.24, on splitting one’s own soul off from the one soul of rational beings, is about my tie to other people, which Article 1 states. The step in 10.25 about whoever breaks the law is the middle of the argument and is not about what happens to me; the conclusion it leads to is quoted.
articles.limit: Article 1 already says that resenting what happens cuts me off from the whole, and Article 3 that I accept what happens and do not complain. Claim 3’s “Displeased with it, I stand apart and separate myself from the common nature” is close to Article 3’s item from 5.8, that each time I am displeased with what happens I cut through the connection of the whole, and its “brought me forth too” is close to Article 3’s first claim, that what happens comes from the same causes that produced me. Claim 2 is close to Article 2, whose fourth claim says that doing my work makes me content and whose item from 7.30 says that my mind then has all that belongs to it. Claim 2 is nearly the same as Article 18’s first claim, that a good state of soul and good actions are enough for me. The same words of Seneca’s Ep. 98.2 back that claim and this article’s claim 1. Claims 1 and 2 are also near Article 12, which says that I keep watch over what is within me rather than guess what others think, and that I am content with my present state. What this article adds is that my happiness or unhappiness is decided in my own soul, and that distress, anger and fear are a flight from a master. The section has two strands that no passage joins: 2.5, 7.14 and 9.24 are about my own soul, 10.25 is about the law of the whole, and only 4.24 touches both, so it is quoted in two claims. Claim 1 rests on two short passages, each of which gives one side of it.

135 characters. ‘The part of me that rules’ puts the ruling part of 7.14 and 9.24 in plain words. ‘Resent an event that has happened’ shows the fault is a refusal of the event itself, joining 4.24’s displeasure with 10.25’s not wanting a thing to have happened. Nature (4.24) and law (10.25) are named side by side in place of ‘order’ and are not merged. The opening narrows to past events. Fear and the future stay in c3.
marcus_revision.limit: Only 4.24 and 10.25 speak of a source that sends events, and in different terms: the common nature that also brought me forth, and law as the one who deals out what falls to each. The opening names them side by side and does not claim they are one thing. 2.5, 7.14 and 9.24 say nothing of fate, so the opening’s second sentence is not their doctrine. ‘Resent’ is our word for 4.24’s displeasure and for 10.25’s distress and anger. The opening narrows to events that have happened, while c3 keeps fear and the present and future from 10.25. The passages judge the refusal of an event. They say nothing about what to do next and prescribe no remedy, so the article neither forbids nor directs later action. ‘The part of me that rules’ is our plain wording for the ruling part, and no passage says what its proper work is. The beggar image must be read with 4.24’s civic reason and one soul of rational beings. ‘I look to myself for what I need’ in c2 is inferred from the beggar warning and the 9.24 reproach, not stated by either. No passage gives a method beyond dismissing an impression and saying ‘enough’, and what ‘enough’ refers to in 9.24 is our reading.

here as anywhere
I am ready to go

statement.kind: A fact faced, and how to live under it
statement.form: Claims 1 and 2 are the ground: death is near, and dying is nothing much. Claims 3 and 4 say how to live meanwhile: without pretence, and here as anywhere. The said-once items give a way to stay free, a daily exercise, two pictures of failing and the way back, and an argument by cases that holds whether or not death comes soon.
