seneca.becomes: With Seneca, four claims gain a second author: that death is near, that I am ready to go, that I do not pretend, and, in claim 4, both “wherever I am” and preferring death to living another way. He adds what can serve as a reason for the article, though he does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were meant or a pretence. He adds words to say each night, and he limits the readiness to die: I go out of life, I do not flee from it, and I keep clear of a longing to die.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains what can serve as a reason, though Seneca does not offer it as one: death will show whether my brave words were really meant or a pretence.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: For whom is it not near, ready as it is in every place and at every moment?
piece.follows: Everyone is near death, since death is ready everywhere and always.
piece.context: Letter 30: Seneca reports the old, failing Bassus on the fear of death. The words say that death, “it”, is near to everyone, in every place and at every moment.
gives: any moment now I will be dead

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I shall not tremble at the end, I am already prepared
piece.follows: Seneca will not tremble at the end, because he is already prepared for it.
piece.context: Letter 54: Seneca has just come through an attack of asthma, which doctors call rehearsing death. By “the end” he means his own death.
gives: I am ready to go

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Do you not know that to die is also one of the duties of life?
piece.follows: Dying is one of the duties of life.
piece.context: Letter 77, on taking one’s own life: someone says he wants to live on because of the duties he is carrying out honourably. Seneca answers that dying is a duty too.
gives: one of the acts of my life

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: wherever you leave off, if you leave off well, it is whole.
piece.follows: A life that ends well is whole, wherever it ends.
piece.context: Letter 77, on taking one’s own life: a journey stopped halfway is incomplete, Seneca says, but a life is not incomplete if it is honourable. In the words quoted, “it” is the life.
gives: whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Never will this flesh drive me to fear, never to a pretence unworthy of a good man
piece.follows: Seneca will never let his body drive him into fear or into a pretence unworthy of a good man.
piece.context: Letter 65: Seneca calls his body a chain on his freedom. “This flesh” is his body, and the pretence is one he might put on to protect it.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: I was not born for one corner; this whole world is my country.
piece.follows: Seneca was not born for one corner; the whole world is his country.
piece.context: Letter 28: Lucilius travels to shake off his gloom, and Seneca says it goes with him. This is the conviction Seneca tells Lucilius to live by instead.
gives: wherever I am

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: To die sooner or later does not matter; to die well or badly does matter. And to die well is to escape the danger of living badly.
piece.follows: What matters is dying well, and dying well is escaping the danger of living badly.
piece.context: Letter 70, on the proper time to end one’s life: the wise man lives as long as he ought; Seneca then blames a captive who chose to live on in a tyrant’s cage.
gives: I would rather die
than live another way

items.label: why
items.t: What I have shown so far, in word or deed, proves nothing. I will take death’s word for what progress I have made: on the day I die, with the tricks and the paint set aside, I will see whether my brave words were really meant or a pretence.
items.why: In this section Marcus sets the nearness of death beside a life without pretence and does not say why the two belong together. Seneca says that death will test whether his brave words against fortune were meant or a pretence; reading that as the reason is the editor’s link.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: What we have shown so far, whether in deeds or in words,” I say, “is nothing.
support.follows: Nothing we have shown so far, in words or deeds, proves anything.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the old Seneca speaks to himself as if the day that judges all his years had come. “What we have shown so far” is what he has said and done.
gives: What I have shown so far, in word or deed, proves nothing

support.author: seneca
support.quote: As to what progress I have made, I shall take death’s word.
support.follows: Seneca will take death’s word for how far he has progressed.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the progress is Seneca’s progress in philosophy, which, he says, his words so far cannot prove.
gives: I will take death’s word for what progress I have made

support.author: seneca
support.quote: with the tricks and the paint set aside, I shall pass judgment on myself: whether I say brave things or mean them, whether all the defiant words I have flung at fortune were a pretence and a piece of acting.
support.follows: On the day of his death, with the tricks and the paint set aside, Seneca will judge whether his brave words were meant or a pretence.
support.context: Letter 26, on old age and death: the day Seneca is making ready for is the day of his death, when he judges himself with the tricks and the paint set aside.
gives: on the day I die, with the tricks and the paint set aside, I will see whether my brave words were really meant or a pretence

items.label: practice
items.t: When I go to sleep, I say, glad and cheerful: “I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given.” If god adds a tomorrow, I receive it gladly.
items.why: 7.40 says to live through every day as the last, and gives no words for it. Seneca gives words to say when each day ends, and a way to take the next morning.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: as we go to sleep let us say, glad and cheerful: “I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given.”
support.follows: We should go to sleep glad and say that we have lived and have finished the course fortune gave us.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: Pacuvius held his own funeral feast every evening; Seneca turns the custom to a good use. The course is the course of one’s life.
gives: When I go to sleep, I say, glad and cheerful
I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If god adds a tomorrow, let us receive it gladly.
support.follows: If god adds a tomorrow, we should receive it gladly.
support.context: Letter 12, on old age: said right after the bedtime words “I have lived”. The added tomorrow is the next morning, taken as a gift.
gives: If god adds a tomorrow, I receive it gladly

items.t: Seneca agrees that leaving life can be right, but he limits it. The brave and wise man does not flee from life but goes out of it, and above all he avoids the lust for dying that seizes even the noble. Marcus says to leave if others will not allow a life by nature; Seneca adds that the leaving must not be a flight, nor come from a longing to die. The limit concerns going to death rather than waiting for it; it limits the claim and does not contradict it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: A brave and wise man ought not to flee from life but to go out of it.
support.follows: A brave and wise man does not flee from life; he goes out of it.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: having argued against fearing death, Seneca turns to how one should leave life: by going out of it, not by fleeing from it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: And above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying.
support.follows: Above all, a brave and wise man avoids the longing to die that has taken hold of many.
support.context: Letter 24, on despising death: “the lust for dying” is an unconsidered leaning towards dying, which Seneca says seizes the noble and the spiritless alike.

amend.t: ; death will show whether my brave words were really meant or a pretence
; but I do not flee from life, I go out of it, and I keep clear of a longing to die

passages.title: On an old man’s calm before death
passages.text: He used to say that this torment at least we feel by our own doing: that we tremble just when we believe death is near us. For whom is it not near, ready as it is in every place and at every moment? “But let us consider,” he said, “just when some cause of dying seems to be approaching, how much nearer the other causes are, the ones that are not feared.”

passages.title: On asthma and rehearsing death
passages.text: Be assured of this about me: I shall not tremble at the end, I am already prepared, I give no thought to a whole day. As for you, praise and imitate the man who is not sorry to die though he is glad to live: for what virtue is there in going out when you are being thrown out? Yet there is virtue here too: I am indeed being thrown out, but as though I were going out. And the reason the wise man is never thrown out is that to be thrown out is to be driven from a place you leave unwillingly: the wise man does nothing unwillingly; he escapes necessity, because he wants what it is going to force on him. Farewell.

passages.title: On a friend’s calm, chosen death
passages.text: “But I,” he says, “want to live, I who do many things honourably; it is against my will that I am leaving the duties of life, which I carry out faithfully and diligently.” What? Do you not know that to die is also one of the duties of life? You are leaving no duty; for no fixed number is laid down that you must complete.

passages.title: On a friend’s calm, chosen death
passages.text: A journey will be incomplete if you stop in the middle of it or short of the place you were making for. A life is not incomplete if it is honourable; wherever you leave off, if you leave off well, it is whole. But often one must leave off both bravely and for reasons that are not the greatest; for the reasons that hold us are not the greatest either.

passages.title: On causes and the worth of studying nature
passages.text: Never will this flesh drive me to fear, never to a pretence unworthy of a good man; never will I lie to do honour to this little body. When it seems right, I shall break up my partnership with it. And even now, while we are stuck together, we shall still not be partners with equal shares: the mind will take all the rights for itself. Contempt for one’s own body is sure freedom.

passages.title: On travel as no cure for the mind
passages.text: But once you have removed that ill, every change of place will become pleasant. Though you are driven out to the farthest lands, though you are set down in any corner of barbarian country, that dwelling, whatever it is like, will be hospitable to you. Who you are when you come matters more than where you come to, and for that reason we ought not to sign our mind over to any place. One must live with this conviction: “I was not born for one corner; this whole world is my country.”

passages.title: On choosing the right time to die
passages.text: To die sooner or later does not matter; to die well or badly does matter. And to die well is to escape the danger of living badly. So I consider most unmanly the saying of that man of Rhodes who, when he had been thrown into a cage by a tyrant and was being fed like some wild animal, said to someone who advised him to refuse food: “A human being should hope for everything while he lives.”

passages.title: On old age, and death as the test of progress
passages.text: “What we have shown so far, whether in deeds or in words,” I say, “is nothing. Those are slight and deceptive guarantees of what the mind is, and wrapped in much flattering ornament. As to what progress I have made, I shall take death’s word. So it is not timidly that I am readying myself for that day on which, with the tricks and the paint set aside, I shall pass judgment on myself: whether I say brave things or mean them, whether all the defiant words I have flung at fortune were a pretence and a piece of acting.

passages.title: On old age and living each day fully
passages.text: There was no day on which he did not carry himself out for burial. What he used to do from a bad conscience let us do from a good one, and as we go to sleep let us say, glad and cheerful: “I have lived, and I have finished the course that Fortune had given.” If god adds a tomorrow, let us receive it gladly. The happiest man, and the untroubled owner of himself, is the one who waits for tomorrow without anxiety; whoever has said “I have lived” rises every day to a gain.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: A brave and wise man ought not to flee from life but to go out of it. And above all, that passion too should be avoided which has taken hold of many: the lust for dying. For there is, my Lucilius, an unconsidered leaning of the mind towards dying too, as there is towards other things, and it often seizes men who are noble and of the keenest character, and often the spiritless and the downcast. The former scorn life; the latter find it a burden.

claims.t: My time is short: very soon I will leave all this behind, and any moment now I will be dead. What is left now is little.
claims.shared: All three say that the end is close, each in its own words: “very soon” (10.12), “any moment now” (4.30), “what is left now is little” (10.17).
claims.changed: 10.12 speaks of “such a person” and 4.30 speaks to “you”; the claim says “I”. 10.17 does not say what is left; the claim takes it to be time.

support.quote: having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people
support.follows: The person described has understood that very soon they must leave all this behind and go from among people.
gives: My time is short
very soon I will leave all this behind

support.quote: Any moment now you will be dead
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that he will be dead any moment now.
gives: My time is short
any moment now I will be dead

support.quote: What is left now is little.
support.follows: Marcus tells himself that little is left now.
gives: My time is short
What is left now is little

claims.t: I am ready to go, and I go as one who suffers nothing bad: dying is nothing much, one of the acts of my life. If my mind has been disciplined and cleansed, then whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished.
claims.shared: 5.23 and 6.2 both say that dying matters little: “Why do you think it anything much?” (5.23) and “Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting … whether dying” (6.2). 5.23 and 3.9 both describe someone ready to leave: “There is smoke, and I leave” (5.23), a life that fate does not overtake unfinished (3.9).
claims.changed: 5.23 says that one should go out of life as one who suffers nothing bad; the claim keeps this as the manner of going, and extends to any death the calm that 5.23 speaks of for one case: when others do not allow one to live rightly. 6.2 says only that dying should make no difference to doing what is fitting; “dying is nothing much” is wider. “I am ready to go” is said without 3.9’s condition; the claim’s last sentence keeps it.

support.quote: as one who is suffering nothing bad
support.follows: If one has to go out of life, one goes as someone who is suffering nothing bad.
gives: I go as one who suffers nothing bad

support.quote: There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much?
support.follows: When there is smoke, Marcus leaves, and he asks why one should think leaving any great matter.
gives: I am ready to go
dying is nothing much

support.quote: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting while shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act.
support.follows: Whether I am cold or warm, praised or spoken ill of, dying or doing something else, it should make no difference to doing what is fitting.
gives: dying is nothing much

support.quote: For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die.
support.follows: Dying is one of the acts of life.
gives: one of the acts of my life

support.quote: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus
support.follows: A mind that has been disciplined and cleansed has nothing festering in it.
gives: If my mind has been disciplined and cleansed

support.quote: Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the drama through.
support.follows: Whenever death comes to such a person, their life is not left unfinished, like a play an actor walks out of.
gives: I am ready to go
whenever death comes my life is not cut off unfinished

claims.t: I do not pretend or play a part. The finer thing is to leave this life without ever having tasted pretence, with nothing affected or hidden in me.
claims.shared: 9.2 and 7.40 both refuse pretence: “any pretence” (9.2) and “nor to play a part” (7.40). In the Greek the two are one word, the noun ὑπόκρισις and its verb.
claims.changed: 9.2 says that going without having tasted pretence would have been the finer course, one already missed; the claim calls it the finer thing without saying that I can still have it, and says “leave this life” for 9.2’s “go from among people”. 9.2 names lying, luxury and vanity beside pretence; the claim keeps pretence. From 3.9’s longer list the claim keeps “affected” and, as “hidden”, “lurking in a hole”.

support.quote: It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity.
support.follows: It would have been finer to leave life without ever having tasted lying, pretence, luxury or vanity.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part
The finer thing is to leave this life without ever having tasted pretence

support.quote: nor to play a part
support.follows: A perfect character does not play a part.
gives: I do not pretend or play a part

support.quote: nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole
support.follows: In a cleansed mind there is nothing slavish, affected or hidden, and nothing that has to answer for itself.
gives: with nothing affected or hidden in me

claims.t: The place makes no difference: I can live here the way I mean to live, according to nature, wherever I am. If the people around me do not allow it, I would rather die than live another way.
claims.shared: Both say that the life one means to live can be lived where one is: “so you can live here” (5.23), “it makes no difference whether there or here” (10.17). Both call it a life by nature, and both say what to do if others will not have it: “if they do not allow it, then go out of life” (5.23), “If they do not bear it, let them kill that person” (10.17).
claims.changed: 5.23 speaks of going out of life oneself, 10.17 of being killed by others; the claim says only “die”. In 10.17 “that way” is open: it may mean living as those people live. 10.17 says that the place makes no difference if a person lives in the universe as in a city; the claim does not repeat that condition.

support.quote: As you have in mind to live once you have gone out, so you can live here.
support.follows: The life one plans to live after leaving can be lived here already.
gives: The place makes no difference
I can live here the way I mean to live

support.quote: Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city.
support.follows: One can live as on a mountain anywhere, since the place makes no difference to someone whose city is the universe.
gives: The place makes no difference
I can live here the way I mean to live
wherever I am

support.quote: Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature.
support.follows: Marcus asks that people see and study a true human being living according to nature.
gives: according to nature

support.quote: And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living being.
support.follows: What Marcus wants is what fits the nature of a rational and social creature.
gives: according to nature

support.quote: But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well
support.follows: If others do not let one live that way, one should go out of life.
gives: If the people around me do not allow it
I would rather die

support.quote: If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.
support.follows: If people cannot bear a person who lives by nature, being killed by them is better than living that way.
gives: If the people around me do not allow it
I would rather die
than live another way

single.quote: But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.label: Free while I stay
single.t: As long as nothing leads me out of life, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.why: Only 5.23 says that staying is free. “Of that kind” in the quote refers to the smoke just before it: something that makes staying impossible. 10.23’s first case, living here and being used to it, is about staying too, but it does not say that staying is free.
single.follows: Until something like the smoke leads Marcus out, he stays, free, and no one stops him from doing what he wants.

single.quote: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb
single.label: Every day as the last
single.t: I live through every day as if it were my last, neither feverish nor numb.
single.why: Only 7.40 in this section gives an exercise for each day. Its last words, on playing no part, are quoted in claim 3.
single.follows: A perfect character lives each day as the last, without agitation and without numbness.

single.quote: But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around.
single.label: The next best course
single.t: If I have tasted lying and pretence, the next best thing is at least to be sick of them when I die. I do not stay sitting beside vice: a corrupt mind is a worse plague than any sickness of the air.
single.why: Only 9.2 gives a way back for someone who has already failed: to grow sick of these things before the end and to flee the plague.
single.follows: Having tasted these vices, the next best course is to die sick of them, since staying with vice is staying with a worse plague.

single.quote: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence.
single.label: The piglet at the sacrifice
single.t: When I am pained or displeased at anything, I am like the piglet at the sacrifice that kicks and squeals, and no less so when I lament alone on my bed, in silence.
single.why: Only 10.28 pictures what failing looks like. Its last sentence, on following what happens willingly, is left to Article 10.
single.follows: Whoever is pained or displeased at what happens is like a sacrificial piglet kicking, even when they lament in silence.

single.quote: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be cheerful.
single.label: Three cases
single.t: Either I go on living here, and I am used to it by now; or I go away from here, as I wanted; or I die, and my service is complete. There is no other case, so I can be cheerful.
single.why: Only 10.23 argues by cases, and it holds whether or not death comes soon, so it stands under “If I doubt it”. Its “completed your service” is close to 3.9, but it is kept whole here. Its “so” is Marcus’s own.
single.follows: Whether one lives on here, goes away or dies, there is no fourth case, and in each one can be cheerful.

members.text:
It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out
of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood,
dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride. But if this cannot be, yet it
is some comfort for a man joyfully to depart as weary, and out of love
with those; rather than to desire to live, and to continue long in those
wicked courses. Hath not yet experience taught thee to fly from the
plague? For a far greater plague is the corruption of the mind, than any
certain change and distemper of the common air can be. This is a plague
of creatures, as they are living creatures; but that of men as they are
men or reasonable.
members.english: It would have been the mark of a finer man to go from among people without having tasted lying, or any pretence or luxury or vanity. But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around. For the latter is a plague of living beings, insofar as they are living beings; the former is a plague of human beings, insofar as they are human beings.
members.greek: Χαριεστέρου μὲν ἦν ἀνδρός, ἄγευστον ψευδολογίας καὶ πάσης ὑποκρίσεως καὶ τρυφῆς καὶ τύφου γενόμενον ἐξ ἀνθρώπων ἀπελθεῖν. τὸ δ’ οὖν κορεσθέντα γε τούτων ἀποπνεῦσαι δεύτερος πλοῦς. ἢ προῄρησαι προσκαθῆσθαι τῇ κακίᾳ καὶ οὔπω σε οὐδὲ ἡ πεῖρα πείθει φεύγειν ἐκ τοῦ λοιμοῦ; λοιμὸς γὰρ διαφθορὰ διανοίας πολλῷ γε μᾶλλον ἤπερ ἡ τοῦ περικεχυμένου τούτου πνεύματος τοιάδε τις δυσκρασία καὶ τροπή· αὕτη μὲν γὰρ ζῴων λοιμός, καθὸ ζῷά ἐστιν, ἐκείνη δὲ ἀνθρώπων,καθὸ ἄνθρωποί εἰσιν.

members.text:
He hath got loose from the bonds of his body, and perceiving that
within a very little while he must of necessity bid the world farewell,
and leave all these things behind him, he wholly applied himself, as to
righteousness in all his actions, so to the common nature in all things
that should happen unto him. And contenting himself with these two
things, to do all things justly, and whatsoever God doth send to like
well of it: what others shall either say or think of him, or shall do
against him, he doth not so much as trouble his thoughts with it. To go
on straight, whither right and reason directed him, and by so doing to
follow God, was the only thing that he did mind, that, his only business
and occupation.
members.english: Such a person has stripped off the body and, having taken in that very soon they will have to leave all these things behind as they go from among people, has given their whole self over: to justice in what they do themselves, and to the nature of the whole in the other things, those that happen. What anyone will say or think about them, or do against them, they do not even let into their mind, being content with these two things: if they themselves act justly in what is being done now, and if they love what is being allotted to them now. They have let go of all busyness and all eager pursuits, and want nothing else than to keep a straight course right through, by way of the law, and to follow god, who keeps a straight course right through.
members.greek: ἐξεδύσατο τὸ σῶμα καὶ ἐννοήσας ὅτι ὅσον οὐδέπω πάντα ταῦτα καταλιπεῖν ἀπιόντα ἐξ ἀνθρώπων δεήσει, ἀνῆκεν ὅλον ἑαυτὸν δικαιοσύνῃ μὲν εἰς τὰ ὑφ’ ἑαυτοῦ ἐνεργούμενα, ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἄλλοις συμβαίνουσι τῇ τῶν ὅλων φύσει. τί δ’ ἐρεῖ τις ἢ ὑπολήψεται περὶ αὐτοῦ ἢ πράξει κατ’ αὐτοῦ, οὐδ’ εἰς νοῦν βάλλεται, δύο τούτοις ἀρκούμενος, εἰ αὐτὸς δικαιοπραγεῖ τὸ νῦν πρασσόμενον καὶ φιλεῖ τὸ νῦν ἀπονεμόμενον ἑαυτῷ· ἀσχολίας δὲ πάσας καὶ σπουδὰς ἀφῆκε καὶ οὐδὲν ἄλλο βούλεται ἢ εὐθεῖαν περαίνειν διὰ τοῦ νόμου καὶ εὐθεῖαν περαίνοντι ἕπεσθαι τῷ θεῷ.

members.text:
Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to
that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and
perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external
accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou
shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is,
to be just in all his actions.
members.english: Any moment now you will be dead, and you are not yet simple, nor untroubled, nor free of the suspicion that you could be harmed from outside, nor gracious towards everyone, nor someone who places wisdom only in acting justly.
members.greek: Ἤδη τεθνήξῃ καὶ οὔπω οὔτε ἁπλοῦς οὔτε ἀτάραχος οὔτε ἀνύποπτος τοῦ βλαβῆναι ἃν ἔξωθεν οὔτε ἵλεως πρὸς πάντας οὔτε τὸ φρονεῖν ἐν μόνῳ τῷ δικαιοπραγεῖν τιθέμενος.

members.text:
In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst
not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered:
nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no
malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed. The life of
such an one, death can never surprise as imperfect; as of an actor, that
should die before he had ended, or the play itself were at an end, a man
might speak.
members.english: In the mind of someone who has been disciplined and thoroughly cleansed you would find nothing full of pus, nor indeed anything stained, nor anything festering under the skin. Nor does fate overtake their life while it is unfinished, as one might say of a tragic actor who leaves before finishing and playing the drama through. And further, nothing slavish, nothing affected, nothing tied to anything, nothing split off, nothing liable to be called to account, nothing lurking in a hole.
members.greek: Οὐδὲν ἂν ἐν τῇ διανοίᾳ τοῦ κεκολασμένου καὶ ἐκκεκαθαρμένου πυῶδες οὐδὲ μὴν μεμολυσμένον οὐδὲ ὕπουλον εὕροις· οὐδὲ ἀσυντελῆ τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἡ πεπρωμένη καταλαμβάνει, ὡς ἄν τις εἴποι τὸν τραγῳδὸν πρὸ τοῦ τελέσαι καὶ διαδραματίσαι ἀπαλλάσσεσθαι· ἔτι δὲ οὐδὲν δοῦλον οὐδὲ κομψὸν οὐδὲ προσδεδεμένον οὐδὲ ἀπεσχισμένον οὐδὲ ὑπεύθυνον οὐδὲ ἐμφωλεῦον.

members.text:
Either thou dost Continue in this kind of life and that is it,
which so long thou hast been used unto and therefore tolerable: or thou
doest retire, or leave the world, and that of thine own accord, and then
thou hast thy mind: or thy life is cut off; and then mayst thou
rejoice that thou hast ended thy charge. One of these must needs be.
Be therefore of good comfort.
members.english: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be cheerful.
members.greek: Ἤτοι ἐνταῦθα ζῇς καὶ ἤδη εἴθικας· ἢ ἔξω ὑπάγεις καὶ τοῦτο ἤθελες· ἢ ἀποθνῄσκεις καὶ ἀπελειτούργησας. παρὰ δὲ ταῦτα οὐδέν. οὐκοῦν εὐθύμει.

members.text:
So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as
one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill. For whether here,
or there, if the whole world be but as one town, it matters not much for
the place. Let them behold and see a man, that is a man indeed, living
according to the true nature of man. If they cannot bear with me, let
them kill me. For better were it to die, than so to live as they would
have thee.
members.english: What is left now is little. Live as on a mountain. For it makes no difference whether there or here, if a person, wherever they are, lives in the universe as in a city. Let human beings see, let them study, a true human being living according to nature. If they do not bear it, let them kill that person. For that is better than to live that way.
members.greek: Ὀλίγον ἐστὶ τὸ ὑπολειπόμενον τοῦτο. ζῆσον ὡς ἐν ὄρει· οὐδὲν γὰρ διαφέρει ἐκεῖ ἢ ὧδε, ἐάν τις πανταχοῦ ὡς ἐν πόλει τῷ κόσμῳ. ἰδέτωσαν, ἱστορησάτωσαν οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἄνθρωπον ἀληθινὸν κατὰ φύσιν ζῶντα. εἰ μὴ φέρουσιν, ἀποκτεινάτωσαν· κρεῖττον γὰρ ἢ οὕτως ζῆν.

members.text:
Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and
conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day:
never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as
one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
members.english: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb nor to play a part.
members.greek: Τοῦτο ἔχει ἡ τελειότης τοῦ ἤθους, τὸ πᾶσαν ἡμέραν ὡς τελευταίαν διεξάγειν καὶ μήτε σφύζειν μήτε ναρκᾶν μήτε ὑποκρίνεσθαι.

members.text:
'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As
thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such
place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here. And if
they will not suffer thee, then mayest thou leave thy life rather than
thy calling, but so as one that doth not think himself anyways wronged.
Only as one would say, Here is a smoke; I will out of it. And what a
great matter is this! Now till some such thing force me out, I will
continue free; neither shall any man hinder me to do what I will, and
my will shall ever be by the proper nature of a reasonable and sociable
creature, regulated and directed.
members.english:
Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute.

As you have in mind to live once you have gone out, so you can live here. But if they do not allow it, then go out of life as well, yet as one who is suffering nothing bad. There is smoke, and I leave. Why do you think it anything much? But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want. And I want what accords with the nature of the rational and social living being.
members.greek: Οὔτε τραγῳδὸς οὔτε πόρνη. Ὡς ἐξελθὼν ζῆν διανοῇ, οὕτως ἐνταῦθα ζῆν ἔξεστιν· ἐὰν δὲ μὴ ἐπιτρέπωσι, τότε καὶ τοῦ ζῆν ἔξιθι, οὕτως μέντοι ὡς μηδὲν κακὸν πάσχων. καπνὸς καὶ ἀπέρχομαι· τί αὐτὸ πρᾶγμα δοκεῖς; μέχρι δέ με τοιοῦτον οὐδὲν ἐξάγει, μένω ἐλεύθερος καὶ οὐδείς με κωλύσει ποιεῖν ἃ θέλω· θέλω δὲ κατὰ φύσιν τοῦ λογικοῦ καὶ κοινωνικοῦ ζῴου.

members.text:
Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether
only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or
commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for
that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties
and actions of our lives.
members.english: Let it make no difference to you whether you do what is fitting while shivering or warm, and whether drowsy or having slept enough, and whether spoken ill of or praised, and whether dying or doing some other kind of act. For this too is one of the acts of life, the one in which we die. So in this too it is enough to manage well what is at hand.
members.greek: Μὴ διαφέρου πότερον ῥιγῶν ἢ θαλπόμενος τὸ πρέπον ποιεῖς, καὶ πότερον νυστάζων ἢ ἱκανῶς ὕπνου ἔχων, καὶ πότερον κακῶς ἀκούων ἢ εὐφημούμενος, καὶ πότερον ἀποθνῄσκων ἢ πράττων τι ἀλλοῖον· μία γὰρ τῶν βιωτικῶν πράξεων καὶ αὕτη ἐστί, καθ’ ἣν ἀποθνῄσκομεν· ἀρκεῖ οὖν καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτης τὸ παρὸν εὖ θέσθαι.

members.text:
As a pig that cries and flings when his throat is cut, fancy to
thyself every one to be, that grieves for any worldly thing and takes
on. Such a one is he also, who upon his bed alone, doth bewail
the miseries of this our mortal life. And remember this, that Unto
reasonable creatures only it is granted that they may willingly and
freely submit unto Providence: but absolutely to submit, is a necessity
imposed upon all creatures equally.
members.english: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence. Picture also how we are bound, and that to the rational living being alone it has been given to follow willingly what happens, while simply to follow is a necessity for all.
members.greek: Φαντάζου πάντα τὸν ἐφ’ ᾡτινιοῦν λυπούμενον ἢ δυσαρεστοῦντα ὅμοιον τῷ θυομένῳ χοιριδίῳ καὶ ἀπολακτίζοντι καὶ κεκραγότι· ὅμοιος καὶ ὁ οἰμώζων ἐπὶ τοῦ κλινιδίου μόνος σιωπῇ. τὴν ἔνδεσιν ἡμῶν καὶ ὅτι μόνῳ τῷ λογικῷ ζῴῳ δέδοται τὸ ἑκουσίως ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γινομένοις, τὸ δὲ ἕπεσθαι ψιλὸν πᾶσιν ἀναγκαῖον.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 10.12 is 10.11b, 4.30 is 4.37, 3.9 is 3.8, 10.23 is 10.22, 10.17 is 10.15, 7.40 is 7.69 and 5.23 is 5.28b–29; 9.2, 6.2 and 10.28 are the same.

Joins 5.23 and 10.17 in claim 4 although one speaks of going out of life oneself and the other of being killed; both say that dying is the answer when others will not allow a life by nature. In 10.17 “that way” is open, and the claim’s “another way” keeps it open.

Takes 9.2’s “pretence” and 7.40’s “play a part” as one thing, because the Greek uses one word for both. 3.9’s “affected” is a different word, smart or showy in a bad sense, and backs only its own part of claim 3.

Leaves to Article 10 the claim that acting justly now and taking what is allotted are enough, though 10.12 (“content with these two things”), 4.30 (“wisdom only in acting justly”), 6.2 (“it is enough to manage well what is at hand”) and 10.28 (“follow willingly what happens”) say it here too. Leaves out as well: 5.23’s opening “Neither a tragic actor nor a prostitute”, which closes a part of the chapter on anger and has no verb; 10.12’s “What anyone will say or think about them … they do not even let into their mind” and the rest of 4.30’s list, which concern what others do and belong with Articles 8 and 12; 9.2’s last sentence, which only explains the two plagues; and 10.28’s “Picture also how we are bound”, whose Greek, as it stands, does not form a grammatical sentence.
articles.limit: Much of this section is said elsewhere: Article 10 already says that death is near and that justice in what I do and peace with what is allotted are enough, Article 3 that I accept what happens, and Article 6 that nothing comes too early; 7.40’s every day as the last is Article 9’s claim 4 and Article 10’s claim 2, the refusal of pretence is in Article 9’s claim 1, a life complete whenever it ends is Article 31’s claim 5 (without this article’s condition), and Articles 12 and 18 already say that where I am makes no difference. What this article adds is the readiness to go, the refusal of pretence set beside death, and the indifference of place joined to a willingness to die rather than live otherwise. In claim 4, what others “do not allow” concerns the outward conditions of a life, where and among whom I live, not the power to act justly, which Article 13 (claim 2) and Article 8 (claim 4) say no one can take from me. The article also states that dying is nothing much without arguing for it, beyond calling it one of the acts of life.

claims.t: My time is short. Any moment now I will be dead, and very soon I will leave all these things behind.
claims.shared: Adds to the opening what is left behind. “All this” became “all these things” so the reference is clear. The 10.17 sentence was folded into the joint first phrase to avoid saying shortness twice.

claims.t: Dying is one of the acts of my life and nothing much. When I leave life, I leave as one who suffers nothing bad. If my mind is disciplined and cleansed, fate does not overtake my life while it is unfinished. I am then not like a tragic actor who leaves before playing the drama through.
claims.shared: The actor is now a comparison, as in 3.9, and is no longer confused with the role-playing actor of 5.23. “When I leave life” is anchored to 5.23d. “Nothing much” has joint support from 5.23 and 6.2. The completeness claim stays conditional on the cleansed mind and is 3.9 alone. “Suffers nothing bad” is 5.23 alone and judges the leaving without denying it.

single.quote: But as long as nothing of that kind leads me out, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.label: Free while I stay
single.t: As long as nothing leads me out of life, I stay, free, and no one will prevent me from doing what I want.
single.why: Existing wording kept, since no pilot wording was supplied. It rests on 5.23 alone. “Nothing of that kind” refers to the smoke and is given as “nothing leads me out of life” so the line reads clearly alone. Staying free is the default. “What I want” is limited by the next sentence of 5.23, which is kept in the margin.
single.follows: Until something like the smoke leads Marcus out, he stays, free, and no one stops him from doing what he wants.

single.quote: Perfection of character has this: to live through every day as the last, and neither to be feverish nor to go numb
single.label: Every day as the last
single.t: Perfection of character is to live through every day as the last, neither feverish nor numb.
single.why: Rests on 7.40 alone. Kept as the speaker’s definition of perfection so the ideal is not claimed as attained. The third negative, playing a part, sits in c3.
single.follows: A perfect character lives each day as the last, without agitation and without numbness.

single.quote: But at any rate to breathe one’s last having at least grown sick of these things is the next best course. Or have you chosen to stay sitting beside vice, and does not even experience yet persuade you to flee from the plague? For the corruption of the mind is a plague, far more so than any such unhealthy mixture and change of this air that is poured around.
single.label: The next best course
single.t: To breathe my last having at least grown sick of vice is the next best course. Have I chosen to stay sitting beside vice? Does experience not yet persuade me to flee the plague? Corruption of the mind is a plague far worse than any unhealthy change of the air.
single.why: Rests on 9.2 alone. The reproachful questions stay questions, where the earlier line turned them into a vow. “These things” is given as “vice”, the quote’s own word. The plague is moral corruption, not death.
single.follows: Having tasted these vices, the next best course is to die sick of them, since staying with vice is staying with a worse plague.

single.quote: Picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on their little bed, alone, in silence.
single.label: The piglet at the sacrifice
single.t: I picture everyone who is pained or displeased at anything whatever as like the piglet that is being sacrificed and kicks and squeals. Like it too is the one who laments on a little bed, alone, in silence.
single.why: Rests on 10.28 alone. Kept as a picturing exercise in the third person, so the comparison stays a comparison. It does not say the pain is unreal.
single.follows: Whoever is pained or displeased at what happens is like a sacrificial piglet kicking, even when they lament in silence.

single.quote: Either you live here, and by now you are used to it; or you are going out from here, and that is what you wanted; or you are dying, and you have completed your service. Besides these there is nothing. So be cheerful.
single.label: Three cases
single.t: Either I live here, and by now I am used to it. Or I am going out from here, and that is what I wanted. Or I am dying, and I have completed my service. Besides these there is nothing, so let me be cheerful.
single.why: Rests on 10.23 alone. Semicolons removed. Leaving “here” and dying remain separate cases, and “here” is left unspecified as in the source. The ending stays a self-exhortation.
single.follows: Whether one lives on here, goes away or dies, there is no fourth case, and in each one can be cheerful.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 10.12 is 10.11b, 4.30 is 4.37, 3.9 is 3.8, 10.23 is 10.22, 10.17 is 10.15, 7.40 is 7.69 and 5.23 is 5.28b–29; 9.2, 6.2 and 10.28 are the same.

Semicolon removed and “may die” dropped, since the sources say death is near, not merely possible. Every phrase rests on two passages. The line states a resolve: 4.30 and 9.2 show the speaker still falling short.
marcus_revision.limit: These lines state a resolve and an ideal, not an achievement: 4.30 and 9.2 are self-reproach, and 3.9 and 10.12 describe an ideal figure. Leaving life in 5.23 and being killed in 10.17 are conditional on being prevented from living rightly, and they differ in agency. Neither supports seeking death. The actor of 3.9 is an unfinished drama and is not the role-playing actor of 5.23 and 7.40. “What I want” in 5.23 means what accords with the nature of a rational and social being. The first-person wording and the fusion of passages are our editorial interpretation.

statement.kind: A ground, the rule it supports, and words to say
statement.form: Claim 1 is the ground: wherever I am, a good lot is one I assign myself, and a good state of soul and good actions are enough. Claim 2 is the rule for acting and for accepting: what I do is for other people, and what happens I accept. Claim 3 gives words that hand the choice of gifts, losses and place to another. The statement joins the “wherever” of 8.43 and 5.30 to the giving and taking back of 10.16; that joining is the editor’s.

seneca.becomes: With Seneca, all three claims gain a second author. For the first: any land I am driven to can be a hospitable home, the mind is itself the cause of a happy life or a wretched one, and the real good comes from a good conscience, honourable plans and right actions. For the second: a good man bears whatever happens to him as something that has happened by the divine law. For the third: a prayer hands to Jupiter the choice of where I am led. The article gains two grounds (who I am matters more than where I come to; a spirit within treats me as I treat it), two things under “In action” (how to hold what is given; making something of whatever fortune I receive) and, under “Practice”, a rehearsal of poverty and exile. Nothing is added under “If I doubt it”. He limits the first claim: some places harm a mind still recovering, and where he may choose he avoids them.
seneca.statement: With Seneca the statement stands and gains a ground: who I am when I come matters more than where I come to. His limit on the first claim touches the statement’s “wherever” too: for a mind not yet perfected some places are harmful, and where I may choose I avoid them.

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Though you are driven out to the farthest lands, though you are set down in any corner of barbarian country, that dwelling, whatever it is like, will be hospitable to you.
piece.follows: Once the mind’s trouble is removed, the place I am driven to, whatever it is like, will be hospitable to me.
piece.context: Letter 28, on travel that does not cure a gloomy mind: Lucilius needs a change of soul, not of scene. “That dwelling” is any land, once the mind’s trouble is removed.
gives: Wherever I am put
I can be content there

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: For the mind is stronger than any fortune, and itself leads its own things in either direction, and is for itself the cause of a happy life and of a wretched one.
piece.follows: The mind is stronger than any fortune and is itself the cause of a happy life or a wretched one.
piece.context: Letter 98, on not depending on Fortune’s gifts. Seneca has just said that Fortune hands us only the material for goods and evils; the mind turns it to good or evil.
gives: A good lot is one I assign myself

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: from a good conscience, from honourable plans, from right actions
piece.follows: The real good comes from a good conscience, honourable plans and right actions.
piece.context: Letter 23, on true joy: rejoice only in what comes from your own store. The question answered is where the real good comes from; these are the first three of the five sources Seneca names for it.
gives: a good state of soul
good actions

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: whatever happens to him he will bear with a calm mind; for he will know that it has happened by the divine law
piece.follows: A good man bears calmly whatever happens to him, because he knows it happened by the divine law.
piece.context: Letter 76, on the honourable as the only good. “He” is the good man, who is of the highest piety towards the gods; the divine law is the one by which all things go forward.
gives: What happens to me, I accept
whatever it is
as something that comes from the gods

piece.author: seneca
piece.quote: Lead me, O father and ruler of the high heaven, wherever you have decided: there is no delay in obeying; I am here, and eager.
piece.follows: The speaker asks Jupiter to lead him wherever Jupiter has decided, and promises to obey without delay.
piece.context: Letter 107, on obeying the order of the universe, ends with lines of the Stoic Cleanthes that Seneca has put into Latin. They are spoken to Jupiter.
gives: I hand the choice over

items.label: why
items.t: Who I am when I come matters more than where I come to, and for that reason I do not sign my mind over to any place. I was not born for one corner: the whole world is my country.
items.why: Marcus says that he will be content wherever he is thrown and gives as the ground the state of the divinity within him. He does not say in this section, as Seneca does, that who I am counts for more than where I come to, or that the whole world is my country.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Who you are when you come matters more than where you come to, and for that reason we ought not to sign our mind over to any place.
support.follows: Who I am counts for more than where I come to, so the mind should not be signed over to any place.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel that fails to cure a gloomy mind. Seneca has just said that, once the mind’s trouble is gone, any land is hospitable; “you” is Lucilius.
gives: Who I am when I come matters more than where I come to
for that reason I do not sign my mind over to any place

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I was not born for one corner; this whole world is my country.
support.follows: I should live with the conviction that I was not born for one corner and that the whole world is my country.
support.context: Letter 28: words Seneca gives Lucilius to live by, after saying that a restless traveller needs a change of soul. “This whole world” is set against the one corner.
gives: I was not born for one corner
the whole world is my country

items.label: why
items.t: A sacred spirit sits within me as my guardian and observes the bad and the good that are mine. As I treat it, so it treats me.
items.why: 8.43 says that wherever I am thrown the divinity within me will be gracious, and that it is content if its state and its actions follow from its make-up; the claim keeps the state and the actions and leaves the divinity out. Seneca too speaks of a spirit within, and says what Marcus does not say here: it observes the bad and the good that are mine, and how it treats me depends on how I treat it.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn.
support.follows: A sacred spirit sits in each of us as observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours, and it treats us as we treat it.
support.context: Letter 41 opens by telling Lucilius not to pray to heaven for a sound mind: God is near him, with him, within him. The “sacred spirit” is that god within each person.
gives: A sacred spirit sits within me as my guardian and observes the bad and the good that are mine
As I treat it, so it treats me

items.label: action
items.t: What I am given I use but do not boast of, as something deposited with me that is going to leave. I do not let it stick fast to me, so that when it is led away it leaves without tearing me at all.
items.why: 8.31 says to take without conceit and to let go readily, and does not say what is taken. 10.16 says that nature gives and takes back. Seneca names the things, the advantages that opinion calls goods, and says how to hold them between the giving and the taking back.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let us use them, not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as things deposited with us that are going to leave.
support.follows: I should use such things sparingly and without boasting, as things deposited with me that are going to leave.
support.context: From Letter 74, on virtue as the only good. The things to be used, “them”, are the advantages that opinion calls goods, which Seneca says are in our possession but outside ourselves.
gives: What I am given I use but do not boast of
as something deposited with me that is going to leave

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Let all those things come to us as additions and not stick fast to us, so that, if they are led away, they may leave without tearing us at all.
support.follows: Such things should come to me as additions without sticking fast, so that when they leave they do not tear me at all.
support.context: Letter 74, on virtue as the only good. Seneca has just said that what opinion calls goods are only “advantages”, our chattels and not parts of us; “all those things” means these.
gives: I do not let it stick fast to me
when it is led away it leaves without tearing me at all

items.label: action
items.t: I display virtue in my own country if I can and in exile if I cannot, able-bodied if I can and disabled if I cannot. Whatever fortune I receive, I make out of it something worth remembering, as the sculptor Phidias would have made the best that could be made out of his material.
items.why: Marcus says here that I act for the good of others and accept what happens; he does not say what I do with the place or the fortune I am handed. Seneca does: I work with it as a sculptor works with the material he is given. He grants with his “if he can” that one fortune is preferable to another, which no passage of Marcus in this section does.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: In the same way the wise man will display virtue in riches if he is allowed, and if not, in poverty; in his own country if he can, and if not, in exile; as a general if he can, and if not, as a soldier; able-bodied if he can, and if not, disabled. Whatever fortune he receives, he will make out of it something worth remembering.
support.follows: The wise man displays virtue at home if he can and in exile if he cannot, and makes something worth remembering out of whatever fortune he receives.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and misfortune: what Seneca draws from Phidias, who made the best statue each material allowed. Poverty, exile and disability are the poorer materials.
gives: I display virtue in my own country if I can and in exile if I cannot, able-bodied if I can and disabled if I cannot
Whatever fortune I receive, I make out of it something worth remembering

support.author: seneca
support.quote: If you had offered him marble, if you had offered him a still cheaper material, he would have made the best that could be made out of it.
support.follows: Offered marble or something cheaper still, Phidias would have made the best that could be made out of it.
support.context: Letter 85, on the wise man and misfortune: he is not pressed by bad things but uses them. “Him” is the sculptor Phidias, who worked in bronze as well as ivory.
gives: as the sculptor Phidias would have made the best that could be made out of his material

items.label: practice
items.t: Whatever can happen, I think of it as going to happen. If I become poor, I will be among the greater number; if I become an exile, I will think myself born in the place I am sent to.
items.why: Marcus’s words are said to whoever throws him, and they leave the place open. Seneca thinks of each thing that can happen before it does, and for poverty and exile he gives the answer to have ready; his answer to exile is to think of the new place as one’s birthplace.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: Whatever can happen, let us think of it as going to happen.
support.follows: Whatever can happen should be thought of as something that is going to happen.
support.context: Letter 24, on the fear of a lawsuit. Seneca reminds Lucilius that death, exile and pain have hung over him since birth, and that he was born to these things.
gives: Whatever can happen, I think of it as going to happen

support.author: seneca
support.quote: I will become poor: I will be among the greater number. I will become an exile: I will think myself born in the place I am sent to.
support.follows: If I become poor I will be among the greater number, and if I become an exile I will think of the place I am sent to as my birthplace.
support.context: Letter 24, to Lucilius, who fears losing a case in court. Seneca has told him to turn from his own case to what can befall anyone; “I” is anyone saying this.
gives: If I become poor, I will be among the greater number
if I become an exile, I will think myself born in the place I am sent to

items.t: Seneca agrees that any land can be a home once the mind is at peace (Ep. 28.4), but he does not treat all places alike. Some places are not wholesome enough for a mind that is recovering and not yet perfected, and he says we ought to choose where we live with our character in mind. This limits the claim and does not contradict it. The harm he names does not depend on choosing: it falls on such a mind whether or not it chose the place. His remedy does depend on it: where he may choose his own place, he keeps away from such places, and where he may not, he says that one may live quietly even in the forum if necessary.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: for a good mind too, one that is not yet perfected and is recovering, there are some places that are not wholesome enough
support.follows: Some places are not wholesome enough for a mind that is recovering but is not yet perfected.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel. Seneca likens such places to oppressive places that test even the strongest health; the mind meant is a good one still recovering, not yet perfected.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: But if one might choose one’s own place, I would flee far from even the sight and the neighbourhood of the forum
support.follows: Given the choice, Seneca would keep far away from the forum.
support.context: Letter 28, on travel. Seneca has just said that one may live quietly even in the forum, the most turbulent of places, if necessary; this is what he adds at once.

support.author: seneca
support.quote: We ought to choose a place that is healthy not only for the body but also for our character.
support.follows: I should choose where I live with my character in mind as well as my body.
support.context: Letter 51, on Baiae, which Seneca left the day after he came because self-indulgence has claimed it. He says the wise man avoids such places without hating any place as such.

amend.t: ; who I am when I come matters more than where I come to
; but some places harm a mind still recovering, and where I may choose I pick a place that is healthy for my character

passages.title: On travel as no cure for the mind
passages.text: But once you have removed that ill, every change of place will become pleasant. Though you are driven out to the farthest lands, though you are set down in any corner of barbarian country, that dwelling, whatever it is like, will be hospitable to you. Who you are when you come matters more than where you come to, and for that reason we ought not to sign our mind over to any place. One must live with this conviction: “I was not born for one corner; this whole world is my country.”

passages.title: On not depending on fortune’s gifts
passages.text: All the things that Fortune looks on become fruitful and pleasant on this condition: that the one who has them also has himself and is not in the power of his own things. For those people are wrong, Lucilius, who judge that Fortune gives us anything good or anything evil: she gives the material for goods and evils, and the beginnings of things that, in our keeping, will turn out for evil or for good. For the mind is stronger than any fortune, and itself leads its own things in either direction, and is for itself the cause of a happy life and of a wretched one.

passages.title: On finding true joy within
passages.text: Do you ask what that is, or where it comes up from? I will tell you: from a good conscience, from honourable plans, from right actions, from contempt for the things of chance, from the peaceful and unbroken course of a life that keeps to one road. For those who leap from one set of purposes to another, or do not even leap but are carried across by some accident, how can they have anything certain or lasting, when they are suspended and wandering?

passages.title: On learning in old age, and virtue as the only good
passages.text: You must grant that the good man is a man of the highest piety towards the gods. So whatever happens to him he will bear with a calm mind; for he will know that it has happened by the divine law by which all things go forward. If that is so, the only good for him will be what is honourable; for in this lies obeying the gods, and not flaring up at sudden events or bewailing his lot, but patiently accepting fate and doing what is commanded.

passages.title: On accepting fate willingly
passages.text: Lead me, O father and ruler of the high heaven, wherever you have decided: there is no delay in obeying; I am here, and eager. Suppose I am unwilling: I shall go along groaning, and as a bad man I shall be made to do what I was allowed to do as a good one. The fates lead the willing; the unwilling they drag.

passages.title: On the god within us
passages.text: This is what I say, Lucilius: a sacred spirit sits within us, the observer and guardian of the bad and the good that are ours. As it has been treated by us, so it treats us in its turn. And indeed no one is a good man without god: or can anyone rise above fortune unless helped by him? It is he who gives advice that is grand and lofty. In each and every good man a god (which god is uncertain) lives.

passages.title: On virtue as the only safe good
passages.text: Let all those things come to us as additions and not stick fast to us, so that, if they are led away, they may leave without tearing us at all. Let us use them, not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as things deposited with us that are going to leave. Whoever has possessed them without the use of reason has not kept them long; for good fortune itself, unless it is kept within measure, weighs itself down. If he has trusted in goods that are the quickest to run away, he is soon deserted, and, so that they can desert him, he is struck down. Few have been allowed to lay their good fortune down gently: the rest fall together with the things among which they stood high, and the very things that had lifted them up weigh them down.

passages.title: On rejecting even moderate passions
passages.text: You think he is pressed by bad things? He uses them. It was not only out of ivory that Phidias knew how to make statues; he made them out of bronze. If you had offered him marble, if you had offered him a still cheaper material, he would have made the best that could be made out of it. In the same way the wise man will display virtue in riches if he is allowed, and if not, in poverty; in his own country if he can, and if not, in exile; as a general if he can, and if not, as a soldier; able-bodied if he can, and if not, disabled. Whatever fortune he receives, he will make out of it something worth remembering.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: Turn these things over in your mind; you have often heard them and often said them, but whether you have truly heard them, whether you have truly said them, prove in action. For this charge that is commonly thrown at us is a most shameful one: that we handle the words of philosophy, not its deeds. What? Have you learned now for the first time that death hangs over you, now exile, now pain? You were born to these things. Whatever can happen, let us think of it as going to happen.

passages.title: On facing feared troubles and death
passages.text: I will become poor: I will be among the greater number. I will become an exile: I will think myself born in the place I am sent to. I will be bound: what of it? Am I unbound now? Nature has bound me fast to this heavy weight of my body. I will die: what you are saying is this, I will cease to be able to be ill, I will cease to be able to be bound, I will cease to be able to die.

passages.title: On travel as no cure for the mind
passages.text: Can anything be as turbulent as the forum? Even there one may live quietly, if it should be necessary. But if one might choose one’s own place, I would flee far from even the sight and the neighbourhood of the forum; for just as oppressive places test even the strongest health, so for a good mind too, one that is not yet perfected and is recovering, there are some places that are not wholesome enough.

passages.title: On luxurious resorts and soft living
passages.text: We ought to choose a place that is healthy not only for the body but also for our character. Just as I would not want to live among torturers, so I would not want to live among taverns either. To see drunk people wandering along the shores, and the revels of people out sailing, and the lakes noisy with the music of bands, and the other offences that self-indulgence, as if set free from the laws, not only commits but makes public: what need is there of that?

claims.t: Wherever I am put, my lot can be good and I can be content there. A good lot is one I assign myself: a good state of soul and good actions. These are enough for me.
claims.shared: 8.43 and 5.30 both say “wherever”, and both say that I am well off there: in 8.43 the divinity within me is gracious, in 5.30 my lot is good. Both then name what that rests on, and both name how the soul is and how it acts (8.43: “the state it is in and the way it acts”; 5.30: “good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions”). 8.43’s “content” and 9.5’s “It is enough” are the same verb in the Greek.
claims.changed: The claim says “soul”, as 5.30 does, where 8.43 says “the divinity within me”. 8.43 does not call the state good; it says the state and the way of acting “follow from its own make-up”. 5.30 lists three things; the claim drops “good impulses”, which stand between the soul’s turnings and its actions. In 8.43 it is the divinity within me that is content, and the claim says that I am, and that these are enough for me. The words quoted from 9.5 name only the judgment; in the passage the same “It is enough” also governs the social action and the well-pleased disposition, which are quoted in claim 2. 5.30 says “yourself”; the claim says “myself”.

support.quote: For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious
support.follows: Even in the place I am thrown to, the divinity within me will be gracious.

I can be content there

support.quote: wherever caught, a person whose lot is good

support.quote: “whose lot is good” means having assigned yourself a good lot

support.quote: good lots are good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions

support.follows: Three present things are enough, and the first is a judgment with a firm grasp of what is there.

claims.t: What I do, I do for the good of other people. What happens to me, I accept, whatever it is, as something that comes from the gods.
claims.shared: All three passages set what I do beside what happens to me and give one rule for each. For what happens, 8.22 and 12.8 both say “accept” and both name the gods or god; 12.8 and 9.5 both say “everything”. For what I do, 8.22 says “the doing of good to human beings” where 9.5 says “social”.
claims.changed: 9.5 says “well pleased”, which is warmer than “accept”; the claim keeps the word that 12.8 and 8.22 share. 9.5 names “the external cause” and not the gods. 12.8 measures what I do by god’s praise, not by the good of other people; that half of 12.8 stands alone under “Why”.

support.quote: Am I doing something? I do it, referring it to the doing of good to human beings.
support.follows: Whatever I am doing, I do it with the good of other people as its aim.
gives: What I do, I do for the good of other people

support.quote: the present action should be social
support.follows: What I am doing at this moment should be a social action.
gives: What I do, I do for the good of other people

support.quote: Is something happening to me? I accept it, referring it to the gods and to the spring of all things, from which everything that comes about is wound together.
support.follows: When something happens to me, I accept it and trace it back to the gods and to the one source of everything that comes about.

as something that comes from the gods

support.follows: A human being is able to accept everything god assigns, whatever it turns out to be.

whatever it is
as something that comes from the gods

support.quote: the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause

claims.role: Words that hand over the choice
claims.t: I hand the choice over: to nature I say “Give what you want, take back what you want”, and about where I am put I say “Pick me up and throw me wherever you want”. My words to nature are said in obedience to it and good will towards it, not in bold defiance.
claims.shared: Both passages are spoken to a “you”, and both leave the choice to it in nearly the same words: “what you want” (10.16) and “wherever you want” (8.43). The Greek verb is the same in both.
claims.changed: 10.16 is about things given and taken back, 8.43 about the place I am thrown to; the claim keeps the two sayings apart. 8.43 does not say who is addressed, and the claim does not make it nature. Only 10.16 says in what spirit its words are said, so the last sentence speaks only of the words to nature and rests on 10.16 alone. 8.43 names no spirit; its next words state a confidence, that the divinity within will be gracious there too.

support.quote: To nature, which gives everything and takes everything back
support.follows: Nature gives everything and takes everything back.

support.follows: The educated and modest person tells nature to give what it wants and to take back what it wants.

single.quote: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise
single.label: A great power
single.t: To do nothing but what god is going to praise is in my power, as it is in every human being’s, and it is a great power.
single.why: Only this passage calls the rule a power, and only it measures what I do by god’s praise; 8.22 and 9.5 measure it by the good of other people. The same sentence goes on to accepting what god assigns, which is quoted under “In action”.
single.follows: A human being has the power to do only what god is going to praise, and it is a great power.

single.quote: To take without conceit, and to let go readily.
single.label: Taking, letting go
single.t: I take without conceit, and I let go readily.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of how I take and how I let go. It does not say what is taken, so it is not joined to 10.16, where it is nature that gives and takes back.
single.follows: Whatever is taken should be taken without conceit and let go readily.

single.quote: How easy it is to push away and wipe out every impression that is troublesome or out of place, and at once to be in a complete calm.
single.label: When I am troubled
single.t: When an impression troubles me or is out of place, I can push it away and wipe it out, and at once be completely calm. This is easy.
single.why: Only this passage speaks of an impression that troubles me and of calm. It is kept as what losing my contentment looks like, with the way back.
single.follows: A troublesome or out-of-place impression is easy to push away and wipe out, and complete calm follows at once.

members.text:
How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto
him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and
that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
members.english: How great a power a human being has: to do nothing other than what god is going to praise, and to accept everything god assigns to them, whatever it is.
members.greek: Ἡλίκην ἐξουσίαν ἔχει ἄνθρωπος μὴ ποιεῖν ἄλλο ἢ ὅπερ μέλλει ὁ θεὸς ἐπαινεῖν, καὶ δέχεσθαι πᾶν ὃν νέμῃ αὐτῷ ὁ θεός.

members.text:
Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there
also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is
well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and
with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are
suitable and agreeable.
members.english: Pick me up and throw me wherever you want. For there too I will have the divinity within me gracious, that is, content if the state it is in and the way it acts follow from its own make-up.
members.greek: Ἆρόν με καὶ βάλε, ὅπου θέλεις. κἀκεῖ γὰρ ἕξω τὸν ἐμὸν δαίμονα ἵλεων, τουτέστιν, ἀρκούμενον, εἰ ἔχοι καὶ ἐνεργοίη κατὰ τὸ ἑξῆς τῇ ἰδίᾳ κατασκευῇ.

members.text:
If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present
action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God,
be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
members.english: It is enough that the present judgment should have a firm grasp of what is there, that the present action should be social, and that the present disposition should be well pleased with everything that happens from the external cause.
members.greek: Ἀρκεῖ ἡ παροῦσα ὑπόληψις καταληπτικὴ καὶ ἡ παροῦσα πρᾶξις κοινωνικὴ καὶ ἡ παροῦσα διάθεσις εὐαρεστικὴ πρὸς πᾶν τὸ παρὰ τῆς ἐκτὸς αἰτίας συμβαῖνον.

members.text:
Give what thou wilt, and take away what thou wilt, saith he that is
well taught and truly modest, to Him that gives, and takes away. And it
is not out of a stout and peremptory resolution, that he saith it, but
in mere love, and humble submission.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.8 is the first part of 12.11, 8.43 is the first part of 8.45, 9.5 is 9.6, 10.16 is 10.14, 8.22 is 8.23, 5.30 is the end of 5.36 and 8.31 is 8.33; 5.2 is the same.

Says “a good state of soul” for two different things: the state of the divinity within me, when it follows from its own make-up (8.43), and good turnings of the soul (5.30). Only 5.30 uses the word “good”. The translators note that Marcus elsewhere treats the divinity within as one’s own mind and reason.

Reads 8.43’s “content if …” as naming what the divinity within is content with: its state and its way of acting. The translators give another reading, “content, provided that …”, which makes the clause a condition on the whole promise. “These are enough for me” leans on the first reading; 9.5’s “It is enough” backs the same words independently.

Reads 5.30 from where the 1634 edition cuts it, in the middle of a sentence. The opening words, “Once I was”, stand in the passage before, so “wherever caught, a person whose lot is good” has no verb here. The claim takes it with the definition that follows, which is complete, and says only that my lot “can be” good.

Joins 8.43 to 10.16 because both hand the choice to a “you”. The Greek of 8.43 does not say who that is, and the article does not make it nature. The obedience and good will of 10.16 are kept to the words spoken to nature.
Places the calm of 5.2 under “When it breaks”. The passage does not mention place or lot; it is read as the way back when an impression disturbs my contentment.

Keeps the translators’ reading of 12.8, ὃ ἂν νέμῃ (“whatever he assigns”), for the transmitted ὃν, which does not fit the grammar of the sentence. Their note says the edition’s text was given from memory and is unchecked, and no printed edition could be consulted for this article; the English of 1634 (“whatsoever God doth send”) reads it the same way. Claim 2’s “whatever it is” does not rest on 12.8 alone: 9.5’s “everything that happens” backs the same words.
articles.limit: Much of this article is said elsewhere. Claim 2 repeats Article 3 (I accept whatever happens) and Articles 1 and 2 (what I do aims at the common good), and adds only that the two stand side by side as one rule. Claim 1’s “wherever” is already Article 17’s claim 4 (I can live as I mean to wherever I am) and Article 12’s claim 1 (where I am is like any retreat); its “enough” is Article 16’s claim 2 (what I have in myself is enough), and Article 2 says that doing my own work makes me content. Claim 3 stands near Article 6, which already takes the universe’s side; and the said-once item from 5.2 is Article 7’s claim 3 (when I take away the judgment there is calm) and Article 21’s claim 3 (I keep wiping out impressions). What this article adds is that a good lot is one I assign myself, and that the same measure holds for whatever is given or taken back as for the place; claim 3 adds the spoken words that hand over gifts, losses and place. That part rests mainly on 5.30, a fragment cut from a sentence in the past tense, and on 10.16. No passage joins “wherever I am put” to “whatever is given or taken back” in one sentence; the statement does, and its “equally” is marked as the editor’s. In the statement, “taken back” is said by 10.16 alone; 12.8 backs only “whatever is given me”.

claims.t: A good lot is one I assign myself: good turnings of the soul, good impulses, good actions. In whatever place I am, the divinity within me is content if its state and the way it acts follow from its own make-up. It is enough that my present judgement has a firm grasp of what is there and that my present action serves other people.
claims.shared: Gives the reason behind the opening: the lot is self-assigned (5.30 only), contentment is conditional (8.43 only), and present judgement and present social action are enough (9.5, with 8.22 for the social aim). “It is enough that my present judgement” removes the misleading “for the present”. The pilot’s “refused” and “I do not wait for somewhere better” go beyond the quotes and stay out.

decisions: Quotes the project’s own translation from the Greek. Passage numbers are those of Casaubon’s 1634 translation. In modern editions 12.8 is the first part of 12.11, 8.43 is the first part of 8.45, 9.5 is 9.6, 10.16 is 10.14, 8.22 is 8.23, 5.30 is the end of 5.36 and 8.31 is 8.33; 5.2 is the same.

Pilot wording restored, with “even somewhere I would not have chosen” cut because no quotation states it and the line must stay within 140 characters. “Put” replaces the throwing scenario. “Can” and “depends on” keep the condition in 8.43 and promise no success. “My life” renders “lot” in 5.30 in plain words and is editorial.
marcus_revision.limit: The outside source is called god, the gods and the spring, nature, or the external cause, and the passages do not equate these. The will addressed in 8.43 is unnamed, and “a will that is not mine” in c3 does not identify it with nature. The lot is assigned by god in 12.8 but self-assigned in 5.30, and the article leaves that unreconciled. “My life” in the opening is an editorial rendering of “lot”. Contentment in 8.43 is conditional, and the power in 12.8 is a capacity, not an achievement. The sufficiency in 9.5 has three parts. c1 states judgement and action, and the third, a disposition well pleased with what comes from the external cause, is carried only as acceptance in c2 and in the margin. The words to nature in 10.16 belong to a third person of a certain character, and their tone qualifier applies only to those words. Ease in 5.2 covers impressions only. No passage says acceptance is easy, that the place is one I would have refused, or why what is assigned should be welcomed.
